- **Eval-driven iteration**: maintain a growing golden test set drawn from real failures so regressions are caught before the next release.

## Incident Response for AI

Define severity levels (e.g., SEV1 = harmful/unsafe output or outage, SEV3 = minor quality regression). For each:

- **Detection**: alerts, user reports, monitoring anomalies.
- **Roles**: incident commander, comms lead, on-call engineer; the PM often owns user/stakeholder communication and the decision to roll back.
- **Mitigation**: kill switch via feature flag, fallback to previous model or rules-based system, prompt patch, rate limiting.
- **Postmortem**: blameless review, root cause, add a regression test to your eval set.

## Iteration Cadence

Treat the launch as the beginning. Run a regular review (weekly early on) of metrics and feedback, prioritize fixes vs. enhancements using impact and effort, and tie every change back to a measurable hypothesis. Close the loop: ship → measure → learn → repeat.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a percentage ramp during an AI feature rollout?
options: To limit exposure so problems are caught while affecting few users
To skip the need for monitoring
quiz.why: A percentage ramp progressively exposes the feature, so any issues surface while only a small fraction of users are affected, allowing safe observation and rollback.

quiz.q: Which metric is an example of an operational (not model-quality) metric?
quiz.why: p95 latency is an operational metric. Hallucination rate, groundedness, and win-rate are all measures of model quality.

quiz.q: Why is implicit feedback (e.g., whether users edit or discard AI output) valuable?
options: It is cheaper to store than explicit ratings
It reveals real user satisfaction even when users don't leave explicit feedback
It eliminates the need for human review
It guarantees the model won't drift
quiz.why: Most users never click thumbs up/down, but their behavior—accepting, editing, or discarding output—is a high-volume, honest signal of quality and satisfaction.

quiz.q: During a SEV1 incident where the AI produces harmful output, what is the fastest mitigation?
options: Use the feature-flag kill switch or fall back to a safe baseline
Wait for the next scheduled release
quiz.why: A feature-flag kill switch or fallback to a previous safe model/rules system instantly contains harm without requiring a redeploy or retraining.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what should you add to your eval set after resolving an AI incident, and why?
quiz.answer: Add a regression test based on the failure case so the same issue is automatically caught before future releases.
quiz.why: Capturing real failures as eval cases builds a growing golden test set that prevents regressions and institutionalizes learning from incidents.

quiz.q: Name two things every rollout stage should have defined before ramping.
quiz.answer: Entry gates (conditions to advance) and rollback criteria (thresholds that trigger a pullback), each with an owner.
quiz.why: Defining advancement gates and rollback triggers in advance—with clear ownership—prevents indecision and slow responses during a live problem.

apm-m4-l04-capstone-pitch-a-complete-ai-.title: Capstone: Pitch a Complete AI Product Plan
objectives: Synthesize strategy, roadmap, PRD, eval plans, and metrics into a single coherent AI product proposal
Structure a compelling executive pitch narrative that ties user problem to business value
Define both product success metrics and AI-specific quality/eval metrics with clear targets
Articulate AI-specific risks (data, model, safety, cost) and concrete mitigations
Anticipate and answer tough leadership questions about ROI, feasibility, and trade-offs
Self-assess the proposal against a portfolio-ready rubric
apm-m4-l04-capstone-pitch-a-complete-ai-.body:
## Capstone Overview

This is where it all comes together. Across this course you learned to identify AI opportunities, write PRDs, design evaluation plans, choose metrics, and manage stakeholders. The capstone asks you to **package all of that into one cohesive proposal and pitch it** as if you were seeking executive funding and headcount.

The deliverable is two things: (1) a written **AI Product Plan** (your portfolio artifact) and (2) a **10-minute mock leadership pitch** with Q&A.

## The AI Product Plan: Required Sections

A strong plan reads as a tight story, not a data dump. Include:

1. **Problem & Opportunity** — Who is the user, what painful job are they doing, and how big is the prize? Quantify with TAM/usage data where possible.
2. **Why AI, Why Now** — Justify that AI is the right tool (vs. rules/heuristics). Name the capability unlock (e.g., unstructured text understanding) and the enabling shift (cheaper inference, better models).
3. **Solution & Strategy** — Your product concept, the wedge, and the moat. One crisp sentence of positioning.
4. **Roadmap** — Phased plan: crawl (validate), walk (scale), run (differentiate). Tie phases to learning milestones, not just features.
5. **PRD Highlights** — Core user stories, the happy path, and the human-in-the-loop design. Include what is explicitly out of scope.
6. **Evaluation Plan** — How you measure model quality offline (golden datasets, rubrics, LLM-as-judge) and online (A/B, shadow mode). Define acceptance thresholds before launch.
7. **Metrics & Targets** — Separate **product metrics** (adoption, retention, task success, time saved) from **model metrics** (accuracy, precision/recall, hallucination rate, latency, cost per query). Always name a North Star and guardrail metrics.
8. **Risks & Mitigations** — Data quality, model drift, safety/bias, cost overruns, regulatory exposure. Pair each risk with a mitigation and an owner.
9. **Ask** — The decision you want: budget, headcount, timeline, and the go/no-go gate.

## Crafting the Pitch Narrative

Leadership pitches reward clarity over completeness. Use a simple arc:

- **Hook** (problem framed as money or pain) →
- **Insight** (why this is solvable now with AI) →
- **Solution** (your product) →
- **Proof** (eval results, prototype, or comparable benchmarks) →
- **Plan & Ask** (roadmap, metrics, what you need).

Lead with the conclusion. Executives are busy—state the ask early, then support it. Use one chart per idea. Pre-empt objections by addressing the biggest risk yourself.

## AI-Specific Pitch Tips

- **Be honest about uncertainty.** AI outcomes are probabilistic. Show how your eval plan de-risks the bet rather than pretending the model is perfect.
- **Frame metrics in business terms.** "95% precision" means little; "fewer than 1 wrong escalation per 100, saving 200 agent-hours/month" lands.
- **Show the cost model.** Inference cost per query × volume is a real P&L line. Executives will ask.
- **Define the guardrail.** What's the safety/quality floor below which you would not ship?

## Anticipating Tough Questions

Prepare answers for: *What if the model isn't accurate enough? How much does this cost at scale? What's the build vs. buy decision? How do we measure success in 90 days? What's the biggest reason this fails?* Strong PMs rehearse these.

## Self-Assessment Rubric

Score your plan 1-5 on: problem clarity, AI justification, eval rigor, metric quality (leading + guardrail), risk realism, and pitch storytelling. Anything scoring ≤3 is your revision priority before adding it to your portfolio.

quiz.q: Why should an AI product pitch translate '95% precision' into business terms like hours saved?
options: Because precision is not a real metric
Executives fund outcomes, not raw benchmark numbers
It makes the model more accurate
Business terms are always more impressive
quiz.why: Leadership cares about business impact. Translating model metrics into dollars or hours makes the value concrete and fundable, whereas a raw benchmark figure is hard to act on.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly separates product metrics from model metrics?
options: Adoption & retention vs. hallucination rate & latency
Cost per query vs. inference cost
quiz.why: Product metrics (adoption, retention, task success) measure user/business outcomes; model metrics (hallucination rate, latency, precision) measure system quality. Keeping them separate clarifies what success means.

quiz.q: When should acceptance thresholds for model quality be defined?
options: After launch, based on user complaints
Before launch, as part of the eval plan
quiz.why: Defining acceptance thresholds before launch prevents moving the goalposts and creates an objective go/no-go gate, which de-risks the bet.

quiz.q: What makes a roadmap phase strong in an AI product plan?
options: It lists as many features as possible
It is tied to a learning milestone, not just features
quiz.why: Crawl-walk-run phases should be organized around what you need to learn or validate, so each phase reduces uncertainty before scaling investment.

quiz.q: Name one AI-specific risk an executive will likely ask about, and a mitigation you would pair with it.
quiz.answer: Example: Cost overruns from inference at scale — mitigation: model a cost-per-query budget, cache results, and set a usage-based guardrail with an owner. (Other valid risks: model drift with monitoring/retraining; bias/safety with eval audits; data quality with validation pipelines.)
quiz.why: AI introduces risks beyond traditional products. Pairing each named risk with a concrete mitigation and an owner shows leadership the bet is managed, not hopeful.

quiz.q: In the pitch narrative arc, what should come immediately after the 'Hook'?
options: The Insight — why it's solvable now with AI
quiz.why: After hooking with the problem, the Insight explains why this is newly solvable with AI, setting up the credibility for your solution before proof and the ask.

cse-m1-l01-zero-trust-foundations-and-th.title: Zero Trust Foundations and the Microsoft Security Stack
objectives: State the three Zero Trust principles and explain what each one changes about traditional network security
Name the six Zero Trust pillars and give a real control for each
Explain the cloud shared-responsibility model and identify who secures identity, data, and the host across SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS
Map each Microsoft security product to the Zero Trust pillar it primarily defends
Justify why identity is the new perimeter and what 'verify explicitly' means in practice
Position SC-500 architect responsibilities relative to MD-102/MS-102 administrator tasks
cse-m1-l01-zero-trust-foundations-and-th.body:
## Why This Lesson Exists

Every later module in this course — Conditional Access, PIM, Intune and Defender for Endpoint, Purview data governance, Sentinel SIEM/SOAR — is a *piece* of one architecture. If you learn each product in isolation you become a button-clicker. If you learn the **model first**, you become an architect who can explain *why* a control exists and *where* it fits. That model is **Zero Trust**, and this lesson is the map you'll keep returning to.

The old model was a **castle-and-moat**: a hard network perimeter (firewall, VPN) with a soft, trusted interior. Once you were 'inside', you were trusted. That assumption is now fatal: users work from anywhere, apps are SaaS, data lives in the cloud, and a single phished credential drops an attacker straight 'inside'. Zero Trust replaces *implicit trust based on network location* with *explicit verification on every request*.

## The Three Zero Trust Principles

Microsoft frames Zero Trust around three principles. Memorize them — they are the lens for every design decision.

1. **Verify explicitly.** Always authenticate and authorize based on *all* available signals: identity, location, device health, service or workload, data classification, and anomalies. Never trust something just because it is on the corporate network.
2. **Use least-privilege access.** Limit users with **just-in-time (JIT)** and **just-enough-access (JEA)**, risk-based adaptive policies, and data protection. Standing admin rights are the enemy; access should be the minimum needed, for the shortest time needed.
3. **Assume breach.** Operate as though an attacker is already inside. **Segment** access (by network, identity, app, and data), **minimize blast radius**, encrypt end-to-end, and use analytics to **detect** and **respond**. Logging and visibility are not optional.

A useful test: for any control you build, ask which principle it serves. Conditional Access requiring MFA = *verify explicitly*. PIM eligible roles = *least privilege*. Sentinel detections and segmentation = *assume breach*.

## The Six Zero Trust Pillars

Principles are the *philosophy*; pillars are *where you apply it*. Microsoft organizes Zero Trust into six pillars (sometimes shown as a wheel around a central policy engine):

| Pillar | What it protects | Example control |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity** | Users, service principals, workload identities | Strong/phishing-resistant MFA, Conditional Access, PIM |
| **Endpoints** | Laptops, phones, servers, IoT | Intune compliance, Defender for Endpoint EDR |
| **Apps** | SaaS and line-of-business applications | App governance, app-enforced session controls, OAuth app review |
| **Data** | Files, emails, structured data, AI prompts | Purview sensitivity labels, DLP, encryption |
| **Infrastructure** | VMs, containers, PaaS, on-prem servers | Defender for Cloud, hardening, JIT VM access |
| **Network** | Segmentation, traffic flows | Micro-segmentation, private endpoints, encrypted transport |

At the center sits a **policy engine** that takes signals from every pillar and makes an allow/deny/limit decision. In the Microsoft stack, **Conditional Access is that engine** for identity-centric access — which is exactly why Lesson 2 is dedicated to it.

## The Cloud Shared-Responsibility Model

Zero Trust lives inside the **shared-responsibility model**, which defines *who* secures *what* between you and the cloud provider. The split shifts by service type:

- **On-premises:** you own everything — physical, host, OS, network, apps, data, identity.
- **IaaS** (e.g., an Azure VM): Microsoft owns the physical host and hypervisor; *you* still own the OS, applications, network configuration, data, and identities.
- **PaaS** (e.g., Azure SQL, App Service): Microsoft also takes the OS and runtime; you own data, identities, and access configuration.
- **SaaS** (e.g., Microsoft 365): Microsoft runs almost the whole stack; you *still* own your **data**, your **identities/accounts**, and the **access** you grant.

The constant across all models: **data and identities are always your responsibility.** That single fact is why this course starts with identity. Microsoft running the datacenter does not protect you from an over-privileged admin or an un-reviewed guest account — those are yours to govern.

## Mapping the Microsoft Security Stack to the Pillars

Here is the product map you'll use for the rest of the course:

- **Identity → Microsoft Entra ID.** Authentication, Conditional Access (the policy engine), Identity Protection (risk), PIM (JIT admin), Identity Governance (access reviews, entitlement management, B2B). *This is Module 1.*
- **Endpoints → Microsoft Intune + Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.** Intune sets and reports device **compliance** (which Conditional Access consumes); Defender for Endpoint provides **EDR**, attack surface reduction, and threat analytics. *Module 2.*
- **Apps → Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps / Entra app governance.** Discovery, OAuth app risk, session controls.
- **Data → Microsoft Purview.** Sensitivity labels, data loss prevention (DLP), insider risk, and AI/Copilot data governance. *Module 3.*
- **Infrastructure → Microsoft Defender for Cloud.** Cloud security posture management (CSPM) and workload protection. *Module 4/5.*
- **Visibility & automation (cross-pillar) → Microsoft Defender XDR + Microsoft Sentinel.** Defender XDR correlates signals across identity, endpoint, email, and apps into unified **incidents**; Sentinel is the cloud-native **SIEM/SOAR** that ingests everything, hunts with **KQL**, and automates response with playbooks. *Module 4 and 5.*

Notice the flow: each pillar **produces signals**, Conditional Access **acts** on identity signals in real time, and Defender XDR/Sentinel **observe and respond** across all of them — a direct expression of *assume breach*.

## Identity Is the New Perimeter — and Where SC-500 Sits

Because users, apps, and data are scattered beyond any network edge, the **identity** is the one consistent thing present in every access request. That is what 'identity is the new perimeter' means: instead of asking *'is this packet inside the firewall?'* we ask *'is this verified identity, on a healthy device, with acceptable risk, allowed to reach this app and this data right now?'* Conditional Access answers that question on every sign-in.

Finally, position your own growth. **MD-102** (endpoint admin) and **MS-102** (Microsoft 365 admin) certify you to *operate* services: enroll devices, manage licenses, configure mailboxes. **SC-500** (and this course) is the level above — *designing and operating the security architecture*: how identity, endpoint, data, and SIEM controls combine to enforce Zero Trust, and how you detect and respond when they're tested. You already know how to administer the parts; this course teaches you to architect the whole.

quiz.q: Which set correctly lists the three core principles of Zero Trust as Microsoft defines them?
options: Encrypt everything, patch everything, log everything
Verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, assume breach
Trust the internal network, distrust the internet, audit quarterly
Single sign-on, multifactor authentication, password rotation
quiz.why: Zero Trust rests on three principles: verify explicitly (authenticate and authorize on all available signals), use least-privilege access (just-enough and just-in-time), and assume breach (segment, minimize blast radius, verify end-to-end). The other options are useful practices but are not the three principles.

quiz.q: An attacker steals valid user credentials and connects from inside the corporate network. Which Zero Trust principle most directly limits the damage?
options: Verify explicitly, because the network location is no longer treated as proof of trust
Encrypt data at rest, because the files are protected
Perimeter firewalling, because the VPN blocks the attacker
Annual access recertification, because the account will eventually be reviewed
quiz.why: Zero Trust never treats network location as trust. 'Verify explicitly' re-evaluates every access request against signals such as identity, device compliance, and risk — so a valid credential from a trusted network is still challenged, unlike the legacy 'trusted internal network' model.

quiz.q: In the cloud shared-responsibility model, which item is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility across SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS?
options: The physical datacenter and host hypervisor
quiz.why: Regardless of service model, the customer always owns their data and their identities/accounts (and the access granted to them). Physical hosts and the hypervisor are always Microsoft's; OS and network responsibility shift depending on whether the service is SaaS, PaaS, or IaaS.

quiz.q: Which Microsoft product is the primary control plane for the IDENTITY pillar of Zero Trust?
quiz.why: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is the identity provider and policy decision point — authentication, Conditional Access, Identity Protection, and PIM all live here. Intune governs endpoints, Purview governs data, and Sentinel provides cross-pillar visibility and automation.

quiz.q: Why is identity described as 'the new perimeter' in cloud-first environments?
options: Because firewalls no longer exist in the cloud
Because users, apps, and data are distributed beyond any network boundary, so the identity is the consistent control point for every access decision
Because all traffic is internal once you adopt the cloud
quiz.why: When SaaS apps, remote users, and data live outside the corporate LAN, there is no single network edge to defend. The identity — verified with strong, phishing-resistant auth and evaluated by Conditional Access — becomes the consistent enforcement point for who can access what, from which device, under what risk.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, explain how SC-500 architect-level responsibilities differ from the MD-102/MS-102 administrator tasks you may already know, and give one concrete example of a task at each level.
quiz.answer: MD-102 and MS-102 focus on administering and configuring individual services — for example, enrolling a device in Intune or assigning licenses and managing mailboxes in Microsoft 365. SC-500 sits above this: it is about designing and operating a cross-product security architecture — deciding how identity, endpoint, data, and SIEM controls fit together to enforce Zero Trust across the estate. A concrete architect-level task is designing a layered Conditional Access baseline with PIM and Identity Protection that feeds incidents into Microsoft Sentinel and Defender XDR, then defining the response automation — a system-design and policy decision rather than a single-service configuration step.
quiz.why: Administrator certifications are scoped to operating specific services; the SC-500 security architect role is scoped to designing the end-to-end Zero Trust security posture and how the products integrate, automate, and respond together.

cse-m1-l02-architecting-conditional-acce.title: Architecting Conditional Access Policies
objectives: Describe Conditional Access as the policy decision point that enforces Zero Trust 'verify explicitly'
Decompose a policy into assignments, conditions, grant controls, and session controls
Select the correct signals — sign-in risk, user risk, device compliance, location, client app — for a given scenario
Choose appropriate grant controls including require MFA, require compliant device, and require phishing-resistant MFA
Apply report-only mode and a phased rollout to deploy policies without locking users out
Design break-glass emergency accounts and exclude them from blocking policies
Assemble a layered Conditional Access baseline expressed as Microsoft Graph JSON
cse-m1-l02-architecting-conditional-acce.body:
## Conditional Access Is the Policy Engine

In Lesson 1 we said Zero Trust has a central policy engine that turns signals into decisions. In Microsoft Entra ID, that engine is **Conditional Access (CA)**. Think of it as an `if-then` statement evaluated on **every sign-in**: *IF* a particular user, accessing a particular resource, under particular conditions (risk, device, location, app), *THEN* allow, block, or allow only with extra controls.

CA is where 'verify explicitly' becomes real. It does not replace authentication — it sits *after* the first factor and decides what else is required before a token is issued. Because tokens gate access to every Microsoft 365 and integrated app, CA is the single most important identity control you will design. Get it right and a stolen password is nearly useless; get it wrong and you either lock out your company or leave the door open.

## Anatomy of a Policy: Assignments vs. Access Controls

Every CA policy has two halves.

**Assignments (the IF):**
- **Users and groups** — who the policy targets, with **exclusions** (this is where break-glass accounts go).
- **Target resources** — cloud apps, user actions (e.g., *register security info*), or authentication context.
- **Conditions / signals** — the contextual inputs: sign-in risk, user risk, device platforms, device state (compliant/hybrid-joined), locations, and client apps (browser, mobile/desktop, legacy).

**Access controls (the THEN):**
- **Grant controls** — block access, or grant *only if* controls are met: require MFA, require **phishing-resistant** MFA, require a **compliant device**, require hybrid-joined device, require approved client app, require app protection policy. Combine with *require all* or *require one*.
- **Session controls** — shape the session even after access is granted: **sign-in frequency**, **persistent browser**, **app-enforced restrictions** (e.g., limited web-only access to Exchange/SharePoint), and Conditional Access App Control via Defender for Cloud Apps.

## The Signals That Drive Decisions

CA is only as smart as the signals it can read. The key ones:

- **User/group membership** — the baseline scope.
- **Sign-in risk** (from Microsoft Entra **Identity Protection**) — the probability *this specific sign-in* is not the legitimate user (impossible travel, anonymous IP, malware-linked IP).
- **User risk** (also Identity Protection) — the probability the *account itself* is compromised (leaked credentials found, atypical behavior over time).
- **Device compliance / state** — comes from **Microsoft Intune**: is the device enrolled, compliant with policy (encryption, OS version, defender healthy), or hybrid-joined? This is the bridge between the identity and endpoint pillars.
- **Location** — named locations / trusted IPs or country-based conditions.
- **Client app** — modern auth browser/desktop vs. **legacy authentication** (POP, IMAP, SMTP, older Office). Legacy auth can't do MFA and should be blocked outright.

## A Realistic Policy as Graph JSON

CA policies are objects you can read and deploy via Microsoft Graph. Below is a policy that **requires phishing-resistant MFA for all users on all apps**, in **report-only** mode, excluding break-glass accounts. Note `grantControls.authenticationStrength` referencing the built-in phishing-resistant strength.

```json
{
  "displayName": "CA001 - Require phishing-resistant MFA for all users",
  "state": "enabledForReportingButNotEnforced",
  "conditions": {
    "users": {
      "includeUsers": ["All"],
      "excludeUsers": [
        "<break-glass-1-objectId>",
        "<break-glass-2-objectId>"
      ]
    },
    "applications": {
      "includeApplications": ["All"]
    },
    "clientAppTypes": ["all"]
  },
  "grantControls": {
    "operator": "AND",
    "authenticationStrength": {
      "id": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000004"
    }
  }
}
```

A second policy blocks **legacy authentication**, which cannot satisfy MFA at all:

```json
{
  "displayName": "CA002 - Block legacy authentication",
  "state": "enabledForReportingButNotEnforced",
  "conditions": {
    "users": { "includeUsers": ["All"], "excludeUsers": ["<break-glass-1-objectId>"] },
    "applications": { "includeApplications": ["All"] },
    "clientAppTypes": ["exchangeActiveSync", "other"]
  },
  "grantControls": { "operator": "OR", "builtInControls": ["block"] }
}
```

Deploy and inspect policies with Graph PowerShell, for example `Get-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy` and `New-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -BodyParameter $json`.

## Safe Rollout: Report-Only, What If, and Phasing

Never flip a tenant-wide blocking policy straight to **On**. The discipline:

1. **Report-only mode** (`enabledForReportingButNotEnforced`) — the policy is evaluated on real sign-ins and the result is logged (would-grant / would-block / would-require-control) **without** affecting users. Watch the sign-in logs and the report-only workbook for days.
2. **What If tool** — simulate a specific user, app, and conditions to see which policies apply and why.
3. **Phased enforcement** — pilot on a small group, then ring out to the org; keep exclusion groups for users who need temporary relief.
4. **Monitor after enabling** — confirm no spike in failures or help-desk tickets before declaring success.

This is the difference between an architect and someone who locks out the CEO on a Friday afternoon.

## Break-Glass Accounts and the Layered Baseline

**Break-glass (emergency access) accounts** are your insurance against a CA mistake or an MFA-provider outage locking everyone out. Best practice: at least **two** cloud-only accounts (`*.onmicrosoft.com`), Global Administrator, with **long unique passphrases** stored offline, **excluded** from blocking CA policies, and wired to **alerts on every sign-in** so any real use is noticed immediately.

With that safety net, layer the baseline from broad hygiene to adaptive response:

1. **Block legacy authentication** (CA002 above) — kills the easiest password-spray path.
2. **Require MFA / phishing-resistant MFA for all users** (CA001) — the core 'verify explicitly' control.
3. **Require a compliant or hybrid-joined device for sensitive/admin apps** — ties access to Intune endpoint health.
4. **Identity Protection risk policies** — **high sign-in risk → block**; **high user risk → require secure password change** (self-remediation via MFA).

Each layer maps to a Zero Trust principle, and every layer carries the same break-glass exclusion. That is a defensible, portfolio-grade Conditional Access architecture.

quiz.q: In Zero Trust terms, what role does Conditional Access play?
options: It is the data classification engine for files and email
It is the policy decision point that evaluates signals and enforces access decisions in real time
It is the endpoint EDR sensor that detects malware
It is the SIEM that stores and queries long-term logs
quiz.why: Conditional Access is the identity policy engine: at sign-in it gathers signals (user, risk, device, location, app) and outputs a decision — allow, block, or allow-with-controls. That real-time enforcement is exactly 'verify explicitly'. Classification is Purview, EDR is Defender for Endpoint, and the SIEM is Sentinel.

quiz.q: A Conditional Access policy is built from assignments and access controls. Which option lists the assignment (the 'if') components correctly?
options: Users/groups, target resources (apps/actions), and conditions (risk, device, location, client app)
Sensitivity labels, retention policies, and DLP rules
Antivirus signatures, firewall rules, and IP allow-lists only
Mailbox permissions, license SKUs, and group memberships only
quiz.why: Assignments define WHO and WHAT a policy applies to: users and groups (with exclusions), target resources such as cloud apps or user actions, and conditions like sign-in risk, user risk, device platform/state, locations, and client apps. The access controls (grant and session) then define the THEN.

quiz.q: Which grant control gives the strongest protection against real-time phishing and adversary-in-the-middle token theft?
options: Require multifactor authentication using SMS text messages
Require a password change every 30 days
Require phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 security key, passkey, or Windows Hello for Business)
Require security questions in addition to a password
quiz.why: Phishing-resistant MFA — FIDO2/passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, or certificate-based authentication — binds the credential to the legitimate site and device, defeating adversary-in-the-middle proxies that can relay SMS or push approvals. SMS and security questions are phishable; password rotation does nothing against token theft.

quiz.q: Why should you deploy a new blocking Conditional Access policy in report-only mode first?
options: Report-only mode encrypts the sign-in logs
Report-only evaluates the policy and logs what WOULD happen without enforcing it, so you can find impact before locking users out
Report-only mode automatically excludes all guests
It is required before you can assign any users
quiz.why: Report-only mode runs the policy logic against real sign-ins and records the result (would grant / would block / would require control) in the sign-in logs and the What If tool, without affecting users. This lets you validate scope and catch unintended impact — like blocking a service account — before turning the policy On.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of break-glass (emergency access) accounts, and how should they relate to Conditional Access?
options: They are everyday admin accounts that should be in every MFA policy
They are highly-protected, monitored emergency accounts that are EXCLUDED from blocking CA policies so a misconfigured policy or MFA outage can't lock everyone out
They are guest accounts used for vendor access
They are disabled accounts kept for auditing only
quiz.why: Break-glass accounts are a small number of cloud-only, highly-protected accounts excluded from policies that could otherwise cause a tenant-wide lockout (for example if an MFA provider fails or a CA policy is misconfigured). They use long, unique credentials, are tightly monitored with alerts on every sign-in, and are used only in emergencies.

quiz.q: In three to five sentences, design a minimal but layered Conditional Access baseline for a mid-sized tenant and explain what each layer enforces and why the order/exclusions matter.
quiz.answer: Layer one blocks legacy authentication protocols for all users, because legacy auth cannot do MFA and is the most common path for password-spray attacks. Layer two requires MFA (ideally phishing-resistant) for all users accessing all cloud apps, establishing the 'verify explicitly' baseline. Layer three requires a compliant or hybrid-joined device for sensitive or admin applications, tying access to endpoint health from Intune. Layer four uses Identity Protection signals so that high sign-in risk is blocked and high user risk forces a secure password change. Across all of these, a small set of break-glass accounts is excluded so a misconfiguration or MFA outage cannot lock administrators out of the tenant.
quiz.why: A good baseline layers controls from broad hygiene (block legacy auth, require MFA) to targeted hardening (compliant device for sensitive apps) to adaptive risk response (Identity Protection), always with break-glass exclusions to preserve recoverability.

cse-m1-l03-privileged-identity-managemen.title: Privileged Identity Management and Just-in-Time Admin
objectives: Contrast standing access with eligible (just-in-time) access and explain why standing privilege is dangerous
Configure PIM role settings: activation duration, require MFA, require justification, and approval workflow
Distinguish eligible vs. active assignments and time-bound vs. permanent assignments
Create recurring access reviews for privileged roles and act on the results
Use PIM for Groups to bring just-in-time access to group-based and non-role permissions
Enable and triage PIM alerts and articulate the principle of zero standing privilege
Make a user eligible for a privileged role using Microsoft Graph PowerShell
cse-m1-l03-privileged-identity-managemen.body:
## The Problem: Standing Privilege

Most breaches that end in disaster pass through a **privileged account**. The traditional model gives admins **standing access** — a permanent role assignment that is live every second of every day. That means the powerful permissions are *always* there to be stolen: phish the password, steal the token, or ride an open session, and the attacker instantly *is* a Global Administrator. There is no activation gate, no fresh MFA, no time limit, no second pair of eyes.

Zero Trust's least-privilege principle says access should be **just-enough** and **just-in-time (JIT)**. Applied to admin roles, the end state is **zero standing privilege**: nobody walks around with live admin rights. Instead they hold *eligibility* and elevate only when they actually need to, for a short, audited window. The tool that delivers this in Microsoft Entra ID is **Privileged Identity Management (PIM)**.

## Eligible vs. Active, Permanent vs. Time-Bound

PIM describes assignments along two axes:

- **Eligible vs. Active.** An **eligible** assignment grants *nothing* until the user **activates** it through PIM. An **active** assignment means the permissions are in effect now. The whole point of PIM is to make powerful roles *eligible* by default.
- **Permanent vs. Time-bound.** Either type can be permanent or given a start/end date. Best practice for privileged roles is **eligible + time-bound** so even the eligibility itself expires and must be renewed.

So a hardened design looks like: *Alice is **eligible** for Global Administrator until the end of the quarter; when she needs it she **activates** for up to 4 hours with MFA, a justification, and approval.* Outside those activations, her account has no admin power at all — there is nothing for an attacker to steal.

## Activation: MFA, Justification, Approval, and Duration

What happens at activation is controlled per role in **PIM role settings**. The levers you'll set:

- **Require Microsoft Entra MFA on activation** — a fresh strong-auth challenge at elevation time (verify explicitly, again).
- **Require justification** — the user types *why*, creating an audit trail.
- **Require approval** — one or more designated approvers must say yes before the role activates; great for the most sensitive roles.
- **Require ticket information** — tie elevation to a change/incident ticket.
- **Maximum activation duration** — the time box, e.g., 1–8 hours. When it expires, permissions are automatically removed.

Tune by sensitivity: a Global Administrator might require MFA + justification + approval with a 2–4 hour cap; a lower-impact role might need only MFA and justification. The tighter the role, the tighter the gate.

## Making a User Eligible with Graph PowerShell

PIM assignments are schedule requests in Microsoft Graph. The snippet below creates an **eligible** assignment for a role using the `Microsoft.Graph` PowerShell SDK. Replace the IDs with your tenant's values (find role definition IDs with `Get-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleDefinition`).

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory"

$params = @{
  action           = "adminAssign"
  justification    = "Make Alice eligible for Helpdesk Administrator"
  roleDefinitionId = "729827e3-9c14-49f7-bb1b-9608f156bbb8"  # Helpdesk Administrator
  directoryScopeId = "/"
  principalId      = "<alice-objectId>"
  scheduleInfo     = @{
    startDateTime = (Get-Date).ToString("o")
    expiration    = @{
      type     = "afterDuration"
      duration = "P90D"   # eligible for 90 days, then must be renewed
    }
  }
}

New-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleEligibilityScheduleRequest -BodyParameter $params
```

This grants Alice **no live access** — it only makes her *eligible*. She must still activate through PIM (portal or `New-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleAssignmentScheduleRequest` with `action = "selfActivate"`), passing whatever MFA/justification/approval the role settings demand.

## Access Reviews of Privileged Roles

PIM controls *how* a role is used, but **eligibility lists still grow**. People change teams, projects end, and old eligibility lingers. **Access reviews** close that gap: schedule a **recurring** review (e.g., monthly or quarterly) of each privileged role's eligible and active members. Reviewers — a manager, a designated owner, or the users themselves via self-attestation — confirm each assignment is still needed; anything not approved is **removed automatically**. For privileged roles, configure reviews to **require justification** and to **remove access on denial or no response**, so silence defaults to *least privilege*, not to lingering rights.

## PIM for Groups, Alerts, and Zero Standing Privilege

Not every permission is a directory role. **PIM for Groups** extends JIT to **group membership and ownership**: make a user *eligible* for a group, and activating it grants whatever the group confers — access to a SaaS app, an Azure RBAC scope, or a bundle of permissions — under the same MFA, justification, approval, and duration controls. This is how you bring zero standing privilege to things that aren't native PIM roles.

Finally, turn on **PIM alerts** and triage them: *'Administrators aren't using their privileged roles'* (prune them), *'Roles are being assigned outside of PIM'* (close the back door), *'There are too many Global Administrators'*, and *'Roles activated too frequently.'* Each alert is a nudge back toward the goal: **zero standing privilege** — eligibility instead of standing rights, short activated windows instead of permanent power, approvals and reviews keeping the whole system honest.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between an 'eligible' and an 'active' PIM role assignment?
options: Eligible means the user can use the role anytime; active means it is disabled
Eligible means the user must activate the role (with MFA/justification) before using it; active means the permissions are granted right now
Eligible roles are read-only; active roles are read-write
There is no functional difference; the terms are interchangeable
quiz.why: An eligible assignment grants nothing until the user activates it through PIM — typically requiring MFA, a justification, and sometimes approval — and the activation is time-bound. An active assignment means the role's permissions are in effect immediately. Eligible-by-default is the just-in-time model that drives toward zero standing privilege.

quiz.q: Why is permanent (standing) Global Administrator access considered a serious risk?
options: It costs more in licensing than eligible access
A permanently-assigned high-privilege account is always available to an attacker who compromises it, with no activation barrier or time limit
It prevents the user from signing in to non-admin apps
quiz.why: Standing privilege means the powerful permissions are live 24/7. If the account is phished or its token stolen, the attacker immediately has full admin with no JIT activation gate, no fresh MFA challenge, and no time box. PIM shrinks that exposure window to only the minutes the role is actually activated.

quiz.q: Which combination of PIM activation settings best enforces Zero Trust for a Global Administrator role?
options: No MFA, no justification, 7-day activation, no approval
Require MFA on activation, require justification, short maximum activation duration, and require approval
Require justification only, with permanent activation
Require approval only, with MFA disabled
quiz.why: Strong PIM settings for a top-tier role combine require MFA at activation (verify explicitly), require a written justification (accountability), a short maximum duration such as a few hours (least privilege in time), and an approval workflow so a second person authorizes the elevation. Together these minimize both the window and the unilateral use of privilege.

quiz.q: What problem does PIM for Groups solve that role-based PIM alone does not?
options: It backs up group membership to storage
It brings just-in-time, time-bound, approval-gated activation to membership/ownership of groups — useful for app roles, Azure resources, or roles not directly PIM-enabled
It converts security groups into distribution lists
It disables Conditional Access for group members
quiz.why: PIM for Groups makes users *eligible* for group membership or ownership, so activating the group grants whatever that group confers — access to an app, an Azure RBAC scope, or a bundle of permissions — under the same JIT, MFA, justification, and approval controls. It extends zero standing privilege beyond directory roles.

quiz.q: Why should privileged roles be subject to recurring access reviews even when PIM is enforced?
options: Access reviews replace the need for MFA
Eligibility itself accumulates over time; reviews confirm each person still NEEDS to be eligible and remove stale assignments
Access reviews are required to activate a role
They automatically delete the user account if not reviewed
quiz.why: PIM controls *how* a role is used (JIT activation), but eligibility lists still grow as people change jobs. Recurring access reviews force reviewers (or the users themselves) to attest that each eligible assignment is still justified, removing accumulated, forgotten, or role-changed access — closing the gap PIM activation alone doesn't address.

quiz.q: In three to five sentences, explain the principle of 'zero standing privilege' and describe how PIM, access reviews, and approval workflows together move a tenant toward it.
quiz.answer: Zero standing privilege means no account holds active high-privilege permissions by default; privilege exists only as eligibility that must be activated for a short, justified window. PIM delivers this by making admin roles eligible rather than active, so even a compromised admin account has no live privilege until someone passes MFA, supplies a justification, and waits out an approval. Maximum activation durations time-box the access so it auto-expires, and approval workflows ensure a second person authorizes sensitive elevations. Recurring access reviews then prune the eligibility lists so people who no longer need a role lose even the ability to activate it. Together they collapse the attack surface from a permanent target down to a brief, audited, approved window.
quiz.why: Zero standing privilege is the end state of least-privilege-in-time: eligibility plus JIT activation (PIM), time-boxing and approvals to constrain each use, and access reviews to keep the eligibility set minimal and current.

cse-m1-l04-identity-governance-access-re.title: Identity Governance: Access Reviews, Entitlement Management, and B2B
objectives: Describe the Microsoft Entra Identity Governance suite and the problem each component solves
Design entitlement management with access packages, catalogs, and lifecycle policies that automatically expire access
Configure access reviews for groups, applications, and guest users with sensible recurrence and auto-removal
Automate joiner/mover/leaver events with lifecycle workflows
Secure external collaboration using B2B and cross-tenant access settings (inbound/outbound trust)
Explain cross-tenant synchronization and when to use it instead of guest invitations
Use guest access reviews to prevent guest sprawl and enforce least privilege
cse-m1-l04-identity-governance-access-re.body:
## From Admin Elevation to the Whole Lifecycle

Lesson 3 governed *admin elevation* with PIM. But least privilege has to apply to **everyone, all the time** — the new hire on day one, the employee who changes departments, the contractor who finishes a project, and the partner guest who was invited two years ago and never removed. **Microsoft Entra Identity Governance** is the suite that automates this whole lifecycle so access is granted appropriately, reviewed regularly, and removed promptly — without an admin manually babysitting every change.

The suite has four workhorses we'll cover: **entitlement management** (how access is requested and granted), **access reviews** (how access is recertified), **lifecycle workflows** (how joiners/movers/leavers are automated), and **B2B / cross-tenant** controls (how external people collaborate safely). All four serve one goal: keep *who-can-access-what* minimal and current.

## Entitlement Management: Access Packages and Catalogs

Manually adding people to groups and apps doesn't scale and leaves no governance trail. **Entitlement management** fixes this with **access packages**.

- An **access package** bundles everything a role needs: security and Microsoft 365 groups, enterprise applications, and SharePoint sites — plus a **policy** describing *who can request it*, *who approves*, and *how long it lasts*.
- A **catalog** is the container that holds those resources and packages. Catalogs enable **delegation**: a department owner can manage packages for their own resources without being a tenant admin (least privilege for governance itself).
- **Lifecycle policies** on the package set **automatic expiration** — access lapses after N days or on a date unless the user re-requests and is re-approved. Nothing is permanent by default.

The user experience: someone visits the **My Access** portal, requests the *'Finance App — Analyst'* package, the finance owner approves, and the right groups/apps/sites are granted automatically — then auto-removed at expiry. Request, approve, expire: governed end-to-end.

## Access Reviews for Groups, Apps, and Guests

Grants drift. People change roles, projects end, and yesterday's appropriate access becomes today's risk. **Access reviews** force periodic **attestation**:

- Scope a review to a **group**, an **application's** assigned users, a **privileged role** (from Lesson 3), or **guest users**.
- Choose **reviewers**: resource owners, managers, or the users themselves (self-attestation).
- Set **recurrence** (weekly/monthly/quarterly) and an **auto-apply** action: **remove access if denied or not reviewed**, so inaction defaults to least privilege rather than lingering rights.

For sensitive resources, require the reviewer to **provide a justification** and enable **decision helpers** (e.g., flag users who haven't signed in). Reviews are the recertification heartbeat of governance.

## Lifecycle Workflows: Joiner / Mover / Leaver

**Lifecycle workflows (LCW)** automate the **JML** events that historically caused the worst access hygiene problems — especially the **leaver**, where forgotten accounts become standing attack surface.

- **Joiner:** triggered relative to `employeeHireDate` — e.g., *2 days before start*, enable the account, add it to baseline groups, generate a temporary access pass, send a welcome email.
- **Mover:** on attribute change (department/job title) — adjust group memberships and entitlements.
- **Leaver:** triggered relative to `employeeLeaveDateTime` — disable the account, remove from all groups, revoke sessions/tokens, and reassign or remove access.

Workflows are built from configurable **tasks** and run on a schedule, with execution history for audit. Pairing LCW with HR-driven inbound provisioning means a person's access tracks their employment automatically.

## Secure B2B and Cross-Tenant Access Settings

External collaboration is essential and dangerous. **B2B collaboration** lets partners sign in with *their own* identity (no password for you to manage) as a **guest** in your tenant. **Cross-tenant access settings** make that Zero-Trust-aligned by defining trust **per partner tenant** (and a default):

- **Inbound** — which external users/groups and which of *your* apps they can reach.
- **Outbound** — which of *your* users can access *partner* tenants and apps.
- **Trust settings** — whether you **trust the partner's MFA and device-compliance claims**, so a guest who already did phishing-resistant MFA in their home tenant doesn't have to repeat it, and your Conditional Access can require a *compliant device* even for guests.

A hardened default blocks broad external access and explicitly allows named partner tenants and apps — external access by exception, not by default.

## Cross-Tenant Sync and Stopping Guest Sprawl

For organizations that span **multiple tenants** (mergers, multi-national subsidiaries), inviting guests one by one doesn't scale. **Cross-tenant synchronization (CTS)** automatically **provisions, updates, and deprovisions** B2B users from a source tenant into a target tenant and keeps them in sync — users appear and disappear automatically as their home tenant changes. Use CTS for *same-organization* multi-tenant scenarios; use ordinary B2B invitations for *one-off* external partners.

Whatever the mechanism, guests **accumulate silently** — invited for a project, never removed. That **guest sprawl** is forgotten attack surface. Counter it with **guest-focused access reviews**: recurring reviews of all guests (or guests in sensitive groups), with **remove-on-no-response**, plus inactivity decision helpers to catch guests who haven't signed in for months. 

Step back and see the loop: lifecycle workflows provision and deprovision, access packages grant and auto-expire, access reviews recertify, and guest reviews prune external accounts. Together they keep the identity estate minimal and current — the living embodiment of least privilege, and the identity foundation the rest of this course's Zero Trust architecture is built on.

quiz.q: What core problem does entitlement management (access packages) solve?
options: It encrypts files shared with external users
It bundles the resources a role needs (groups, apps, SharePoint sites) into a requestable package with approval and automatic expiration, so access is governed end-to-end
It replaces Conditional Access for guest sign-ins
It stores admin passwords in a vault
quiz.why: An access package bundles related resources (security/M365 groups, enterprise apps, SharePoint sites) plus the policy for who can request them, who approves, and when they expire. Users request access in one place, approvers grant it, and lifecycle policies auto-expire it — governing the full request-to-removal lifecycle instead of manual one-off grants.

quiz.q: In entitlement management, what is the role of a catalog?
options: It is a list of blocked applications
It is a container that groups the resources and access packages for delegated administration, so non-admins can own packages for their own apps/groups
It is the audit log of all sign-ins
It is a Conditional Access policy set
quiz.why: A catalog is a container of resources (groups, apps, sites) and the access packages built from them. It enables delegation: a department lead can be made a catalog owner and manage access packages for their own resources without being a tenant-wide admin — a least-privilege, self-service governance model.

quiz.q: Which scenario is the best fit for a lifecycle workflow?
options: Encrypting an email with a sensitivity label
Automatically running joiner tasks (enable account, add to groups, send welcome) a set number of days before a new hire's start date, and leaver tasks at termination
Activating a PIM role for four hours
quiz.why: Lifecycle workflows automate joiner/mover/leaver (JML) events based on attributes like employeeHireDate and employeeLeaveDateTime — provisioning access before day one and, critically, deprovisioning it at departure so access doesn't linger. That automation is the operational backbone of least privilege across the user lifecycle.

quiz.q: What do cross-tenant access settings control in B2B collaboration?
options: The color theme of the guest sign-in page
Inbound and outbound trust between your tenant and specific partner tenants — which users/apps are allowed, and whether you trust their MFA and device compliance claims
The amount of storage guests can use in SharePoint
Whether guests can change their own passwords
quiz.why: Cross-tenant access settings define, per partner tenant (or as a default), which inbound external users and outbound internal users may collaborate, which apps are in scope, and whether you trust the partner's MFA and device-compliance claims so guests don't have to re-satisfy MFA. This is how you make B2B both usable and Zero-Trust-aligned.

quiz.q: When is cross-tenant synchronization (CTS) preferable to standard B2B guest invitations?
options: Never — CTS and B2B are identical
When a multi-tenant organization wants users from one tenant automatically provisioned and kept in sync as B2B members in another tenant, instead of inviting and managing them one by one
When you want to block all external access
When you only need to share a single SharePoint file with one person
quiz.why: Cross-tenant synchronization automatically creates, updates, and deprovisions B2B users across tenants in the same organization, keeping identities in sync without manual invitations. It's ideal for mergers or multi-tenant enterprises; one-off external sharing is still better served by a standard B2B guest invite.

quiz.q: In three to five sentences, explain how access packages, access reviews, lifecycle workflows, and guest access reviews work together to enforce least privilege across the identity lifecycle, and why this matters for Zero Trust.
quiz.answer: Lifecycle workflows handle the joiner and mover and leaver events automatically, so accounts are provisioned just before they're needed and deprovisioned the moment someone leaves, eliminating orphaned access. Access packages govern in-life entitlements: users request bundled resources, approvers grant them, and lifecycle policies auto-expire the access so nothing is permanent by default. Access reviews periodically force attestation that each remaining group, app, and especially guest assignment is still justified, removing anything stale. Guest access reviews specifically curb guest sprawl, because external accounts otherwise accumulate silently and become forgotten attack surface. Together they keep the set of who-can-access-what minimal and current, which is exactly the least-privilege foundation Zero Trust depends on.
quiz.why: The four controls cover provisioning (lifecycle workflows), in-life entitlement (access packages with expiry), periodic recertification (access reviews), and external-account hygiene (guest reviews) — a closed loop that continuously drives toward least privilege, the core of Zero Trust identity.

cse-m2-l01-intune-compliance-and-configu.title: Intune Compliance Policies and Configuration Baselines
objectives: Compare device enrollment models (Windows Autopilot, Automatic Enrollment, BYOD/MAM) and pick the right one per scenario.
Author an Intune compliance policy that checks OS version, BitLocker, firewall, Defender real-time protection, and device threat level.
Deploy configuration profiles and a settings-catalog security baseline that enforce BitLocker, firewall, and ASR.
Configure compliance actions for noncompliance, including 'mark device noncompliant' with a grace period and end-user notifications.
Explain how compliance state flows into Conditional Access as the 'require compliant device' grant control.
Validate compliance and configuration results from the Intune admin center and on the endpoint.
cse-m2-l01-intune-compliance-and-configu.body:
## Why device trust comes first

Zero Trust says *never trust, always verify* — and one of the strongest things you can verify is the health of the device making the request. In Microsoft Intune you build that verification in two halves: **configuration profiles / security baselines** that *enforce* a hardened state, and **compliance policies** that *evaluate* the device and stamp it compliant or noncompliant in Microsoft Entra ID. Conditional Access then consumes that stamp. Get this layer right and the automated isolation you build in Lesson 3 becomes almost free.

## Enrollment models: choose deliberately

Before a device can be governed it must be known to Intune. Pick the model that matches ownership and use case:

- **Windows Autopilot** — corporate Windows devices provisioned zero-touch from the OEM/reseller; the device joins Entra ID and enrolls automatically.
- **Automatic enrollment** — when a user Entra-joins a Windows device, MDM enrollment happens automatically (configured under *Devices > Enrollment*).
- **Hybrid Entra join** — on-prem AD-joined devices that also register in Entra; common in migration scenarios.
- **MAM / App protection (BYOD)** — personal phones where you protect *app data* (Outlook, Teams) without enrolling or fully managing the device.

Rule of thumb: full device management (and therefore compliance + configuration profiles) for corporate devices; MAM for unmanaged personal devices.

## Building a compliance policy

In the Intune admin center go to **Devices > Compliance > Create policy**, platform **Windows 10 and later**. Concrete settings to set:

- **Device Health**: Require BitLocker = *Require*; Require Secure Boot = *Require*; Code integrity = *Require*.
- **Device Properties**: Minimum OS version = e.g. `10.0.22631` (Windows 11 23H2 or later).
- **System Security**: Firewall = *Require*; Antivirus = *Require*; Microsoft Defender Antimalware real-time protection = *Require*; Encryption of data storage = *Require*.
- **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint**: *Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score* = **Medium**. This is the line that ties compliance to MDE's threat level — remember it for Lesson 3.

Assign the policy to a device or user group. A device that fails any rule will (after its action schedule) be marked noncompliant.

## Actions for noncompliance and grace periods

On the **Actions for noncompliance** tab you control the user experience and timing:

- **Mark device noncompliant** with *Schedule (days after noncompliance)* = `0` for immediate, or `1`–`3` to grant a **grace period** so users can self-remediate before access is cut.
- **Send email to end user** using a configured notification message template, optionally CC'ing the helpdesk.
- **Remotely lock** or **Retire the noncompliant device** for high-stakes scenarios.

Grace periods are a usability/security trade-off: too long and a risky device keeps access; `0` days gives the tightest containment, which is what you want for the threat-level rule.

## Enforcing settings with profiles and the settings catalog

Compliance *checks* but does not *fix*. Use **Devices > Configuration > Create > New policy > Settings catalog** to actively enforce. Search the catalog and add, for example:

- **BitLocker**: require encryption, XTS-AES 256, silent enablement, and escrow the recovery key to Entra ID.
- **Microsoft Defender Firewall**: enable Domain/Private/Public profiles, default inbound = block.
- **Attack Surface Reduction**: set ASR rules to *Block* (covered in depth in Lesson 2).

A simple way to read effective BitLocker state on an endpoint:

```powershell
# Confirm BitLocker is on and fully encrypted
Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C: |
  Select-Object MountPoint, VolumeStatus, EncryptionPercentage, ProtectionStatus
```

## Security baselines as a fast hardening start

Instead of hand-picking hundreds of settings, deploy a **security baseline** (Devices > Security baselines) — Microsoft's recommended preconfigured set for Windows, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Microsoft Edge. Treat the baseline as your starting point, then layer targeted settings-catalog profiles for anything the baseline doesn't cover. Watch for **conflicts**: when two profiles set the same setting differently, Intune reports the device as *Conflict* and applies neither, so keep ownership of each setting clear.

## Closing the loop into Conditional Access

None of this blocks anything yet. Compliance state is just metadata until a **Conditional Access** policy uses it. In Entra create a policy targeting your users and cloud apps, and under *Grant* select **Require device to be marked as compliant**. Now a noncompliant Windows device is denied at sign-in to Exchange Online, SharePoint, and your SaaS apps. Validate end-to-end: break a rule (e.g., disable the firewall), confirm the device flips to noncompliant in *Devices > All devices*, and confirm sign-in is blocked. That round trip is exactly what you will automate in Lesson 3.

quiz.q: Which Intune compliance setting turns a Defender for Endpoint machine-risk score into a pass/fail compliance result?
options: Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score (device threat level)
quiz.why: The 'Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score' setting maps the MDE-reported threat level (Clear/Low/Medium/High) onto compliance, which is the hinge for the automated isolation loop later in the module.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a configuration profile and a compliance policy in Intune?
options: They are the same feature with different names
A configuration profile enforces/sets settings on the device; a compliance policy only evaluates and reports a state
A compliance policy enforces settings; a configuration profile only reports
Configuration profiles only apply to iOS
quiz.why: Configuration profiles and security baselines actively push and enforce settings (e.g., turn BitLocker on). Compliance policies evaluate the device against rules and produce a compliant/noncompliant state used by Conditional Access.

quiz.q: A compliance policy's action for noncompliance is set to 'Mark device noncompliant' with a schedule of 1 day. What happens?
options: The device is given a one-day grace period before its state flips to noncompliant
The user is blocked from sign-in for one day
Nothing until an admin manually approves
quiz.why: Setting the schedule to 1 day creates a grace period: the device is treated as compliant for one day after first failing, giving the user time to remediate before the state flips and Conditional Access reacts.

quiz.q: Where in Intune would you most efficiently configure dozens of granular Windows hardening settings (firewall, ASR, BitLocker) from a single searchable surface?
quiz.why: The Settings Catalog exposes the full library of Windows CSP settings in one searchable place, and is the modern recommended way to build configuration profiles and security baselines.

quiz.q: For an unmanaged personal phone accessing only Outlook and Teams, which enrollment approach is most appropriate?
options: App protection policies / MAM without device enrollment
quiz.why: MAM (app protection policies) protects corporate data inside managed apps without enrolling or fully managing the personal device, which is the right fit for BYOD where you only need to govern app data.

quiz.q: In 2-4 sentences, explain why deploying a compliance policy alone does not actually block a noncompliant device from reaching corporate resources, and what you must add.
quiz.answer: A compliance policy only evaluates the device and stamps it compliant or noncompliant in Entra ID; by itself it changes nothing about access. To enforce access decisions you must pair it with a Conditional Access policy that uses the 'Require device to be marked as compliant' grant control. Only then does a noncompliant state actually block sign-in to apps like Exchange Online or SharePoint.

cse-m2-l02-defender-for-endpoint-onboard.title: Defender for Endpoint: Onboarding and Attack Surface Reduction
objectives: Describe MDE's cloud-plus-sensor architecture and the role of the Intune connector.
Onboard Windows devices to MDE through an Intune endpoint detection and response (EDR) policy.
Deploy Attack Surface Reduction rules and run an audit-then-block rollout to avoid breaking business apps.
Identify several real ASR rules by name and GUID and explain what each blocks.
Enable controlled folder access, network protection, and tamper protection.
Interpret the exposure score and security recommendations in Defender Vulnerability Management.
cse-m2-l02-defender-for-endpoint-onboard.body:
## MDE architecture in one picture

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is a cloud service plus a sensor that is already built into Windows. The endpoint sensor streams behavioral telemetry to the **Microsoft Defender portal** (security.microsoft.com), where detections, the device inventory, vulnerability data, and automated investigation all live. There is no separate agent to install on modern Windows — you simply **onboard** the device (register its sensor with your tenant) and configure the antivirus/EDR engine. Onboarding plus the Intune connector is what makes a device both *protected* and *governable*.

## The Intune <-> MDE connector

First wire the two services together. In the **Microsoft Defender portal**: *Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features* and turn on **Microsoft Intune connection**. Then in the **Intune admin center**: *Endpoint security > Microsoft Defender for Endpoint* and confirm the connection status is *Available* with *Connect Windows devices...* set to **On**. This service-to-service trust does two jobs: it lets Intune onboard devices, and — crucially for Lesson 3 — it lets MDE report each device's **risk level** back to Intune so compliance can react to it.

## Onboarding through an Intune EDR policy

With the connector live, onboarding is a policy push. Go to **Endpoint security > Endpoint detection and response > Create policy** (platform Windows). Because the connector is on, Intune fills in the onboarding blob automatically; set *Sample sharing* and *Expedite telemetry reporting frequency* as desired, then assign to your device group. Confirm success two ways:

```powershell
# On an onboarded device, sense service should be running
Get-Service -Name Sense | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

# Quick MDE protection state
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMRunningMode, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, IsTamperProtected
```

Within ~10-15 minutes the device appears under *Assets > Devices* in the Defender portal.

## Attack Surface Reduction: audit, tune, then block

ASR rules block the behaviors attackers rely on. The golden rule is **never deploy straight to block** — start in **Audit**, watch what *would* have been blocked, add exclusions, then enforce. Configure rules in Intune under *Endpoint security > Attack surface reduction > Create policy > Attack Surface Reduction Rules*. Real rules worth knowing:

- **Block credential stealing from lsass.exe** — `9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2` (stops Mimikatz-style credential dumping).
- **Block all Office applications from creating child processes** — `d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a`.
- **Block executable content from email client and webmail** — `be9ba2d9-53ea-4cdc-84e5-9b1eeee46550`.
- **Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands** — `d1e49aac-8f56-4280-b9ba-993a6d77406c`.
- **Block Win32 API calls from Office macros** — `92e97fa1-2edf-4476-bdd6-9dd0b4dddc7b`.
- **Use advanced protection against ransomware** — `c1db55ab-c21a-4637-bb3f-a12568109d35`.

Each rule's per-setting state is *Not configured / Audit / Block / Warn*. You can manage ASR audit/block centrally; on an endpoint you can confirm with PowerShell:

```powershell
# 1 = Block, 2 = Audit, 6 = Warn, 0 = Not configured
(Get-MpPreference).AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids
(Get-MpPreference).AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions
```

Review hits in the Defender portal's **attack surface reduction report**, add `AttackSurfaceReductionOnlyExclusions` for confirmed false positives, then flip to Block ring by ring.

## Controlled folder access and network protection

Two more proactive controls live in the same ASR policy family:

- **Controlled folder access** — anti-ransomware: only trusted apps may write to protected folders (Documents, Desktop, etc.). Roll it out in audit first too, because line-of-business apps often need to be explicitly allowed.
- **Network protection** — extends SmartScreen to all processes, blocking outbound connections to malicious domains/IPs and phishing sites. Also start in audit, then set to Block.

## Tamper protection and exposure score

**Tamper protection** locks Defender's own settings — real-time protection, cloud-delivered protection, and signature updates — so malware, scripts, or even local admins cannot switch them off. Enable it tenant-wide in the Defender portal (*Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features*) and/or via an Intune Antivirus/Security Experience policy.

Finally, **Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management** continuously assesses every onboarded device and produces an **exposure score** and a prioritized list of **security recommendations** (missing patches, weak configurations, risky software). A lower exposure score means a smaller attack surface; treat the top recommendations as your hardening backlog. Together, ASR plus a falling exposure score plus tamper protection give you a measurably harder fleet — and a reliable risk signal to feed the automated loop next.

quiz.q: What does the Intune connector to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint primarily enable?
options: It establishes trust so MDE can share device risk with Intune and Intune can onboard/deploy EDR policy
quiz.why: The connector creates the service-to-service trust that lets Intune onboard devices to MDE and lets MDE report each device's risk level back to Intune for compliance evaluation.

quiz.q: Why deploy ASR rules in audit mode before block mode?
options: Audit mode is required by licensing
Audit mode logs what would be blocked so you can find false positives before enforcing
Block mode does not generate any telemetry
Audit mode is faster to deploy
quiz.why: Audit mode records the events a rule would have blocked without actually blocking them, letting you discover legitimate business apps that would break and add exclusions before flipping to block.

quiz.q: Which ASR rule specifically protects against credential theft tooling like Mimikatz reading the LSASS process?
options: Block executable content from email client and webmail
Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)
Block Office applications from creating child processes
quiz.why: The 'Block credential stealing from lsass.exe' rule (GUID 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2) stops tools from dumping credentials out of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service.

quiz.q: What does Controlled Folder Access protect against?
options: Ransomware modifying files in protected folders by only allowing trusted apps to write
quiz.why: Controlled Folder Access guards designated folders so only trusted/allowed applications can modify their contents, blocking ransomware-style mass file encryption.

quiz.q: Tamper protection in MDE primarily prevents what?
options: Malware or local admins from disabling Defender features such as real-time protection
quiz.why: Tamper protection locks critical Defender settings (real-time protection, cloud-delivered protection, security intelligence updates) so they cannot be turned off by malware, scripts, or even local administrators.

quiz.q: In 2-4 sentences, outline a safe production rollout plan for a new ASR rule across a 5,000-device fleet.
quiz.answer: Start by deploying the rule in audit mode to a small pilot ring and review the ASR audit events and the attack surface reduction report for legitimate apps that would be blocked. Add per-path or per-publisher exclusions for confirmed false positives, then expand audit to the full fleet for a week or two. Once telemetry is clean, flip the rule to block for the pilot ring, validate, and progressively roll block mode out ring by ring while monitoring the Action center and user reports.

cse-m2-l03-risk-based-automated-device-i.title: Risk-Based Automated Device Isolation
objectives: Trace the end-to-end risk-based isolation loop from MDE detection to Conditional Access block.
Configure the Intune compliance rule that maps the MDE machine risk level to a noncompliant state.
Build the Conditional Access policy that enforces 'require compliant device' on the right apps.
Tune the loop's timing so containment happens in seconds without human intervention.
Trigger and reverse MDE device isolation and 'restrict app execution' actions.
Validate the whole loop with a controlled test detection and document the evidence for a portfolio.
cse-m2-l03-risk-based-automated-device-i.body:
## The closed loop, end to end

Project 1's centerpiece is a containment loop with **no human in it**. Three controls you already met now talk to each other:

1. **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** sees malicious behavior on a device and raises its **machine risk level** (Low -> Medium -> High).
2. **Intune compliance** has a rule: *require the device to be at or under the machine risk score = Medium*. A High-risk device instantly fails and is stamped **noncompliant** in Entra ID.
3. **Conditional Access** has a policy: *require device to be marked compliant*. The moment the device is noncompliant, sign-in to Exchange Online, SharePoint, Teams, and SaaS apps is **blocked**.

Detection to lockout takes seconds, and nobody opened a ticket. Your job in this lesson is to build and prove each link.

## Link 1: MDE produces the risk signal

This is already running from Lesson 2 — onboarded devices report risk, and the Intune connector carries that risk into Intune. Confirm the connector is **Available** (Intune > *Endpoint security > Microsoft Defender for Endpoint*) and that *Connect Windows devices...* is **On**. Without this trust, the risk level never reaches compliance and the loop is dead.

## Link 2: compliance converts risk into a state

Edit (or create) your Windows compliance policy and set the **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** rule:

```text
Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score:  Medium
```

Threshold meanings:

- **Clear** — strictest; any detection (Low+) makes the device noncompliant.
- **Low** — Low is tolerated; Medium/High fail.
- **Medium** — Low/Medium tolerated; only **High** fails. A common production balance.
- **High** — most permissive; only the very worst flips the device.

Set the *Actions for noncompliance* schedule to **0 days** so the state flips immediately — a grace period here would defeat the purpose.

## Link 3: Conditional Access enforces the block

In Entra, *Protection > Conditional Access > New policy*:

- **Users**: your target population (exclude a break-glass account).
- **Target resources**: Office 365 (Exchange, SharePoint, Teams) and your SaaS apps.
- **Grant**: *Require device to be marked as compliant*.
- Enable in **Report-only** first, confirm in the *Conditional Access Insights* workbook, then set to **On**.

Now the loop is wired: risk -> noncompliant -> blocked.

## Tuning the timing

'Seconds' depends on a few knobs. MDE raises risk almost immediately on detection. Intune re-evaluates compliance on a sync, so the device check-in cadence matters; the noncompliance schedule should be **0 days**. Conditional Access evaluates at sign-in and via **Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)**, which can revoke active sessions in near real time rather than waiting for token expiry. The net effect is containment that feels instantaneous to the attacker and invisible to your SOC queue.

## Deeper containment: isolate and restrict app execution

Conditional Access blocks *cloud* access, but a compromised device can still attack the *local network*. For that, use MDE response actions from the device page in the Defender portal (or via the API/automation):

- **Isolate device** — cuts the machine off from all network communication except its link back to the Defender service, stopping lateral movement while you investigate. Choose *Full* or *Selective* isolation.
- **Restrict app execution** — applies a code-integrity policy so only Microsoft-signed processes can run, neutering most malware without fully isolating the device.
- **Run antivirus scan**, **Collect investigation package**, and **Initiate automated investigation** for follow-up.

Both isolation and restriction are reversible with one click (*Release from isolation* / *Remove app restriction*) once the threat is handled. These can be triggered manually, by automation in Defender XDR (next lesson), or by your own Logic App / Graph automation (Module 5).

## Validate and capture evidence

Prove it safely. On a dedicated pilot device, trigger a benign detection (e.g., the **EICAR** test string or a Microsoft MDE simulation). Then watch the chain:

```powershell
# Generates a harmless EICAR detection to exercise the pipeline
$e = 'X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*'
Set-Content -Path "$env:TEMP\\eicar.com" -Value $e
```

Confirm: device risk rises in the Defender portal -> device shows **noncompliant** in Intune -> a browser sign-in to Outlook/SharePoint is blocked by Conditional Access. Screenshot each stage with timestamps. Resolve the alert, confirm the device returns to **compliant**, and verify access is restored. That documented round trip is the deliverable for Project 1.

quiz.q: In the automated isolation loop, what is the correct order of cause and effect?
options: Conditional Access blocks -> Intune marks noncompliant -> MDE detects
MDE raises machine risk -> Intune marks device noncompliant -> Conditional Access blocks access
