- **Allow trusted Microsoft services** — a firewall exception (`--bypass

quiz.q: Which statement about Azure Storage encryption at rest is correct?
options: Encryption at rest is optional and must be enabled per account
All data is always encrypted with 256-bit AES; you cannot turn it off, but you can supply your own key
Encryption only applies to blobs, not files, queues, or tables
Encryption at rest requires the premium performance tier
quiz.why: Azure Storage service-side encryption is always on for every account and resource type (blobs, files, queues, tables, disks) using 256-bit AES, and it cannot be disabled. What you choose is key management, Microsoft-managed keys by default, or customer-managed keys (CMK) in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM, with optional infrastructure (double) encryption for a second layer.

quiz.q: You want to prevent anyone from using the account access keys to reach blob data, so that all access goes through Microsoft Entra ID. What do you configure?
options: Rotate both account keys every 24 hours
Set allowSharedKeyAccess to false to disallow Shared Key authorization on the account
Delete key1 and keep only key2
Enable a read-only lock on the storage account
quiz.why: Setting allowSharedKeyAccess=false disallows Shared Key authorization, so requests signed with the account keys (and account/service SAS derived from them) are rejected; only Microsoft Entra ID authorization is accepted. This is also a prerequisite for protecting the account with Entra Conditional Access. Rotating or deleting keys does not stop key-based access by itself.

quiz.q: Which SAS type is the most secure and why?
options: Account SAS, because it can grant access to every service at once
Service SAS, because it never expires
User delegation SAS, because it is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the account key
A SAS embedded in the connection string, because it is easiest to distribute
quiz.why: A user delegation SAS is secured with a user delegation key obtained from Microsoft Entra ID rather than the storage account key, so it carries the signer's identity, can be constrained by RBAC, and is not invalidated by account-key rotation. Account and service SAS are signed with the account key, are harder to revoke, and keep you dependent on shared-key authorization.

quiz.q: What is the most effective way to make a storage account unreachable from the public internet while still allowing a VM in your virtual network to use it?
options: Create a Private Endpoint and set public network access to disabled
Add the VM's public IP to the storage firewall allow list
quiz.why: A Private Endpoint gives the storage account a private IP inside your VNet and, combined with public network access disabled, removes the public endpoint entirely so traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone. Secure transfer and versioning do not control network reachability, and allow-listing a public IP still leaves the public endpoint exposed.

quiz.q: Which combination of features provides ransomware resilience for blob data?
options: Soft delete, versioning, point-in-time restore, and immutable (WORM) policies
Premium performance tier and the hot access tier
quiz.why: Soft delete retains deleted blobs and containers for a recovery window, versioning preserves prior versions on overwrite, point-in-time restore rolls a container back to an earlier state, and time-based or legal-hold immutability makes data WORM (write once, read many) so even an admin cannot alter or delete it during the retention period. Encryption and redundancy protect confidentiality and availability but do not by themselves let you recover from malicious deletion or overwrite.

quiz.q: In 3-4 sentences, explain why moving the storage data plane from account keys to Microsoft Entra ID plus Azure RBAC improves security, and name one role you would assign for read-only blob access.
quiz.answer: Account keys are long-lived shared secrets that grant full control of all data in the account and can generate SAS tokens, so anyone who obtains a key effectively owns the data and the access is hard to attribute or revoke without rotating the key and breaking other consumers. Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC instead authenticates a specific user or managed identity and authorizes only the least-privilege data action they need, with full audit, Conditional Access, and central revocation. For read-only blob access you would assign the Storage Blob Data Reader role, scoped to the container or account; Storage Blob Data Contributor or Owner grant write and delete. Disabling shared key authorization then guarantees every request is identity-based.
quiz.why: Entra ID plus RBAC replaces a shared, all-powerful secret with per-identity, least-privilege, auditable, centrally revocable access; Storage Blob Data Reader is the correct role for read-only blob access, and disabling shared key enforces the model.

cse-m6-l02-securing-azure-sql-and-databa.title: Securing Azure SQL and Databases
objectives: Enforce Microsoft Entra authentication and Entra-only authentication, disabling SQL logins
Authorize applications with managed identities and least-privilege contained database users
Isolate Azure SQL with Private Link, firewall rules, and Deny public network access
Distinguish TDE (data at rest) from Always Encrypted (hidden from DBAs/operators) and choose correctly
Configure TDE customer-managed keys, enforce TLS 1.2, and use Always Encrypted with secure enclaves
Apply Data Discovery & Classification, Dynamic Data Masking, Row-Level Security, and Ledger
Audit to Log Analytics/Sentinel and enable Microsoft Defender for SQL (VA + threat protection)
cse-m6-l02-securing-azure-sql-and-databa.body:
## The Database Is the Crown Jewels

Storage holds your files, but the **database holds your most structured, most queried, most regulated data** — customer PII, payment records, health data. An attacker who reaches it does not need to reassemble anything; it is already indexed for them. So we secure Azure SQL as **defense in depth**: even if one layer fails, the next still stands.

The layers, in the order an attacker hits them:

1. **Identity** — who can authenticate at all (Microsoft Entra, Entra-only auth, managed identities).
2. **Network** — from where they can reach the server (Private Link, firewall, Deny public access).
3. **Encryption** — what they see if they get the bits (TDE at rest, TLS in transit, Always Encrypted).
4. **Data protection** — what a *legitimate* query is allowed to return (classification, masking, Row-Level Security, Ledger).
5. **Detection** — what we notice when something is wrong (auditing, Defender for SQL).

This lesson centers on **Azure SQL Database** and **SQL Managed Instance**, noting where they differ. The controls map almost one-to-one, but their network models differ, which we will call out.

## Authentication: Microsoft Entra and Entra-Only

Every Azure SQL logical server is created with a **SQL administrator login** (username and password). That password-based SQL authentication is the oldest and weakest surface: it is a static secret, it bypasses Conditional Access, and it cannot do MFA.

The fix is **Microsoft Entra authentication** (formerly Azure AD authentication). You assign a **Microsoft Entra admin** to the server, then map Entra users, groups, and managed identities to database principals. Entra identities get **Conditional Access, MFA, and central lifecycle management** — disable the user in Entra and database access dies with it.

The senior move is to go further and enable **Microsoft Entra-only authentication**, a server-level switch that **disables SQL authentication entirely**. After this, no one can connect with a SQL username and password; only Entra principals work.

```bash
# Set the Entra admin, then disable SQL logins entirely (Entra-only auth)
az sql server ad-admin create \
  --resource-group rg-data --server sql-prod-eus \
  --display-name "SQL Admins" --object-id <entra-group-object-id>

az sql server ad-only-auth enable \
  --resource-group rg-data --server sql-prod-eus
```

Once Entra-only auth is on, the static SQL admin password is no longer a usable entry point — you have removed an entire category of credential attack.

## Authorize Apps with Managed Identities and Least-Privilege Roles

Applications should **never carry a database password**. Instead, give the app a **managed identity** (system-assigned or user-assigned), then create a **contained database user** mapped to that identity. The app requests an Entra token and connects with no secret to store, leak, or rotate.

```sql
-- Run in the target database, connected as the Entra admin
CREATE USER [app-orders-api] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;   -- the managed identity's name
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [app-orders-api];
ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER [app-orders-api];
-- Grant only what this app needs; do NOT add db_owner
```

This is **least privilege** at the data tier. The app gets `db_datareader`/`db_datawriter` (or a **custom role** scoped to specific tables/procedures), never `db_owner`. Human admins authenticate as **themselves** through Entra groups, so every action is attributable. The combination — managed identity for apps, Entra groups for humans, least-privilege roles for both — means there is no shared secret anywhere in the system.

## Network Isolation: Private Link, Firewalls, and Deny Public Access

By default an Azure SQL **logical server has a public endpoint**. Lock it down in layers.

- **Server-level firewall rules** allow specific public IP ranges and apply to *all* databases on the server. **Database-level firewall rules** (set via `sp_set_database_firewall_rule`) are scoped to one database and are evaluated first — useful for tight per-database control.
- **Private Endpoint (Azure Private Link)** is the strongest control: it projects the server onto a **private IP inside your VNet**, so application traffic never traverses the public internet.
- **Deny public network access** (the `publicNetworkAccess = Disabled` server property, set via `--enable-public-network false`) then closes the public endpoint entirely, forcing every connection through the private path.
- **Virtual network rules** (service endpoints) are an older middle ground that allow specific subnets without a private IP.

```bash
# Force all traffic private: disable the public endpoint
az sql server update --resource-group rg-data --name sql-prod-eus \
  --enable-public-network false
# Then create a Private Endpoint into the app subnet (Private Link)
```

**Managed Instance differs here.** SQL Managed Instance is **natively deployed inside a delegated subnet** of your VNet — its isolation comes from **subnet delegation** (the subnet is delegated to `Microsoft.Sql/managedInstances`) plus a network security group and route table, rather than from a public endpoint you bolt Private Link onto. So MI is VNet-isolated by design, while SQL Database opts into isolation with Private Link and Deny public access.

## Encryption at Rest: TDE with Service-Managed vs Customer-Managed Keys

**Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)** encrypts the database, its **log files, and its backups at rest** — protecting you against theft of the underlying disks, files, or backup media. It is **on by default** for Azure SQL. Crucially, TDE is *transparent*: the **engine holds the key and decrypts data to serve queries**, so it is invisible to applications — and that means **a DBA or cloud operator with engine access can still see plaintext**. TDE defends the media, not against privileged insiders.

Two key-management options:

- **Service-managed key** (default) — Microsoft creates and rotates the TDE protector. Zero effort.
- **Customer-managed key (CMK / BYOK)** — the **TDE protector lives in your Azure Key Vault** (or Managed HSM). You control rotation and, critically, **revocation**: remove Key Vault access and the database becomes inaccessible, giving you a cryptographic kill switch for compliance.

```bash
# Point the server's TDE protector at a customer-managed key in Key Vault (BYOK)
az sql server key create --resource-group rg-data --server sql-prod-eus \
  --kid "https://kv-data.vault.azure.net/keys/tde-key/<version>"

az sql server tde-key set --resource-group rg-data --server sql-prod-eus \
  --server-key-type AzureKeyVault \
  --kid "https://kv-data.vault.azure.net/keys/tde-key/<version>"
```

## TLS in Transit and Always Encrypted

Data in motion is protected by **TLS**. Set the server's **minimal TLS version to 1.2** so clients cannot negotiate weak, deprecated protocols:

```bash
az sql server update --resource-group rg-data --name sql-prod-eus \
  --minimal-tls-version 1.2
```

Now the layer exams love to test. **Always Encrypted** is fundamentally different from TDE. Encryption and decryption happen **in the client driver**, using a **column encryption key** that is itself protected by a **column master key stored outside SQL** (in Key Vault or a client certificate store). The **database engine only ever stores and returns ciphertext** — it never has the keys. The payoff: sensitive columns are **hidden even from DBAs, cloud operators, and anyone with full server access**, because plaintext exists only inside the trusted client. Use it for the few truly sensitive columns (SSNs, card numbers) that even administrators must not see.

The classic limitation: because the engine sees only ciphertext, server-side operations are limited — practically **equality comparisons** with *deterministic* encryption, and nothing for *randomized* encryption. **Always Encrypted with secure enclaves** removes that limit. A **secure enclave** is a protected r

quiz.q: What is the key difference between Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) and Always Encrypted in Azure SQL?
options: They are the same feature with two names

TDE encrypts data at rest on disk and the engine decrypts it to serve queries, so DBAs and cloud operators can see plaintext; Always Encrypted encrypts in the client driver so the engine never sees plaintext, hiding data from high-privilege admins
Always Encrypted only protects backups, while TDE protects live data
TDE encrypts data in the client, while Always Encrypted encrypts on the server
quiz.why: TDE protects against theft of the physical media, files, and backups by encrypting data at rest; the SQL engine holds the key and decrypts data to process queries, so anyone with high privileges on the server (a DBA or Microsoft operator) can see plaintext. Always Encrypted moves encryption into the client driver using keys the server never has, so the engine stores and returns only ciphertext, protecting sensitive columns from the very administrators who run the database.

quiz.q: How do you ensure that only Microsoft Entra identities can authenticate to an Azure SQL logical server, with SQL username/password logins blocked entirely?
options: Enable Microsoft Entra-only authentication on the server
Set the server firewall to deny all IPs
Rotate the SQL admin password daily
quiz.why: Microsoft Entra-only authentication is a server-level setting that disables SQL authentication so only Entra principals (users, groups, and managed identities) can connect. It removes password-based SQL logins as an attack surface and centralizes access in Entra ID for Conditional Access, MFA, and lifecycle management. Firewall rules restrict where connections originate but do not disable SQL logins.

quiz.q: An application running on an Azure VM or App Service needs to connect to Azure SQL without any secret in its configuration. What is the recommended approach?
options: Embed the SQL admin password in an environment variable
Use a managed identity and create a contained database user FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER with least-privilege roles
Share one SQL login across all applications
Store the connection string with credentials in the app's source code
quiz.why: A managed identity gives the app an Entra identity with no secret to store or rotate; you create a contained user in the database mapped to that identity using CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER and grant only the database roles it needs (for example db_datareader). The app then obtains a token and connects with no password, eliminating credential leakage and manual rotation.

quiz.q: Which Azure SQL configuration prevents the database from being reachable over the public internet and forces traffic through a private IP in your virtual network?
options: A Private Endpoint (Private Link) combined with Deny public network access
quiz.why: A Private Endpoint gives the logical server a private IP inside your VNet via Azure Private Link, and setting public network access to Disabled (Deny public network access) blocks all internet-facing connections so traffic only flows over the private path. TLS, masking, and TDE protect data but do not control network reachability.

quiz.q: What two capabilities does Microsoft Defender for SQL provide?
options: SQL Vulnerability Assessment (baseline scans of misconfigurations) and Advanced Threat Protection alerts (SQL injection, anomalous access, brute force)
Replacing the need for auditing and firewalls
quiz.why: Defender for SQL bundles SQL Vulnerability Assessment, which scans the database against a security baseline and flags misconfigurations and excessive permissions, with Advanced Threat Protection, which raises alerts on suspicious behavior such as SQL injection, access from unusual locations, and brute-force attempts. It is a detection and posture layer that complements, but does not replace, identity, network, and encryption controls.

quiz.q: In 3-4 sentences, explain when you would choose Always Encrypted with secure enclaves over standard Always Encrypted, and what tradeoff each makes.
quiz.answer: Standard Always Encrypted keeps sensitive column data hidden from the database engine and from high-privilege admins, but because the engine only sees ciphertext it can support very limited server-side operations, essentially equality lookups with deterministic encryption and nothing rich like range or pattern matching. Always Encrypted with secure enclaves adds a trusted execution environment inside the engine where keys and plaintext can be used in isolation, so you can run range queries, LIKE comparisons, and in-place encryption while the rest of the engine and operators still never see plaintext. You choose secure enclaves when you need both confidentiality from administrators and richer query functionality on the protected columns. The tradeoff is added configuration (enclave-capable hardware, attestation) in exchange for keeping data usable while still protected.
quiz.why: Standard Always Encrypted maximizes confidentiality but restricts operations to equality on deterministic columns; secure enclaves preserve that confidentiality while enabling range, pattern, and in-place operations through a trusted enclave, at the cost of extra setup and attestation.

cse-m6-l03-azure-network-security.title: Azure Network Security: NSGs, Firewall, and Private Link
objectives: Author stateful NSG rules using priority ordering, default rules, service tags, and ASGs
Decide between subnet and NIC association and between NSGs and Azure Firewall
Centralize egress through Azure Firewall with FQDN filtering, threat intel, and Premium IDPS/TLS
Place each control at its layer — NSG and DDoS at L3-4, Azure Firewall at L3-L7, and WAF at L7
Remove public exposure with Private Endpoints and Private Link, and contrast Service Endpoints
Secure administrative access with Azure Bastion and Just-in-Time VM access
Gain visibility with Network Watcher, VNet flow logs, and Traffic Analytics into Sentinel
cse-m6-l03-azure-network-security.body:
## Defense in Depth: Know Your Layer

The single most important habit in Azure network security is to know **which OSI layer each control defends**, because each tool sees a different part of the traffic and they are meant to stack:

- **Network Security Groups (NSGs)** — **Layer 3-4** only. They filter on IP address, port, and protocol and cannot read inside an HTTP request.
- **Azure Firewall** — primarily **Layer 3-4**, but also **Layer 7-aware**: its application rules filter by FQDN/URL (reading the HTTP Host header / TLS SNI), and the Premium SKU adds IDPS and TLS inspection (L3-L7).
- **Web Application Firewall (WAF)** — **Layer 7**. It is an HTTP-aware reverse proxy that inspects the HTTP request content and body for injection and cross-site scripting, which Azure Firewall application rules do not.
- **Azure DDoS Protection** — **Layer 3-4**, absorbing volumetric and protocol floods before they reach your resources.
- **Private Link / Private Endpoints** — not a filter at all but a **connectivity** control: it replaces a public IP with a **private IP plus private DNS** so the resource is never on the internet.

A senior design uses all of them together: DDoS at the edge, a WAF in front of web apps, NSGs and Azure Firewall segmenting and controlling east-west and egress traffic, and Private Endpoints removing public PaaS exposure entirely.

## Network Security Groups (NSGs)

An **NSG** is a **stateful** packet filter you attach to a **subnet** or a **NIC** (or both). Stateful means you allow a flow in one direction and the return traffic is permitted automatically — you do not write a matching reverse rule.

Each rule is a 5-tuple match — **source**, **source port**, **destination**, **destination port**, **protocol** — plus a **priority** (100-4096) and an **allow/deny** action. The mechanics that trip people up:

- Rules are processed **lowest priority number first**. The **first match wins** and evaluation stops, so a priority-200 allow beats a priority-300 deny.
- Every NSG ships with **default rules** at priorities 65000-65500 that you cannot delete: inbound allows intra-VNet traffic (`AllowVNetInBound`) and the Azure load balancer, then `DenyAllInBound`; outbound allows VNet and internet, then `DenyAllOutBound`. Your rules sit *above* these defaults.
- **Subnet vs NIC**: a subnet NSG applies to every NIC in the subnet (broad, coarse); a NIC NSG applies to one VM (granular). When both are present, inbound traffic is evaluated at the **subnet first then the NIC**, and outbound the reverse — and traffic must be allowed by **both**.

```bash
# Allow HTTPS from the internet to the web tier
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group rg-prod --nsg-name nsg-web \
  --name Allow-HTTPS-Inbound --priority 200 \
  --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes Internet \
  --destination-port-ranges 443 \
  --destination-asgs asg-web
```

## Service Tags and Application Security Groups

Two features make NSG rules maintainable at scale instead of brittle IP lists:

- **Service tags** are Microsoft-managed labels for the IP ranges of a service — `Internet`, `VirtualNetwork`, `AzureLoadBalancer`, `Storage`, `Sql`, `AzureKeyVault`, `AzureCloud`, and many regional variants. Microsoft updates the underlying prefixes for you, so a rule that allows the `Storage` tag keeps working as Azure's address space changes.
- **Application Security Groups (ASGs)** are logical groupings of **NICs by workload role**. You put your web VMs in `asg-web` and your database VMs in `asg-db`, then write intent-based rules — *allow `asg-web` to `asg-db` on 1433* — without referencing a single IP. As the workload scales in and out, ASG membership follows the VMs and the rules keep holding. This is the modern, declarative way to do microsegmentation inside a VNet.

## Azure Firewall

NSGs are great for cheap, distributed Layer 3-4 segmentation, but they have no FQDN awareness, no centralized logging, and no threat intelligence. **Azure Firewall** is the managed, stateful, highly available **network firewall-as-a-service** you put in the **hub** of a hub-and-spoke topology to control and inspect traffic centrally.

Rules live in a **Firewall Policy** and are organized into **rule collections**, processed in a fixed order:

1. **DNAT rules** — translate an inbound public IP:port to a private destination (publishing a service).
2. **Network rules** — Layer 3-4 allow/deny by IP, port, protocol, and **service tags / FQDN tags**.
3. **Application rules** — Layer 7-aware **FQDN filtering** for HTTP/S and SQL, e.g. allow outbound only to `*.windowsupdate.com` or `*.ubuntu.com`.

On top, **threat intelligence-based filtering** supports two modes — **Alert only**, or **Alert and deny** — for traffic to and from known-malicious IPs and domains from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence feed. To make the firewall the actual egress point, you attach a **user-defined route (UDR)** to each spoke subnet with a **default route `0.0.0.0/0` whose next hop is the firewall's private IP** — now all outbound and inter-spoke traffic is forced through it. **Forced tunneling** extends this by routing the firewall's own internet-bound traffic back to an on-premises edge over VPN/ExpressRoute for inspection there.

```bicep
// Force all spoke egress through the hub firewall
resource udr 'Microsoft.Network/routeTables@2023-09-01' = {
  name: 'rt-spoke-default'
  location: location
  properties: {
    routes: [
      {
        name: 'default-to-firewall'
        properties: {
          addressPrefix: '0.0.0.0/0'
          nextHopType: 'VirtualAppliance'
          nextHopIpAddress: '10.0.1.4' // Azure Firewall private IP
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

## Azure Firewall Premium: IDPS and TLS Inspection

The **Premium** SKU adds two capabilities that matter for regulated and high-assurance estates:

- **IDPS (Intrusion Detection and Prevention System)** — signature-based detection that can **alert** or **alert and deny** on known exploit patterns in network traffic, including matching against thousands of rules updated by Microsoft.
- **TLS inspection** — the firewall **decrypts outbound HTTPS**, inspects the plaintext (so IDPS and application rules can see the real content), then re-encrypts. It uses an intermediate CA certificate, typically issued from your own **Key Vault**, that clients trust.

Premium also brings **URL filtering** (beyond whole-FQDN) and **web categories**. The trade-off is cost and the operational care TLS inspection demands, so most teams enable it selectively on the egress paths that need deep inspection.

## Web Application Firewall (WAF) at Layer 7

NSGs and Azure Firewall cannot see that a request body contains `' OR 1=1--`. That is the job of the **Web Application Firewall**, a **Layer 7** control that runs in one of two places:

- **Application Gateway WAF** — a **regional** Layer 7 load balancer / reverse proxy in front of web apps in a VNet.
- **Azure Front Door WAF** — a **global**, edge-based WAF for internet-facing apps, blocking attacks close to the user.

Both use **Microsoft-managed rule sets** built on the **OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS)** to block injection, cross-site scripting, and other Top 10 attacks, plus optional **bot protection** and custom rate-limit/geo rules. The critical operational setting is the mode:

- **Detection mode** — logs what *would* be blocked, used to tune rules and find false positives without breaking the app.
- **Prevention mode** — actually **blocks** matching requests.

The standard rollout is to run in detection first, tune out false positives, then switch to prevention.

## Azure DDoS Protection

Every Azure public IP gets **always-on, platform-level** DDoS defense for free (basic infrastructure protection). The **paid tiers** add adaptive, application-aware mitigation:

- **DDoS Network Protection** — enabled on a **VNet**, it protects **all public IP resources** in that VNet with adaptive real-time tuning,

quiz.q: How are Network Security Group rules evaluated when traffic arrives?
options: All rules are evaluated and the most permissive wins
Rules are processed in priority order, highest number first, and all must allow
Rules are processed in priority order, lowest number first, and the first match (allow or deny) stops evaluation
Rules are evaluated randomly until a deny is found
quiz.why: NSGs are stateful and evaluate rules by priority from the lowest number (highest priority) to the highest. The first rule that matches the 5-tuple is applied and processing stops, so a lower-numbered allow can override a higher-numbered deny. Default rules (priorities 65000-65500) sit at the bottom, allowing intra-VNet and load balancer traffic and denying everything else inbound.

quiz.q: What does an Application Security Group (ASG) let you do that a raw IP-based rule does not?
options: Inspect HTTP request bodies for SQL injection
Group VMs by workload role so NSG rules reference the group instead of hardcoded IP addresses
Absorb volumetric DDoS attacks at the network edge
Encrypt traffic between two subnets automatically
quiz.why: An ASG is a logical grouping of network interfaces by application role (for example web or db). NSG rules can use ASGs as source or destination, so you write intent-based rules like "allow web to db on 1433" without maintaining IP lists. As VMs scale in and out, membership updates and the rules keep working, which is far more maintainable than static IP prefixes.

quiz.q: A workload must reach Azure Storage with no traffic traversing the public internet and no public endpoint exposed. Which option best meets this?
options: A Private Endpoint, which projects a private IP from your subnet to the storage account over Private Link and is resolved via a private DNS zone
A Service Endpoint, because it gives the storage account a private IP in your VNet
An NSG rule allowing the Storage service tag outbound
Azure Firewall application rule allowing the storage FQDN
quiz.why: A Private Endpoint creates a network interface with a private IP from your subnet that maps to the PaaS resource through Azure Private Link, and a private DNS zone (privatelink.blob.core.windows.net) resolves the public name to that private IP. The public endpoint can then be disabled. A Service Endpoint keeps the resource's public IP and only optimizes the path plus VNet firewall rules, so it does not remove public exposure.

quiz.q: At which layer does a Web Application Firewall operate, and how does it differ from an NSG?
options: Layer 3-4, identical to an NSG but faster
Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), inspecting request content for attacks like SQL injection and XSS, whereas an NSG filters by IP, port, and protocol at Layer 3-4
Layer 7, but only for outbound traffic
quiz.why: A WAF on Application Gateway (regional) or Azure Front Door (global edge) is a Layer 7 reverse proxy that inspects HTTP requests against managed rule sets (the OWASP Core Rule Set) to block injection, cross-site scripting, and similar attacks. An NSG and Azure Firewall operate at Layer 3-4 on addresses and ports and cannot see inside an HTTP payload, which is why you layer a WAF in front of web apps.

quiz.q: Why deploy Azure Bastion and Just-in-Time VM access instead of opening RDP/SSH to the internet?
options: They eliminate standing internet-exposed management ports; Bastion gives browser-based RDP/SSH with no public IP on the VM, and JIT opens ports only on demand for a limited time
They are required for VNet peering to work
They replace the need for any NSG rules
quiz.why: Internet-exposed RDP (3389) and SSH (22) are a primary brute-force and ransomware entry point. Azure Bastion is a managed PaaS jumpbox that brokers RDP/SSH over TLS in the browser so VMs need no public IP. Just-in-Time VM access (a Defender for Servers feature) keeps the management ports closed in the NSG and opens them only for a requested source, port, and time window, shrinking the exposure window to near zero.

quiz.q: In 3-4 sentences, explain the role of Azure Firewall in a hub-and-spoke topology and how forced tunneling or a default route changes traffic flow. Name one Premium-tier capability.
quiz.answer: In a hub-and-spoke design, Azure Firewall is deployed in the hub VNet as a central, stateful, managed egress and inspection point for all spoke workloads. You attach a user-defined route (UDR) with a 0.0.0.0/0 default route whose next hop is the firewall's private IP to the spoke subnets, forcing all outbound (and inter-spoke) traffic through the firewall for network, application (FQDN), and threat-intelligence filtering instead of letting it egress directly to the internet. Forced tunneling extends this by routing the firewall's own internet-bound traffic back to an on-premises edge over VPN/ExpressRoute for inspection there. One Premium-tier capability is IDPS (intrusion detection and prevention) or TLS inspection, which decrypts and inspects outbound HTTPS for signatures.
quiz.why: Azure Firewall centralizes egress control in the hub; a default route (0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall private IP) forces spoke traffic through it, and forced tunneling sends internet-bound traffic to on-prem. Premium adds IDPS and TLS inspection. This is the canonical secure hub-and-spoke pattern.

cse-m6-l04-key-vault-and-platform-encryp.title: Azure Key Vault, Secrets, and Platform Encryption
objectives: Choose between Key Vault Standard, Premium (HSM-backed keys), and Managed HSM for a given requirement
Secure the vault with Azure RBAC data-plane roles using least privilege over legacy access policies
Eliminate secrets from code using managed identities and Key Vault references in app settings
Protect the vault with soft delete, purge protection, firewall, and Private Endpoint
Manage the secret and key lifecycle with versioning, expiry, and auto-rotation policies
Encrypt Storage, Azure SQL TDE, and managed disks with customer-managed keys via envelope encryption
Compare Azure Disk Encryption, encryption at host, and server-side encryption, and alert with Defender for Key Vault
cse-m6-l04-key-vault-and-platform-encryp.body:
## The Root of Trust for the Platform

Across this module you hardened **storage accounts**, **Azure SQL databases**, and the **network** around them. Strip away the configuration and every one of those protections comes down to one thing: a **key**. Azure Storage encrypts blobs with a key; Azure SQL **Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)** encrypts the database with a key; a managed disk is encrypted with a key. **Azure Key Vault** is where those keys, along with application **secrets** and **certificates**, live and are governed. That makes Key Vault the **root of trust** for the entire platform: if the vault is wrong, everything it protects is wrong. This lesson closes the module by tying the keys back to the resources they protect.

Key Vault manages three object types, and the distinction matters:

- **Secrets** — arbitrary protected strings: connection strings, API keys, passwords.
- **Keys** — cryptographic keys (RSA, EC) used for **wrap/unwrap, sign/verify**, never exported in the clear; these are what back customer-managed encryption.
- **Certificates** — X.509 certificates with lifecycle management, built on top of keys and secrets.

## Standard, Premium, and Managed HSM

Choose the protection level for your keys deliberately:

- **Standard** — keys are protected by software (still encrypted at rest in Microsoft's infrastructure). Fine for most secrets and certificates.
- **Premium** — adds **HSM-backed keys** protected by **FIPS 140-3 Level 3** validated HSMs (legacy keys were FIPS 140-2 Level 2) in a **multi-tenant** HSM pool. Use it when a key must never exist outside an HSM boundary, including most CMK scenarios.
- **Azure Key Vault Managed HSM** — a fully managed, **single-tenant** service backed by **FIPS 140-3 Level 3** validated HSMs, with a dedicated HSM pool and a customer-controlled security domain. Both Premium and Managed HSM reach FIPS 140-3 Level 3; choose Managed HSM when you need single tenancy / a dedicated cryptographic boundary, not a higher FIPS level.

The rule of thumb: **Standard** for secrets and certificates, **Premium** when CMK or compliance requires an HSM, **Managed HSM** when you need a dedicated, single-tenant cryptographic boundary.

## Access Model: Azure RBAC over Legacy Access Policies

Key Vault has two authorization models for the **data plane** (the operations that read secrets and use keys). The **legacy access policy** model grants coarse permission sets per identity and is managed separately from the rest of Azure. **Azure RBAC is the recommended model** and is what you should use for new vaults: it is granular, role-based, least-privilege, and managed consistently with every other Azure resource.

Assign the **narrowest** built-in data-plane role for the job:

- **Key Vault Secrets User** — read secret values. This is what an application's managed identity gets.
- **Key Vault Crypto User** — use keys to encrypt/decrypt, wrap/unwrap, sign/verify (but not manage them).
- **Key Vault Administrator** — full data-plane management; reserve for break-glass and platform engineers.

Switch the vault to RBAC and grant a role at the vault scope:

```bash
# Put the vault on the Azure RBAC authorization model
az keyvault update --name kv-platform-prod \
  --resource-group rg-platform \
  --enable-rbac-authorization true

# Grant an app's managed identity read-only access to secrets (least privilege)
az role assignment create \
  --assignee "<managed-identity-object-id>" \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/rg-platform/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/kv-platform-prod"
```

Never hand an application **Administrator** when **Secrets User** will do. Least privilege at the vault is the difference between a leaked token reading one secret and an attacker owning every key you have.

## Eliminating Secrets from Code

In Module 5 the theme was automation without standing credentials. Key Vault is how that lands for applications. **Never store credentials in code or config.** Instead, give the workload a **managed identity** and let it fetch secrets at runtime.

- **System-assigned managed identity** — tied to the lifecycle of one resource (a VM, App Service, Function). Deleted with the resource. Use it for a 1:1 identity.
- **User-assigned managed identity** — a standalone identity you can attach to **many** resources. Use it when several workloads share an identity or you want the identity to outlive any single resource.

The app authenticates to **Microsoft Entra ID** with its managed identity, gets a token, and reads the secret. No password is ever stored. For App Service and Functions you do not even need code: use a **Key Vault reference** in app settings, and the platform resolves it at runtime:

```text
@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-platform-prod.vault.azure.net/secrets/SqlConnectionString/)
```

The app sees a normal setting; the value is fetched from Key Vault under the resource's managed identity. The plaintext connection string never lives in your repo, your pipeline, or your configuration files.

## Protecting the Vault Itself

Because the vault is the root of trust, it gets its own defenses:

- **Soft delete** is **on by default** and cannot be disabled. Deleted vaults and objects are retained for a configurable period (7-90 days) so you can **recover from accidental deletion**.
- **Purge protection** goes further: during the retention window it **blocks permanent deletion even by an administrator**. Once enabled it cannot be turned off for the life of the vault. This is what stops a compromised admin or a rogue script from destroying the keys that encrypt your data. **For any vault holding CMK, purge protection is mandatory.**

```bash
az keyvault update --name kv-platform-prod \
  --resource-group rg-platform \
  --enable-purge-protection true
```

- **Network restriction** — set the firewall to **deny public access** and reach the vault over a **Private Endpoint**, so secrets never traverse the public internet. This is the same network discipline you applied to storage and SQL earlier in the module.
- **Diagnostic logging** — send **AuditEvent** logs to **Log Analytics / Microsoft Sentinel** so every secret read and key operation is recorded and huntable.

## Secret and Key Lifecycle: Versioning, Expiry, Rotation

Every object in Key Vault is **versioned**: updating a secret creates a new version while old versions remain addressable, so rotation never breaks a consumer mid-flight. Set **activation and expiry dates** on secrets and keys so stale credentials age out instead of living forever.

For keys, configure an **auto-rotation policy** so Key Vault generates a new key version on a schedule, and use **Event Grid near-expiry notifications** to drive rotation of secrets that Key Vault cannot rotate itself (for example, rotating a database password and writing the new value back). The goal is that no human is the rotation mechanism:

```bash
# Auto-rotate a key 30 days before expiry, with an 18-month lifetime
az keyvault key rotation-policy update \
  --vault-name kv-platform-prod --name cmk-storage \
  --value '{"lifetimeActions":[{"trigger":{"timeBeforeExpiry":"P30D"},"action":{"type":"Rotate"}}],"attributes":{"expiryTime":"P18M"}}'
```

## Customer-Managed Keys: Closing the Loop with Storage and SQL

This is where Key Vault connects back to Lessons 1 and 2. By default Azure encrypts storage, SQL, and disks with **Microsoft-managed keys** at no effort. **Customer-managed keys (CMK / BYOK)** let you supply and control the key instead, using **envelope encryption**: the service encrypts data with a **data encryption key (DEK)**, then **wraps** that DEK with your **key encryption key (KEK)** in Key Vault. The service stores only the wrapped DEK, so if you disable or revoke the KEK, the data becomes unreadable.

That revocability is the benefit. The cost is **ownership**: with CMK **you own the availability and rotation of the key**. An accident

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between Key Vault soft delete and purge protection?
options: Soft delete lets you recover a deleted vault or object during the retention period; purge protection blocks permanent deletion during that window even by administrators
They are the same feature under two names
Purge protection deletes objects faster; soft delete keeps them forever
Soft delete encrypts secrets; purge protection rotates them
quiz.why: Soft delete (on by default) retains deleted vaults and objects for a retention period so you can recover from accidental deletion. Purge protection goes further by blocking any purge of that soft-deleted data during the retention window, so not even a vault administrator or a compromised account can permanently destroy keys, which is critical when those keys encrypt your storage and databases.

quiz.q: When should you choose Azure Key Vault Managed HSM over the Premium vault tier?
options: When you want the cheapest option for storing a few app secrets
When you need FIPS 140-3 Level 3, single-tenant dedicated HSM pool validated HSMs with full control of the key boundary
When you do not need HSM protection at all
When you only store certificates, never keys
quiz.why: Both Premium and Managed HSM provide FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM-backed keys; Managed HSM is single-tenant with a dedicated pool and customer-controlled security domain, so choose it when regulation or sovereignty demands single tenancy.

quiz.q: Why are managed identities the preferred way for an app to read a secret from Key Vault?
options: They store the secret directly in the application source code
They disable RBAC so any app can read any secret
The application authenticates to Microsoft Entra ID with an identity Azure manages, so no credential is ever stored in code or config
They require you to embed a client secret in the app settings
quiz.why: A managed identity gives the app a Microsoft Entra identity whose credential Azure provisions and rotates automatically, so the app requests a token and reads the secret at runtime with no password in code or configuration. Combined with a least-privilege role like Key Vault Secrets User, this removes the bootstrapping secret that plaintext connection strings always reintroduce.

quiz.q: In customer-managed key (CMK) encryption of Azure Storage or SQL TDE, what does envelope encryption mean?
options: The data is mailed on an encrypted disk
A data encryption key encrypts the data, and your Key Vault key (the key encryption key) wraps that data encryption key
Microsoft keeps a copy of your key in every region
The key and the data are stored in the same blob
quiz.why: With envelope encryption the service encrypts data with a symmetric data encryption key (DEK), then wraps that DEK with your key encryption key (KEK) held in Key Vault. The service only stores the wrapped DEK, so revoking or disabling the KEK renders the data unreadable, which is the power and the responsibility of CMK; you now own the availability and rotation of that key.

quiz.q: Why does Azure RBAC for the data plane improve on legacy vault access policies?
options: Access policies are more granular than RBAC
RBAC provides a unified, role-based, least-privilege model managed alongside other Azure resources, with roles like Key Vault Secrets User and Crypto User scoped per vault or secret
RBAC removes the need for any permissions
Access policies integrate with Microsoft Entra ID but RBAC does not
quiz.why: The legacy access policy model grants broad permission sets per identity and is managed separately from the rest of Azure. Azure RBAC is Microsoft's recommended model, offering granular built-in roles (Key Vault Secrets User, Crypto User, Administrator) that you assign with least privilege at the vault or individual object scope, consistent with how you control every other Azure resource.

quiz.q: In 3-4 sentences, explain why Key Vault is described as the "root of trust" for the storage and database protections built earlier in this module, and name one operational risk you accept when you move from Microsoft-managed keys to customer-managed keys.
quiz.answer: Key Vault holds the keys that encrypt the storage accounts, Azure SQL databases, and managed disks hardened earlier, so the confidentiality of all that data ultimately depends on the keys and access controls inside the vault, making it the single root of trust for platform encryption. If the vault is compromised or its keys are destroyed, the protected data is exposed or rendered permanently unreadable, which is why soft delete, purge protection, RBAC, and network isolation matter so much. When you move to customer-managed keys you accept responsibility for the key's availability and rotation, so an accidentally disabled, deleted, or expired key, or a vault that becomes unreachable, can take your storage and databases offline. That operational ownership is the trade-off for the control and revocability CMK provides.
quiz.why: Key Vault is the root of trust because the keys that encrypt storage, SQL TDE, and disks live there, so its protection determines the security of everything downstream; the main CMK trade-off is that you now own key availability and rotation, and a lost or disabled key can make data unreadable.

cse-m7-l01-capstone-zero-trust-endpoint-.title: Capstone: Automated Zero-Trust Endpoint Isolation System
objectives: Explain the Zero Trust signal-sharing loop that connects Defender for Endpoint, Intune compliance, and Conditional Access
Configure an Intune compliance policy that maps the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint machine risk score to a device compliance state
Build a Conditional Access policy that requires a compliant or Intune-managed device to grant access
Verify the connector between Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is enabled and exchanging signals
Safely simulate a high-severity detection and validate that access is revoked end to end
Assemble the architecture diagram, policy exports, and demo video that make this a hireable portfolio artifact
cse-m7-l01-capstone-zero-trust-endpoint-.body:
## Scenario

A finance manager's corporate laptop opens a malicious attachment and ransomware begins encrypting files and attempting lateral movement. In a traditional shop, a SOC analyst eventually sees an alert, opens a ticket, and starts manually pulling access, minutes or hours later. By then the blast radius is enormous. Your capstone removes the human from the critical path. The moment **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** classifies the machine as high risk, the device is judged noncompliant by **Intune**, and **Conditional Access** in **Entra ID** revokes the user's access to Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and a federated **AWS** application, all within seconds. This is Zero Trust signal sharing in action: the endpoint, the device-management plane, and the identity plane all speaking the same language.

This project is the showpiece for Modules 1 (Zero Trust Identity & Entra ID) and 2 (Modern Endpoint Security). It proves you can design a closed-loop, automated containment control, exactly what enterprise hiring managers mean when they say 'Zero Trust'.

## Architecture

The control loop has four moving parts and one connector that glues two of them together:

1. **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE)** runs on the laptop. On active malware it raises the **machine risk score** to High.
2. The **MDE-to-Intune connector** shares that risk signal into Intune.
3. An **Intune compliance policy** contains the rule *Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score = Medium*. A High score therefore makes the device **noncompliant**.
4. A **Conditional Access policy** with the grant control *Require device to be marked as compliant* gates Exchange, SharePoint, and the federated AWS app. A noncompliant device fails the grant.

Signal flow, in one line:

`MDE detects malware -> risk = High -> Intune compliance = Noncompliant -> Conditional Access grant fails -> tokens revoked (CAE) -> access denied to M365 + AWS`

Because **Entra ID** is the identity provider for the AWS app, cutting the identity off at the token-issuance point isolates the user across clouds, not just inside Microsoft 365. Draw this as a left-to-right diagram with the laptop on the left and the three protected workloads on the right; that single diagram is the centerpiece of your portfolio writeup.

## Step-by-step build

**Step 0 - Prerequisites.** Use a Microsoft 365 E5 / Defender for Endpoint evaluation tenant. Onboard at least one Windows test device to MDE, enroll it in Intune, and confirm the user is licensed for Entra ID P1/P2.

**Step 1 - Enable the connector.** In the Intune admin center go to **Endpoint security > Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** (Connectors and tokens). Turn the connection **On** and enable *Connect Windows devices ... to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint* and *Allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to enforce Endpoint Security Configurations*. In the Defender portal, confirm the Intune connection shows **Enabled**. This bidirectional handshake is what carries the risk score.

**Step 2 - Build the compliance policy.** Create a Windows 10/11 compliance policy. Under **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint**, set *Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score* to **Medium**. Set the *Mark device noncompliant* action to **Immediately** (0 days) so there is no grace period during a real incident. Assign it to your test user group.

**Step 3 - Build the Conditional Access policy.** In Entra ID > **Conditional Access**, create a policy: Users = the test group; Target resources = Office 365 (Exchange + SharePoint) and the AWS enterprise application; Grant = **Require device to be marked as compliant** (and optionally *Require Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device*). Start in **Report-only** mode, then flip to **On** once you have validated it does not lock you out.

**Step 4 - Federate the AWS app (if not already).** Add AWS as an enterprise application using Entra ID as the SAML/OIDC IdP, and include it in the Conditional Access target resources so the same compliance grant governs it.

## Validation / Testing

Never detonate real ransomware on a production network. Use the **MDE evaluation lab**, which provisions isolated test VMs, or run a Microsoft-provided safe simulation. Two safe ways to drive the chain:

- **MDE Evaluation Lab + simulation:** spin up a lab device and run one of the bundled attack simulations (or the EICAR test file for AV). Watch the device's **risk level** climb in the Defender portal.
- **Tampering / controlled detection:** trigger a benign high-severity alert in the lab so MDE assigns a High risk score.

Then verify each link:

1. **Defender portal** > Device inventory: risk level shows **High**.
2. **Intune** > Device > Compliance: state flips to **Noncompliant** (may take a few minutes to sync).
3. **Sign-in logs** (Entra ID): a fresh sign-in to Outlook/SharePoint/AWS shows **Failure** with reason *device not compliant*; the Conditional Access tab names the policy that blocked it.
4. **Token revocation timing:** confirm **Continuous Access Evaluation** is shortening the cut-off for existing sessions. Note the realistic latency in your writeup, this honesty impresses interviewers.
5. **Remediation / self-heal:** clear the threat in the lab, watch risk drop to Medium or below, Intune returns to **Compliant**, and access is automatically restored. Demonstrating the loop closing both ways is the strongest part of the demo.

Keep a test plan table: *Link | How tested | Expected | Observed | Pass/Fail*. That table is a portfolio artifact in its own right.

## What to put in your portfolio

- **Architecture diagram** (the signal-flow diagram above) as a clean PNG/SVG.
- **Policy exports**: the Intune compliance policy JSON and the Conditional Access policy JSON (export via Graph or the portal). Redact tenant IDs.
- **A 3-5 minute demo video**: screen-record the detection, the compliance flip, the blocked sign-in, and the self-healing restore.
- **A one-page design doc**: the scenario, the threat it mitigates, design decisions (why CAE matters, why immediate noncompliance, blast-radius scoping), and known limitations.
- **A GitHub repo** with the exported policies, the diagram source, and a README that frames the business value: *contains a compromised endpoint in seconds, across M365 and federated SaaS, with zero analyst involvement*.

Frame the resume bullet around impact, for example: 'Designed and tested an automated Zero Trust endpoint-isolation control (Defender for Endpoint + Intune compliance + Conditional Access) that revokes access to M365 and federated AWS within seconds of a high-severity detection.'

quiz.q: In this system, what is the direct trigger that causes Intune to mark the laptop noncompliant?
options: A user manually reports the device as lost
Defender for Endpoint raises the machine risk score above the threshold set in the compliance policy
Conditional Access blocks the sign-in first, which tells Intune to act
The antivirus signature file becomes more than 24 hours old
quiz.why: The compliance policy contains a rule 'Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score'. When Defender for Endpoint elevates the machine risk to High (above the allowed Medium), Intune evaluates the device as noncompliant. That is the signal that the rest of the chain depends on.

quiz.q: Why does Conditional Access, not Intune, perform the actual access revocation to Exchange and SharePoint?
options: Intune cannot see cloud applications at all
Conditional Access is the policy decision point at the identity layer that gates access to apps based on the device compliance signal
Exchange and SharePoint ignore Intune entirely
Conditional Access is faster because it runs on the device
quiz.why: Intune only computes and stores the compliance state of the device. Conditional Access is the enforcement point in Entra ID: its grant control 'Require device to be marked as compliant' reads that state at sign-in and token refresh, so a noncompliant device fails the grant and loses access to every app in scope, including federated SaaS.

quiz.q: A federated AWS application is in scope of the Conditional Access policy. Why does isolating the Windows laptop also cut off that AWS app?
options: Defender for Endpoint installs an agent inside AWS
Because Entra ID is the identity provider issuing the SAML/OIDC token, and Conditional Access evaluates device compliance before that token is issued
AWS polls Intune directly every minute
The laptop's local firewall blocks the AWS endpoints
quiz.why: When AWS uses Entra ID as its identity provider, every sign-in flows through Entra. Conditional Access evaluates the compliant-device grant before issuing the federation token, so a noncompliant device cannot obtain a token for the AWS app even though the workload lives in another cloud. This is the power of centralizing identity.

quiz.q: What prerequisite makes the Defender for Endpoint risk score visible to Intune in the first place?
options: A manually exported CSV uploaded to Intune each morning
The Microsoft Defender for Endpoint connector in Intune must be turned On, with device compliance evaluation enabled
A third-party MDM bridge running on each laptop
A Logic App copying alerts between portals
quiz.why: Under Endpoint security or Connectors and tokens, the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint connector must be enabled and set to connect Windows devices and share signals for compliance. Without that connector the machine risk score never reaches Intune, and the compliance rule has nothing to evaluate.

quiz.q: When you test the chain, why might access NOT be revoked instantly even after the device shows noncompliant?
options: Conditional Access only runs once per week
Existing access tokens remain valid until they expire or Continuous Access Evaluation revokes them; sign-in re-evaluation or CAE drives the cut-off
The device must be physically rebooted for any policy to apply
quiz.why: Conditional Access is evaluated at sign-in and token refresh. An already-issued access token can linger until expiry unless Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) signals the resource to revoke it near-real-time. Understanding token lifetime and CAE is what separates a demo that 'eventually' blocks from one that contains the threat in seconds.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, justify the design choice of using device-compliance-based Conditional Access for containment rather than simply having an analyst manually disable the user account when an alert fires.
quiz.answer: The automated compliance-to-Conditional-Access loop responds in seconds with no human in the path, which matters because ransomware spreads far faster than an analyst can triage and act. It also scopes the response to the affected device and its identity context rather than nuking the user everywhere, and it reverses automatically once the device is remediated and risk drops back to acceptable. Manual account disablement is slower, error-prone under pressure, and creates a recovery burden, whereas this design is consistent, auditable, and self-healing. It embodies the Zero Trust principle of assume breach and verify continuously using shared signals.
quiz.why: The grading answer should connect speed of containment, blast-radius scoping, and self-healing reversibility to the Zero Trust 'assume breach' pillar, and contrast those with the latency and human error of manual response.

cse-m7-l02-capstone-pre-ai-data-security.title: Capstone: Pre-AI Deployment Data Security Audit (Purview)
objectives: Explain why Copilot inherits a tenant's existing permissions and why oversharing is the core AI data-security risk
Design a sensitivity label taxonomy and auto-labeling rules that classify proprietary IP and sensitive financial data at scale
Author DLP policies that block sharing of labeled data externally and to unapproved generative AI applications
Apply oversharing remediation, restricted SharePoint search, and the Copilot data-protection controls in Purview
Validate the controls with seeded test data and measure tenant readiness before enabling Copilot
Assemble the audit report, policy exports, and before/after evidence that make this a hireable portfolio artifact
cse-m7-l02-capstone-pre-ai-data-security.body:
## Scenario

Leadership wants **Microsoft 365 Copilot** rolled out to the whole company next quarter to boost productivity. Security is sounding the alarm: 'If we turn this on today, will Copilot expose salary spreadsheets, the unreleased product roadmap, and the M&A folder to half the company?' They are right to worry. Copilot does not invent new access, it **respects every existing Microsoft 365 permission**, which means a decade of over-permissive SharePoint sites and 'share with everyone' links becomes instantly discoverable through natural-language prompts. Your job as the security architect is to run a **pre-AI deployment data security audit** and stand up **Microsoft Purview** as the control layer that makes the tenant safe for AI.

This capstone is the marquee project for Module 3 (Data Security & AI Governance with Purview). It proves you can do the single most in-demand 2026 security task: get an organization Copilot-ready without leaking the crown jewels.

## Architecture

Think of Purview as three protective layers wrapped around Copilot, plus a readiness gate:

1. **Classification layer - Sensitivity labels + auto-labeling.** Define a label taxonomy (e.g., Public, Internal, Confidential, Highly Confidential\Financial, Highly Confidential\IP). Auto-labeling policies crawl **SharePoint Online and OneDrive**, using sensitive information types (SITs), exact data match (EDM), and trainable classifiers to tag proprietary IP and sensitive financial data automatically.
2. **Movement-control layer - DLP.** Data Loss Prevention policies use those labels and classifiers to **block external sharing** of labeled content and to **block paste/upload of sensitive data into unapproved generative AI tools** via Endpoint and browser DLP.
3. **Access-minimization layer - Oversharing remediation + Restricted Search.** Use **SharePoint Advanced Management** data-access governance reports to find oversharing, then remediate. Turn on **Restricted SharePoint Search** to allow-list a curated set of sites so Copilot and enterprise search cannot surface unsecured content during rollout.
4. **Copilot-aware controls.** Purview's **AI data-security** features (DSPM for AI / data protection for Copilot) let labels and DLP apply to Copilot interactions, and let you audit Copilot prompts and responses.

Diagram it as concentric rings: data at the center, then labels, then DLP, then access minimization, with Copilot reaching in through all three rings. That ring diagram is your portfolio centerpiece.

## Step-by-step build

**Step 0 - Prerequisites.** Use an M365 E5 / E5 Compliance evaluation tenant with Copilot licensing (or trial). Seed a test SharePoint site and a few OneDrive accounts with realistic but **synthetic** documents (see Validation). Confirm Purview roles are assigned.

**Step 1 - Build the label taxonomy.** In the Purview portal under **Information Protection > Labels**, create the labels above. For Highly Confidential\Financial and \IP, configure **encryption** and content marking. Publish them in a **label policy** scoped to your users.

**Step 2 - Auto-label at scale.** Create **auto-labeling policies** (service-side) for SharePoint/OneDrive: match the financial label on built-in financial SITs (credit card, bank account, plus a custom EDM for internal account IDs) and match the IP label on a trainable classifier or a keyword/document-property rule (e.g., documents containing 'PROPRIETARY - DO NOT DISTRIBUTE'). Run them first in **simulation mode** to preview matches before enforcing.

**Step 3 - Author DLP policies.** Create DLP policies that, for content carrying the Financial or IP labels: **block sharing with people outside the organization**; and via **Endpoint DLP + the Purview browser extension / network protection**, **block or warn on paste and upload to unapproved generative AI sites** while allowing the approved enterprise Copilot. Start with **Audit/Test with notifications**, then move to **Block**.

**Step 4 - Reduce oversharing.** Run **SharePoint Advanced Management** data-access governance reports to find sites with 'Everyone' / 'Everyone except external users' access and overshared links. Remediate the worst offenders. Enable **Restricted SharePoint Search** to allow-list vetted sites for Copilot/search while remediation continues.

**Step 5 - Turn on Copilot-aware protection.** In **DSPM for AI**, enable the data-protection and auditing controls so labels and DLP apply to Copilot, and so prompts/responses are auditable.

## Validation / Testing

Validate against **ground truth** using seeded synthetic data, never real secrets:

- **Seed test documents** with known fake patterns: fake credit-card and IBAN numbers (financial), a doc clearly marked 'PROPRIETARY - DO NOT DISTRIBUTE' (IP), and benign 'Public' docs as negative controls.
- **Classification test:** confirm auto-labeling applies the right labels (check the document's label and Content Explorer). Record precision: did any Public doc get mislabeled (false positive)? Did any sensitive doc get missed (false negative)?
- **DLP test:** attempt to share a labeled financial doc with an external address, expect a block and policy tip. Attempt to paste seeded IP text into an unapproved public AI site in the browser, expect a block/warn; confirm the approved Copilot still works.
- **Oversharing test:** as a low-privilege test user, run a Copilot prompt like 'summarize our latest financial results' or 'show me the product roadmap' before and after remediation. Before, Copilot may surface the seeded sensitive doc; after restricted search and remediation, it should not.
- **Readiness metrics:** report a simple scorecard, percentage of sensitive sites remediated, number of overshared links removed, classifier precision/recall on the seeded set, and number of DLP blocks observed. This turns 'it feels safer' into measurable readiness.

Keep a *Control | Test | Expected | Observed | Pass/Fail* table and capture screenshots of each block and label, these are gold in your portfolio.

## What to put in your portfolio

- **The concentric-ring architecture diagram** (data -> labels -> DLP -> access minimization -> Copilot).
- **A written audit report**: executive summary of the oversharing risk, the controls deployed, before/after readiness metrics, and a go/no-go recommendation for Copilot.
- **Policy exports**: label definitions, auto-labeling policy config, and DLP policy config (export via Graph/PowerShell where possible). Redact tenant specifics.
- **Before/after evidence**: screenshots of the Copilot prompt surfacing the seeded doc *before*, and being blocked *after*; DLP policy tips; Content Explorer showing labels applied.
- **A GitHub repo** with the diagram, exported configs, the seeded-data generator script, and a README framing the business value.

Resume bullet, impact-first: 'Led a pre-Copilot data security audit in Microsoft Purview, deployed auto-labeling, DLP, and oversharing remediation that reduced overshared sites by X% and blocked sensitive data from leaving to unapproved AI tools, clearing the tenant for safe Microsoft 365 Copilot rollout.'

quiz.q: Why is oversharing the central risk when deploying Microsoft 365 Copilot?
options: Copilot uploads tenant data to the public internet by default
Copilot respects existing permissions, so any content a user can already access can be surfaced and summarized by Copilot, amplifying pre-existing oversharing
Copilot creates new permissions on every file it reads
quiz.why: Copilot enforces the user's existing Microsoft 365 permissions, it does not grant new access. The danger is that years of 'shared with everyone' SharePoint sites and over-permissive links mean a user can already reach far more than anyone realized, and Copilot makes that latent oversharing instantly discoverable through natural-language search and summarization.

quiz.q: What is the role of auto-labeling in this capstone?
options: It encrypts every email in the tenant regardless of content
It automatically applies sensitivity labels to content matching classifiers (e.g., financial data, IP) so downstream DLP and protection can act on it at scale
It deletes any file older than 90 days
It replaces the need for DLP policies completely
quiz.why: Auto-labeling uses sensitive information types, trainable classifiers, and keyword/EDM rules to apply sensitivity labels across SharePoint and OneDrive without relying on users. Those labels become the hook that DLP, encryption, and Copilot controls use to enforce protection consistently at scale.

quiz.q: Which DLP capability most directly addresses the fear of staff pasting proprietary data into an unapproved public AI tool?
options: Purview DLP for the browser/endpoint with controls that detect and block paste or upload of sensitive content to unapproved generative AI sites
A firewall rule that blocks all internet access
Renaming the files so the AI cannot read them
quiz.why: Purview Endpoint DLP (with the browser integration) can detect sensitive content being pasted or uploaded into generative AI sites and either warn or block it. Combined with the broader sensitive AI-site controls, this targets the exact exfiltration path the business fears without blocking the entire internet.

quiz.q: Why apply restricted SharePoint search or SharePoint Advanced Management as part of Copilot readiness?
options: To make SharePoint search faster for everyone
To temporarily constrain what Copilot and enterprise search can return while you remediate oversharing, so Copilot cannot surface unsecured content during rollout
To disable SharePoint entirely during the audit
quiz.why: Restricted SharePoint Search lets you allow-list a curated set of sites for Copilot and enterprise search while you fix oversharing elsewhere, acting as a guardrail during rollout. SharePoint Advanced Management adds data-access governance reports and site lifecycle controls to find and reduce oversharing systematically.

quiz.q: When validating, why seed purpose-built test data rather than testing only on real documents?
options: Seeded test data with known sensitive patterns lets you prove the classifiers, labels, and DLP fire correctly and measure precision without risking real exposure
Microsoft requires synthetic data for all DLP
quiz.why: Seeding documents that contain known fake credit-card numbers, fake account IDs, and clearly marked 'PROPRIETARY' IP gives you ground truth. You can confirm auto-labeling tags them, DLP blocks the right actions, and Copilot cannot surface them, and you can measure false positives and negatives, which you cannot do reliably against messy real data alone.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, explain how labels, DLP, and oversharing remediation work together as layers to make a tenant safe for Copilot, rather than relying on any single control.
quiz.answer: Sensitivity labels classify and can encrypt the data so protection travels with the file, giving every other control a consistent signal to act on. DLP then uses those labels (and content classifiers) to stop the data from leaving the trust boundary or being pasted into unapproved AI tools, controlling movement. Oversharing remediation and restricted search reduce who can reach the data in the first place, so even Copilot's permission-respecting search cannot surface content the user should never have been able to open. Together they form defense in depth: classify, control movement, and minimize access, so no single failure exposes the crown jewels to AI.
quiz.why: A strong answer ties each layer to a distinct function, labels classify/protect, DLP controls movement, oversharing remediation minimizes access, and frames them as defense in depth that survives a single control failing.

cse-m7-l03-capstone-cloud-threat-hunting.title: Capstone: Enterprise Cloud Threat-Hunting Dashboard
objectives: Stand up a Microsoft Sentinel workspace and connect Entra, M365, Azure Activity, and AWS data connectors
Write a custom KQL scheduled analytics rule that detects impossible-travel / concurrent anomalous logins
Map alert entities (account, IP) so detections drive automated response
Build a Logic App playbook that disables the account and routes the case to PIM and analyst review
Validate the detection-to-response flow end to end with controlled test sign-ins
Build a Workbook dashboard and assemble the KQL, playbook, and screenshots into a hireable portfolio artifact
cse-m7-l03-capstone-cloud-threat-hunting.body:
## Scenario

The CISO is tired of swivel-chairing between the Entra portal, the Microsoft 365 admin center, the Azure portal, and the AWS console to answer one question: 'Are we under attack right now?' Leadership wants **one centralized security dashboard across the multi-cloud estate**, with automated response for the obvious wins. Your capstone delivers exactly that with **Microsoft Sentinel**: a single SIEM/SOAR workspace that ingests identity and cloud signals, detects **impossible travel** (the same user appearing in two distant locations within minutes, classic credential theft), automatically contains the account, and visualizes it all for leadership.

This is the headline project for Modules 4 (Cloud SIEM & SOAR with Sentinel) and 5 (Security Automation with PowerShell, Graph, and Logic Apps). It proves you can run a cloud SOC, write detections in KQL, and automate response, the core of a modern security engineering role.

## Architecture

Five components, left to right:

1. **Ingestion - Data connectors.** A Sentinel workspace on a Log Analytics workspace, with connectors for **Microsoft Entra ID** (SigninLogs, AuditLogs), **Microsoft 365** (Defender/Office activity), **Azure Activity**, and **AWS** (CloudTrail / AWS security data via the S3 connector). Now Entra sign-ins and AWS API activity live in one query surface.
2. **Detection - Custom KQL analytics rule.** A scheduled rule runs the impossible-travel query on **SigninLogs** every few minutes, emitting an alert/incident when the same user signs in from two far-apart locations inside a short window.
3. **Enrichment - Entity mapping.** The rule maps **Account** (UserPrincipalName) and **IP** as entities so the incident is investigable and the playbook can act on the account.
4. **Response - Logic App playbook.** An automation rule triggers a **Sentinel playbook** (Logic App) that **disables the user in Entra ID via Microsoft Graph**, posts the case to the SOC channel/ticket, and routes it to **PIM**/analyst review for a governed restore.
5. **Reporting - Workbook dashboard.** A Sentinel **Workbook** visualizes sign-ins by country, top risky IPs, impossible-travel incidents over time, and AWS activity, the leadership view.

## The impossible-travel KQL

The heart of the project. This scheduled rule self-joins `SigninLogs` to pair two successful sign-ins by the same user, then flags pairs that are geographically far apart but close in time, for example one from Massachusetts and one from a foreign IP within 10 minutes:

```kusto
let timeWindow = 10m;
let lookback = 1h;
let successful =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ResultType == 0                 // successful sign-ins only
    | extend City = tostring(LocationDetails.city),
             Country = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion),
             Lat = todouble(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.latitude),
             Lon = todouble(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.longitude)
    | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, City, Country, Lat, Lon;
successful
| join kind=inner (
    successful
    | project-rename TimeGenerated2 = TimeGenerated, IPAddress2 = IPAddress,
                     City2 = City, Country2 = Country, Lat2 = Lat, Lon2 = Lon
  ) on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated < TimeGenerated2                     // ordered pair, no self-match
| where TimeGenerated2 - TimeGenerated <= timeWindow        // within the short window
| where Country != Country2 or IPAddress != IPAddress2      // genuinely different origin
| extend DistanceKm = geo_distance_2points(Lon, Lat, Lon2, Lat2) / 1000.0
| where DistanceKm > 500                                    // implausibly far apart
| extend MinutesApart = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated2, TimeGenerated)
| project UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated, City, Country, IPAddress,
          TimeGenerated2, City2, Country2, IPAddress2, DistanceKm, MinutesApart
```

Key ideas: filter to **successful** sign-ins (`ResultType == 0`), **self-join on UserPrincipalName** to compare two events for one identity, use `geo_distance_2points` for great-circle distance, and require both a large distance and a short time gap. In the rule wizard, set the schedule (run every 5-10 min, lookback 1h), map **Account = UserPrincipalName** and **IP = IPAddress**, and set incident creation on.

## Step-by-step build

**Step 0 - Prerequisites.** An Azure subscription with a Log Analytics workspace, an Entra tenant generating sign-ins, and (optionally) an AWS account for the AWS connector. Use evaluation/free tiers.

**Step 1 - Onboard Sentinel.** Create/choose a Log Analytics workspace and enable Microsoft Sentinel on it.

**Step 2 - Connect data.** Install the **Microsoft Entra ID** connector and enable SigninLogs + AuditLogs (via Diagnostic settings). Add **Microsoft 365** and **Azure Activity** connectors. Add the **Amazon Web Services** connector (S3-based) to pull CloudTrail. Confirm tables populate (`SigninLogs`, `AWSCloudTrail`).

**Step 3 - Create the analytics rule.** New > **Scheduled query rule**; paste the KQL; set frequency/lookback; map entities; enable **Create incidents**; set severity Medium/High.

**Step 4 - Build the playbook.** Create a **Logic App** playbook triggered by *Microsoft Sentinel incident*. Steps: parse the **Account** entity; call **Microsoft Graph** (or the Entra connector) to **disable the user** (`accountEnabled = false`) and/or revoke sessions; post an adaptive card to Teams/create a ticket; add a task to **review in PIM**. Attach it via an **automation rule** so qualifying incidents run it automatically (or with analyst approval).

**Step 5 - Build the workbook.** Create a **Workbook** with tiles: sign-ins by country (map), impossible-travel incidents over time, top source IPs, and AWS CloudTrail activity. This is the leadership dashboard.

## Validation / Testing

Drive the whole chain safely:

- **Simulate impossible travel:** with a dedicated **test account**, sign in from your normal location, then within a few minutes sign in again through a **VPN exit node in another country**. Two far-apart successful sign-ins now exist in `SigninLogs`. (Alternatively, inject crafted sample `SigninLogs` rows.)
- **Confirm detection:** run the KQL manually in Logs to see the pair returned; then wait for the scheduled rule to fire and create an **incident** with the account and IP entities mapped.
- **Confirm response:** verify the playbook ran, the **test account is disabled** in Entra (and sessions revoked), the **Teams card/ticket** posted, and a **PIM/analyst review** task exists.
- **Confirm false-positive handling:** repeat using a *trusted* corporate VPN IP that you have added to **trusted named locations**, and show the rule does NOT fire, demonstrating your tuning.
- **Confirm dashboard:** the Workbook shows the incident on the map and timeline.

Keep a *Stage | Test | Expected | Observed | Pass/Fail* table and capture screenshots at each stage.

## What to put in your portfolio
