quiz.q: True or false — Chroma can store a vector together with the original text and metadata.
quiz.why: Each Chroma record holds the embedding, the source document text, an id, and optional metadata like source or page.

m3-l09-chunking.title: Chunking strategies
objectives: Explain why chunking is needed for retrieval and long documents
Compare fixed-size, recursive, and semantic chunking strategies
Choose a sensible chunk size and overlap for a use case
Implement character and token-based chunking in Python
Preserve structure and attach metadata to each chunk
Evaluate chunking quality by inspecting retrieved results
m3-l09-chunking.body:
## Why chunking?

A language model can only read so much text at once, and a retrieval system works best when each stored piece is small and focused. **Chunking** is the act of splitting a long document into smaller pieces, called **chunks**, before you embed and store them.

If you store an entire 50-page PDF as one item, a search for one fact returns all 50 pages, most of it irrelevant. If you split it into paragraph-sized chunks, search returns just the passages that matter. Good chunking is often the single biggest lever on the quality of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system.

## The trade-off: size vs precision

Chunk size is a balance. **Large chunks** carry more surrounding context but dilute relevance and may overflow limits. **Small chunks** are precise but can lose the context needed to answer.

A common starting point is roughly **500 to 1000 tokens** per chunk. Size in **tokens**, not characters, because models limit and bill by tokens. A rough rule of thumb is one token per four characters of English, but count properly when it matters.

## Overlap

If you cut strictly every N tokens, you will sometimes slice a sentence or idea in half. **Overlap** repeats a small slice of text between neighbouring chunks so the idea survives in at least one chunk. A typical overlap is 10 to 20 percent of the chunk size.

```python
def chunk_text(text, size=800, overlap=100):
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + size
        chunks.append(text[start:end])
        start = end - overlap   # step back to create overlap
    return chunks

doc = open("report.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
print(len(chunk_text(doc)))
```

This is **fixed-size** chunking: simple and fast, but blind to structure.

## Smarter strategies

**Recursive chunking** splits on a priority list of separators — paragraphs first, then lines, then sentences, then words — so cuts land on natural boundaries. **Semantic chunking** groups sentences by meaning, keeping related ideas together. Recursive is the practical default for most text.

```python
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=800,
    chunk_overlap=100,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""],
)
chunks = splitter.split_text(doc)
print(len(chunks), "chunks")
```

## Metadata matters

Each chunk should travel with **metadata**: the source file, a title, a page or section number. This lets you cite where an answer came from and filter retrieval. Without it, a correct answer is hard to trust.

## Sizing by tokens with Claude

When the downstream model is Claude, count tokens with the Anthropic SDK so chunks fit your budget exactly. Keep your A P I key in the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
for i, ch in enumerate(chunks):
    n = client.messages.count_tokens(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ch}],
    ).input_tokens
    print(f"chunk {i}: {n} tokens")
```

## Your task

Take a long text file, chunk it three ways — fixed-size, recursive, and recursive with metadata — and inspect the boundaries of the first few chunks for each.

quiz.q: Why do we chunk documents before putting them in a retrieval system?
options: To fit context limits and improve retrieval relevance
quiz.why: Chunks keep each retrieved piece focused and small enough to fit the context window, so search returns relevant passages instead of whole documents.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of chunk overlap?
options: To avoid cutting a key idea exactly at a boundary
quiz.why: Overlap repeats a little text between neighbouring chunks so a sentence or idea split across a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk.

quiz.q: Which strategy splits on natural separators like paragraphs, then sentences, falling back to characters only if needed?
quiz.why: Recursive chunking tries a priority list of separators (paragraph, line, sentence, word) so splits land on natural boundaries before resorting to raw character cuts.

quiz.q: True or false: chunk size should always be measured in characters, never tokens.
quiz.why: False. Because models bill and limit by tokens, sizing chunks in tokens is often more reliable; characters are a convenient approximation only.

quiz.q: Name one useful piece of metadata to store alongside each chunk and say why.
quiz.answer: The source document name or page number, so retrieved answers can cite where they came from.
quiz.why: Metadata such as source, title, page, or section lets you trace, filter, and cite chunks, which is essential for trustworthy RAG answers.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is a reasonable default starting point for chunk size and overlap?
quiz.answer: Around 500 to 1000 tokens per chunk with roughly 10 to 20 percent overlap, then tune by inspecting results.
quiz.why: These defaults balance enough context per chunk against retrieval precision; you adjust based on document type and observed answer quality.

m3-l10-rag.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
objectives: Explain why RAG reduces hallucinations and keeps answers up to date
Describe the RAG pipeline: chunk, embed, store, retrieve, generate
Turn text into embedding vectors and store them in a vector database
Retrieve the most relevant chunks using cosine similarity
Build a prompt that grounds Claude in the retrieved context
Cite sources and recognise common RAG failure modes
m3-l10-rag.body:
## Why RAG?

A language model only knows what it learned during training. Ask it about your company handbook, last week's news, or a private PDF and it will either refuse or, worse, **hallucinate** a confident wrong answer.

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** fixes this. Instead of retraining the model, we *retrieve* the most relevant pieces of your own text and paste them into the prompt as context. The model then answers from facts you supplied. As a maths graduate this is a familiar idea: an open-book exam beats a closed-book one.

## The RAG pipeline

RAG has two phases. **Indexing** (done once, offline):

1. **Chunk** — split documents into small passages.
2. **Embed** — turn each chunk into a vector (a list of numbers capturing meaning).
3. **Store** — save the vectors in a vector database.

**Querying** (every question):

4. **Embed the question** with the same model.
5. **Retrieve** the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question.
6. **Generate** — give those chunks plus the question to the LLM.

## Embeddings and similarity

An **embedding** maps text to a point in high-dimensional space so that similar meanings sit near each other. We measure closeness with **cosine similarity** — the cosine of the angle between two vectors. A value near 1 means very similar; near 0 means unrelated.

```python
import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

# Retrieve top-k chunks for a query embedding
def top_k(query_vec, chunk_vecs, k=3):
    scores = [cosine_similarity(query_vec, c) for c in chunk_vecs]
    return sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: scores[i], reverse=True)[:k]
```

## Grounding the generation with Claude

Once you have the top chunks, build a prompt that tells the model to answer **only** from that context. Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in code.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def answer(question, context_chunks):
    context = "\n\n".join(context_chunks)
    prompt = (
        f"Use ONLY the context to answer. If the answer is not there, "
        f"say 'I don't know'.\n\nContext:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    )
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text
```

## Failure modes and good habits

RAG is powerful but not magic. Watch for: **bad chunking** (passages too big or split mid-idea), **retrieval misses** (the right chunk never surfaces), and **ignored context** (the model answers from memory anyway). Improve results by tuning chunk size, retrieving a few extra chunks, asking the model to **cite** which chunk it used, and instructing it to admit when it doesn't know.

## Your task

Take three short text files, chunk and embed them, store the vectors, and build a tiny question-answering loop that retrieves the top chunks and grounds Claude in them.

quiz.q: What problem does RAG primarily solve?
options: It makes the model train faster
It grounds answers in external, up-to-date documents the model never memorised
It removes the need for a prompt
quiz.why: RAG retrieves relevant text from your own data and adds it to the prompt, so the model answers from facts instead of guessing from memory.

quiz.q: In the RAG pipeline, what is an embedding?
options: A copy of the user's question
A numeric vector that captures the meaning of a piece of text
quiz.why: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) where texts with similar meaning sit close together, enabling semantic search.

quiz.q: Which metric is commonly used to measure how similar two embedding vectors are?
quiz.why: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors; values near 1 mean the texts are semantically close.

quiz.q: Why do we split documents into smaller chunks before embedding?
quiz.answer: So each vector captures a focused idea and retrieval returns precise, relevant passages that fit in the prompt, rather than whole documents.
quiz.why: Chunking keeps embeddings meaningful and lets you pass only the relevant pieces into the limited context window.

quiz.q: What should you do in the prompt to reduce the chance the model invents facts not in the retrieved context?
quiz.answer: Instruct it to answer only from the provided context and to say 'I don't know' when the context lacks the answer.
quiz.why: Grounding instructions plus retrieved context keep the model honest and let it admit gaps instead of hallucinating.

quiz.q: True or false: RAG requires retraining or fine-tuning the language model.
quiz.why: False. RAG adds knowledge at inference time through the prompt, so you can update your data without touching the model.

m3-l11-evaluation.title: Evaluating LLM apps
objectives: Explain why LLM apps need evaluation, not just spot-checking
Build a small, representative evaluation dataset with inputs and expected outputs
Choose metrics that fit the task: exact match, similarity, or rubric scores
Write code-based (deterministic) checks for structured outputs
Use an LLM-as-judge to grade open-ended responses against a rubric
Track results over time so you can catch regressions before users do
m3-l11-evaluation.body:
## Why evaluate at all?

When you build an ordinary program, you write tests: given an input, you assert the exact output. LLM apps are harder — the same prompt can give slightly different wording each time, and "correct" is often a matter of degree. But that does **not** mean you skip measuring. It means you measure deliberately.

Without evaluation you are flying blind. You tweak a prompt, it *feels* better, you ship it — and you've quietly broken three other cases. An **evaluation** (an "eval") turns "feels better" into a number you can compare.

## The three ingredients of an eval

Every eval has the same shape:

1. A **dataset** — a list of inputs paired with what a good answer looks like.
2. A **task** — the function that runs your app on each input.
3. A **metric** — a rule that scores each output, giving you one number overall.

Keep the dataset small but representative: 20–50 hand-picked cases that cover the easy path *and* the tricky edges. And hold it back — don't tune your prompt on the very examples you grade on, or you're just memorising.

## Picking a metric

Match the metric to the task:

- **Exact match** — for fixed outputs like classification labels. Did the model output exactly `positive`?
- **Similarity** — for short factual answers where wording varies; compare against the expected answer.
- **Rubric score** — for open-ended text (a summary, an email). Here there is no single right string, so you grade against explicit criteria.

## Code-based checks

Whenever there's a programmatic ground truth, check it with code — it's free, instant, and deterministic. Here we grade a sentiment classifier built on the Claude Messages API.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

dataset = [
    {"text": "I love this!", "label": "positive"},
    {"text": "This is terrible.", "label": "negative"},
    {"text": "It arrived on Tuesday.", "label": "neutral"},
]

def classify(text):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5",
        max_tokens=10,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"Reply with one word — positive, negative, or neutral:\n{text}"}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text.strip().lower()

correct = sum(classify(row["text"]) == row["label"] for row in dataset)
print(f"Accuracy: {correct / len(dataset):.2f}")
```

## LLM-as-judge

For open-ended outputs there's no string to match, so you ask a *second* model call to grade the answer against a rubric. Use a clear rubric and force a numeric score so you can average it.

```python
def judge(question, answer):
    rubric = (
        "Score 1-5 how accurate and helpful the answer is. "
        "Reply with ONLY the integer."
    )
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=5,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"{rubric}\n\nQ: {question}\nA: {answer}"}],
    )
    return int(msg.content[0].text.strip())

score = judge("What is the capital of France?", "Paris is the capital of France.")
print(f"Judge score: {score}/5")
```

## Track it over time

Save each run's score next to the prompt and model you used. The moment a change drops the number, you've caught a **regression** before your users did. That single habit — a held-out dataset, a metric, a recorded score — is what separates a hobby prompt from a production LLM app.

## Your task

Build a tiny `evals/` folder for one of your own prompts: a `dataset.jsonl` with 10 cases, and a script that prints one accuracy or average-score number.

quiz.q: Why is spot-checking a few prompts by hand a poor way to evaluate an LLM app?
quiz.answer: It isn't repeatable or representative — small manual checks miss edge cases, can't catch regressions when you change the prompt or model, and don't give you a number you can track over time.
quiz.why: Evaluation needs a fixed dataset and a metric so results are comparable across changes.

quiz.q: Which metric is the right fit for grading a classifier that must output exactly 'positive', 'negative', or 'neutral'?
quiz.why: A fixed label set has one correct answer per item, so exact match against the expected label is simplest and most reliable.

quiz.q: What is 'LLM-as-judge'?
options: Letting the model pick its own training data
Using a second LLM call to grade an output against a rubric
A tool that auto-fixes failing tests
quiz.why: For open-ended answers there's no single correct string, so you prompt a model to score the output against explicit criteria.

quiz.q: When you change your prompt and your eval accuracy drops from 0.92 to 0.78, what has happened?
options: A regression — the change made the app worse on your test set
quiz.why: A drop on a fixed test set is a regression; catching it before shipping is the whole point of evals.

quiz.q: Give one reason to prefer a code-based check over an LLM judge when both could work.
quiz.answer: Code-based checks are deterministic, free, and instant — so for structured or exact-match outputs they're cheaper and more reliable than spending a model call to judge.
quiz.why: Use the LLM judge only where there's no programmatic ground truth, like tone or open-ended quality.

quiz.q: Why should your evaluation dataset be kept separate from the examples you use to design the prompt?
quiz.answer: So you measure generalisation, not memorisation — if you tune the prompt on the same examples you grade on, a high score may just mean you overfit to those cases.
quiz.why: A held-out test set gives an honest estimate of how the app behaves on unseen inputs.

m3-l12-frameworks.title: Frameworks: LangChain / LlamaIndex
objectives: Explain what an LLM framework is and the problem it solves
Compare LangChain (general orchestration) and LlamaIndex (data/RAG focus)
Build a simple prompt-to-model chain with LCEL
Load documents, index them, and query with LlamaIndex
Understand retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) at a high level
Know when a framework helps and when raw SDK calls are simpler
m3-l12-frameworks.body:
## Why frameworks?

By now you can call a language model directly with the Anthropic SDK. That works well for a single request. But real applications need more: a prompt template here, a model call there, your own documents pulled in, maybe a tool the model can use. Wiring all that by hand gets messy fast.

A **framework** gives you reusable building blocks for these jobs so you write less plumbing and focus on your logic. The two best known in the LLM world are **LangChain** and **LlamaIndex**.

## LangChain vs LlamaIndex

Think of them as overlapping but with different centres of gravity.

- **LangChain** — broad orchestration. Prompts, models, output parsers, tools, agents, memory. Good when your app has several steps chained together.
- **LlamaIndex** — data-first. Loading documents, splitting them, indexing, and retrieving the right chunks. Built for **RAG** (retrieval-augmented generation).

They are not rivals you must choose between forever — many projects use both. Start with the one that matches your main need.

## A simple LangChain chain (LCEL)

**LCEL** (LangChain Expression Language) composes components with the pipe `|` operator: a prompt feeds a model, the model feeds a parser.

```python
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template("Explain {topic} in one sentence.")
model = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=1024)
chain = prompt | model | StrOutputParser()

print(chain.invoke({"topic": "eigenvalues"}))
```

The key reads from the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable — never hard-code it.

## RAG with LlamaIndex

RAG means: **retrieve** relevant text, then **generate** an answer grounded in it. This lets the model answer questions about *your* documents — things it was never trained on.

```python
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader

docs = SimpleDirectoryReader("my_notes").load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs)
engine = index.as_query_engine()

print(engine.query("What did my notes say about gradient descent?"))
```

Under the hood it splits your files into chunks, embeds them as vectors, finds the closest chunks to your question, and passes them to the model as context.

## When NOT to use a framework

Frameworks add layers. For a single, simple model call with no retrieval and no tools, the raw Anthropic SDK is clearer:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise photosynthesis."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Reach for a framework when you have multiple steps, retrieval over data, tools, or agents.

## Your task

Pick a folder of your own notes or PDFs and build a tiny RAG app with LlamaIndex that answers a question about them. Keep your API key in an environment variable.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a framework like LangChain?
options: To orchestrate LLMs, prompts, tools, and data into apps
To store your API keys securely
quiz.why: LangChain provides reusable building blocks to wire prompts, models, retrievers, and tools together — it does not train models.

quiz.q: Which framework is most focused on connecting your own documents to an LLM (RAG)?
quiz.why: LlamaIndex specialises in loading, indexing, and retrieving over your data, though LangChain can do RAG too.

quiz.q: In a RAG pipeline, why do we retrieve documents before calling the model?
quiz.answer: To give the model relevant, up-to-date context it was not trained on, reducing hallucinations.
quiz.why: Retrieval injects your specific facts into the prompt so the answer is grounded in real source material.

quiz.q: What does LCEL stand for and what is it for?
quiz.answer: LangChain Expression Language — a declarative way to compose components into chains using the pipe operator.
quiz.why: LCEL lets you connect prompt, model, and output parser with a clean, streamable, composable syntax.

quiz.q: When might you skip a framework and call the SDK directly?
options: For a single, simple model call with no retrieval or tools
When you need many chained steps
When building a large RAG system
quiz.why: For one-off simple calls a framework adds overhead; the raw Anthropic SDK is clearer and has fewer moving parts.

quiz.q: True or false — frameworks store your API key for you so you do not need environment variables.
quiz.why: False. You still keep secrets like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in environment variables; the framework just reads them.

m4-l01-prompt-patterns.title: Prompt-engineering patterns
objectives: Write a clear instruction with a role, task, and constraints
Use a system prompt to set persistent behaviour
Steer output with few-shot examples
Force machine-readable answers with structured output
Split hard problems into a chain of smaller prompts
Call the Claude Messages API in Python with a model id and max_tokens
Evaluate a prompt and iterate instead of guessing
m4-l01-prompt-patterns.body:
## Why prompt patterns?

A **prompt** is the text you send to a language model. Beginners type a question and hope. Engineers use **patterns** - reusable shapes that turn a vague request into a reliable, testable instruction. For your portfolio projects this is the difference between a demo that works once and a feature that works every time.

Think of it like a function signature: a good prompt states the **role**, the **task**, the **inputs**, and the **constraints** on the output.

## Pattern 1: role, task, constraints

Don't just say *"summarise this"*. Say who the model is, what to do, and what the answer must look like.

```text
You are a careful financial analyst.
Summarise the email below in exactly 3 bullet points.
Do not invent numbers. If a figure is missing, write "not stated".
```

The role sets tone, the task is the verb, and the constraints (3 bullets, no invented numbers) make the output predictable - and therefore testable.

## Pattern 2: system prompt + few-shot

The **system prompt** sets persistent behaviour for the whole conversation. **Few-shot** prompting adds a few worked examples so the model copies the pattern. Here is a minimal Claude Messages API call in Python:

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You label support tickets. Reply with one word: billing, bug, or other.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "My card was charged twice."},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "billing"},
        {"role": "user", "content": "The app crashes on login."},
    ],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)  # -> bug
```

The earlier user/assistant pair is the single example that teaches the format.

## Pattern 3: structured output

When your code needs to *read* the answer, ask for JSON and parse it - never string-match prose.

```python
import json
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
        'Extract name and city as JSON keys "name" and "city": '
        '"Ada Lovelace lives in London."'}],
)
data = json.loads(msg.content[0].text)
print(data["city"])  # -> London
```

## Pattern 4: prompt chaining

If one prompt is doing too much, break it into steps where each output feeds the next: **extract -> summarise -> format**. Each step is simple, so each step is easy to check and fix. This is the single biggest reliability win in real projects.

## Your task

Take one feature in your portfolio project and rewrite its prompt using **role, task, constraints** plus one **few-shot example**. Keep your key in `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

quiz.q: What is the role of a system prompt?
options: It sets persistent behaviour and persona for the whole conversation
It is the user's first question
It limits how many tokens you are billed for
quiz.why: The system prompt frames who the model is and how it should behave across every turn, separate from the per-message user content.

quiz.q: What is few-shot prompting?
options: Asking the same question several times
Giving a few worked input-output examples so the model copies the pattern
Using fewer tokens to save money
Calling the model with a tiny max_tokens
quiz.why: Few-shot means including a handful of example pairs in the prompt so the model infers the format and style you want.

quiz.q: Why ask the model for JSON output instead of free text?
options: JSON can be parsed reliably by your code without fragile string-matching
The model thinks harder in JSON
It is the only format the API accepts
quiz.why: Structured output (e.g. JSON) lets your program read fields directly, instead of guessing meaning from prose that varies each run.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is prompt chaining and when would you use it?
quiz.answer: Splitting a task into a sequence of prompts where each step's output feeds the next; use it when one prompt is doing too much or accuracy drops.
quiz.why: Chaining keeps each step simple and checkable - extract, then summarise, then format - which is far more reliable than one giant prompt.

quiz.q: Name one reason you should keep your API key in an environment variable, not in your code.
quiz.answer: So the secret is never committed to Git or shared, keeping it out of your portfolio repo and version history.
quiz.why: Hard-coded keys leak when you push to GitHub; reading ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment keeps the secret private.

quiz.q: What does the temperature-free, deterministic-leaning approach of giving explicit constraints buy you?
options: More predictable, on-spec answers that are easier to test
quiz.why: Explicit constraints (length, format, what to avoid) narrow the model's choices, so outputs vary less and are easier to evaluate.

m4-l02-guardrails.title: Guardrails & hallucination control
objectives: Explain what a hallucination is and why LLMs produce them
Add input guardrails to block prompt injection and off-topic requests
Add output guardrails that validate structure and content before use
Ground answers in retrieved context and cite sources
Force structured JSON output and validate it with a schema
Let the model abstain and say 'I don't know' when unsure
Log refusals and failures so you can measure and improve
m4-l02-guardrails.body:
## What is a hallucination?

A **hallucination** is when a language model produces output that sounds confident and fluent but is factually wrong or completely made up. Large language models predict the next likely token from patterns in their training data — they have no built-in sense of truth. So when they don't know something, they often *guess* in a way that reads exactly like a correct answer.

For a portfolio project this matters enormously. A demo that invents a fake legal clause, a wrong dosage, or a non-existent function call looks impressive until someone checks it. **Guardrails** are the controls you put around the model to catch problems before they reach the user.

## Input guardrails

The first line of defence is checking the request *before* it reaches the model. This blocks **prompt injection** (a user trying to override your instructions), off-topic requests, and obvious abuse — and saves you the API cost of a doomed call.

```python
BANNED = ["ignore previous", "reveal your prompt", "system prompt"]

def check_input(text: str) -> bool:
    low = text.lower()
    if any(phrase in low for phrase in BANNED):
        return False        # block it
    if len(text) > 4000:
        return False        # too long / suspicious
    return True
```

Keyword lists are crude; in production you'd use a small classifier or a moderation model. But the idea is the same: **untrusted input is validated first.**

## Grounding: answer from sources

The single most effective way to cut hallucinations is **grounding** — retrieve real documents and tell the model to answer *only* from them. This is the core of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Crucially, you also give the model permission to abstain.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

SYSTEM = (
    "Answer using ONLY the provided context. "
    "If the answer is not in the context, reply exactly: "
    "'I don't know based on the provided sources.' Cite the source id."
)

def ask(question: str, context: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        temperature=0,
        system=SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text
```

Setting `temperature=0` makes answers more deterministic, and the system prompt makes "I don't know" an acceptable, expected output.

## Output guardrails & structured output

Treat the model's reply as **untrusted output**. Ask for JSON, then *validate* it with a schema before any downstream code uses it. If validation fails, you can reject, retry, or fall back — never act on unverified data.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError
import json

class Answer(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    confidence: float
    source_id: str

def validate(raw: str) -> Answer | None:
    try:
        return Answer(**json.loads(raw))
    except (ValidationError, json.JSONDecodeError):
        return None   # malformed -> reject and retry
```

## Logging, evaluation & the abstain rule

Guardrails are only useful if you **measure** them. Log every blocked input, every failed validation, and every "I don't know". Those logs become your evaluation set: you can count how often the model abstains correctly versus hallucinates.

A simple rule sums it up: **a confident wrong answer is worse than an honest "I don't know".** Reward abstention. Your task: add input checks, grounding, and JSON validation to one of your portfolio apps, and log every refusal.

quiz.q: What is an LLM 'hallucination'?
options: Confident, fluent output that is factually wrong or made up
quiz.why: A hallucination is plausible-sounding text the model invented; it is not grounded in any real source and may be completely false.

quiz.q: Why does grounding (RAG) reduce hallucinations?
options: It gives the model real source text to answer from
quiz.why: By retrieving relevant documents and putting them in the prompt, the model answers from supplied facts instead of guessing from memory.

quiz.q: What is the safest behaviour when the context does not contain the answer?
options: Say 'I don't know' or that the answer isn't in the sources
quiz.why: Abstaining is correct: a confident wrong answer is far more dangerous than admitting the information is missing.

quiz.q: Name one input guardrail you can add before sending a user's message to the model.
quiz.answer: Detect and block prompt injection / off-topic / disallowed requests (e.g. with a classifier, allowlist, or moderation check).
quiz.why: Input guardrails stop malicious or out-of-scope requests reaching the model, reducing both abuse and wasted cost.

quiz.q: Why validate the model's output against a JSON schema before using it?
quiz.answer: The model can return malformed or unexpected JSON; validating catches it so your app doesn't crash or act on bad data.
quiz.why: Treat model output as untrusted input: parse, validate the shape and values, and reject anything that fails before it reaches downstream code.

quiz.q: Which setting most directly makes answers more repeatable and less random?
quiz.why: Lower temperature makes sampling more deterministic, which is useful for factual, structured, or guardrailed tasks.

m4-l03-eval-harness.title: Evaluation harnesses
objectives: Explain what an evaluation harness is and why vibes are not enough
Build a small labelled dataset of inputs and expected outputs
Write metrics: exact match, contains, and an LLM-as-judge score
Loop over cases, call the model, and aggregate a pass rate
Pin the model and keep settings deterministic for fair comparison
Track results over time so you can catch regressions
Wire the harness into a simple CI check
m4-l03-eval-harness.body:
## Why you need an eval harness

When you tweak a prompt and the output looks nicer, how do you *know* it actually got better? You don't — unless you measure it. An **evaluation harness** is a small program that runs your AI app over a fixed set of test cases and scores the results. It turns "this feels better" into a number you can compare run to run.

As a maths graduate this should feel natural: you're defining a function from (input, expected) pairs to a score, then aggregating.

## The three ingredients

Every harness has three parts:

1. A **dataset** — a list of inputs paired with expected answers (or a rubric).
2. A **metric** — a function that scores one model output against the expected answer.
3. A **runner** — a loop that calls the model for each case, scores it, and aggregates.

Keep the dataset small and fixed at first (10-30 cases). A frozen dataset is what makes results comparable.

## A minimal dataset

Store cases as plain data so they're easy to read and extend:

```python
cases = [
    {"input": "What is 2 + 2?", "expected": "4"},
    {"input": "Capital of France?", "expected": "Paris"},
    {"input": "Is 7 prime?", "expected": "yes"},
]
```

## Calling the model and scoring

Pin the model so re-runs are comparable. We use the Anthropic Claude Messages API:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def run_case(prompt: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=256,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text.strip()

def contains_score(output: str, expected: str) -> int:
    return 1 if expected.lower() in output.lower() else 0

passed = 0
for case in cases:
    out = run_case(case["input"])
    passed += contains_score(out, case["expected"])

print(f"Pass rate: {passed}/{len(cases)}")
```

## LLM-as-judge for free-form answers

Exact match breaks on essays, summaries, and explanations. For those, ask a second model call to grade the answer against a short rubric, returning a number you can average. Keep the judge prompt strict and ask for just a score so it's easy to parse.

## Wiring it into CI

Turn the harness into a test that fails when quality drops, then run it on every pull request:

```bash
# fail the build if the eval pass rate is below threshold
pytest tests/test_eval.py -q
```

Now a prompt change that quietly makes things worse gets caught before it ships.

## Your task

Build a 10-case dataset for a small task you care about, write a `contains` metric, and print a pass rate.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an evaluation harness?
options: To deploy the model to production
To measure model output quality against a fixed dataset
quiz.why: An eval harness runs your app over a known set of cases and scores the outputs, turning 'it feels better' into a number you can track.

quiz.q: Why is a single fixed dataset important for fair comparison?
quiz.answer: It keeps the inputs and expected answers constant, so any change in score comes from your code or prompt, not from different test data.
quiz.why: If the dataset moves, you can't tell whether a score change is a real improvement or just easier examples.

quiz.q: Which metric is best when answers are free-form text and exact match is too strict?
quiz.why: LLM-as-judge uses a separate model call to grade an answer against a rubric, handling wording differences that break exact match.

quiz.q: Why pin the model ID (e.g. claude-sonnet-4-6) in your harness?
quiz.answer: So results are comparable over time; an unpinned or changing model could shift scores for reasons unrelated to your code.
quiz.why: Reproducibility: pinning the model isolates your changes as the cause of any score movement.

quiz.q: What does a regression mean in the context of an eval harness?
options: The pass rate dropped after a change
quiz.why: A regression is when a change lowers your score versus the last run — exactly what the harness exists to catch.

quiz.q: Why run the eval harness in CI (continuous integration)?
quiz.answer: To automatically catch quality drops on every commit or pull request before they reach users.
quiz.why: CI makes the eval a gate: if the pass rate falls below a threshold, the build fails and you investigate before merging.

m4-l04-agents.title: Agents & multi-step workflows
objectives: Explain what an LLM agent is and how it differs from a single prompt
Define tools the model can call, with names, descriptions, and input schemas
Run the agentic loop: call, read tool_use, execute, feed results back
Use the Anthropic tool runner to handle the loop for you
Decide when a simple workflow beats a full agent
Add guardrails: step limits, error handling, and human approval for risky actions
m4-l04-agents.body:
## What is an agent?

Up to now you've sent one prompt and read one reply. An **agent** does more: it runs a **loop**. The model decides on an action — usually calling a **tool** — you run that action, hand the result back, and the model decides what to do next. It keeps going until the task is finished.

Think of it like long division. You don't solve it in one step; you repeat *estimate, multiply, subtract, bring down* until there's nothing left. An agent repeats *think, act, observe* the same way.

## Tools: giving the model hands

A **tool** is a function the model is allowed to call. You describe it with a name, a plain-English description, and an `input_schema` (JSON Schema) for its arguments. The model never runs your code — it just *asks* to, and your program does the running.

```python
tools = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get the current weather for a city.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["city"]
    }
}]
```

## The agentic loop

When the model wants a tool, the response comes back with `stop_reason == "tool_use"`. You execute the tool, append a `tool_result`, and call the API again. Repeat until `stop_reason == "end_turn"`.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Lagos?"}]
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024, tools=tools, messages=messages)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = []
    for b in resp.content:
        if b.type == "tool_use":
            out = run_tool(b.name, b.input)   # your code
            results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": out})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
```

## Let the SDK run the loop

Writing that loop by hand is good for understanding. In practice the SDK's **tool runner** does it for you — you define tools as typed functions and iterate the results.

## Workflow vs agent

Not everything needs an agent. If you can write the steps down in advance — *extract, then summarise, then email* — that's a **workflow**, and a workflow is cheaper, faster, and far easier to debug. Reach for a full agent only when the path genuinely can't be planned ahead.

## Guardrails

An unbounded loop can spin forever or do something irreversible. Always add a **step limit**, handle tool errors gracefully, and require **human approval** before risky actions like sending money or deleting data.

## Your task

Build a tiny two-tool agent (e.g. a calculator and a search stub) and watch the loop call them in turn.

quiz.q: What makes an agent different from a single LLM call?
options: It loops — calling tools and deciding the next step until done
quiz.why: An agent runs a loop: the model picks an action (often a tool), you run it, feed the result back, and it decides what to do next.

quiz.q: When Claude wants to call a tool, what is the stop_reason on the response?
quiz.why: stop_reason becomes "tool_use". You execute the tool, return a tool_result, and call the API again to continue.

quiz.q: In a tool definition, what does input_schema describe?
options: The JSON shape of the arguments the tool expects
quiz.why: input_schema is JSON Schema describing the tool's parameters, so the model knows exactly what arguments to supply.

quiz.q: Why prefer a fixed workflow over an open-ended agent when you can?
quiz.answer: A workflow is more predictable, cheaper, faster, and easier to debug; reach for an agent only when the path can't be fully specified in advance.
quiz.why: Agents add cost and latency and are harder to reason about. Use the simplest tier that solves the task.

quiz.q: Name one guardrail you should add to an agentic loop.
quiz.answer: A maximum step (iteration) limit, error handling on tool calls, or human approval before irreversible actions.
quiz.why: Without limits an agent can loop forever or take harmful actions; bounds and approval gates keep it safe.

m4-l05-architecture.title: Application architecture
objectives: Explain what application architecture is and why it matters for portfolio projects
Identify the core layers: frontend, backend, model/API, and data store
Separate concerns so each layer has one clear responsibility
Understand the request flow from user click to model response and back
Keep secrets like API keys out of the frontend and in environment variables
Choose between monolith and simple service split for a small project
Draw a clear architecture diagram to include in your portfolio
m4-l05-architecture.body:
## What is application architecture?

**Application architecture** is the high-level design of how the parts of your app fit together. Not the line-by-line code — the *shape*. Which components exist, what each one does, and how they talk to each other.

For a portfolio AI app, getting this right means a recruiter can read your diagram and instantly understand your thinking. That clarity is worth as much as the code itself.

## The core layers

Most AI web apps have four layers:

- **Frontend** — what the user sees and clicks (the browser).
- **Backend** — your server code; holds secrets and business logic.
- **Model / API** — the Claude Messages API that does the A I work.
- **Data store** — a database or files where you keep state.

The golden rule is **separation of concerns**: each layer has *one* job. That makes the system easy to change, test, and explain.

## The request flow

Follow a single click through the system. The user types a question and presses send. The frontend sends that text to your backend. The backend validates it, attaches the secret key, and calls the model. The model replies, the backend cleans it up, and the frontend shows it.

The frontend never talks to the model directly. The backend is a **trusted middle layer**.

```python
# backend: app.py (Flask)
import os
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
from anthropic import Anthropic

app = Flask(__name__)
client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env

@app.post("/ask")
def ask():
    user_text = request.json["question"]
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_text}],
    )
    return jsonify({"answer": msg.content[0].text})
```

## Keep secrets out of the frontend

Your `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is like a password. If it sits in browser code, anyone can open dev tools and steal it. Keep it on the **server**, loaded from an environment variable — never committed to Git.

```bash
# set the key in your shell or a .env file (gitignored)
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

# .gitignore
.env
```

## Monolith vs services

For a small portfolio project, start with a **monolith** — one deployable app containing frontend and backend. It is simpler to build, deploy, and reason about. Split into separate services only when there is a real reason: different scaling needs, separate teams, or independent deploys. Do not add microservices just to look advanced.

## Your task

Draw the architecture diagram for one of your projects: boxes for each layer, arrows for the request flow, and a note on where the secret key lives. Add it to your README.

quiz.q: In a typical AI web app, where should your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live?
options: In the backend, read from an environment variable
quiz.why: The key must stay server-side in an env var. If it is in the frontend, anyone can read it from the browser and steal it.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of 'separation of concerns'?
options: It makes the app run faster
Each part has one job, so it is easier to change and test
It removes the need for a database
It hides the code from users
quiz.why: When each layer does one thing, you can change or fix one part without breaking the others, and you can test them independently.

quiz.q: Which layer is responsible for calling the Claude Messages API and shaping the prompt?
quiz.why: The backend holds the secret key and business logic, so it calls the model API. The frontend just sends user input and shows results.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is application architecture?
quiz.answer: The high-level design of how an application's parts (frontend, backend, model, data) are split up and connected.
quiz.why: Architecture is the shape of the system — which components exist and how they talk — not the line-by-line code inside them.

quiz.q: Why might you start a small portfolio project as a monolith rather than many microservices?
quiz.answer: A monolith is simpler to build, deploy, and reason about; microservices add overhead you rarely need at small scale.
quiz.why: For a one-person portfolio project, a single deployable app is easier and faster; you split into services only when there is a real reason.

quiz.q: What does the backend act as between the user and the model API?
quiz.answer: A trusted middle layer (a proxy/gateway) that holds secrets, validates input, and forwards requests.
quiz.why: The backend shields the API key, controls what gets sent, and lets you add logging, limits, and error handling in one place.

m4-l06-fastapi-ai.title: FastAPI for AI apps
objectives: Understand what a web API is and why AI apps need one
Build a FastAPI app with a POST endpoint
Validate request and response data with Pydantic models
Call the Anthropic Claude Messages API from an endpoint
Keep your API key safe in an environment variable
Run the server locally with uvicorn and test it
Read auto-generated docs at the /docs page
m4-l06-fastapi-ai.body:
## Why AI apps need an API

You have working A I logic — a function that takes a prompt and returns a Claude response. But a function only runs inside one Python process. To let a website, a mobile app, or a teammate use it, you expose it as a **web API**: a server that listens for HTTP requests and returns answers.

**FastAPI** is a modern Python framework that makes this fast to build, automatically validates your data, and generates interactive docs for free.

## Your first endpoint

An **endpoint** is a URL plus an HTTP verb that runs a function. For sending data like a prompt we use **POST**. The `@app.post` decorator wires a path to a handler.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

Run it locally with uvicorn, the A S G I server:

```bash
pip install fastapi uvicorn anthropic
uvicorn main:app --reload
```

## Validating data with Pydantic

Never trust raw input. A **Pydantic** `BaseModel` declares exactly what fields you expect and their types. FastAPI parses the incoming JSON into that model, rejects bad requests with a clear error, and documents the schema automatically.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str

class ChatResponse(BaseModel):
    reply: str
```

## Calling Claude from an endpoint

Inside the handler, create an Anthropic client and call the **Messages API**. The client reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment — keep keys out of your code.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

@app.post("/chat", response_model=ChatResponse)
def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": req.prompt}],
    )
    return ChatResponse(reply=msg.content[0].text)
```

## Testing and docs

With the server running, open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`. FastAPI generates an interactive Swagger page from your models — you can send a real request from the browser. Set your key first:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
```

## Your task

Build a small FastAPI service with a `/chat` POST endpoint that calls Claude, validate the request with a Pydantic model, and test it from the `/docs` page.

quiz.q: What does an API let you do?
options: Let one program call another over HTTP
quiz.why: An A P I (Application Programming Interface) lets programs talk to each other — here, a client sends a request and your server returns a response over HTTP.

quiz.q: Which decorator defines a POST endpoint in FastAPI?
quiz.why: @app.post("/path") registers a function to handle POST requests, which is the right verb for sending data like a prompt.

quiz.q: What is Pydantic used for in FastAPI?
options: Validating and parsing request and response data
quiz.why: A Pydantic BaseModel declares the shape of your data; FastAPI uses it to validate incoming JSON and document the schema automatically.

quiz.q: Where should your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live?
quiz.answer: In an environment variable, not hard-coded in the source.
quiz.why: Hard-coding secrets risks leaking them in Git. The Anthropic client reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment by default.

quiz.q: What command runs a FastAPI app named app in main.py during development?
quiz.answer: uvicorn main:app --reload
quiz.why: Uvicorn is the A S G I server; main:app points to the app object in main.py, and --reload restarts on code changes.

quiz.q: What URL shows FastAPI's auto-generated interactive docs?
quiz.why: FastAPI serves interactive Swagger U I at /docs out of the box, generated from your Pydantic models and endpoints.

m4-l07-streamlit.title: Building UIs with Streamlit
objectives: Understand what Streamlit is and why it suits data and AI portfolios
Install Streamlit and run an app with streamlit run
Display text, data, and charts with st.write, st.dataframe, and st.line_chart
Collect user input using widgets like st.text_input, st.slider, and st.button
Understand Streamlit's rerun model and use st.session_state to keep state
Wire a Claude API call into an interactive app with secrets kept safe
Cache slow work with st.cache_data so the app stays fast
m4-l07-streamlit.body:
## Why Streamlit?

You have written scripts and notebooks that do clever things — but a recruiter cannot run a `.py` file. **Streamlit** turns a plain Python script into a web app you can share with a link. No HTML, CSS, or JavaScript needed: you write Python, Streamlit draws the page.

For an AI portfolio this is gold. A working, clickable app that calls a model is far more persuasive than a screenshot.

## Install and run

Streamlit installs with pip. You launch an app with the `streamlit run` command — not plain `python`.

```bash
pip install streamlit
streamlit run app.py
```

This opens your app in the browser, usually at http://localhost:8501, and reloads automatically when you save the file.

## Display and input

Every widget is a function. `st.write` shows almost anything; `st.dataframe` shows a table; input widgets return the user's value.

```python
import streamlit as st

st.title("My first app")
name = st.text_input("Your name")
if st.button("Greet"):
    st.write(f"Hello, {name}!")
```

## The rerun model

Here is the one idea that confuses everyone: **every interaction reruns the whole script from top to bottom**. A button click, a slider drag — the entire file runs again. To remember values between runs, use `st.session_state`, a dictionary that survives reruns.

```python
if "count" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.count = 0
if st.button("Add one"):
    st.session_state.count += 1
st.write("Count:", st.session_state.count)
```

## Calling Claude from your app

Keep your key in an environment variable (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) or `.streamlit/secrets.toml` — never in the code. Because the script reruns often, wrap slow or paid work carefully and only call the model on a button press.

```python
import streamlit as st
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
prompt = st.text_area("Ask Claude")
if st.button("Send"):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    st.write(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Cache the slow parts

Loading a big CSV or computing a chart on every rerun is wasteful. Decorate the function with `@st.cache_data` and Streamlit reuses the result when inputs do not change.

```python
@st.cache_data
def load_data(path):
    return pd.read_csv(path)
```

## Your task

Take a script from an earlier lesson and **wrap it in a Streamlit app** with at least one input widget and one output. Bonus: deploy it free on Streamlit Community Cloud.

quiz.q: How do you start a Streamlit app from the terminal?
quiz.why: Streamlit apps launch with the command streamlit run app.py, which opens the app in your browser.

quiz.q: What happens every time a user interacts with a widget in Streamlit?
options: The whole script reruns top to bottom
The page reloads from the server cache
quiz.why: Streamlit reruns the entire script on every interaction — this simple model is why st.session_state and caching matter.

quiz.q: Which object keeps values alive across reruns?
quiz.why: st.session_state is a dictionary-like store that persists across reruns for a single user session.

quiz.q: Why should you put your Anthropic API key in .streamlit/secrets.toml or an environment variable instead of in the code?
quiz.answer: So the secret key is never hard-coded or pushed to GitHub, keeping it private and out of version control.
quiz.why: Hard-coded keys leak when you share or commit code; secrets files and env vars keep credentials separate and gitignored.

quiz.q: What does st.cache_data do?
quiz.answer: It stores the result of an expensive function so repeated runs with the same inputs return instantly instead of recomputing.
quiz.why: Because the script reruns on every interaction, caching avoids repeating slow work like loading data or calling an API.

quiz.q: Which function would you use to show a pandas DataFrame as an interactive table?
quiz.why: st.dataframe renders a scrollable, sortable interactive table; st.table renders a simpler static one.

m4-l08-files-pdfs.title: Working with files & PDFs
objectives: Open, read and write files safely with the with statement
Choose the right mode and encoding for text files
Work with paths cleanly using pathlib
Read and write CSV data with the csv and pandas libraries
Extract text from PDFs using pypdf
Send extracted document text to Claude for summarisation and extraction
Handle missing files and bad input gracefully
m4-l08-files-pdfs.body:
## Why files matter for your portfolio

Real projects live on data, and that data sits in **files**: text logs, CSV exports, JSON config, and a lot of **PDFs** — invoices, reports, contracts. A portfolio project that ingests a folder of documents and produces a clean summary looks far more impressive than another toy notebook.

In this lesson you'll read and write files safely, parse CSVs, pull text out of PDFs, and hand that text to Claude to summarise or extract structured fields.

## Opening files the safe way

Always use the `with` statement. It closes the file automatically when the block ends — even if an error is thrown. Specify the **mode** (`r` read, `w` write, `a` append) and the **encoding**.

```python
# Read a whole text file
with open("notes.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()

# Write a new file (overwrites!)
with open("out.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Hello\n")
```

## Paths and CSVs

Use `pathlib` for paths so your code works on Windows, macOS and Linux. For tabular data, `pandas` reads and writes CSV in one line.

```python
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

data_dir = Path("data")
df = pd.read_csv(data_dir / "sales.csv")
print(df.head())
df.to_csv(data_dir / "clean.csv", index=False)
```

## Extracting text from PDFs

Install `pypdf`, loop over the pages, and call `extract_text()`. Note that PDFs are messy — text can arrive out of order, and scanned (image-only) PDFs return nothing until you run OCR.

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader

reader = PdfReader("report.pdf")
pages = [page.extract_text() or "" for page in reader.pages]
full_text = "\n".join(pages)
```

## Sending document text to Claude

Once you have the text, let an **A I** model do the reading. Send the extracted text as the message content and ask Claude to summarise or pull out fields. Keep your key in the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Summarise this report in 5 bullets:\n\n" + full_text}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Your task

Build a small script that reads every PDF in a `docs/` folder, extracts the text, and writes a one-paragraph Claude summary of each into a CSV.

quiz.q: Why prefer the with statement when opening a file?
options: It closes the file automatically, even on error
quiz.why: with open(...) as f: guarantees the file is closed when the block ends, even if an exception is raised.

quiz.q: Which file mode opens a file for writing and erases existing content?
quiz.why: "w" truncates (empties) the file before writing. Use "a" to append, "r" to read.

quiz.q: What encoding should you almost always specify when reading text files?
quiz.answer: utf-8
quiz.why: Passing encoding="utf-8" avoids garbled characters and platform-dependent defaults across Windows, macOS and Linux.

quiz.q: Which library reliably extracts text from a PDF in Python?
quiz.why: pypdf reads PDF pages and exposes extract_text(); pandas is for tables, requests for HTTP, json for JSON.

quiz.q: After extracting messy PDF text, how do you get a clean summary with Claude?
quiz.answer: Pass the extracted text inside the content of a messages.create call to the Claude Messages API.
quiz.why: You send the raw text as the user message content and ask Claude to summarise or extract fields; keep the API key in an env var.

quiz.q: True or false — pypdf's extract_text always returns perfectly clean, structured text.
quiz.why: False. Scanned or complex-layout PDFs often need cleaning, and image-only PDFs need OCR before any text is available.

m4-l09-secrets-config.title: Secrets & configuration management
objectives: Explain why secrets must never live in source code or Git history
Separate configuration from code using environment variables
Load secrets safely with a .env file and python-dotenv
Protect secrets with .gitignore and an .env.example template
Call the Anthropic Claude API using a key read from the environment
Know how secrets are injected in CI/CD and cloud deployments
Respond correctly when a secret leaks
m4-l09-secrets-config.body:
## Why secrets must leave your code

A **secret** is any value that grants access: an API key, a database password, a token. The golden rule is simple — secrets never belong in source code. If you hard-code a key, anyone who reads your repo can use it, and once it is pushed to Git it lives in the **history** forever, even after you delete the line.

This matters for your portfolio. Public GitHub repos are scanned constantly by bots, and a leaked Anthropic or cloud key can be abused within minutes, running up a bill on your account.

## Configuration belongs in the environment

The fix is to separate **configuration** from **code**. Your code stays the same everywhere; only the settings change between your laptop, a teammate's machine, and production. The standard place to put those settings is **environment variables** — named values the operating system hands to your program at run time.

```python
import os

api_key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]   # raises if missing
debug = os.getenv("DEBUG", "false")          # default if missing
```

Use `os.environ[...]` when the value is required, and `os.getenv(name, default)` when it is optional.

## The .env file for local development

Typing `export VAR=...` every session is tedious, so locally we keep settings in a **.env** file and load them with **python-dotenv**. The `.env` file is for your machine only — it must never be committed.

```bash
# .env  (NEVER commit this file)
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-your-real-key-here
DEBUG=true
```

```python
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()                                # reads .env into the environment
key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]
```

## Protect it with .gitignore and a template

Two files keep you safe. Add `.env` to **.gitignore** so Git ignores it, and commit an **.env.example** with the variable *names* but fake values, so teammates know what to set.

```bash
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
```

The `.env.example` is committed; the real `.env` is not.

## Using a secret with the Claude API

The Anthropic client reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment automatically — you never pass the key in code.

```python
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from anthropic import Anthropic

load_dotenv()
client = Anthropic()                         # picks up ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Secrets in CI/CD and the cloud

Your `.env` never leaves your laptop, so how does a deployed app get its keys? Through the platform's encrypted **secret store**. In GitHub Actions you add **repository secrets** and reference them in the workflow; the host injects them as environment variables at run time.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
steps:
  - run: python app.py
    env:
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
```

If a key ever leaks, **rotate** it — revoke the old one and generate a new one. Deleting the file is not enough.

quiz.q: Where should an API key like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live?
options: In an environment variable, loaded at runtime
In the README so teammates can find it
Committed to Git in a config.py
quiz.why: Secrets belong in the environment (or a secret manager), never in source code. Code reads them at runtime via os.environ.

quiz.q: Why must the .env file be added to .gitignore?
quiz.answer: So it is never committed to Git, keeping real secrets out of the repository and its history.
quiz.why: Once a secret is pushed to a shared or public repo it is considered compromised, even after deletion, because it stays in history.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an .env.example file?
options: It stores the real production keys
It is a committed template listing variable names with no real values
quiz.why: .env.example is committed and documents which variables are needed, using placeholder values so teammates know what to set.

quiz.q: True or false — deleting a leaked key from a file and committing the fix makes the repo safe.
quiz.why: False. The key remains in Git history. You must rotate (revoke and regenerate) the key, not just delete it.

quiz.q: In Python, how do you read an environment variable named ANTHROPIC_API_KEY?
quiz.answer: os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] or os.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY").
quiz.why: The os module exposes the environment; getenv returns None (or a default) if the variable is missing instead of raising.

quiz.q: How are secrets provided to a deployed app or a CI/CD pipeline?
options: You commit the .env file to the deploy branch
Through the platform's secret store or repository secrets, injected as env vars
You email them to the server
You paste them into the build log
quiz.why: Platforms like GitHub Actions and cloud hosts provide encrypted secret stores that are injected as environment variables at run time.

m4-l10-putting-together.title: Putting it together
objectives: Scope a focused project that tells a clear story to recruiters
Wire data, an LLM call, and an interface into one working app
Keep API keys and secrets out of your code with environment variables
Write a README that lets anyone run your project in minutes
Add basic tests and error handling so the demo doesn't break
Deploy or record a demo so the project is easy to view
Present the project with results, trade-offs, and next steps
m4-l10-putting-together.body:
## The goal: one project that proves it

After four months you can write Python, use Git, query data, and call an LLM. This lesson is about **putting it together** into a single portfolio project a recruiter can open, understand, and run.

The aim is not size — it's a **finished, focused** project that tells a clear story: *here is a real problem, here is how I used AI to solve it, here is the result.*

## Scope it small, ship it whole

Pick one narrow problem. A good shape is: take some **input**, send it to **Claude**, return a useful **output**, wrapped in a small interface.

Examples that work well: a CV-to-cover-letter helper, a support-ticket classifier, a notes summariser. Each is small enough to finish and clear enough to explain.

Write down, in one sentence, what done looks like. Then build to that and stop.

## The core: data in, Claude in the middle, result out

Here is the heart of almost every project — a clean call to the Claude Messages API. Keep your key in an environment variable, never in the code.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def summarise(text: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarise in 3 bullets:\n{text}"}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text
```

## Make it runnable by a stranger

A project a reviewer can't run might as well not exist. Pin your dependencies and set the key from the shell.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...   # Windows: set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
streamlit run app.py
```

Your `requirements.txt` should pin versions, for example `anthropic==0.39.0` and `streamlit==1.39.0`, so it installs the same way every time.

## Polish: README, tests, and a demo

Three things turn code into a portfolio piece:

- **README** — one-line description, a screenshot, setup steps, and how to run it.
- **A test or two** — even one `assert` that your function returns text proves you think about correctness.
- **A demo** — deploy it or record a 60-second screen capture, and link it at the top of the README.

Add simple error handling so a missing key or empty input shows a friendly message instead of a stack trace.

## Present it like an engineer

When you talk about the project, cover three things: **the result**, the **trade-offs** you made (why this model, why this scope), and **what you'd do next**. That honesty is exactly the judgement employers are hiring for.

## Your task

Ship one end-to-end project this week: scope it in a sentence, build the data-to-Claude-to-output core, write the README, and record a short demo.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in a portfolio project?
options: Paste it directly in the code
In an environment variable, read with os.environ
In the README so reviewers can use it
In a public config.json committed to GitHub
quiz.why: Secrets belong in environment variables (or a .env file that is git-ignored), never hard-coded or committed where others can see them.

quiz.q: Which file makes a portfolio project easy for a stranger to run?
options: All of these help, but the README is the entry point
quiz.why: A clear README explains what the project does and how to run it; requirements.txt and LICENSE support it, but the README is what a recruiter reads first.

quiz.q: Why scope a portfolio project narrowly rather than building something huge?
options: A finished, focused project beats an impressive unfinished one
quiz.why: One small project you actually finished and can demo cleanly is far more convincing than a sprawling one that doesn't run.

quiz.q: Name one thing your README should always include so someone can run your project.
quiz.answer: Setup/install and run instructions (e.g. install dependencies, set the API key, run the command).
quiz.why: Without clear setup and run steps, even great code is useless to a reviewer who can't get it started.

quiz.q: In one phrase, what should the final slide of a project presentation cover?
quiz.answer: Results, trade-offs you made, and what you would do next.
quiz.why: Closing with results and honest next steps shows engineering judgement, which is what employers are really assessing.

quiz.q: What does pinning versions in requirements.txt (e.g. anthropic==0.39.0) protect against?
options: A future package update silently breaking your app
quiz.why: Pinned versions make the project reproducible: it installs the same dependencies today and months from now, so it keeps working.

m5-l01-deploy-platforms.title: Deployment platforms
objectives: Explain what deployment means and why localhost is not enough
Tell apart static hosts, app platforms (PaaS), and serverless functions
Match a platform to a project: Streamlit, FastAPI, or a static front end
Configure environment variables and secrets safely on a host
Pin dependencies with requirements.txt for reproducible deploys
Read build logs and diagnose a failed deployment
m5-l01-deploy-platforms.body:
## What deployment really means

**Deployment** is moving your app from your laptop to a server that anyone on the internet can reach. While you build, you run things on `localhost` — address `127.0.0.1` — which always means *this machine*. Send that link to a friend and it points at *their* computer, not yours.

To go public you need a **host**: a machine (or managed service) that is always on, has a public address, and runs your code. Your job is to package the app, tell the host how to start it, and hand over your secrets safely.

## Three kinds of platform

Not every app needs the same host. The three families you'll meet:

- **Static hosts** (Netlify, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages) — serve pre-built files only: HTML, CSS, JavaScript. No Python runs. Great for a portfolio site or a React front end.
- **Platform-as-a-Service / PaaS** (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Streamlit Cloud, Hugging Face Spaces) — you give it code, it builds and runs a long-lived process. Perfect for a FastAPI or Streamlit AI app.
- **Serverless functions** (Vercel Functions, AWS Lambda) — your code runs only when a request arrives, then scales to zero. Cheap at idle, but **cold starts** add latency and there are time limits.

## Pinning dependencies

The host is a fresh machine — none of your packages are installed. A `requirements.txt` lists exactly what to install so the build is reproducible.

```bash
pip freeze > requirements.txt
cat requirements.txt
# anthropic==0.39.0
# fastapi==0.115.0
# uvicorn==0.32.0
```

## Secrets and environment variables

Never hard-code an API key, and never commit a `.env` file. Read keys from the environment, and set the real values in the platform's secrets panel.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one line."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Picking a platform

For this course, **Streamlit Community Cloud** and **Hugging Face Spaces** are the fastest free routes to a live AI demo — connect a GitHub repo and they build it for you. Reach for **Render** when you need a plain FastAPI backend with a public URL. Use a static host only for a front end with no Python.

## Your task

Pick one app you've built. Write its `requirements.txt`, move every secret to an environment variable, push to GitHub, and deploy it to Streamlit Cloud or Hugging Face Spaces. Share the live link.

quiz.q: Why can't you just send a friend your localhost URL to use your app?
quiz.answer: localhost (127.0.0.1) only refers to the machine the request comes from, so it points at their computer, not yours; the app must be hosted on a public server with a real domain.
quiz.why: localhost always resolves to the local machine, so a public, reachable host is required for others to access your app.

quiz.q: Which platform type runs your code only when a request arrives and scales to zero when idle?
quiz.why: Serverless functions spin up on demand per request and cost nothing while idle, but have cold starts and time limits.

quiz.q: Where should your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live when deployed?
options: In the platform's secrets / environment variables settings
In the README so teammates can find it
quiz.why: Secrets belong in the host's environment-variable settings, never in code or version control where they can leak.

quiz.q: What is the main job of requirements.txt during deployment?
options: It lists the Python packages the host must install
quiz.why: The host reads requirements.txt to pip install the exact packages your app needs, making the build reproducible.

quiz.q: Name one trade-off of serverless functions compared with an always-on PaaS app.
quiz.answer: Cold starts: the first request after idle is slow while the function boots; there are also execution time limits unsuited to long-running tasks.
quiz.why: Serverless saves money at idle but adds latency on cold starts and caps how long a single request can run.

quiz.q: A static host like Netlify or GitHub Pages can run your Python FastAPI backend.
quiz.why: False. Static hosts only serve pre-built files (HTML, CSS, JS); running Python server code needs a PaaS or serverless platform.

m5-l02-docker.title: Docker basics
objectives: Explain what a container is and why "works on my machine" stops being a problem
Tell the difference between an image and a container
Write a simple Dockerfile for a Python AI app
Build an image and run it as a container with docker build and docker run
Pass secrets like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in safely with environment variables
Map ports so you can reach a running app from your browser
Use .dockerignore and a requirements.txt for clean, reproducible builds
m5-l02-docker.body:
## Why Docker?

You have built an A I app that runs on your laptop. But "it works on my machine" is not a deployment plan. The server might have a different Python version, missing libraries, or different settings. **Docker** solves this by packaging your code *and* everything it needs — Python, libraries, files — into a single portable unit called a **container** that runs the same everywhere.

Think of a container as a sealed lunchbox: whatever you put in stays exactly as packed, no matter whose fridge it ends up in.

## Images vs containers

This is the one distinction to nail. An **image** is the read-only blueprint — built once, stored on disk. A **container** is a running instance of that image. One image, many containers, like a class and its objects in code.

```bash
docker build -t myapp .     # build the image (blueprint)
docker run myapp            # start a container from it
docker ps                   # list running containers
```

## Writing a Dockerfile

A **Dockerfile** is a recipe: each line is a step Docker runs to build your image. Start from an official base image, copy your code in, install dependencies, then say how to start.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

Copying `requirements.txt` *before* the rest of your code lets Docker cache the slow `pip install` step, so rebuilds are fast when only your code changes.

## Secrets and the Anthropic API

Never bake an API key into the image — anyone who pulls it can read the layers. Keep keys in **environment variables** and pass them in at run time. Your code reads the key from the environment; Docker hands it over with `-e` or `--env-file`.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello from inside a container!"}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Then run it without ever writing the key into a file the image keeps:

```bash
docker run -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY myapp
```

## Ports and persistence

If your app serves a web page or A P I, you must **map a port** so your browser can reach inside the container. The format is `host:container`. Also remember containers are **ephemeral**: files written inside vanish when the container is removed, unless you mount a **volume**.

```bash
docker run -p 8000:80 myapp        # localhost:8000 -> port 80 inside
docker run -v $(pwd)/data:/app/data myapp
```

## Your task
