It gives every prediction traceability, so you can tell which model version produced a given result
quiz.why: Returning the model_version with each prediction provides traceability and auditability: when results are investigated later, you can map a response back to the exact model that produced it, which is essential for debugging and governance.

quiz.q: Which Dockerfile choice best follows production best practice for a model service?
options: Run the container as root so it can write anywhere
Use a slim base image, create and switch to a non-root user, and install pinned deps with --no-cache-dir
Install dependencies without a requirements file to stay flexible
Use the full python image and run pip install with no version pins
quiz.why: A slim base reduces image size and attack surface, a non-root user limits blast radius if the container is compromised, and pinned dependencies installed with --no-cache-dir give deterministic, lean builds.

quiz.q: If you run uvicorn with 4 workers serving a 500 MB model, roughly how much memory do the loaded models consume in total?
options: About 500 MB, because workers share one copy of the model
About 125 MB, because the model is split across workers
About 2 GB, because each of the 4 workers holds its own copy of the model
Zero, because the model lives only on disk
quiz.why: Each worker is a separate process with its own memory space and loads its own copy of the model via the lifespan handler. Four workers each holding a 500 MB model use roughly 2 GB combined, so you must size worker count against model footprint and host RAM.

quiz.q: In two or three sentences, explain why feeding model input through a Pydantic request schema is safer than reading raw values straight from the request body, and give one concrete failure it prevents.
quiz.answer: A Pydantic schema validates and coerces incoming data against declared types and constraints before your prediction code ever runs, so malformed or missing fields are rejected with a clear 422 error instead of crashing deep in the model call. It documents the exact contract callers must follow and centralizes validation in one place. A concrete failure it prevents is passing a string or null where the model expects a numeric feature, which would otherwise raise an opaque error inside scikit-learn or produce a garbage prediction.
quiz.why: Pydantic enforces the input contract at the edge of the service, converting validation into predictable, well-typed errors and protecting the model from receiving inputs of the wrong type, shape, or range.

dsc-m6-l02-experiment-tracking-and-model.title: Experiment Tracking and Model Registry with MLflow
objectives: Explain why experiment tracking is essential for reproducibility and comparing model runs
Log parameters, metrics, and artifacts for a run using the MLflow tracking API
Log a trained scikit-learn model with mlflow.sklearn using the MLflow 3.x name= argument
Compare and rank runs visually in the MLflow UI to select the best model
Register a model and manage versions, promoting them with aliases such as champion
Load a registered model back by alias to serve predictions in production
dsc-m6-l02-experiment-tracking-and-model.body:
## Why Tracking Matters

Every data scientist has lived this nightmare: a model scored beautifully last Tuesday, but nobody recorded the exact features, hyperparameters, or random seed that produced it. **Experiment tracking** ends the guesswork. A tracking tool records the inputs and outputs of every training run so results are **reproducible** and **comparable**.

MLflow is the de facto open-source standard. This lesson uses **MLflow 3.x** (install with `pip install "mlflow>=3,<4"`). The core abstractions are:

- An **experiment** groups related runs (e.g., all attempts at a churn model).
- A **run** is a single execution: its params, metrics, artifacts, and model.

With tracking in place, "which params gave that score?" becomes a query, not a memory test.

## Logging a Run

You wrap training in `mlflow.start_run()` and log three kinds of information: **parameters** (the knobs you set), **metrics** (the scores you measured), and **artifacts** (any output files such as plots or reports).

```python
import mlflow
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

mlflow.set_experiment("churn-model")

with mlflow.start_run():
    model = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)

    mlflow.log_params({"C": 1.0, "max_iter": 1000})
    mlflow.log_metrics({"f1": 0.82, "roc_auc": 0.90})
    mlflow.log_artifact("confusion_matrix.png")
```

Each `with` block is one run. Re-run the script with different settings and MLflow keeps a tidy history of every attempt.

## Logging the Model Itself

Params and metrics describe a run, but you also want the **trained model** saved so it can be reloaded later. The `mlflow.sklearn` flavor serializes the estimator along with its environment.

```python
with mlflow.start_run():
    # ... log_params / log_metrics ...
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model")  # MLflow 3.x (2.x used artifact_path=)
```

**Version note:** MLflow 3.x uses `name=` to identify the logged model. MLflow 2.x used `artifact_path=` instead, so older tutorials will show `mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, artifact_path="model")`. The behavior is the same; only the keyword changed. Pinning your MLflow version keeps the API unambiguous.

## Comparing Runs in the MLflow UI

Start the UI locally with:

```bash
mlflow ui
```

Then open `http://localhost:5000`. Select your experiment and you will see a table of runs, one row each, with columns for every param and metric. From here you can:

- **Sort** by a metric (e.g., highest `roc_auc`) to find the best run instantly.
- **Select several runs** and click *Compare* to see side-by-side params and metric charts.
- **Drill into** any run to view its artifacts and logged model.

This visual comparison replaces spreadsheets full of copy-pasted numbers and makes model selection an evidence-based decision.

## The Model Registry

Tracking answers "what did I try?" The **Model Registry** answers "what is in production?" It is a centralized store of named models, each with numbered **versions** and a lifecycle.

The simplest path is to register a model at log time with `registered_model_name`:

```python
with mlflow.start_run():
    # ... log params and metrics first ...
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
        model,
        name="model",
        registered_model_name="churn-model",
    )
```

You can also register an existing run's model after the fact:

```python
result = mlflow.register_model(
    "runs:/<run_id>/model", "churn-model")
```

The first registration creates **Version 1**; each subsequent one increments to Version 2, 3, and so on. Nothing is overwritten, so you can always roll back.

## Promoting with Aliases

How do you say "this version is the one production should serve"? The **modern** approach is **aliases**: human-readable pointers like `champion` or `challenger` that you attach to a specific version.

```python
from mlflow import MlflowClient

client = MlflowClient()
client.set_registered_model_alias(
    name="churn-model", alias="champion", version=3)
```

When a better model arrives, repoint `champion` to the new version. Consumers reference the alias, never a hard-coded number.

**Version note:** older MLflow used **stage transitions** (`Staging`, `Production`) via `transition_model_version_stage`. Stages are now deprecated in favor of aliases, which are more flexible because you can define as many as you need.

## Loading a Registered Model for Serving

This closes the loop with the deployment workflow from the previous lesson. Instead of shipping a pickle file by hand, your serving code pulls the current champion straight from the registry by alias:

```python
import mlflow.sklearn

model = mlflow.sklearn.load_model(
    "models:/churn-model@champion")
predictions = model.predict(X_new)
```

The URI `models:/churn-model@champion` resolves the alias to whatever version is current, so promoting a new model needs **no code change** in the service. You could also load a fixed version with `models:/churn-model/3` when you need strict pinning. This alias-based loading is the bridge from experimentation to reliable, reproducible production serving.

quiz.q: What is the primary value of experiment tracking with MLflow?
options: It records params, metrics, and artifacts so runs are reproducible and comparable
It removes the need for any version control system
It only works with deep learning frameworks
quiz.why: Tracking captures the inputs (params), outputs (metrics), and artifacts of every run, so you can reproduce a result months later and answer 'which parameters gave that score?' by comparing runs instead of guessing.

quiz.q: In MLflow 3.x, which keyword argument names the saved model when calling mlflow.sklearn.log_model()?
quiz.why: MLflow 3.x uses name= to identify the logged model (e.g., name="model"). The older 2.x API used artifact_path=, which is why pinning the version matters when reading code or docs.

quiz.q: Which MLflow call records numeric performance values such as f1 and roc_auc for a run?
quiz.why: log_metrics() stores numeric scores. log_params() stores hyperparameters like C and max_iter, log_artifacts() stores output files like plots, and log_model() stores the serialized model.

quiz.q: What is the modern, recommended way to mark a registered model version as the one production should use?
options: Delete all older versions so only one remains
Assign an alias like 'champion' to a version with set_registered_model_alias
Retrain the model from scratch each deployment
quiz.why: Aliases (e.g., champion) are the modern promotion mechanism; you point an alias at a specific version with MlflowClient().set_registered_model_alias(). Stage transitions (Staging/Production) are the older, now-discouraged API.

quiz.q: Which URI loads the registered model version currently carrying the 'champion' alias?
quiz.why: The alias syntax uses an @ between the model name and the alias: models:/churn-model@champion. The slash form (models:/name/version) is for a numeric version, and runs:/ refers to a run artifact, not a registered model.

quiz.q: Name the MLflow function, typically used as a context manager with 'with', that opens a new tracked run.
quiz.answer: mlflow.start_run
quiz.why: mlflow.start_run() begins a run; used as 'with mlflow.start_run():' it ensures the run is properly closed and that all params, metrics, and the model are logged under that single run.

dsc-m6-l03-monitoring-models-drift-and-p.title: Monitoring Models in Production: Drift and Performance
objectives: Explain why production models decay and why offline metrics are not enough
Define and distinguish data drift from concept drift with concrete examples
Detect drift statistically using the KS test and the Population Stability Index
Build a reference-vs-current drift report with Evidently and read its output
Monitor live performance by recomputing Module 3 metrics as labels arrive
Design alerting thresholds and retraining triggers that respond to drift
dsc-m6-l03-monitoring-models-drift-and-p.body:
## Why Models Decay in Production

A model is a snapshot of the world at training time, but the world keeps moving. Customer behavior shifts, competitors launch products, fraudsters change tactics, an upstream team renames a column. None of these events touch your code, yet each can quietly erode accuracy. This is **model decay**, and it is the default outcome, not the exception.

The trap is trusting your **offline metrics**. A 0.92 ROC-AUC on a held-out test set tells you how the model did on data that looks like the past; it says nothing about next month. Production monitoring closes that gap by continuously asking two questions: *has the incoming data changed?* and *is the model still right?*

## Data Drift vs. Concept Drift

These two terms are constantly confused, so define them precisely.

- **Data drift** (covariate shift): the distribution of the **inputs** `P(X)` changes. Example: your loan model was trained mostly on applicants aged 30-45, but a new marketing campaign brings in mostly 18-25 year-olds. The features look different from what the model saw in training.
- **Concept drift**: the **relationship** between inputs and target `P(y | X)` changes. The inputs may look identical, but their meaning has shifted. Example: a spam filter's emails look statistically the same, but spammers invent new tricks, so the same words now imply spam far less reliably. The learned mapping is simply wrong now.

Why it matters: data drift is detectable **without labels** because you only need the inputs. Concept drift usually requires **ground truth** to confirm, because you must observe that the same `X` now yields a different `y`. In practice you monitor input drift as an early warning and performance metrics as confirmation.

## Detecting Drift Statistically

Drift detection compares a **reference window** (often the training or a known-good period) against a **current window** (recent production data), feature by feature.

For a single continuous feature, the two-sample **Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test** compares the two empirical distributions and needs nothing beyond SciPy:

```python
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp

stat, p_value = ks_2samp(ref_df["income"], cur_df["income"])
if p_value < 0.05:
    print(f"Drift suspected in 'income' (KS={stat:.3f}, p={p_value:.4f})")
```

The **Population Stability Index (PSI)** is the classic credit-risk metric. It bins a feature and sums `(cur% - ref%) * ln(cur% / ref%)` across bins. Rule of thumb: **< 0.1 stable, 0.1-0.2 moderate, > 0.2 significant shift**. Both KS and PSI are dependency-light and easy to run on a schedule.

## A Concrete Drift Report with Evidently

Hand-rolling a test per column does not scale to hundreds of features. **Evidently** automates this: you pass a reference and a current dataframe, and a preset picks an appropriate test per column and renders an HTML report.

```python
from evidently import Report
from evidently.presets import DataDriftPreset

report = Report(metrics=[DataDriftPreset()])
result = report.run(reference_data=ref_df, current_data=cur_df)
result.save_html("drift.html")
```

The report shows, per feature, the test used, the drift score, and whether drift was detected, plus an overall dataset drift share. Note that **Evidently's API has evolved across versions** (the modern 0.4+/0.6+ pattern uses `Report` with presets); always check the current docs at https://docs.evidentlyai.com/ for the exact imports your installed version expects.

An important complement is **NannyML**, which can **estimate performance without labels** using algorithms like CBPE, giving an estimated ROC-AUC before ground truth lands. Use Evidently for drift and NannyML for label-free performance estimation to cover the gap while labels are delayed.

## Monitoring Live Performance Once Labels Arrive

Drift is a leading indicator; the lagging, ground-truth indicator is **actual performance**. When labels finally arrive (a user churns, a loan defaults, a ticket is resolved), recompute the **exact same scikit-learn metrics from Module 3** over rolling windows so the numbers are comparable to your offline baseline.

```python
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, recall_score, classification_report

# y_true: labels that just arrived; probs/labels: stored predictions
window_auc = roc_auc_score(y_true, probs)
window_recall = recall_score(y_true, labels)
print(classification_report(y_true, labels))

if window_auc < 0.80:            # agreed SLO threshold
    raise_alert("ROC-AUC below SLO", window_auc)
```

Log these per window into a time series and plot the trend. A slow downward slope in recall or ROC-AUC is decay in action, and it lets you connect a performance drop back to the drift you already flagged.

## Alerting and Retraining Triggers

Detection is useless without a response policy. Build a tiered playbook:

1. **Validate first.** Rule out a pipeline bug: a schema change, a flood of nulls, or a unit change (dollars to cents) often masquerades as drift.
2. **Alert, don't auto-fire.** A single noisy window should notify the owning team, not trigger a retrain. Require a **sustained** breach (drift share above threshold for N consecutive windows).
3. **Retrain on real evidence.** Trigger retraining when a live metric falls below its **SLO** (e.g., recall < 0.80) or when sustained, confirmed drift coincides with a falling label-free performance estimate.
4. **Retrain safely.** Train on fresh, representative data, validate against the current production model, promote only if it wins, and keep the old model for rollback.

Never wire `eval()` or arbitrary code execution into an alerting pipeline; keep triggers as explicit, reviewable thresholds. Monitoring is a control loop: detect, confirm, decide, act, and verify the fix held.

A complete stack has three layers: **input drift** (Evidently/PSI/KS, available immediately), **estimated performance** (NannyML, available before labels), and **measured performance** (Module 3 sklearn metrics, available once labels land). Wire each into dashboards and alerts, and your models stop decaying in silence.

quiz.q: A spam classifier's input email distribution looks unchanged, but spammers have invented new tactics so the SAME features now imply 'spam' less often. What is this called?
quiz.why: Concept drift is a change in the relationship between features and the target P(y|X). The inputs look stable but the meaning of those inputs has shifted, so the learned mapping is now wrong.

quiz.q: Which statistical test is a natural choice for detecting drift in a single CONTINUOUS feature by comparing a reference window to a current window?
quiz.why: scipy.stats.ks_2samp compares two empirical distributions of a continuous variable and returns a statistic and p-value, making it a dependency-light way to flag distribution shift in one feature.

quiz.q: Why is monitoring input drift valuable even BEFORE ground-truth labels arrive?
options: Drift metrics replace the need for labels permanently
Input distributions never change in production
Labels are often delayed, so drift is an early proxy warning that performance MAY be degrading
Drift only matters for regression models
quiz.why: Ground truth often lags by days or weeks. Input and prediction drift can be measured immediately, giving an early signal to investigate before delayed labels confirm a performance drop.

quiz.q: A Population Stability Index (PSI) of 0.30 between the reference and current distribution of a feature most likely indicates:
options: A significant, actionable population shift worth investigating
A data type error in the column
Perfect stability between the two windows
quiz.why: By common rule of thumb, PSI below 0.1 is stable, 0.1-0.2 is moderate, and above 0.2-0.25 signals a major shift. A PSI of 0.30 is a strong signal to investigate.

quiz.q: Which tool can ESTIMATE a model's performance in production WITHOUT immediately available ground-truth labels?
quiz.why: NannyML provides performance-estimation algorithms (such as CBPE for classification) that estimate metrics like ROC-AUC from model confidence and drift before labels arrive, complementing label-based monitoring.

quiz.q: Describe a sensible alerting and retraining policy for a model whose input drift report fires but whose labels have not yet arrived. What checks would you run and what would trigger an actual retrain?
quiz.answer: open
quiz.why: A strong answer: first confirm the drift is real and not a pipeline bug (schema change, nulls, unit change); quantify it (which features, how large the PSI/KS shift); estimate performance impact with a label-free method like NannyML; alert the owning team rather than auto-retraining on a single noisy signal; and trigger a retrain only when a sustained threshold is crossed or, once labels arrive, when a live metric (e.g., ROC-AUC or recall) drops below an agreed SLO, retraining on fresh representative data and validating before promotion.

dsc-m6-l04-orchestration-and-the-mlops-l.title: Orchestrating the ML Lifecycle (Capstone)
objectives: Describe the MLOps lifecycle as a continuous loop connecting serving, tracking, and monitoring
Explain why orchestration is needed to schedule and automate pipeline steps
Model a pipeline as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) using a modern orchestrator API
Build a minimal, readable Airflow TaskFlow or Prefect pipeline that retrains and re-deploys
Set up a CI/CD workflow that runs pytest and deploys on merge with GitHub Actions
Productionize an existing model end to end: serve, track, monitor for drift, and schedule retraining
dsc-m6-l04-orchestration-and-the-mlops-l.body:
## The MLOps Lifecycle Is a Loop

Everything in this module clicks together when you stop seeing deployment as the finish line and start seeing it as one stop on a **continuous loop**:

```
data -> train -> track -> serve -> monitor -> retrain -> (back to data)
```

- **Data**: fresh data arrives from your warehouse or stream.
- **Train**: you fit the model (Module 3).
- **Track**: you log params, metrics, and artifacts with **MLflow** (Lesson 2).
- **Serve**: you expose predictions behind **FastAPI + Docker** (Lesson 1).
- **Monitor**: you watch for **data drift** and performance decay (Lesson 3).
- **Retrain**: drift or a schedule triggers a new run, and the loop closes.

The job of MLOps is to make this loop **automated, reproducible, and observable** instead of a sequence of manual notebook runs.

## Why Orchestration?

The steps above have **dependencies**: you cannot serve a model you have not trained, and you should not retrain before validating new data. Running them by hand does not scale and is not reproducible.

An **orchestrator** (Apache Airflow, Prefect, Dagster) lets you declare the steps and dependencies once, then **schedule** them, **retry** failures, **backfill** history, and **alert** on errors. You express the workflow as a **DAG** — a Directed Acyclic Graph — where each node is a task and each edge is a dependency. "Acyclic" means no task can loop back onto itself, so the engine can always compute a valid run order.

## A Minimal Pipeline as a DAG

Modern Airflow uses the **TaskFlow API** (`@dag` / `@task` decorators), which is far cleaner than the legacy operator style. Each `@task` function becomes a node; calling one with another's return value creates the dependency edge.

```python
from datetime import datetime
from airflow.decorators import dag, task

@dag(schedule='@daily', start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), catchup=False)
def churn_pipeline():
    @task
    def extract() -> str:
        # pull fresh data, return a path/URI
        return 'data/churn_latest.parquet'

    @task
    def check_drift(path: str) -> bool:
        # compare live vs training distribution (Lesson 3)
        return True  # drift detected

    @task
    def train_and_track(path: str) -> str:
        # fit model, log to MLflow, return run/model URI
        return 'models:/churn/Staging'

    @task
    def deploy(model_uri: str):
        # promote + redeploy the FastAPI service (Lesson 1)
        print(f'Deploying {model_uri}')

    p = extract()
    if_drift = check_drift(p)
    model = train_and_track(p)
    deploy(model)

churn_pipeline()
```

The graph reads top to bottom: extract feeds drift-check and training; training feeds deploy. Airflow schedules it daily and retries any failed task.

## CI/CD for ML

Orchestration automates the *runtime* loop; **CI/CD** automates *shipping the code* behind it. On every push or pull request, **Continuous Integration** runs your tests so a broken pipeline never reaches production. On merge, **Continuous Delivery** deploys.

Here is a minimal, valid GitHub Actions workflow that runs `pytest`, then deploys only on the main branch:

```yaml
name: ml-ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -q
  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh
```

Tests should cover your code **and** your pipeline: schema checks, a tiny end-to-end run on sample data, and a check that the model meets a minimum metric threshold before promotion.

## Putting It All Together

The full lifecycle: code lives in Git; **CI** tests every change; on merge, **CD** ships the pipeline and serving image; the **orchestrator** runs the DAG on schedule; each run **trains** and **tracks** to MLflow; the best model is **served** via FastAPI; **monitoring** watches drift; and drift or the schedule **retrains**. Humans stay in the loop only for approvals and incidents.

## Mini-Project Brief: Productionize Your Module 3 Model

Take the predictive model from the **Module 3 mini-project (dsc-m3-l04)** and productionize it end to end using everything in this module. Keep it small but complete.

1. **Serve it** — wrap the saved pipeline in a **FastAPI** app with a `/predict` endpoint and containerize it with a **Dockerfile** (Lesson 1).
2. **Track training** — refactor training into a script that logs params, metrics, and the model artifact to **MLflow** and registers it (Lesson 2).
3. **Add a drift check** — write a function that compares a recent data batch against the training distribution and returns a drift flag (Lesson 3).
4. **Wire a pipeline** — connect extract -> drift-check -> train+track -> deploy as an Airflow TaskFlow (or Prefect) DAG on a daily schedule.
5. **Write a runbook** — a one-page Markdown doc: how to deploy, how to roll back, what the alerts mean, and who to page.

## Deliverables

- `app/main.py` (FastAPI) + `Dockerfile` that serves the model.
- `train.py` that logs a run to MLflow and registers the model.
- `monitoring/drift.py` with a drift-detection function and threshold.
- `pipeline.py` defining the scheduled DAG (TaskFlow `@dag`/`@task` or Prefect `@flow`/`@task`).
- `.github/workflows/ml-ci.yml` running `pytest` on push and deploying on merge.
- `tests/` with at least one pipeline test and one API test.
- `RUNBOOK.md` covering deploy, rollback, alerts, and on-call.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the MLOps lifecycle?
options: A continuous loop: data, train, track, serve, monitor, then retrain
A one-time linear process that ends the moment the model is deployed
Only the model-training step in isolation
A technique for avoiding version control
quiz.why: MLOps is a loop, not a one-shot deployment. Data flows into training, runs are tracked, the model is served, production is monitored, and drift or new data triggers retraining, closing the loop.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of an orchestrator such as Apache Airflow or Prefect?
options: To replace your machine learning model with a rules engine
To automatically label your training data
To schedule and automate the steps of a pipeline expressed as a DAG
To store model artifacts and nothing else
quiz.why: An orchestrator schedules, runs, retries, and monitors the dependent steps of a workflow. Those steps are expressed as a DAG so the engine knows the order and dependencies.

quiz.q: In a CI/CD pipeline for ML, what should run automatically on every push or pull request?
options: A full retrain on the entire production dataset
Automated tests such as pytest against the code and the pipeline
A manual code review with no automation
Deletion of the held-out test set
quiz.why: CI runs your automated tests on every change so broken code or a broken pipeline is caught before merge. Heavy retraining and deployment are separate, often gated steps.

quiz.q: What does a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) guarantee about a pipeline?
options: That every task always runs at the same time in parallel
That tasks may form cycles and loop back on themselves
That no task will ever fail at runtime
That tasks run in a defined order with no circular dependencies
quiz.why: A DAG is directed and acyclic: edges define dependencies and order, and the absence of cycles means a task can never depend on itself, directly or transitively.

quiz.q: Why add a scheduled drift check as a step in the lifecycle?
options: To make model training run faster
To replace the need for a held-out test set
To detect when incoming data diverges from training data and trigger retraining
To reduce the number of input features automatically
quiz.why: Data drift degrades a deployed model silently. A scheduled drift check (Lesson 3) flags divergence between live and training data so the pipeline can alert or retrain before performance collapses.

quiz.q: Name the experiment-tracking tool from Lesson 2 you would use to log parameters, metrics, and model artifacts during each automated training run.
quiz.answer: MLflow
quiz.why: MLflow records parameters, metrics, and artifacts per run and provides a model registry, so every orchestrated retrain is reproducible and comparable to past runs.

hd1-l01-how-a-computer-works.title: How a computer works: hardware, software & the boot process
objectives: Explain the difference between hardware and software in plain terms
Describe the input-process-output-storage model every computer follows
List the main stages of the boot process in order
Identify the role of the BIOS/UEFI firmware and the operating system
Recognise the four core hardware components and what each one does
Use the right vocabulary to describe a computer to a customer or colleague
hd1-l01-how-a-computer-works.body:
## Hardware vs software

Every computer is two things working together. **Hardware** is the physical equipment you can touch: the processor, memory, drives, screen, keyboard, and the board that links them. **Software** is the set of coded instructions that tells the hardware what to do — the **operating system** and the apps you run.

A useful way to remember it: hardware is the *body*, software is the *thoughts and instructions*. Neither is useful without the other. As a helpdesk technician, half your job is deciding whether a problem is hardware or software, so this distinction matters from day one.

## The model behind every computer

No matter how big or small, a computer follows the same loop: **input → process → output → storage**.

- **Input**: data comes in (keyboard, mouse, microphone, network).
- **Process**: the **CPU** does the calculations and decisions.
- **Output**: results go out (screen, speakers, printer).
- **Storage**: data is kept for later (drive) or held briefly while in use (**RAM**).

A calculator, a phone, and a data-centre server all follow this exact pattern.

## The four core components

Nearly every machine has four essentials:

- **CPU** (the processor) — does the actual work.
- **RAM** (memory) — fast, temporary workspace for whatever is running right now.
- **Storage** (HDD or SSD) — keeps your files when the power is off.
- **Motherboard** — the main board that connects everything, fed by the **power supply**.

We will open each of these up in later lessons. For now, just learn the names.

## The boot process, step by step

When you press the power button, a precise sequence runs:

1. **Power** flows from the power supply to the motherboard.
2. The motherboard **firmware** (**BIOS** on older PCs, **UEFI** on modern ones) starts first.
3. Firmware runs **POST** (Power-On Self-Test) to confirm RAM, CPU and other essentials are present and healthy.
4. Firmware finds the **boot device** (usually the main drive) and loads the **bootloader**.
5. The bootloader starts the **operating system**.
6. The OS loads drivers and shows you the **login screen** and **desktop**.

If POST fails, you may hear **beep codes** or see an error before any OS appears — a strong clue the problem is hardware.

## BIOS/UEFI and the operating system

Think of **firmware** as the building's caretaker who unlocks the doors and checks the lights work, then hands the keys to the **operating system** — the manager who actually runs the place. You can usually enter firmware settings by tapping a key like **Del**, **F2**, or **F10** right after powering on.

You can confirm key system facts from inside Windows once it boots:

```powershell
systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"OS Name" /C:"System Type" /C:"BIOS Version"
```

## Your task

Watch a computer boot and narrate the stages out loud. Power on a PC and tap the firmware key (often **Del** or **F2**) to peek at the BIOS/UEFI screen, then exit without changing anything. Once Windows loads, open PowerShell, run the `systeminfo` command above, and write down the OS name, system type, and BIOS version. In two sentences, describe what happened between pressing power and seeing the desktop.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the difference between hardware and software?
options: Hardware is the programs; software is the physical parts
Hardware is the physical parts you can touch; software is the instructions that run on it
They are two words for the same thing
Hardware only exists on laptops; software only on desktops
quiz.why: Hardware is the physical equipment (CPU, RAM, drives, screen). Software is the coded instructions, such as the operating system and apps, that tell the hardware what to do.

quiz.q: What is the first piece of code that runs when you press the power button?
options: The firmware (BIOS/UEFI) stored on the motherboard
quiz.why: Before any operating system loads, the motherboard's firmware (BIOS or modern UEFI) runs first. It performs the POST and then locates and hands off to the boot device.

quiz.q: The simple model that describes what every computer does is best summarised as:
quiz.why: Computers take input, process it with the CPU, produce output, and keep data in storage. This four-part model fits everything from a calculator to a server.

quiz.q: What does POST check during boot?
options: That essential hardware like RAM and the CPU is present and working
quiz.why: POST stands for Power-On Self-Test. The firmware quickly checks core hardware before loading the operating system; failures are often signalled by beep codes or on-screen errors.

quiz.q: In your own words, what is the role of the operating system once the computer has booted?
quiz.answer: The operating system manages the hardware and resources and provides a platform so the user and applications can run, giving you a desktop, files, and a way to launch programs.
quiz.why: After firmware hands off, the OS (Windows, macOS, Linux) takes control: it manages memory, the CPU, storage, devices, and presents the interface you actually use.

quiz.q: Name the four core hardware components found in nearly every computer.
quiz.answer: CPU (processor), RAM (memory), storage (drive), and the motherboard, usually powered by a power supply.
quiz.why: These are the essentials: the CPU does the work, RAM holds active data, storage keeps data when powered off, and the motherboard connects everything together.

hd1-l02-inside-the-pc.title: Inside the PC: CPU, RAM, motherboard & power supply
objectives: Explain what the CPU does, including cores, clock speed, and sockets
Describe RAM as volatile memory and identify DIMM versus SODIMM modules
Identify the motherboard's chipset, slots, connectors, and form factors
Explain power supply wattage, common connectors, and PSU safety rules
View your own CPU and RAM details from the Windows command line
Match each component to the job it does in a working PC
hd1-l02-inside-the-pc.body:
## The four parts that make a PC "go"

Open any desktop computer and, past the cables, you will always find the same core team working together. The **CPU** does the thinking, the **RAM** holds the work you are doing right now, the **motherboard** connects everything, and the **power supply** feeds the whole machine. Learn these four and the inside of a PC stops being a mystery.

## The CPU: the brain

The **CPU** (Central Processing Unit) carries out the instructions that make programs run. Three words describe it on a spec sheet. **Cores** are independent workers inside one chip; a 4-core CPU can juggle four jobs at once, so more cores help with multitasking. **Clock speed**, measured in **gigahertz (GHz)**, is how many cycles of work it does per second, so higher is generally faster. The **socket** is the shaped slot on the motherboard the CPU drops into. The socket must match the CPU exactly — an Intel chip will not fit an AMD socket, and vice versa.

The CPU runs hot, so it always sits under a **heatsink and fan** (or a liquid cooler). Never run a PC with that cooler removed.

## RAM: the desk you work on

**RAM** (Random Access Memory) is fast, short-term memory. Think of it as your desk: the bigger the desk, the more papers (programs and files) you can have open at once. RAM is **volatile**, which means it is wiped the moment power is lost — that is why unsaved work vanishes in a crash. **Capacity** is measured in **gigabytes (GB)**; 8 GB is a sensible minimum and 16 GB is comfortable today. Desktop RAM comes on **DIMM** modules; laptops use the smaller **SODIMM**. Installing modules in matched pairs enables **dual-channel**, which lets the CPU reach memory faster.

## The motherboard: the connector of everything

The **motherboard** is the big circuit board everything else plugs into. Its **chipset** manages the traffic between the CPU, memory, and devices. It carries **slots** (the CPU socket, RAM slots, and **PCIe** slots for cards like a graphics card) and **connectors** (for storage, USB, and front-panel buttons). Boards come in **form factors** — sizes that decide how much fits and which case they need. **ATX** is the full-size standard, **Micro-ATX** is smaller, and **Mini-ITX (mITX)** is the tiny one.

## The power supply: feed it safely

The **power supply unit (PSU)** converts wall power into the steady low voltages the parts need. Its **wattage** rating (for example 550 W) is the most power it can deliver — a gaming PC with a hungry CPU and GPU needs more than an office PC. The PSU connects with a large **24-pin** plug to the board, a **CPU power** plug, and **SATA/PCIe** plugs for drives and cards. **Safety rule: never open a PSU.** Its capacitors can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged. A faulty PSU is replaced as a whole sealed unit, never repaired.

## See your own hardware

You do not need to open the case to read your specs. Open **PowerShell** and ask Windows directly:

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, MaxClockSpeed
Get-CimInstance Win32_PhysicalMemory | Select-Object Capacity, Speed
```

Or use the classic one-liner that prints a full system report:

```text
systeminfo
```

## Your task

On your own PC, run the two `Get-CimInstance` commands above. Write down your CPU name, its number of cores, its clock speed in GHz, and your total RAM in GB. Then state in one sentence whether your machine uses DIMM or SODIMM memory and how you can tell (desktop versus laptop).

quiz.q: What is the main job of the CPU?
options: Store files permanently when the power is off
Carry out the instructions that make programs run
Supply electricity to the other parts
Display the picture on the monitor
quiz.why: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the 'brain': it executes the instructions of every program. Permanent storage is the drive's job, electricity is the PSU's job, and the picture comes from the GPU.

quiz.q: Why is RAM described as 'volatile' memory?
options: It loses everything it holds when power is removed
It can only be read, never written
It is the fastest storage in the PC and keeps data forever
quiz.why: Volatile means RAM only holds data while it is powered. Switch the PC off and RAM is wiped, which is why unsaved work is lost in a power cut.

quiz.q: Which motherboard form factor is the larger, full-size standard?
quiz.why: ATX is the full-size standard board with the most slots and ports. Micro-ATX is smaller, Mini-ITX is the smallest, and SODIMM is a type of RAM module, not a board size.

quiz.q: What does the wattage rating on a power supply (PSU) tell you?
options: The maximum power it can deliver to the components
How fast the CPU can run
How much storage the drive has
quiz.why: Wattage is the total power the PSU can supply. A build with a power-hungry CPU and GPU needs a higher-wattage PSU so it does not run short.

quiz.q: Name the type of RAM module used in laptops (the smaller form factor).
quiz.answer: SODIMM
quiz.why: SODIMM (Small Outline DIMM) is the compact RAM module used in laptops and small PCs, while full-size desktops use DIMM modules.

quiz.q: Give one safety reason you should never open or repair a power supply unit.
quiz.answer: PSUs contain capacitors that can store a dangerous high-voltage charge even after the unit is unplugged, so opening one risks a serious electric shock.
quiz.why: Technicians replace a faulty PSU as a whole sealed unit; they never open it. The stored charge in its capacitors can injure or kill even when the PC is off and unplugged.

hd1-l03-storage-explained.title: Storage explained: HDD vs SSD, partitions & file systems
objectives: Explain the difference between an HDD and an SSD and when each is used
Identify common drive form factors and connectors (2.5", M.2, SATA, NVMe)
Describe what a partition is and tell GPT apart from MBR
Match common file systems (NTFS, exFAT, FAT32, ext4) to the right job
Explain what formatting does and how a drive becomes a drive letter
View disks, volumes and partitions safely using built-in Windows tools
hd1-l03-storage-explained.body:
## Why storage matters

Your computer has two kinds of memory. **RAM** is fast but forgets everything when the power goes off. **Storage** is the slower, permanent home for your operating system, programs, and files — it keeps your data even when the PC is switched off. On a helpdesk, you will swap drives, clone systems, and explain to users why their old PC "feels slow." Very often the answer is the drive.

## HDD vs SSD

A **hard disk drive (HDD)** stores data on spinning magnetic **platters**. A tiny mechanical arm with a read/write **head** moves across the platter to find your data. The platters spin at a fixed speed measured in **RPM** (revolutions per minute) — commonly 5400 or 7200. Because parts physically move, HDDs are slower, noisier, and more fragile, but they are **cheap and come in huge capacities**, which makes them great for bulk storage and backups.

A **solid-state drive (SSD)** stores data in **flash memory** chips. There are **no moving parts**, so it is dramatically faster, silent, cooler, and far more resistant to bumps. Swapping an old HDD for an SSD is the single biggest speed upgrade you can give most computers. The trade-off is a higher cost per gigabyte.

## Form factors and connectors

Drives come in different shapes (**form factors**) and use different connectors:

- **2.5\" SATA** — a small rectangular drive that connects with a **SATA** cable. Both HDDs and SSDs use this shape.
- **M.2** — a thin stick that plugs flat onto the motherboard. Pronounced "em dot two."
- **SATA vs NVMe** — the connector is only half the story. A 2.5\" SSD or some M.2 drives use the older **SATA** bus. Faster M.2 drives use **NVMe**, which runs over the high-speed **PCIe** lanes and is many times quicker.

## Partitions: GPT vs MBR

A raw drive is just empty space. A **partition** is a section of the drive treated as a separate unit. One physical disk can hold several partitions. The **partition table** records this layout, and there are two schemes:

- **MBR (Master Boot Record)** — older, limited to **2 TB** and four **primary** partitions.
- **GPT (GUID Partition Table)** — modern, supports huge drives and many partitions. Required for UEFI boot.

## File systems and formatting

A partition still needs a **file system** — the rulebook for how files are stored and named. Common ones:

- **NTFS** — Windows default; permissions, large files, journaling.
- **exFAT** — great for large external/USB drives shared between Windows and Mac.
- **FAT32** — old and simple; can't hold files over 4 GB.
- **ext4** — the common Linux file system.

**Formatting** writes a fresh, empty file system onto a partition — and erases what was there. Once formatted, Windows assigns a **drive letter** (like `C:` or `D:`) so you can use it.

## Viewing drives safely

You can inspect storage without changing anything. Open PowerShell and run these read-only commands:

```powershell
Get-Disk
Get-Volume
Get-Partition
```

You can also open **Disk Management** (`diskmgmt.msc`) for a visual map. The command-line tool **diskpart** can also list disks read-only:

```text
diskpart
list disk
list volume
exit
```

**Warning:** never run format, clean, or delete commands unless you are 100% sure of the disk number. Selecting the wrong disk wipes it permanently.

## Your task

Open PowerShell on your PC and run `Get-Disk`, then `Get-Volume`, then `Get-Partition`. Write down, for your main drive: is it an HDD or SSD, what file system does it use (look at the `Get-Volume` output), and what drive letter is it? Then open Disk Management (`diskmgmt.msc`) and confirm your findings visually — without changing anything.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes an SSD compared with a traditional HDD?
options: It uses spinning platters and a moving read/write head
It stores data in flash memory with no moving parts and is much faster
It is always cheaper per gigabyte than an HDD
It can only be used for the operating system, never for files
quiz.why: An SSD uses flash memory chips with no moving parts, so it is far faster and more shock-resistant than an HDD, which relies on spinning platters and a mechanical head.

quiz.q: What does the RPM rating on a hard drive (HDD) tell you?
options: How fast the platters spin, which affects performance
quiz.why: RPM means revolutions per minute. Faster-spinning platters (e.g. 7200 RPM vs 5400 RPM) generally read and write data quicker on a mechanical HDD.

quiz.q: An M.2 NVMe drive is faster than a 2.5" SATA SSD mainly because:
options: It connects over the PCI Express bus instead of the slower SATA bus
quiz.why: NVMe drives talk to the system over the high-speed PCIe lanes, which carry far more data per second than the older SATA interface used by 2.5" SATA SSDs.

quiz.q: Which partitioning scheme supports drives larger than 2 TB and more than four primary partitions?
quiz.why: GPT (GUID Partition Table) is the modern scheme that handles drives over 2 TB and many partitions. The older MBR scheme is capped at 2 TB and four primary partitions.

quiz.q: Name the default file system Windows uses for its system drive, and give one reason it is chosen.
quiz.answer: NTFS, because it supports large files, security permissions, and journaling that helps recover from crashes.
quiz.why: NTFS is the standard Windows file system; its permissions and journaling make it reliable and secure for the operating system and most internal drives.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does formatting a drive actually do, and why must you be careful?
quiz.answer: Formatting writes a fresh, empty file system onto a partition, which erases the data that was there, so you must always confirm you have selected the correct disk.
quiz.why: Formatting prepares a volume for use but wipes existing files, so picking the wrong disk in a tool like Disk Management or diskpart can destroy data permanently.

hd1-l04-ports-and-peripherals.title: Ports, connectors & peripherals
objectives: Identify common ports (USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, DisplayPort, RJ45, 3.5mm) by their shape
Explain the difference between USB versions and the speeds they offer
Connect the right peripheral to the right port: keyboard, mouse, monitor, webcam, headset
Describe what a docking station does and when to use one
Recognise legacy ports such as VGA, DVI and PS/2 when you meet older equipment
List connected USB and PnP devices from Windows PowerShell
hd1-l04-ports-and-peripherals.body:
## Why ports matter on a helpdesk

A huge share of helpdesk tickets are simply "my monitor won't display" or "my mouse stopped working". Nine times out of ten the fix is knowing **which cable goes in which hole**. If you can identify a port by its **shape**, you can solve these in seconds. Let's learn the common ones.

## USB: the universal connector

**USB** (Universal Serial Bus) is the most common port you'll meet. There are two shapes you must know:

- **USB-A** — the flat **rectangular** connector that only fits one way up (everyone flips it three times). Used for keyboards, mice, flash drives.
- **USB-C** — a small **oval, reversible** connector. No wrong way up. It can carry data, video and power all at once.

USB also comes in **versions** that set the speed. **USB 2.0** is slow (often a black plug). **USB 3.x** is faster (often a **blue** plug). **Thunderbolt** uses the USB-C shape but is even faster and can drive monitors and external drives. Tip: blue inside the port usually means it's a faster USB 3 port.

## Video ports: getting a picture on screen

When a monitor shows "No Signal", check the video cable. The common ones:

- **HDMI** — flat with slightly tapered corners; carries **video and audio**. Most common today.
- **DisplayPort** — similar size to HDMI but with one **squared-off** corner; great for high refresh rates.
- **VGA** — old **blue D-shaped** port with 15 pins; **analogue video only**, no sound.
- **DVI** — older white connector with many pins; a step between VGA and HDMI.

## Audio, networking, legacy and power

- **3.5mm jack** — the round headphone/microphone hole. Green is usually output, pink is microphone.
- **RJ45 (Ethernet)** — squarish 8-pin port with a clip, for **wired networking**. Looks like a fat phone socket.
- **PS/2** — round **purple (keyboard)** or **green (mouse)** legacy ports on older desktops.
- **Power** — desktops use a **barrel** plug or a power lead; many modern laptops charge over **USB-C**.

## Peripherals and docking stations

**Peripherals** are the devices users plug in: **keyboard**, **mouse**, **monitor**, **webcam**, **headset**. Most modern ones use USB-A, USB-C or wireless (Bluetooth/USB dongle).

A **docking station** lets a laptop connect to lots of things with **one cable**. The user plugs in a single USB-C or Thunderbolt lead and instantly gets Ethernet, two monitors, USB devices and charging. Docks are common on office desks and a frequent support topic.

## Listing devices in PowerShell

When a USB device misbehaves, you can list what Windows currently sees. Open **PowerShell** and run:

```powershell
Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Where-Object Class -eq 'USB'
```

To see everything Windows detects (not just USB):

```powershell
Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Select-Object Class, FriendlyName, Status
```

If a device shows a Status of `Error`, that's a strong clue where the problem is.

## Your task

Walk over to a PC (or use a photo of one). Identify and write down **at least five ports** by shape: USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, RJ45 and a 3.5mm jack. Then open PowerShell, run `Get-PnpDevice -PresentOnly | Where-Object Class -eq 'USB'`, and note one USB device it lists.

quiz.q: Which port is small, oval, reversible (works either way up), and can carry power, video and data?
quiz.why: USB-C is the small oval reversible connector. Because it is reversible there is no wrong way up, and a single USB-C port can carry power, video and data at the same time.

quiz.q: A user wants to plug a wired network cable into their laptop. Which port do they need?
quiz.why: RJ45 is the square-ish 8-pin Ethernet port with a little clip. It is wider than a phone jack and is used for wired network connections.

quiz.q: Which of these is a VIDEO connector commonly found on monitors and TVs?
quiz.why: HDMI carries digital video and audio and is the most common modern display connector. RJ45 is networking, PS/2 is legacy keyboard/mouse, and 3.5mm is analogue audio.

quiz.q: Which connector is the older blue D-shaped video port with 15 pins that carries an analogue signal only?
quiz.why: VGA is the legacy blue 15-pin D-shaped port. It carries analogue video only (no audio) and is being replaced by HDMI and DisplayPort.

quiz.q: In one sentence, how can you tell USB-A apart from USB-C just by looking?
quiz.answer: USB-A is the flat rectangular connector that only fits one way up, while USB-C is the small rounded oval connector that is reversible and fits either way.
quiz.why: Shape is the fastest way to identify a port. USB-A is rectangular and one-way; USB-C is oval and reversible.

quiz.q: What is a docking station and why is it useful on a helpdesk?
quiz.answer: A docking station is a hub a laptop connects to (often by a single USB-C or Thunderbolt cable) that adds extra ports such as Ethernet, multiple monitors, USB and power, so a user can connect everything with one click.
quiz.why: Docks let a user plug in once and instantly connect monitors, network, keyboard, mouse and power, which is why they are common on office desks and a frequent support topic.

hd1-l05-operating-systems-overview.title: Operating systems overview: Windows, macOS, Linux & mobile
objectives: Explain what an operating system does, including the kernel, drivers, and file management
Compare a graphical user interface (GUI) with a command line interface (CLI)
Identify the main desktop operating systems and where each is commonly used
Compare Windows editions (Home vs Pro) and the NTFS file system
Describe the difference between Android and iOS on mobile devices
Check the operating system name and version from a terminal
hd1-l05-operating-systems-overview.body:
## What an operating system actually does

An **operating system** (OS) is the master program that sits between you and the hardware. Without it, a PC is just metal and silicon. The OS does several big jobs at once: it manages memory and the **CPU**, talks to hardware through **drivers**, organises your files, and controls who is allowed to do what through **user accounts**.

The heart of the OS is the **kernel**. The kernel decides which program gets the processor, how memory is shared, and how requests reach the hardware. You never click on the kernel directly — everything else is built on top of it.

## GUI vs CLI, drivers, and files

You interact with an OS in two main ways. A **GUI** (graphical user interface) is the windows, icons, and menus you click. A **CLI** (command line interface) is a text prompt where you type commands. Both control the same machine; the CLI is faster for repetitive admin tasks and is a core helpdesk skill.

A **driver** is a small piece of software that teaches the OS how to talk to a specific device — a printer, a graphics card, a webcam. **File management** is how the OS stores and finds your data, using a **file system** to organise folders and permissions.

## Windows: the business standard

**Windows** is by far the most common OS in business, so you will support it most. Two editions matter for the exam:

- **Windows Home** — for everyday personal use.
- **Windows Pro** — adds business features: domain join, Group Policy, and **BitLocker** encryption.

Windows uses the **NTFS** file system, which supports large drives, permissions, and encryption. You can check the version in seconds:

```powershell
Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object OsName, OsVersion
```

Or simply run `winver` to pop up a version window.

## macOS and Linux

**macOS** is Apple's desktop OS and runs only on **Apple hardware**. It is **Unix-based**, which means it shares a heritage with Linux and has a powerful built-in terminal. You will see it on designers' and executives' machines.

**Linux** is **open source** and **free**. Instead of one product, it comes in many **distributions** (distros) such as **Ubuntu**, Debian, and Fedora. Linux dominates **servers** and cloud computing because it is stable, lightweight, and free to deploy at scale.

## Mobile operating systems

Phones and tablets run their own systems. **Android** is **open source**, made by Google, and used by many manufacturers (Samsung, Google, and others). **iOS** (and **iPadOS** on tablets) is **closed source** and runs only on Apple devices, giving Apple tight control over the experience.

## Choosing an OS and the support lifecycle

There is no single "best" OS — you choose based on the job: Windows for business apps, macOS for Apple-centric creative work, Linux for servers and developers. Just as important is the **vendor lifecycle**: every OS reaches **end of support** (end of life), after which it stops receiving security updates. A technician must track these dates, because an unsupported OS is a security risk that needs upgrading or replacing.

> **A date you should know:** **Windows 10 reached end of support on 14 October 2025.** Microsoft offers paid **Extended Security Updates (ESU)** as a temporary bridge, but those machines should be migrated. **Windows 11 is the current supported client OS.** Lifecycle dates move, so always verify the current dates on Microsoft Learn before you act on them.

## Your task

On the computer in front of you, open a terminal and find out exactly which OS and version you are running. On Windows, open **PowerShell** and run `Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object OsName, OsVersion`, then also try `winver`. On macOS or Linux, open the terminal and run `uname -a`. Write down the OS name and version, then look up online whether that version is still in support — and note its end-of-life date if you can find it.

quiz.q: What is the core part of an operating system that manages memory, the CPU, and hardware called?
quiz.why: The kernel is the central part of the OS that controls memory, the processor, and access to hardware. Drivers, the desktop, and the browser all sit above it.

quiz.q: A small business runs accounting software, joins computers to a company network domain, and wants BitLocker drive encryption. Which Windows edition fits best?
quiz.why: Windows Pro adds business features like domain join, Group Policy, and BitLocker encryption that Windows Home does not include.

quiz.q: Which statement about Linux is correct?
options: It is made only by Apple for Apple hardware
It is open source, free to use, and common on servers
It cannot run a graphical desktop
quiz.why: Linux is open source and free, comes in many distributions such as Ubuntu, and is extremely common on servers. It can run with or without a graphical desktop.

quiz.q: Which mobile operating system is closed source and runs only on Apple devices?
quiz.why: iOS (and iPadOS) is Apple's closed, controlled system that runs only on Apple hardware. Android is open source and used by many manufacturers.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain the difference between a GUI and a CLI.
quiz.answer: A GUI (graphical user interface) lets you point and click on windows, icons, and menus, while a CLI (command line interface) lets you type text commands for the computer to run.
quiz.why: Both control the same OS. The GUI is friendlier for everyday use; the CLI is faster and scriptable, which is why helpdesk and admin work often uses it.

quiz.q: Why does it matter to a helpdesk technician that an operating system has reached end of support (end of life)?
quiz.answer: An out-of-support OS no longer receives security updates, so it becomes a serious security risk and usually must be upgraded or replaced.
quiz.why: Vendors set a support lifecycle. Once an OS is past end of life it stops getting patches, leaving known vulnerabilities open, so techs track these dates and plan upgrades.

hd1-l06-setting-up-windows.title: Setting up and navigating Windows
objectives: Navigate the Windows desktop: Start menu, taskbar, system tray, and search
Tell the difference between Settings and the classic Control Panel
Open File Explorer and find the C: drive, This PC, and your user profile
Explain local vs Microsoft accounts and standard vs administrator users
Open Task Manager and use it to end a frozen program
Use essential keyboard shortcuts and check for Windows Update
hd1-l06-setting-up-windows.body:
## The Windows desktop

When Windows finishes loading you land on the **desktop**. Along the bottom is the **taskbar**. On the left of the taskbar is the **Start menu** button — click it (or press the **Windows key**) to find apps, settings, and a search box. Type anything into **Search** and Windows will look for apps, files, and settings at once; this is often the fastest way to open something.

At the right end of the taskbar is the **system tray** (also called the notification area). It holds small icons for things running in the background — network, volume, battery, and updates. Click the little upward arrow to see hidden icons.

## Settings vs Control Panel

Windows has **two** places to change things. **Settings** is the modern app you open from Start; it covers most everyday options like display, network, accounts, and updates. **Control Panel** is the older, classic interface. Microsoft is slowly moving everything into Settings, but some advanced tools still live only in Control Panel.

Open Control Panel quickly from the Run box:

```text
Win+R  ->  type: control  ->  Enter
```

As a technician you will use both, so get comfortable switching between them.

## File Explorer and folders

**File Explorer** is how you browse files and folders. Open it with **Win+E**. In the left pane, click **This PC** to see your drives. The main drive is the **C: drive** ("C colon"), where Windows itself is installed.

Two folders matter most:

- `C:\Windows` — Windows system files. Do not delete things here.
- `C:\Users\<your name>` — your **user profile**, holding your Documents, Downloads, and Desktop.

## User accounts

Every person who signs in has an **account**. A **local account** lives only on that PC. A **Microsoft account** signs in with an email and syncs settings across devices.

Accounts also have a permission level. A **standard user** can run apps but cannot change system-wide settings. An **administrator** can install software and change anything. For safety, most people should be standard users; admin rights are used only when needed.

## Task Manager and shortcuts

When a program freezes, open **Task Manager** with **Ctrl+Shift+Esc**. Select the stuck app and click **End task** to force it closed.

Learn these shortcuts — they make you fast:

```text
Win+E      open File Explorer
Win+R      open the Run box
Win+L      lock the screen
Alt+Tab    switch between open windows
```

From the Run box you can launch tools directly:

```powershell
winver   # shows the exact Windows version and build
cmd      # opens the Command Prompt
control  # opens Control Panel
```

## Windows Update

Keeping Windows patched closes security holes and fixes bugs. Open **Settings**, choose **Windows Update**, and click **Check for updates**. On a helpdesk, "have you installed the latest updates?" is one of your first questions.

## Your task

Open File Explorer with **Win+E** and navigate to `C:\Users` and find your own profile folder. Then press **Win+R**, type `winver`, and write down your exact Windows edition and build number. Finally, open **Settings**, go to **Windows Update**, and note whether your PC is up to date.

quiz.q: Which keyboard shortcut opens File Explorer instantly?
quiz.why: Win+E (the Windows key plus E) opens File Explorer from anywhere in Windows. Win+F opens the Feedback Hub, so it is a tempting but wrong choice.

quiz.q: What is the fastest way to open Task Manager directly?
quiz.why: Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens Task Manager directly. Ctrl+Alt+Del works too, but it shows a menu first, so it is one extra step.

quiz.q: Where are a user's personal Documents, Downloads, and Desktop folders stored by default?
options: In the user profile under C:\Users
quiz.why: Each account gets a profile folder at C:\Users\<name> that holds their Documents, Downloads, Desktop, and settings. Windows system files live in C:\Windows.

quiz.q: Which type of account can install software and change system-wide settings?
quiz.why: An administrator can install programs and change settings for the whole machine. Standard users are limited for safety, which is why helpdesk often elevates a task rather than handing out admin rights.

quiz.q: Name the Run command that displays the exact Windows version and build number.
quiz.answer: winver
quiz.why: Press Win+R, type winver, and press Enter. A small box shows the Windows edition, version, and build, which is the first thing to confirm when troubleshooting.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the difference between Settings and Control Panel?
quiz.answer: Settings is the modern Windows app for most everyday options, while Control Panel is the older classic interface that still holds some advanced or legacy tools.
quiz.why: Microsoft is slowly moving everything into Settings, but technicians still open Control Panel for items that have not moved yet, such as some device and account tools.

hd1-l07-laptops-and-mobile-devices.title: Laptops & mobile devices
objectives: Explain the trade-offs between laptops and desktops (portability, power, repairability)
Identify laptop-specific parts: Li-ion battery, SODIMM RAM, M.2 storage, integrated display, Fn keys, touchpad
Describe how laptops are powered and charged, including AC adapters and USB-C Power Delivery
Explain what a docking station does and when to use one
Compare mobile device types: smartphones, tablets, and 2-in-1s
Diagnose common laptop issues such as overheating, won't charge, and a dim screen
hd1-l07-laptops-and-mobile-devices.body:
## Laptop vs desktop: the trade-offs

A **laptop** packs a whole computer — screen, keyboard, trackpad, battery, and all the internals — into one portable shell. A **desktop** spreads those parts across a roomy case with separate monitor and keyboard. The difference is all about trade-offs.

- **Portability:** laptops win — you can carry them anywhere and run on battery.
- **Power & cooling:** desktops win — bigger cases mean faster parts and better airflow.
- **Repairability & upgrades:** desktops win — parts are modular and easy to swap, while laptops are tightly packed and increasingly have RAM and storage **soldered** to the board.

On a helpdesk you will support far more laptops than you might expect, so knowing their quirks matters.

## Laptop-specific parts

Laptops use shrunk-down versions of familiar components:

- **Battery** — a rechargeable **Lithium-ion (Li-ion)** pack that powers the laptop unplugged.
- **SODIMM RAM** — a **Small Outline DIMM**, the compact memory stick laptops use instead of full-size desktop DIMMs.
- **M.2 storage** — a small stick-shaped SSD that plugs flat onto the board, replacing bulky 2.5-inch drives.
- **Integrated display** — the screen is built in and connected by a delicate ribbon cable.
- **Function (Fn) key** — a modifier that unlocks a second layer of shortcuts (brightness, volume, Wi-Fi) printed on the keys.
- **Touchpad** — the built-in pointing surface that replaces a mouse.

## Power & charging

Most laptops charge from an **AC adapter** (the "power brick") that converts wall power to low-voltage DC. Each adapter supplies a specific wattage — too weak an adapter may run the laptop but not charge it.

Modern laptops increasingly charge over **USB-C Power Delivery (USB-C PD)**, where a single USB-C cable carries power, data, and video at once. That is why one charger can power a phone, tablet, or laptop.

A **docking station** turns a laptop into a desk setup: connect one cable and you instantly get power, monitors, wired network, and USB devices. Great for staff who roam but want a full workstation at their desk.

## Mobile devices

Beyond laptops you will support:

- **Smartphones** — pocket computers with cellular data and touchscreens.
- **Tablets** — larger touchscreens, often with optional keyboards.
- **2-in-1s** — laptops whose screens detach or fold back to act as a tablet.

These share laptop concerns: Li-ion batteries, limited repairability, and wireless connectivity.

## Battery health & common issues

Li-ion batteries age with **heat** and with sitting at very high or very low charge. Keep devices cool and avoid leaving them pinned at 100% in hot spots. Windows can produce a detailed battery report:

```powershell
powercfg /batteryreport
```

That saves an HTML file showing design capacity versus current full-charge capacity — a great way to prove a battery is worn out. You can also query the battery quickly:

```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Battery
```

Common faults to recognise:

- **Overheating** — dust-clogged fans and vents; clean airflow and check it isn't on a soft surface.
- **Won't charge** — try a known-good adapter and cable, check the port for debris, and confirm it isn't simply too hot.
- **Dim screen** — check the brightness Fn keys first, then the power plan and display ribbon.

## Your task

On a Windows laptop, open PowerShell and run `powercfg /batteryreport`. Open the saved HTML file and find the **design capacity** and the **full charge capacity**. Write down both numbers and work out roughly how much battery health has been lost. Then run `Get-CimInstance Win32_Battery` and note the battery status.

quiz.q: Which RAM form factor is designed for laptops because it is physically smaller than a desktop module?
quiz.why: SODIMM (Small Outline DIMM) is the compact memory module used in laptops; full-size DIMMs are used in desktops and would not fit a laptop's tight chassis.

quiz.q: A user's laptop is plugged in but the battery says "plugged in, not charging" and the device feels very hot. What is the most likely first thing to check?
options: Airflow and vents — overheating can pause charging, and blocked vents cause it
quiz.why: Heat and blocked vents are common, cheap-to-fix causes; dust-clogged fans and vents make a laptop run hot and can stop the battery charging. Always check the simple, physical things first.

quiz.q: What does USB-C Power Delivery (PD) let a laptop do?
options: Charge over the same USB-C cable that also carries data and video
quiz.why: USB-C PD negotiates higher voltages and currents so a single USB-C cable can charge the laptop while also moving data and video, which is why many modern laptops charge from a USB-C dock or phone charger.

quiz.q: Why are laptops generally harder to repair and upgrade than desktops?
options: They run a different operating system
Parts are smaller, tightly packed, and often soldered to the board
quiz.why: To stay thin and light, laptops pack components tightly and increasingly solder RAM and storage to the motherboard, so upgrades and repairs are limited compared with a roomy, modular desktop.

quiz.q: What does the Fn (Function) key on a laptop keyboard do?
quiz.answer: It is a modifier key that, when held with another key (often the F1-F12 row), triggers a secondary action such as adjusting screen brightness, volume, Wi-Fi, or the external display.
quiz.why: Laptops cram many controls onto few keys, so Fn unlocks a second layer of hardware shortcuts printed on the keys, like brightness, volume, and toggling the touchpad or wireless.

quiz.q: Name one thing a user can do to look after a Li-ion laptop battery's long-term health.
quiz.answer: Avoid keeping it at extreme charge or heat — for example don't leave it constantly at 100% in a hot place; keeping it cool and roughly between 20% and 80% helps it last longer.
quiz.why: Lithium-ion batteries age faster under high heat and when held at very high or very low charge for long periods, so moderate charge levels and good cooling extend their useful life.

hd1-l08-printers-and-printing.title: Printers and printing
objectives: Explain the differences between inkjet, laser, thermal, and 3D printers
Describe the seven steps of the laser printing process at a high level
Connect a printer over USB, network IP, wireless, or as a shared printer
Explain the role of printer drivers and the Windows print spooler
Troubleshoot common faults like paper jams, streaks, stuck spoolers, and offline printers
Identify the right consumables: toner for laser, ink for inkjet
hd1-l08-printers-and-printing.body:
## Printer types you'll meet on the helpdesk

Most printers fall into a few families. An **inkjet** printer sprays tiny droplets of liquid **ink** onto the page; they are cheap to buy, great for photos, but the ink can smudge and nozzles clog if unused. A **laser** printer uses a laser, a drum, and powdered **toner** fused with heat; they are fast, sharp for text, and cheaper per page in busy offices. A **thermal** printer uses heat to darken special paper or melt a ribbon and is common for **receipts, labels, and shipping**. A **3D** printer is a different beast entirely: it builds physical objects layer by layer from melted plastic filament. As a Tier 1 tech, you'll spend most of your time on laser and inkjet office printers.

## How a laser printer actually works

Laser printing follows **seven steps** in order. You don't need to memorise the physics, but knowing the sequence helps you locate a fault:

1. **Processing** — the printer receives the job and builds the page image in memory.
2. **Charging** — a uniform negative charge is applied to the rotating drum.
3. **Exposing** — the laser writes the image by discharging spots on the drum.
4. **Developing** — toner sticks to the discharged areas, forming the image.
5. **Transferring** — the toner image is moved onto the paper.
6. **Fusing** — heat and pressure melt the toner so it bonds permanently.
7. **Cleaning** — leftover toner and charge are wiped so the drum is ready again.

A repeating mark or **streak** down every page often points to a damaged drum or dirty fuser.

## Connecting printers

There are four common connection methods. **USB** is a direct cable to one PC — simplest, but only that PC can print. **Network / IP** printers sit on the LAN with their own **I P address**, so anyone on the network can reach them. **Wireless (Wi-Fi)** printers join the network without a cable. A **shared** printer is one PC's local printer that it shares out to others. For network printers, knowing the IP lets you browse to the printer's web page or add it directly.

## Drivers and the print spooler

Windows needs a **driver** — software that translates documents into the printer's language. The **print spooler** is a Windows service that accepts jobs, queues them, and feeds them to the printer one at a time. When printing breaks, these two are the usual suspects. List printers and the queue with PowerShell:

```powershell
Get-Printer
Get-PrintJob -PrinterName "Office-Laser"
```

## Common issues and quick fixes

**Paper jams** — power off, gently remove paper in the direction of travel, check for torn scraps. **Streaks or faded print** — low or faulty toner/ink, or a dirty drum. **Stuck spooler** — jobs pile up and nothing prints; clear the queue and restart the service. **Offline printer** — Windows can't reach it; check the cable, Wi-Fi, or IP, and confirm it's the default printer. To clear a hung queue:

```powershell
Get-PrintJob -PrinterName "Office-Laser" | Remove-PrintJob
Restart-Service -Name Spooler
```

## Consumables

Match the supply to the printer: **laser printers use toner cartridges** (dry powder), **inkjets use ink cartridges or tanks** (liquid). Ordering the wrong one is a common Tier 1 mistake. Always note the exact model number before ordering.

## Your task

On a Windows PC, open PowerShell and run `Get-Printer` to list the installed printers. Pick one, run `Get-PrintJob -PrinterName "<name>"` to view its queue, then practise restarting the spooler with `Restart-Service -Name Spooler`. Write down the printer's connection type (USB, network IP, or wireless) and whether it uses toner or ink.

quiz.q: Which printer type uses a laser, a charged drum, and heat to fuse toner onto paper?
quiz.why: A laser printer charges a drum, uses a laser to write the image, attracts powdered toner, then fuses it to the paper with heat and pressure. Inkjets spray liquid ink instead.

quiz.q: A user reports their printer shows as 'Offline' even though it is powered on. What is a sensible FIRST check?
options: Check the cable or network connection and that the printer is set as default
quiz.why: Offline usually means Windows cannot reach the printer. Check the USB cable or network/Wi-Fi connection first before touching consumables or doing anything drastic.

quiz.q: What does the Windows print spooler service do?
options: It fuses toner to the paper
It manages and queues print jobs being sent to printers
It scans documents into the computer
quiz.why: The spooler (Spooler service) accepts print jobs, queues them, and feeds them to the printer in order. If it gets stuck, restarting the service clears the jam.

quiz.q: Which command lists the printers installed on a Windows machine?
quiz.why: Get-Printer is the PowerShell cmdlet that returns the installed printers and their status, a quick first step when diagnosing printing problems.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the difference between toner and ink?
quiz.answer: Toner is the dry powder used by laser printers and fused with heat, while ink is the liquid used by inkjet printers and sprayed onto the page.
quiz.why: Knowing which consumable a printer uses tells you what to order and what causes faults: dry toner streaks versus wet ink smudges or clogged nozzles.

quiz.q: A print job is stuck in the queue and nothing prints. Name a PowerShell command that often fixes this.
quiz.answer: Restart-Service -Name Spooler (after optionally clearing stuck jobs with Get-PrintJob / Remove-PrintJob).
quiz.why: Restarting the Spooler service clears a hung queue so jobs can flow again; it is one of the most common helpdesk printing fixes.

hd1-l09-safety-esd-toolkit.title: Safety, ESD and the technician's toolkit
objectives: Explain what electrostatic discharge is and why tiny static charges destroy components
Apply ESD prevention using an anti-static wrist strap, ESD mat, and anti-static bags
Identify electrical hazards and explain why a PSU and CRT monitor must never be opened
Apply personal and environmental safety practices for lifting, fire, fumes, and cables
Explain how to dispose of batteries, toner, and e-waste safely using SDS sheets
Identify the core tools in a technician's toolkit and what each one is for
hd1-l09-safety-esd-toolkit.body:
## What is ESD and why does it matter

**Electrostatic discharge (ESD)** is the sudden flow of electricity between two objects at different charges — the tiny zap you feel touching a door handle. You only *feel* static above about **3,000 volts**, but sensitive chips inside a PC can be damaged by **less than 100 volts**. That means you can quietly destroy a part — or weaken it so it fails weeks later — without ever feeling a thing. This is why ESD is the number one hazard to the *hardware* you touch.

## Preventing ESD

The goal is to keep you and the equipment at the **same electrical potential** so no charge can jump. This is called **equipotential bonding**.

```text
ESD prevention checklist
[ ] Wear an anti-static wrist strap, clipped to bare metal on the chassis
[ ] Work on an ESD (anti-static) mat, not a carpet
[ ] Touch the metal case before handling any component
[ ] Hold cards by the edges, never the gold contacts or chips
[ ] Keep spare parts inside anti-static bags until needed
[ ] Avoid wool jumpers and shuffling on carpet in socks
```
