Identify the **problem** and gather symptoms, form a **theory** of the likely cause, **test** the theory, fix it, **verify** full functionality, and finally **document** what you did. The tools below slot into that flow: most begin with *finding the evidence* before changing anything.

A quick triage habit: ask what changed. New driver, new update, new app, or new hardware right before the problem started is your strongest lead.

## Event Viewer: find the real error

Vague symptoms ("it just crashes") hide specific errors in the logs. Open **Event Viewer** (`eventvwr.msc`) and look under **Windows Logs > System** and **Application**. Filter for **Error** and **Critical** around the time of the fault.

```powershell
Get-EventLog -LogName System -EntryType Error -Newest 5

Index Time          Source        Message
----- ----          ------        -------
 4821 Jun 16 09:14  disk          The device has a bad block.
 4810 Jun 16 09:02  Service Ctrl  A service terminated unexpectedly.
```

That "bad block" line instantly points you at the disk — now your testing is targeted, not guesswork.

## Repairing system files: sfc then DISM

When Windows itself behaves oddly, suspect corrupt **system files**. Run **System File Checker** from an elevated terminal:

```cmd
sfc /scannow

Verification 100% complete.
Windows Resource Protection found corrupt files and successfully repaired them.
```

If sfc reports it *couldn't* repair everything, the underlying component store is damaged. Repair it with **DISM**, then run sfc again:

```cmd
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
```

## Disk and memory checks

For file-system errors or a failing drive, run **chkdsk**. With `/f` it fixes errors; on the system drive it schedules itself for the next restart because it needs exclusive access.

```cmd
chkdsk C: /f
```

For random crashes that smell like bad RAM, run **Windows Memory Diagnostic**:

```cmd
mdsched
```

It restarts the PC and tests memory before Windows loads, then reports results after boot.

## Recovery: Safe Mode and System Restore

When Windows won't start normally — often after a bad driver — boot into **Safe Mode**, which loads only essential drivers so you can remove the culprit. You reach it from `msconfig` (Boot tab > Safe boot) or the recovery menu. If a recent change broke things, **System Restore** rolls protected system files and settings back to an earlier **restore point** without touching personal files.

The last step of the method is **documentation**. Note the symptom, the root cause, and the exact fix. One solved ticket then becomes searchable knowledge that helps the whole team solve the next one faster.

## Your task

On a test PC, open Event Viewer and find one Error or Warning in the System log — note its Source and time. Open an elevated terminal and run `sfc /scannow`, then record the result line. (Do not run chkdsk /f on your only drive unless you can reboot.) Finally, open `msconfig`, look at the Boot tab and confirm where you would enable Safe boot — then write a short 'troubleshooting note' documenting an imaginary crash: symptom, the log evidence you'd look for, and the tool you'd use to fix it.

quiz.q: A PC shows random crashes. Where do you look first to find the underlying error messages logged by Windows?
quiz.why: Event Viewer records System, Application and Security logs. Filtering for Errors and Critical events around the crash time usually reveals the offending component or driver.

quiz.q: You suspect corrupt protected system files are causing instability. Which command scans and repairs them?
quiz.why: sfc /scannow (System File Checker) scans protected system files and restores correct versions. If sfc can't fix the underlying component store, you then run DISM.

quiz.q: sfc reports it could not repair some files. What is the correct next step before re-running sfc?
options: Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth to repair the component store
Run chkdsk to format the disk
quiz.why: DISM repairs the underlying Windows image / component store that sfc draws from. After DISM completes, re-running sfc /scannow can then succeed.

quiz.q: A user reports the PC won't start normally after installing a bad driver. Which startup option loads Windows with a minimal set of drivers so you can remove it?
quiz.why: Safe Mode boots Windows with only essential drivers and services, letting you uninstall the bad driver or run repairs without the faulty component loading.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does chkdsk /f do and why might it ask to run at next restart?
quiz.answer: chkdsk /f checks the disk for file-system errors and fixes them; it schedules itself for restart when the volume is in use (such as the system drive) because it needs exclusive access to repair it.
quiz.why: A volume that is currently in use can't be locked, so chkdsk defers to the next boot when it can get exclusive access to the drive.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why should you document the root cause and fix at the end of a troubleshooting job?
quiz.answer: So the resolution is searchable for the next technician and the same problem can be recognised and fixed faster, or prevented entirely.
quiz.why: Documentation closes the loop in the troubleshooting methodology and turns one solved ticket into reusable knowledge for the whole team.

hd3-l05-malware-threats-remediation.title: Malware, threats and remediation
objectives: Identify common malware types: virus, worm, trojan, ransomware, spyware
Recognise social-engineering attacks like phishing and tailgating
Follow the CompTIA seven-step malware removal procedure in order
Quarantine an infected system and scan it from a known-good tool
Use Windows Defender and Task Manager to spot and stop suspicious activity
Educate the end user to prevent re-infection
hd3-l05-malware-threats-remediation.body:
## Know your enemy: malware types

You can't fight what you can't name. A **virus** attaches to a file and spreads when that file runs. A **worm** spreads by itself across a network with no user action. A **trojan** disguises itself as something useful to trick you into running it. **Ransomware** encrypts your data and demands payment. **Spyware** quietly harvests information, and a **rootkit** buries itself deep in the OS to hide other malware. Recognising the symptom pattern points you at the right fix.

## The human attack: social engineering

The easiest way past security is often the person, not the firewall. **Phishing** emails impersonate a trusted sender to steal credentials; **spear phishing** targets a specific individual. **Tailgating** is following an authorised person through a secure door. The defence is awareness: legitimate IT never asks for your password by email, and a healthy pause before clicking stops most attacks.

## The CompTIA malware removal steps

A+ expects you to remediate in a fixed order. Memorise it:

1. **Investigate and verify** malware symptoms.
2. **Quarantine** the infected system (disconnect it from the network).
3. **Disable System Restore** in Windows (so restore points can't re-infect).
4. **Remediate**: update anti-malware definitions, then scan and remove — using Safe Mode or a pre-installation/bootable environment if needed.
5. **Schedule scans and run updates**.
6. **Enable System Restore and create a fresh restore point**.
7. **Educate the end user**.

Step 2 matters because an infected PC on the network can spread the threat. Step 3 matters because malware can hide inside restore points.

## Hunting with the tools you have

Start by looking at what's running. **Task Manager** can reveal a strange, resource-hungry process you don't recognise:

```powershell
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, Id, CPU

Name        Id   CPU
----        --   ---
svch0st   6612  912.4
chrome    9120  120.0
```

That misspelled `svch0st` (zero instead of o) is a classic disguise. Then run a full scan with **Windows Security / Microsoft Defender** — from the command line if you like:

```powershell
Start-MpScan -ScanType FullScan
Get-MpThreatDetection
```

For stubborn infections, scan from **Safe Mode** or trusted **bootable media** so the malware can't defend itself.

## Harden and prevent re-infection

Cleaning is only half the job. Confirm **Windows Update** is current, that real-time protection is **on**, and that the firewall is enabled. Then the most important fix of all is human: explain to the user *how* it happened — the dodgy download, the phishing link — so the same mistake doesn't undo your work tomorrow.

## Your task

On your own PC: open Windows Security and confirm Virus & threat protection is on and definitions are up to date. From PowerShell, run `Get-MpComputerStatus` and note whether real-time protection is enabled. Open Task Manager and scan the Processes list for anything you don't recognise (research the name before judging it). Finally, write the seven CompTIA malware-removal steps from memory, in order, and add one sentence on how you would explain a phishing incident to a non-technical user.

quiz.q: A user's files are all encrypted and a message demands payment to unlock them. Which type of malware is this?
quiz.why: Ransomware encrypts the victim's data and demands payment for the decryption key. The other types steal information, push adverts, or hide deep in the OS respectively.

quiz.q: What is the FIRST step in CompTIA's malware removal process once you suspect an infection?
options: Identify and research the malware symptoms
quiz.why: The process begins with investigating and verifying malware symptoms. You can't remediate effectively until you know what you're dealing with.

quiz.q: Why do you disable System Restore (and delete restore points) during malware remediation?
options: Because restore points can re-infect the PC by restoring the malware
To free disk space for the scan
Because Windows requires it before any scan
To make the PC boot faster
quiz.why: Malware can be saved inside restore points. If you clean the system but later restore an infected point, the malware comes right back — so you disable and clear them, then recreate a clean point afterward.

quiz.q: A staff member gets an urgent email 'from IT' asking them to confirm their password via a link. What attack is this, and what should they do?
options: Phishing; do not click, report it to IT
quiz.why: This is phishing — a social-engineering attack that tricks users into revealing credentials. The correct response is to not click, not reply, and report it. Legitimate IT never asks for your password by email.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why should you scan a suspected-infected PC with a tool from a known-good source (such as bootable media or Safe Mode) rather than just trusting the installed antivirus?
quiz.answer: Because sophisticated malware can disable or blind the installed antivirus, so scanning from outside the infected environment (bootable media or Safe Mode) gives a trustworthy result.
quiz.why: Rootkits and advanced malware tamper with the running OS and its security tools, so a scan from a clean external environment is far harder to deceive.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the final step of the malware removal process and why does it matter?
quiz.answer: Educate the end user about safe habits and how the infection happened, because the same behaviour will otherwise lead to re-infection.
quiz.why: Technical cleanup fixes today's problem; user education prevents tomorrow's. It is the final CompTIA remediation step for good reason.

hd3-l06-security-best-practices.title: Security best practices: passwords, MFA & encryption
objectives: Explain why length and uniqueness beat complexity in modern password policy
Configure local account and lockout policies from the command line
Describe how multi-factor authentication stops stolen-password attacks
Enable and check BitLocker full-disk encryption with manage-bde
Save and use a BitLocker recovery key during a lockout
Apply the principle of least privilege to user accounts
hd3-l06-security-best-practices.body:
## Why security is a Tier 1 job

Most breaches do not start with a clever hacker; they start with a weak password, a reused password, or a laptop left on a train. As a helpdesk technician you are the person who actually turns the controls on. Three controls cover the majority of real risk: strong **authentication**, **multi-factor authentication (MFA)**, and **encryption**. Learn these and you protect both the user and the business.

## Passwords and account policy

Forget the old advice about swapping letters for symbols every month. Modern guidance favours **length and uniqueness**: a long **passphrase** is both stronger and easier to remember than `P@ss1!`. You also want an **account lockout** so attackers cannot guess endlessly, and you want to follow **least privilege** — give users a standard account, not local administrator, unless they genuinely need it.

You can inspect and set local policy from the command line:

```cmd
net accounts
:: Lockout threshold: Never  -> set it
net accounts /lockoutthreshold:5 /lockoutduration:15

:: List local users and check who is an admin
net user
net localgroup administrators
```

Sample output:

```cmd
Lockout threshold:                 5
Lockout duration (minutes):        15
```

## Multi-factor authentication

A password is **something you know**. MFA adds **something you have** (a phone or token) or **something you are** (a fingerprint). Even if a password is phished, the attacker cannot complete the login without the second factor. As a technician you will help users enrol in an authenticator app, generate **backup codes**, and recover when a device is lost. The key teaching point for users: approve a prompt **only** when you are the one signing in.

## Full-disk encryption with BitLocker

**BitLocker** encrypts the whole drive so a lost or stolen laptop is just an expensive paperweight, not a data leak. On business machines it usually relies on the **TPM** chip to release the key automatically at boot. Check and enable it with `manage-bde`:

```powershell
# Check status of every drive
manage-bde -status

# Turn BitLocker on for C: and save the recovery key to a file
manage-bde -on C: -recoverypassword
```

Sample output:

```powershell
Volume C: [OSDisk]
    Conversion Status:    Used Space Only Encrypted
    Percentage Encrypted: 100.0%
    Protection Status:    Protection On
```

## Recovery keys — do not skip this

If the TPM, firmware, or boot configuration changes, BitLocker demands the **recovery key**. Save it somewhere off the machine: a Microsoft account, Azure AD/Entra, a printout, or a USB stick stored elsewhere. A recovery key locked inside the drive you cannot open is worthless.

```powershell
# Show the numeric recovery password / key protectors
manage-bde -protectors -get C:
```

## Your task

On a test or virtual machine: run `net accounts` and set a lockout threshold of 5 attempts; confirm the change. Then run `manage-bde -status` to record the encryption state of C:. If BitLocker is available, capture the recovery key with `manage-bde -protectors -get C:` and write where you would store it safely. Summarise in three bullet points how passwords, MFA and encryption each protect a different stage of an attack.

quiz.q: Which password policy gives the best real-world protection against guessing and reuse attacks?
options: Force a change every 30 days with three special characters
Require long, unique passphrases and screen against known-breached passwords
Require exactly eight characters with one capital letter
Disable lockout so users never get blocked
quiz.why: Modern guidance (NIST and Microsoft) favours length and uniqueness over forced rotation and arbitrary complexity, and blocking known-breached passwords stops reuse attacks.

quiz.q: A user's password was phished. What single control would most likely have stopped the attacker from logging in?
quiz.why: MFA requires a second factor the attacker does not have, so a stolen password alone is not enough to sign in.

quiz.q: What does BitLocker protect against?
options: Data being read from a lost or stolen drive
quiz.why: BitLocker provides full-disk encryption, so data on a lost or stolen drive cannot be read without the key or recovery key.

quiz.q: Which command shows the encryption status of all drives on a Windows machine?
quiz.why: manage-bde -status reports protection status, encryption percentage and method for each volume; the other commands lock, refresh policy, or list users.

quiz.q: In one sentence, define the principle of least privilege and give one example.
quiz.answer: Least privilege means giving each user only the access they need to do their job and nothing more — for example, making a normal user a standard account instead of a local administrator.
quiz.why: Limiting privileges shrinks the damage an attacker or mistake can cause, which is why standard accounts are the default and admin rights are granted only when needed.

quiz.q: Why should you save the BitLocker recovery key somewhere other than the encrypted machine itself?
quiz.answer: If you are locked out (for example after a TPM or firmware change) you need the recovery key to unlock the drive, and it is useless if it is stored only on the drive you cannot access.
quiz.why: The recovery key is the fallback when normal unlock fails, so it must live somewhere independent — a Microsoft account, Azure AD, a printout, or a USB key kept elsewhere.

hd3-l07-backup-recovery-imaging.title: Backup, recovery and imaging
objectives: Explain the 3-2-1 backup rule and why it matters
Tell the difference between a file backup, a system image, and a recovery point
Restore user files with File History
Create and restore a system image backup with wbadmin
Describe how disk imaging speeds up rebuilding many machines
Decide which recovery method fits a given failure
hd3-l07-backup-recovery-imaging.body:
## Backups exist for the bad day

Nobody appreciates a backup until a disk dies, a laptop is stolen, or ransomware locks every file. As a technician your job is to make sure that bad day is survivable. That means knowing the difference between backing up **files**, backing up a whole **system image**, and being able to **recover** when something fails. Get this right and a catastrophic failure becomes an inconvenience.

## The 3-2-1 rule

The industry shorthand is **3-2-1**: keep **3 copies** of your data, on **2 different media** (for example an internal disk and an external drive or cloud), with at least **1 copy off-site or offline**. The off-site copy is what saves you from fire, theft, or ransomware that encrypts everything it can reach on the network. A backup that sits next to the original on the same machine is barely a backup at all.

## File backups vs system images

There are two flavours you must keep straight. A **file backup** copies documents, photos and settings — small, frequent, easy to restore one item from. A **system image** is a block-level snapshot of the entire drive: operating system, installed apps and settings as one unit. You restore a file backup to get a document back; you restore an image to rebuild a whole machine after a disk failure.

On Windows, **File History** handles versioned file backups. There is no first-class PowerShell cmdlet for it — File History is turned on and managed from Control Panel, and its settings live in a config file under your profile. So to "check status" from PowerShell you confirm that a configuration exists:

```powershell
# Open the File History control panel to turn it on or check settings
control /name Microsoft.FileHistory
# Check status from PowerShell: a config file means File History has been set up
Get-ChildItem "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\FileHistory\Configuration\" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

If that folder contains a `Config*.xml` file, File History has been configured for the user; an empty or missing folder means it has never been turned on. To restore a single file, open **File History** from Control Panel, browse to the file, pick a version, and click the green restore button.

## System image with wbadmin

For a full image, `wbadmin` is the built-in command-line tool. Run it from an **elevated** prompt:

```cmd
:: Create a system image of C: onto drive E:
wbadmin start backup -backupTarget:E: -include:C: -allCritical -quiet

:: List the backups you have
wbadmin get versions
```

Sample output:

```cmd
Backup time: 16/06/2026 09:14
Backup target: Fixed Disk labelled E:
Version identifier: 06/16/2026-08:14
Can recover: Volume(s), File(s), Application(s), Bare Metal Recovery, System State
```

To recover a whole system, boot into the **Windows Recovery Environment** and choose **System Image Recovery**, pointing it at the image you created.

## Imaging for fleets

**Imaging** takes the system-image idea and scales it. You configure one machine perfectly — the **gold image** — capture it, then deploy that single image to many computers so they all start identical. Tools like DISM capture and apply Windows images (`.wim` files):

```powershell
DISM /Capture-Image /ImageFile:D:\gold.wim /CaptureDir:C:\ /Name:"Gold build"
```

This is how IT departments rebuild a broken laptop in twenty minutes instead of a day.

## Your task

On a test or virtual machine: turn on **File History** to an external or second drive, create a test document, then delete it and restore the previous version. Next, from an elevated prompt run `wbadmin get versions` to inspect any system backups present (or create one with `wbadmin start backup` if you have a spare target). Finally, write two or three sentences mapping each of these failures to the right recovery method: a single deleted file, a dead boot drive, and rebuilding ten identical machines.

quiz.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule recommend?
options: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with 1 copy off-site
quiz.why: 3-2-1 means keep three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with at least one copy stored off-site, so a single failure or disaster can't wipe everything.

quiz.q: A user deleted a single document yesterday and needs it back. Which is the quickest appropriate tool on Windows?
quiz.why: File History keeps versioned copies of user files, so a single deleted or changed document can be restored quickly without touching the rest of the system.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a system image over a file-only backup?
options: It is smaller and faster to create
It restores the whole OS, apps and settings as one unit
quiz.why: A system image is a block-level snapshot of the whole drive, so restoring it brings back the operating system, installed applications and settings together — ideal after a disk failure.

quiz.q: Which command creates a system image backup on Windows?
quiz.why: wbadmin start backup creates a backup including a system image; the others repair files, check the disk, or wipe a disk respectively.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why imaging is useful when setting up many identical computers.
quiz.answer: You configure one machine perfectly, capture it as an image, and deploy that single image to many computers so they all start identical without repeating the setup each time.
quiz.why: Imaging captures a known-good build once and clones it to many devices, saving hours and guaranteeing consistency across a fleet.

quiz.q: Why should at least one backup copy be kept off-site or offline?
quiz.answer: So that a local disaster such as fire, theft, or ransomware that encrypts everything reachable on the network cannot destroy every copy of the data at once.
quiz.why: An off-site or offline copy is isolated from local failures and online threats, which is the whole point of the '1' in the 3-2-1 rule.

hd3-l08-virtualization-and-cloud-basics.title: Virtualization and cloud basics
objectives: Explain what a hypervisor and a virtual machine are
Tell type 1 (bare-metal) from type 2 (hosted) hypervisors
Create and manage a Hyper-V virtual machine from PowerShell
Describe the cloud service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
Tell public, private and hybrid cloud deployment models apart
Recognise common support scenarios involving VMs and cloud apps
hd3-l08-virtualization-and-cloud-basics.body:
## What virtualization actually means

**Virtualization** lets one physical computer pretend to be many. A **virtual machine (VM)** is a complete computer — its own OS, disk, and network — running as software inside another machine. The thing that makes this possible is the **hypervisor**, the software layer that shares the real hardware (CPU, RAM, disk) among several VMs and keeps them isolated from each other.

For a helpdesk technician this is everyday gold: you can test a risky fix, run an old application, or reproduce a user's problem on a throwaway VM without touching a production machine.

## Type 1 vs type 2 hypervisors

There are two kinds. A **type 1 (bare-metal)** hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no host OS underneath — think **Hyper-V** on a server or VMware **ESXi**. A **type 2 (hosted)** hypervisor runs as an application on top of your existing OS — think **VirtualBox** or VMware Workstation on your laptop. Type 1 is for servers and performance; type 2 is for convenience on a desktop.

## Running a VM with Hyper-V

Windows includes **Hyper-V** (a type 1 hypervisor) on Pro and Enterprise editions. Manage it with PowerShell:

```powershell
# See what VMs exist and their state
Get-VM

# Create a new VM with 4 GB RAM and a new virtual disk
New-VM -Name "Test-Win11" -MemoryStartupBytes 4GB -NewVHDPath "C:\VMs\test.vhdx" -NewVHDSizeBytes 60GB

# Start it
Start-VM -Name "Test-Win11"
```

Sample output:

```powershell
Name        State   CPUUsage(%)   MemoryAssigned(M)   Uptime
----        -----   -----------   -----------------   ------
Test-Win11  Running 1             4096                00:00:42
```

## The cloud: someone else's computer, on demand

The **cloud** is computing you rent over the internet instead of owning. The three classic **service models** describe how much the provider manages for you:

- **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent raw VMs, storage and networking, and you manage the OS and apps. Example: an Azure or AWS virtual machine.
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service): you deploy your code onto a managed platform and never touch the servers.
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service): you just use a finished app in the browser. Example: Microsoft 365 or Gmail.

A quick way to spin up cloud infrastructure with the Azure CLI:

```bash
# Log in, then create a resource group and a small VM
az login
az group create --name demo-rg --location uksouth
az vm create --resource-group demo-rg --name demo-vm --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_B1s
```

## Deployment models

Where the cloud lives matters too. **Public cloud** is shared infrastructure run by a provider (Azure, AWS). **Private cloud** is dedicated infrastructure for one organisation. **Hybrid cloud** mixes both — keeping sensitive data private while using public cloud for scale. Regulated industries often choose hybrid for exactly this reason.

## Your task

If you have Windows Pro/Enterprise, enable Hyper-V, then use `Get-VM` to list any existing VMs and `New-VM` to create one (you can delete it afterwards with `Remove-VM`). If Hyper-V is not available, install VirtualBox and create a small Linux VM instead. Then write a short note classifying three real services you use — for example a hosted email service, a rented server, and a code-hosting platform — into IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, and explain your reasoning for each.

quiz.q: What is a hypervisor?
options: A faster type of hard drive
Software that creates and runs virtual machines
quiz.why: A hypervisor is the software layer that creates, runs and manages virtual machines by sharing the physical hardware among them.

quiz.q: Which is a type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor?
quiz.why: Type 1 hypervisors such as Hyper-V or ESXi run directly on the hardware, while type 2 hypervisors like VirtualBox run as an application on top of an existing operating system.

quiz.q: A company uses Microsoft 365 — email and Office in the browser with nothing to install or patch on the server side. Which cloud model is that?
quiz.why: Software as a Service delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet, with the provider managing everything underneath; the customer just uses the app.

quiz.q: Which PowerShell command lists the virtual machines on a Hyper-V host?
quiz.why: Get-VM returns the virtual machines and their state on a Hyper-V host; the others list processes, services, or files.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain the difference between IaaS and PaaS.
quiz.answer: IaaS gives you raw virtual machines, storage and networking that you manage yourself, while PaaS gives you a managed platform to run your code without managing the underlying servers.
quiz.why: IaaS hands you the infrastructure (you patch the OS); PaaS abstracts the servers away so you only deal with your application, trading control for convenience.

quiz.q: Why might an organisation choose a hybrid cloud over a purely public cloud?
quiz.answer: To keep sensitive or regulated data and some workloads on their own private infrastructure while still using public cloud for scale, bursting, or cheaper general workloads.
quiz.why: Hybrid combines private control for sensitive systems with public-cloud flexibility and scale, which is why regulated industries often adopt it.

hd3-l09-linux-and-macos-support.title: Linux and macOS support basics
objectives: Navigate a Linux filesystem and inspect files from the terminal
Use sudo and chmod to manage permissions safely
Install and update software with a package manager like apt
Check disk, memory and processes with df, top and ps
Perform common macOS support tasks and manage software with Homebrew
Know where logs and settings live on Linux and macOS
hd3-l09-linux-and-macos-support.body:
## Why you need more than Windows

Not every machine on the helpdesk runs Windows. Developers, designers and servers run **Linux** and **macOS**, and a confident technician can support all three. The good news: both Linux and macOS share a **Unix** heritage, so the terminal skills you learn here work on both. Once you are comfortable at a shell, a strange-looking system stops being intimidating.

## Moving around Linux

Everything in Linux is a file, and you navigate from the terminal. The essentials:

```bash
pwd            # print working directory
ls -la         # list everything, long format, including hidden files
cd /var/log    # change directory
cat syslog     # show a file's contents
```

Sample output:

```bash
$ ls -la
drwxr-xr-x  2 root root 4096 Jun 16 09:01 .
-rw-r--r--  1 user user  220 Jun 16 08:55 notes.txt
```

That `drwxr-xr-x` string is the **permissions** — read, write, execute for the owner, group and everyone else.

## Permissions, sudo and packages

To change permissions you use **chmod**; to act as the administrator (**root**) for one command you prefix it with **sudo**. To install software on Debian/Ubuntu you use the **apt** package manager.

```bash
chmod +x script.sh           # make a script executable
sudo apt update              # refresh the package list
sudo apt install htop        # install a package and its dependencies
```

Using `sudo` for single commands — rather than logging in as root — is the safe Linux equivalent of least privilege.

## Checking health: disk, memory, processes

When a Linux box is slow or full, three commands answer most questions:

```bash
df -h          # disk space used/free, human-readable
top            # live processes by CPU/memory (press q to quit)
ps aux         # snapshot of all running processes
```

Sample output:

```bash
$ df -h
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        50G   42G  5.2G  90% /
```

Ninety percent full explains a lot. For deeper investigation, logs live in **/var/log** (or via `journalctl` on modern systems).

## Supporting macOS

macOS is Unix underneath, so the same terminal commands work in **Terminal.app**. Day to day you will also use the graphical tools: **Activity Monitor** (the Mac equivalent of Task Manager), **Force Quit** (Cmd+Option+Esc) for a frozen app, **Disk Utility** for drives, and **Time Machine** for backups. For installing developer tools, many Mac users rely on **Homebrew**:

```bash
brew update              # refresh Homebrew
brew install wget        # install a package
brew list                # what's installed
```

You can also read and change hidden settings with `defaults`:

```bash
defaults write com.apple.finder AppleShowAllFiles -bool true
killall Finder           # apply the change
```

## Your task

Get to a Linux shell (a VM, WSL on Windows, or a Raspberry Pi) and do the following: run `pwd`, `ls -la`, and `df -h`, and note your home directory and how full the disk is. Create a file, then use `chmod +x` to make it executable and confirm the permissions changed. Use `sudo apt update` (or your distro's package manager) to refresh the package list. If you have access to a Mac, open Activity Monitor, find the most CPU-hungry process, and write one sentence on what it is and whether it looks normal.

quiz.q: Which command changes the permissions on a file in Linux?
quiz.why: chmod (change mode) sets the read, write and execute permissions on a file or directory; the others change directory, check a Windows disk, or are not real commands.

quiz.q: What does prefixing a command with sudo do?
options: Runs it as the superuser (root) for that command
quiz.why: sudo (superuser do) runs a single command with administrative/root privileges, which is the safe way to perform admin tasks without logging in as root.

quiz.q: On a Debian/Ubuntu system, which command installs a package and its dependencies?
quiz.why: On Debian and Ubuntu the apt package manager handles installs; sudo apt install <package> downloads and installs the package with its dependencies.

quiz.q: A Mac user's application won't quit normally. What is the standard macOS way to force it to close?
options: Force Quit (Cmd+Option+Esc) or kill from Activity Monitor
quiz.why: macOS uses Force Quit, reached with Command-Option-Escape or from Activity Monitor, to close an unresponsive app — there is no Ctrl+Alt+Delete on a Mac.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain what df and top tell you on a Linux machine.
quiz.answer: df shows how much disk space is used and free on each filesystem, while top shows the running processes with their live CPU and memory usage.
quiz.why: df is for storage capacity and top is for live performance and what's consuming CPU/RAM — two of the first things you check when a Linux box is slow or full.

quiz.q: Where would you look first to investigate a problem on a Linux server?
quiz.answer: In the system and application logs, typically under /var/log (for example /var/log/syslog or with the journalctl command on systemd systems).
quiz.why: Linux records events and errors in /var/log and the systemd journal, so that's the first place a technician checks to see what actually went wrong.

hd3-l10-scripting-basics-for-support.title: Scripting basics for support technicians
objectives: Explain why automating repetitive tasks reduces errors and saves time
Store and use values in variables in PowerShell and Bash
Loop over a list of items with foreach / for
Make decisions in a script with if/else
Read a file line by line and act on each line
Run scripts safely and understand basic execution policy and permissions
hd3-l10-scripting-basics-for-support.body:
## Why technicians script

When you have done the same five-step fix forty times, you are not learning — you are wasting time and inviting mistakes. **Scripting** is the cure. A script is just a saved list of commands the computer runs for you, the same way every time. You do not need to be a programmer; four small ideas — **variables**, **loops**, **conditionals**, and reading **input** — cover most of the automation a Tier 1 technician needs. The two languages you will meet are **PowerShell** on Windows and **Bash** on Linux/macOS.

## Variables: name your values

A **variable** is a named box that holds a value, so you set it once and reuse it.

```powershell
$name = "Kwasi"
$logPath = "C:\Logs\app.log"
Write-Host "Checking log for $name at $logPath"
```

In Bash the same idea looks like this (note: no spaces around `=`):

```bash
name="Kwasi"
logPath="/var/log/syslog"
echo "Checking log for $name at $logPath"
```

## Loops: do it for every item

A **loop** repeats an action for each item in a list — perfect for "do this to every user" or "every file".

```powershell
$services = "Spooler", "W32Time", "BITS"
foreach ($svc in $services) {
    $state = (Get-Service $svc).Status
    Write-Host "$svc is $state"
}
```

Sample output:

```powershell
Spooler is Running
W32Time is Running
BITS is Stopped
```

## Conditionals: make decisions

An **if/else** lets the script decide. Here we restart a service only if it is stopped:

```powershell
foreach ($svc in $services) {
    if ((Get-Service $svc).Status -eq "Stopped") {
        Write-Host "$svc is stopped - starting it"
        Start-Service $svc
    } else {
        Write-Host "$svc is fine"
    }
}
```

The Bash equivalent uses `if ... then ... else ... fi` and tools like `systemctl is-active`.

## Reading input from a file

Real automation often reads a list — say, computer names — from a file. In PowerShell, **Get-Content** reads it and you loop over the lines:

```powershell
Get-Content ".\computers.txt" | foreach {
    Write-Host "Pinging $_"
    Test-Connection -ComputerName $_ -Count 1 -Quiet
}
```

The `$_` means "the current line". In Bash you would use `while read line; do ...; done < file`.

PowerShell guards against untrusted scripts with an **execution policy**. If a script refuses to run, check it:

```powershell
Get-ExecutionPolicy
# Restricted
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
```

On Linux you make a script runnable with `chmod +x script.sh` and run it as `./script.sh`. Always read a script before you run it, and test on a non-production machine first.

## Your task

Write a short PowerShell script that defines a list of three service names, loops over them with `foreach`, and uses `if/else` to print whether each is Running or Stopped (use `Get-Service`). Save it as `check-services.ps1` and run it; if it is blocked, check `Get-ExecutionPolicy` and note what you would change. Bonus: create a `computers.txt` file with three names, then use `Get-Content` and a loop to print each line. Write two sentences on one repetitive helpdesk task you could automate this way.

quiz.q: What is the main reason a support technician writes scripts?
options: To make the computer run faster
To automate repetitive tasks consistently and avoid manual mistakes
quiz.why: Scripting automates repetitive work so it runs the same way every time, which saves time and removes the human errors that creep into manual steps.

quiz.q: Which PowerShell loop runs a block of code once for each item in a list?
quiz.why: foreach iterates over a collection, running its block once per item; the others show help, stop a process, or change directory.

quiz.q: What does an if/else statement let a script do?
options: Choose between actions based on whether a condition is true
quiz.why: if/else branches the script: it runs one block when a condition is true and another when it is false, letting the script make decisions.

quiz.q: In PowerShell, which command reads the contents of a text file?
quiz.why: Get-Content reads a file and returns its lines, which you can then loop over; the others print text, delete items, or start a service.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is a variable and why is it useful in a script?
quiz.answer: A variable is a named container that stores a value (like a name, number or path) so you can reuse it and change it in one place instead of repeating the value throughout the script.
quiz.why: Variables make scripts readable and maintainable: change the value once and every use updates, which avoids errors from repeating the same literal everywhere.

quiz.q: Why might a PowerShell script refuse to run, and how do you check the relevant setting?
quiz.answer: The execution policy may block unsigned scripts; you check it with Get-ExecutionPolicy and, if appropriate and permitted, adjust it (for example to RemoteSigned) with Set-ExecutionPolicy.
quiz.why: PowerShell's execution policy is a safety control against running untrusted scripts, so a blocked script usually means the policy needs checking with Get-ExecutionPolicy.

hd4-l01-the-helpdesk-role.title: The Tier 1/2 helpdesk role and career path
objectives: Describe the difference between Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 support
Explain the daily responsibilities of a service desk technician
List the core skills employers expect in an entry-level helpdesk role
Identify the common career paths that start at the helpdesk
Recognise the metrics your performance is measured against
Map your current skills to a realistic first job target
hd4-l01-the-helpdesk-role.body:
## What the helpdesk actually is

The **helpdesk** (or **service desk**) is the single point of contact between an organisation's users and its IT department. When someone's laptop won't connect, their password is locked, or an application throws an error, they contact the helpdesk first. Your job is to capture the problem, fix what you can, and route the rest to the right people.

This is the most common entry point into IT, and for good reason: in one role you touch hardware, software, networking, accounts, and people. That broad exposure is exactly what makes it a launchpad.

## The tiers explained

Support is usually organised into tiers by complexity:

| Tier | Who they are | What they handle |
|------|-------------|------------------|
| Tier 1 | First-line agents | Password resets, common errors, how-to questions, logging tickets |
| Tier 2 | Specialist technicians | Deeper troubleshooting, configuration, issues needing more access |
| Tier 3 | Engineers / vendors | Root-cause work, infrastructure, code, product escalations |

**Tier 1** resolves the bulk of contacts using documented fixes. When an issue needs more knowledge, more access, or more time than the front line can give, it is **escalated** to **Tier 2**. Tiers describe complexity, not seniority of person — a good Tier 1 agent is valuable.

## A typical day

You log in, check the **ticket queue**, and pick up contacts arriving by phone, email, chat, or a self-service portal. A realistic ticket looks like this:

```text
Ticket #48213
User: Maria Okafor (Sales)
Subject: Can't log into email on laptop
Priority: P3
Description: Outlook says "password incorrect" since this morning.
```

You greet the user, confirm details, troubleshoot, document every step, and either **resolve** or **escalate**. Throughout the day you are juggling several tickets while keeping each user informed.

## How your work is measured

Service desks track metrics so they can improve. The ones that affect you most:

- **First Contact Resolution (FCR)** — fixed on the first interaction.
- **Average Handle Time** — how long contacts take.
- **CSAT** — customer satisfaction score from surveys.
- **SLA compliance** — did you respond and resolve within the agreed time.

Good technicians balance speed with quality. Closing tickets fast but wrong just creates repeat contacts.

## The skills employers want

Technical foundations get you the interview; **soft skills** keep you employed. Employers consistently ask for clear written and spoken communication, patience, empathy, and the discipline to **document** everything. You will spend as much energy reassuring a stressed user as you spend fixing the machine.

## Where this leads

The helpdesk is a doorway, not a dead end. Common next steps within two to three years include **systems administrator**, **network technician**, **cloud support**, or **security analyst** — and eventually team lead or IT manager. The broad visibility you get on the desk is what makes those moves possible.

## Your task

Write a short profile of yourself as a job candidate. List three technical skills you already have, two soft skills, and the one entry-level role title you will target first. Then write two sentences explaining which Tier 2 specialism (networking, security, or systems) interests you as a next step, and why.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a Tier 1 support technician?
options: Being the first point of contact and resolving common, documented issues
quiz.why: Tier 1 is the front line: they receive contacts, log tickets, and fix the high-volume, well-documented problems, escalating anything they cannot resolve.

quiz.q: When does a Tier 1 technician escalate a ticket to Tier 2?
options: When the issue is outside their knowledge, access, or the documented fixes
At the end of every shift
Only if the user asks them to
quiz.why: Escalation happens when the issue needs deeper expertise, higher access rights, or steps not covered by the knowledge base — not based on the user's mood.

quiz.q: Which of these is a typical metric used to measure helpdesk performance?
quiz.why: First Contact Resolution (FCR), average handle time, and CSAT are standard service desk metrics; coding output is not relevant to most helpdesk roles.

quiz.q: Which career path most commonly follows a few years on the helpdesk?
options: Systems administrator, network technician, or security analyst
quiz.why: The helpdesk builds broad exposure, so technicians commonly move into sysadmin, networking, security, or cloud roles as the next step.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is the difference between Tier 1 and Tier 2 support?
quiz.answer: Tier 1 handles the first contact and common documented issues, while Tier 2 takes on the more complex problems that need deeper technical knowledge or higher access.
quiz.why: The tiers describe escalating levels of complexity and expertise, not status — most contacts are resolved at Tier 1.

quiz.q: Name two soft skills that matter as much as technical knowledge on a helpdesk, and say why.
quiz.answer: Clear communication and patience matter because you must explain fixes to non-technical users and stay calm with frustrated people, which drives customer satisfaction.
quiz.why: Employers consistently rank communication and empathy alongside technical ability because the helpdesk is a customer-facing role.

hd4-l02-ticketing-systems.title: Ticketing systems: ServiceNow, Jira & Zendesk
objectives: Explain what a ticketing system is and why every service desk uses one
Describe the lifecycle of a ticket from New to Closed
Identify the core fields every ticket should contain
Compare ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, and Zendesk at a high level
Write a clear, well-structured ticket that another technician could pick up
Use ticket categories, priority, and assignment correctly
hd4-l02-ticketing-systems.body:
## Why every service desk uses a ticketing system

A **ticketing system** is the shared workspace where every support request is logged, tracked, and documented. Without one, requests scatter across inboxes, sticky notes, and hallway conversations — and things get lost. With one, every contact becomes a **ticket** with an ID, a status, a history, and an owner. It is the source of truth for the whole team.

Ticketing systems also make work *measurable*. Because every request is recorded, the desk can report on volumes, response times, and recurring problems.

## The lifecycle of a ticket

Every ticket moves through **states**. The names vary slightly by platform, but the shape is the same:

```text
New  ->  In Progress  ->  (On Hold / Pending)  ->  Resolved  ->  Closed
```

- **New** — logged but not yet picked up.
- **In Progress** — a technician is actively working it.
- **On Hold / Pending** — waiting on the user, a vendor, or a part.
- **Resolved** — the fix is applied; awaiting confirmation.
- **Closed** — confirmed fixed and finished.

Never skip states. The status field tells everyone — including the user — exactly where things stand.

## The fields that make a ticket usable

A ticket another technician can pick up cold contains:

- **Requester** and **contact details**
- A specific **subject** naming the system and symptom
- A **description** with symptoms, error text, timing, and what changed
- **Category** (e.g. Email, Network, Hardware)
- **Priority**
- **Assignment** to a person or queue

Compare these two subjects:

```text
Bad:  It's broken
Good: Outlook 365 - "password incorrect" error since 09:00 today
```

The good subject can be triaged, searched, and understood in one glance.

## The three platforms you will meet

Three tools dominate the job market:

| Platform | Strength | Typical home |
|----------|----------|--------------|
| **ServiceNow** | Full enterprise ITSM, ITIL-aligned | Large organisations |
| **Jira Service Management** | Tight link to dev teams, flexible | Software-driven companies |
| **Zendesk** | Friendly, fast, omnichannel | Customer-support-heavy teams |

The good news: they all share the same core concepts. Learn the lifecycle and field discipline once, and you can move between them quickly. The buttons differ; the thinking does not.

## Writing the ticket

When you log a contact, capture the user's words *and* the technical facts. A clean description reads like a short report:

```text
User reports Outlook prompts "password incorrect" repeatedly
since ~09:00. Webmail login works with same password.
No recent password change reported. Laptop, Windows 11, on VPN.
Verified account is not locked in directory.
```

That description tells the next person what was tried and rules things out — it is half the troubleshooting already done.

## Your task

Write a complete ticket for this scenario: a user named Sam in Finance reports that the shared accounting drive 'S:' disappeared from their PC after a reboot this morning; other users can still see it. Include subject, category, priority, and a description with symptoms, timing, and what you have already verified. Aim for the quality of the 'Good' examples above.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a ticketing system?
options: To track, manage, and document every support request in one place
quiz.why: A ticketing system records each request, tracks its status, and keeps a complete history so nothing is lost and work can be measured and audited.

quiz.q: Which sequence best represents a typical ticket lifecycle?
quiz.why: Tickets generally flow New, then In Progress (often via On Hold/Pending), to Resolved once fixed, and finally Closed after confirmation.

quiz.q: Which platform is an IT service management suite most associated with large enterprises?
quiz.why: ServiceNow is a large, enterprise-focused ITSM platform; Zendesk leans toward customer support and Jira toward dev-aligned teams, though all three handle IT tickets.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid a ticket subject like 'It's broken'?
options: It gives no information, so the ticket can't be triaged or searched
quiz.why: A vague subject can't be categorised, prioritised, or found later; a good subject names the system and the symptom, e.g. 'Outlook - password incorrect error'.

quiz.q: List the core fields every well-formed ticket should contain.
quiz.answer: Requester/user, contact details, a clear subject, a detailed description with symptoms and timing, category, priority, and the assignment or queue.
quiz.why: These fields let any technician triage, prioritise, and pick up the ticket without having to chase the user for basics.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why does good ticket hygiene matter to the whole team?
quiz.answer: Clean, complete tickets mean any technician can pick up the work without re-interviewing the user, which speeds resolution and builds a searchable knowledge history.
quiz.why: Tickets are shared records; sloppy ones create rework, while well-written ones become future knowledge-base material.

hd4-l03-itil-fundamentals.title: ITIL fundamentals: incident, problem and change
objectives: Explain what ITIL is and why organisations adopt it
Define a service, value, and the four dimensions in plain terms
Distinguish an incident from a problem with confidence
Describe the goal of change management and why it protects users
Recognise service requests as distinct from incidents
Apply the correct ITIL practice to a real support scenario
hd4-l03-itil-fundamentals.body:
## What ITIL is and why it exists

**ITIL** (the IT Infrastructure Library) is the world's most widely adopted framework of **best practices** for IT service management. It is not a rulebook you must obey to the letter — it is a shared vocabulary and set of sensible practices so that IT teams everywhere work in a consistent, reliable way. The current version is **ITIL 4**.

The central idea is **value**: IT exists to help the business and its users achieve outcomes. A **service** is a way of delivering that value — email, the VPN, the finance system are all services. Your job on the desk is to keep those services flowing.

## The three practices you live by

ITIL 4 has many practices, but a helpdesk technician works with three constantly: **incident management**, **problem management**, and **change enablement**. Get these three clear and most of the framework falls into place.

## Incidents: restore service fast

An **incident** is an **unplanned interruption** to a service, or a reduction in its quality. The phone rings, email is down, a laptop won't boot — those are incidents. The single goal of **incident management** is to **restore normal service as quickly as possible**, even with a temporary fix or **workaround**. You are not required to find the deep cause; you are required to get the user working again.

```text
Incident: "Email is down for the whole Sales floor."
Goal: get Sales back on email ASAP, even via a workaround.
```

## Problems: remove the cause

A **problem** is the **underlying cause** of one or more incidents. If twelve people report the same outage, that is twelve incidents and likely one problem. **Problem management** investigates the root cause so the incidents stop coming back. It is slower, more analytical work — often done by Tier 2 and Tier 3.

```text
12 incidents: "Email down" reported by 12 users
 1 problem:   the failed mail server behind all of them
```

Incidents are the *symptoms*; the problem is the *disease*.

## Changes: improve without breaking things

A **change** is the addition, modification, or removal of anything that could affect services — a server patch, a firewall rule, a new application. **Change enablement** exists to make changes **safely**, because uncontrolled changes are one of the biggest causes of outages. Changes are usually assessed for risk and scheduled, sometimes through a **Change Advisory Board (CAB)**. Low-risk, routine changes may be pre-approved as **standard changes**.

## Service requests: nothing is broken

Not every contact is an incident. When a user wants something provided as a normal offering — software installed, access to a mailbox, a new monitor — that is a **service request**, handled through **request fulfilment**. The test is simple: *is something broken, or does the user want something provided?* Broken means incident; provide means request.

## Your task

For each of the following, label it Incident, Problem, Change, or Service Request, and write one sentence justifying your choice:

1. "My screen is frozen and I have a deadline."
2. "Please give me the Adobe Acrobat licence."
3. The network team plans to replace the core switch on Saturday night.
4. The desk has logged 30 tickets this week all about the VPN dropping; someone needs to find out why.

quiz.q: What is the best plain-English definition of an incident in ITIL?
options: A planned upgrade to a system
An unplanned interruption or reduction in quality of a service
quiz.why: An incident is an unplanned event that breaks or degrades a service; the goal of incident management is to restore normal service as fast as possible.

quiz.q: How does a problem differ from an incident?
options: A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents
A problem is always less urgent than an incident
quiz.why: Incidents are the visible symptoms; a problem is the root cause behind them. Problem management seeks to remove that cause so incidents stop recurring.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of change management (change enablement)?
options: To stop all changes from happening
To make changes safely while minimising risk and disruption
quiz.why: Change enablement aims to maximise successful changes by assessing and controlling risk, so improvements happen without breaking services for users.

quiz.q: A user asks to be given access to a shared mailbox. Which practice is this?
quiz.why: Nothing is broken — the user wants something provided as a standard offering, which is a service request, handled through request fulfilment, not incident management.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain the relationship between incidents and problems using an example.
quiz.answer: If five users separately report the same email outage (five incidents), the single failed mail server behind them is the problem, and fixing the server resolves the root cause.
quiz.why: Many incidents can share one underlying problem; problem management removes the cause so the incidents stop happening.

quiz.q: Why does ITIL insist that most changes go through a controlled process?
quiz.answer: Because uncontrolled changes are a leading cause of outages, a controlled process assesses risk and schedules changes so improvements don't break live services.
quiz.why: Change enablement balances the need to improve with the need to protect stable, working services for users.

hd4-l04-troubleshooting-methodology.title: The troubleshooting methodology (the A+ 6-step model)
objectives: Recite the six steps of the CompTIA A+ troubleshooting methodology in order
Gather information and identify symptoms before changing anything
Form and test one theory of probable cause at a time
Verify full system functionality and apply preventive measures
Document findings, actions, and outcomes in the ticket
Apply the full method to a realistic support scenario
hd4-l04-troubleshooting-methodology.body:
## Why method beats guessing

Beginners often troubleshoot by trying random fixes until something works. It feels productive but it is slow, it breaks things, and you can never explain what fixed the issue. The **CompTIA A+ troubleshooting methodology** is a six-step model that turns troubleshooting into a repeatable, professional process. Learn it once and use it on everything from a frozen laptop to a network outage.

```text
1. Identify the problem
2. Establish a theory of probable cause
3. Test the theory
4. Establish a plan of action and implement the solution
5. Verify full functionality and apply preventive measures
6. Document findings, actions, and outcomes
```

## Step 1: Identify the problem

Before you touch anything, **gather information**. Ask the user what happened, what changed, and when it started. Note exact error messages. A useful question script:

```text
"When did this start?"
"What were you doing right before it happened?"
"Has anything changed recently - updates, new software, a move?"
"Does it happen every time, or sometimes?"
```

Also check the obvious: is it plugged in, is anyone else affected? Identifying scope early tells you whether this is one machine or an outage.

## Step 2: Establish a theory of probable cause

Form a **single, testable theory**. Start with the **most likely and simplest** cause — the famous principle is to question the obvious. "The password is wrong" or "the cable is loose" before "the motherboard has failed." Use your knowledge and the symptoms to make an educated guess, not a wild one.

## Step 3: Test the theory

Now **test it**. If your theory is right, you have found the cause. If it is wrong, form a *new* theory — do not start guessing randomly. Change **one thing at a time** so you always know what affected the result. If you cannot confirm a cause, this is often where you **escalate**.

## Step 4: Plan and implement the solution

With the cause confirmed, decide *how* to fix it, considering impact. Will the fix require a reboot, downtime, or a heads-up to others? Then implement it cleanly. For risky fixes, note a way back.

## Step 5: Verify functionality and prevent recurrence

Confirm the **original symptom is gone** and that **nothing else broke**. Do this *with the user* where possible — they decide whether it is truly fixed. Then think about **prevention**: should a setting change, or a knowledge article be written, so this does not happen again?

## Step 6: Document everything

Finally, **document** the symptoms, the cause, the actions you took, and the outcome in the ticket. This is not paperwork for its own sake — it is what lets the next technician (often future-you) solve the same issue in minutes, and it feeds the **knowledge base**.

## Your task

A user reports: "My laptop won't connect to Wi-Fi since this morning, but my phone connects to the same network fine." Write out how you would work this ticket through all six steps. For each step, write one or two lines: the questions you would ask, your first theory, how you would test it, a plausible fix, how you would verify, and a one-line documentation summary.

quiz.q: What is the correct first step of the A+ troubleshooting methodology?
quiz.why: Step one is always to identify the problem by gathering information, asking the user, and noting symptoms before touching anything.

quiz.q: After you establish a theory of probable cause, what comes next?
options: Test the theory to determine the cause
quiz.why: Step three is to test the theory: confirm whether your suspected cause is correct before you commit to a fix. If not confirmed, form a new theory.

quiz.q: Why should you change only one thing at a time when testing?
options: So you know which change actually fixed or affected the issue
quiz.why: Changing one variable at a time means you can attribute the result to that change; changing several at once hides what actually worked.

quiz.q: What does 'verify full system functionality' mean?
options: Confirm the original issue is fixed and nothing else broke
quiz.why: After applying a fix you confirm the original symptom is gone and the rest of the system still works, ideally with the user, before closing.

quiz.q: List the six steps of the A+ troubleshooting methodology in order.
quiz.answer: 1) Identify the problem; 2) Establish a theory of probable cause; 3) Test the theory; 4) Establish a plan of action and implement the solution; 5) Verify full system functionality and apply preventive measures; 6) Document findings, actions, and outcomes.
quiz.why: Following the steps in order keeps troubleshooting systematic and repeatable rather than a guessing game.

quiz.q: Why is the final documentation step important even after the fix works?
quiz.answer: Documentation records what was wrong and how it was fixed so the same issue can be solved faster next time and feeds the knowledge base.
quiz.why: Good documentation turns one solved ticket into reusable knowledge for the whole team and prevents repeated investigation.

hd4-l05-communication-and-customer-servi.title: Communication and customer service skills
objectives: Open and close a support interaction professionally
Use active listening and confirm understanding before acting
Explain technical things to non-technical users without jargon
Apply techniques to de-escalate a frustrated or angry user
Set expectations clearly and keep users informed
Maintain professionalism, empathy, and proper phone/written etiquette
hd4-l05-communication-and-customer-servi.body:
## The fix is only half the job

A technically perfect resolution delivered rudely is a *bad* support experience. Users remember how you made them feel as much as whether the problem went away. **Communication** and **customer service** are not soft extras on a helpdesk — they are the core of the job. This lesson gives you concrete techniques you can use on your very next call.

## Open and close professionally

Every interaction has a shape. Open warmly, identify yourself, and confirm who you are helping. Close by confirming resolution and inviting follow-up.

```text
Opening:
"Good morning, IT Service Desk, this is Daniel. How can I help today?"

Closing:
"Great, your email is working now. I'll keep the ticket open
until end of day in case anything recurs. Anything else I can help with?"
```

A clear open and close makes you sound calm and in control even when the middle is messy.

## Listen actively and confirm understanding

**Active listening** means giving the user your full attention, letting them finish, and then **restating** the issue in your own words. This catches misunderstandings before you waste time solving the wrong thing.

```text
"So just to confirm - your laptop connects to Wi-Fi at home,
but not in the office since this morning. Is that right?"
```

That one sentence reassures the user you were listening and locks in a shared understanding.

## Drop the jargon

Most users are not technical. Translate. Instead of "your DNS resolver is misconfigured," say "your computer is looking up website addresses in the wrong place — I'll point it to the right one." Plain language respects the user and keeps them with you. Never make someone feel stupid for not knowing IT — that is *your* job, not theirs.

## Set expectations and keep people informed

Uncertainty is what frustrates users most. Always tell them **what happens next and roughly when**. Under-promise and over-deliver.

```text
"This one needs our network team. I'm escalating it now with
all your details. You should hear back within two hours, and
I've put my notes on the ticket so you won't repeat yourself."
```

If you say you will call back, call back — even if it is only to say there is no news yet.

## De-escalating a frustrated user

Angry users are usually frustrated by the *situation*, not by you. Do not take it personally, and never argue or blame other teams. Lead with **empathy**, then move to **action**.

```text
User: "This is the third time this week! It's unacceptable."
You:  "You're right, and I'm sorry - that's genuinely disruptive.
       Let's get you working now, and I'll flag the repeat issue
       so it gets properly investigated."
```

Acknowledge the feeling, take ownership of the next step, and stay calm. Tone of voice matters as much as words.

## Your task

Write a short script for this call: a user phones, clearly stressed, because their presentation file won't open thirty minutes before a big client meeting. Write your opening line, one empathy statement, one sentence confirming the issue back to them, and a closing line that sets expectations. Keep every line jargon-free.

quiz.q: What is 'active listening' on a support call?
options: Fully focusing, not interrupting, and confirming you understood
Reading from a script word for word
quiz.why: Active listening means concentrating on the user, letting them finish, and restating the issue to confirm you understood before you start fixing.

quiz.q: A user is angry about repeated outages. What is the best first response?
options: Acknowledge their frustration and apologise for the impact, then focus on helping
quiz.why: Acknowledging feelings and the impact de-escalates; arguing, dismissing, or blaming others escalates. Empathy first, then action.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid technical jargon with most users?
options: It confuses and alienates non-technical users and slows resolution
quiz.why: Plain language keeps the user with you, reduces confusion and repeat questions, and makes them feel respected rather than talked down to.

quiz.q: What does 'setting expectations' mean in support?
options: Clearly telling the user what will happen next and roughly when
quiz.why: Setting expectations means telling the user the next step and timeframe so they are not left wondering; under-promise and over-deliver.

quiz.q: Give one phrase you can use to show empathy to a frustrated user, and explain why it works.
quiz.answer: Something like 'I completely understand how disruptive this is, and I'm going to help you get it sorted.' It works because it acknowledges their feelings and signals you are on their side.
quiz.why: Empathy phrases validate the user's experience and shift the conversation from conflict to collaboration.

quiz.q: Why is it important to confirm the user's issue back to them before troubleshooting?
quiz.answer: Restating the issue confirms you understood it correctly, catches misunderstandings early, and reassures the user you were listening.
quiz.why: Confirming understanding prevents you from solving the wrong problem and builds trust at the start of the interaction.

hd4-l06-documentation-and-knowledge-base.title: Documentation and knowledge bases
objectives: Explain why documentation is a core helpdesk responsibility, not an afterthought
Write clear, factual ticket notes that capture what was done and why
Structure a knowledge-base (KB) article a user or technician can follow
Distinguish internal documentation from user-facing articles
Apply knowledge-centred service principles in everyday work
Write a usable KB article from a solved ticket
hd4-l06-documentation-and-knowledge-base.body:
## Documentation is the work, not the paperwork

Many beginners treat writing things down as the annoying bit after the real work. Reframe it: on a service desk, **documentation is how your work scales**. A fix you record once can be repeated by anyone in minutes; a fix you keep in your head dies when you go to lunch. Two kinds of writing matter most: **ticket notes** and **knowledge-base articles**.

## Writing good ticket notes

Ticket notes are the running record of what happened. They should let a colleague pick up your ticket cold. Keep them **factual, chronological, and free of blame or opinion** — tickets are official records that can be audited.

```text
10:14 - User reports shared drive S: missing after reboot.
10:18 - Confirmed drive maps fine on a colleague's PC. Scope: 1 user.
10:25 - Found mapped-drive logon script not running; Group Policy
        not applied. Forced gpupdate /force - drive reappeared.
10:30 - Verified with user, S: now present and accessible. Resolved.
```

Notice it records *facts and actions with times*, not "user was clueless." Never write anything in a ticket you would not want the user, your boss, or an auditor to read.

## What a knowledge-base article is

A **knowledge base (KB)** is a searchable library of articles describing how to solve known issues. Some are **internal** (for technicians); some are **user-facing self-help** that deflect tickets entirely. A good article has a predictable structure:

```text
Title:    How to map the shared S: drive (Windows)
Applies to: Windows 11 domain PCs
Symptom:  The S: drive is missing from File Explorer
Steps:
  1. Open File Explorer and click "This PC".
  2. Click the three-dot menu, then "Map network drive".
  3. Choose drive letter S: and enter \\fileserver\shared.
  4. Tick "Reconnect at sign-in" and click Finish.
Expected result: The S: drive appears under "This PC".
```

A **searchable title** uses the words users actually type. Numbered **steps** are unambiguous. An **expected result** lets the reader confirm it worked.

## Internal vs user-facing

Internal docs can be technical and reference tools, scripts, or admin steps. **User-facing** articles use plain language, avoid jargon, and **never expose sensitive detail** such as server names or security settings the public should not see. Always ask: *who will read this?*

## Knowledge-centred service

**Knowledge-Centred Service (KCS)** is the principle that capturing knowledge should be a natural **by-product of solving tickets**, not a separate project. When you solve something new, you write or improve an article as you go. Over time the knowledge base becomes the team's collective memory, and First Contact Resolution climbs because answers are already written down.

## Your task

Take the solved ticket from earlier in the course where Sam's S: drive disappeared (or invent a similar fix you understand). Write a complete, user-facing KB article for it: a searchable title, an 'applies to' line, the symptom, numbered steps in plain language, and an expected result. Then write one sentence on what you would change if the article were internal-only instead.

quiz.q: Why is documentation considered part of the actual job, not extra work?
options: It turns solved issues into reusable knowledge and lets others continue your work
quiz.why: Good notes let any technician resume or repeat a fix without re-investigating, and KB articles deflect future tickets, so documentation directly multiplies the team's capacity.

quiz.q: What makes a good knowledge-base article?
options: Lots of jargon to sound expert
A clear title, the problem, numbered steps, and the expected result
quiz.why: Useful KB articles have a searchable title, a description of the symptom, clear numbered steps, and confirmation of the expected outcome so the reader knows it worked.

quiz.q: What is the difference between internal documentation and a user-facing article?
options: Internal docs can be technical; user-facing articles use plain language and avoid sensitive detail
User-facing articles are for managers only
quiz.why: Internal notes can include technical detail and tools; user-facing self-help articles use plain language and never expose sensitive internal information.

quiz.q: What does 'knowledge-centred service' (KCS) encourage technicians to do?
options: Capture and reuse knowledge as part of solving each issue
quiz.why: KCS treats knowledge capture as a by-product of solving tickets, so the knowledge base grows and improves continuously through normal work.

quiz.q: Write a good, searchable title for a KB article about resetting a forgotten domain password. Explain your choice.
quiz.answer: Something like 'How to reset a forgotten Windows domain password (self-service)'. It names the system, the action, and the context, so users searching 'reset password' will find it.
quiz.why: A searchable title contains the words users actually type and clearly states what the article covers.

quiz.q: Why should ticket notes be factual and free of blame or opinion?
quiz.answer: Tickets are official, shared records that others read and that may be audited, so notes must state facts and actions, not opinions or criticism of users or colleagues.
quiz.why: Professional, factual notes protect everyone, stay useful over time, and avoid creating problems if the ticket is reviewed later.

hd4-l07-slas-priorities-escalation.title: SLAs, priorities and escalation
objectives: Explain what a Service Level Agreement (SLA) is and what it commits to
Calculate priority from impact and urgency using a priority matrix
Distinguish response time targets from resolution time targets
Recognise a major incident and how it is handled differently
Escalate functionally and hierarchically with a complete handover
Prioritise a realistic mixed queue of tickets correctly
hd4-l07-slas-priorities-escalation.body:
## What an SLA actually promises

A **Service Level Agreement (SLA)** is a documented promise between IT and the business about how fast tickets will be handled. It usually sets two separate clocks per priority: a **response time** (how quickly someone acknowledges and starts work) and a **resolution time** (how long is allowed to fix it). When a ticket exceeds its target, that is an **SLA breach** — something the desk works hard to avoid.

```text
Priority  Response target   Resolution target
P1        15 minutes        4 hours
P2        30 minutes        8 hours
P3        4 hours           2 business days
P4        1 business day    5 business days
```

The SLA is why you cannot just work tickets in the order they arrive — some have a much tighter clock than others.

## Priority = impact x urgency

Priority is not about who complains loudest. It is calculated from **impact** (how many people, how critical the service) and **urgency** (how time-sensitive). Most desks use a **priority matrix**:

```text
              Urgency High   Urgency Med   Urgency Low
Impact High      P1            P2            P3
Impact Med       P2            P3            P4
Impact Low       P3            P4            P4
```

A single user who forgot a password is high urgency *to them* but low impact, so it is not a P1. The whole sales floor losing email is high impact *and* high urgency — that is a **P1**.

## Major incidents

A **major incident** is the most severe class: a critical service down, many users affected, the business hurting. These get special handling — a **major incident manager**, a dedicated bridge call, frequent communications, and all-hands focus. As Tier 1, your role is often to **recognise** one early, log it correctly, and raise the alarm rather than quietly working it alone.

## Escalation done well

No single technician can fix everything, so **escalation** is a normal, healthy part of the job. There are two kinds:

- **Functional escalation** — sending the ticket to a team with the right **skills** (e.g. networking).
- **Hierarchical escalation** — raising it up the **management** chain for authority or attention, common on SLA breaches and major incidents.

A clean escalation is a complete **handover**. Bad escalations bounce back and waste everyone's time:

```text
Escalation note:
Ref: INC0048213 | Priority: P2
Summary: Finance shared mailbox not receiving external email since 08:30.
Tried: confirmed mailbox exists, internal mail arrives, checked rules
       (none blocking), verified user permissions OK.
Impact: 6 finance users, month-end deadline today.
Contact: Sam Patel, ext. 4471, available until 17:00.
Reason for escalation: needs mail-flow/transport rule review (Tier 2).
```

That handover lets the next team start immediately, without re-interviewing the user.

## Your task

You have these four tickets open at once. Assign each a priority (P1-P4) using impact and urgency, then list the order you would work them and write one sentence justifying each:

1. The entire warehouse cannot scan stock; shipping is halted.
2. One user's mouse scroll wheel is sticky.
3. A manager cannot open a report needed for a board meeting in one hour.
4. The shared printer on floor 2 is out of toner (a spare is in the cupboard).

quiz.q: What is a Service Level Agreement (SLA)?
options: A documented commitment to respond and resolve within agreed timeframes
quiz.why: An SLA is an agreement between IT and the business defining target response and resolution times, often varying by priority.

quiz.q: How is a ticket's priority normally determined?
quiz.why: Priority comes from a matrix of impact (how many/how critical) and urgency (how time-sensitive), giving a consistent, defensible ranking.

quiz.q: Which scenario is most likely a P1 / major incident?
options: One user wants a larger monitor
The company email system is down for everyone
quiz.why: High impact (everyone) plus high urgency (core service down) makes an organisation-wide email outage a top-priority/major incident.

quiz.q: What is the difference between functional and hierarchical escalation?
options: Functional sends it to a team with the right skills; hierarchical raises it to management for authority or attention
