You assign a remediation to a **device or user group** with a schedule (once, hourly, or daily). Intune then shows, per device, the detection status and remediation status. You can also manage remediations through Graph as `deviceHealthScript` resources.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All'

# List your remediation (device health) scripts via Graph
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/deviceHealthScripts' |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty value |
    Select-Object displayName, id
```

Start with **detection only** (a remediation that just reports) to size the problem, then add the fix and pilot it on a small ring.

## Your task

Build a complete remediation pair for a real issue: a stale DNS cache or a disabled firewall profile (your choice). The **detection** script must read-only check the condition, write a clear single-line status, and exit 0 or 1 correctly. The **remediation** script must fix it **idempotently**, wrap changes in `try/catch`, and exit 0 on success and 1 on failure. State which context (SYSTEM or user) and bitness it needs and why. Finally, use `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` to list the `deviceHealthScripts` in your tenant.

quiz.q: In a proactive remediation, what does an exit code of 1 from the detection script mean?
options: An issue was detected, so the remediation script should run
quiz.why: By contract, detection exit 0 means compliant (no action), and exit 1 means an issue was detected and triggers the remediation script on that device.

quiz.q: Why must a remediation script be idempotent?
options: So running it repeatedly on already-fixed devices causes no harm and produces the same end state
Because Intune only runs it once ever
So it can run without PowerShell
quiz.why: Remediations run on a schedule, so re-running on an already-healthy device must be safe and produce the same correct state without side effects or errors.

quiz.q: By default, in which security context does a proactive remediation run?
options: The local SYSTEM account, unless you choose to run it in the user context
A domain admin account you supply
quiz.why: Remediations run as SYSTEM by default; you can opt to run them in the logged-on user's context, which matters for HKCU registry keys and per-user settings.

quiz.q: What should detection write to standard output to make Intune reporting useful?
options: A short single-line status string via Write-Output describing the finding
quiz.why: The last line written to stdout is surfaced as the pre/post-remediation output in Intune reports, so a concise status string makes triage and reporting far easier.

quiz.q: Name the setting you must enable when a remediation needs to read 64-bit registry or program paths.
quiz.answer: Run script in 64-bit PowerShell (set to Yes); otherwise the script runs in 32-bit and may be redirected to WOW6432Node or miss 64-bit paths.
quiz.why: By default scripts can run 32-bit; enabling 64-bit execution prevents registry/file-system redirection from hiding the real 64-bit state on modern Windows.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why split logic into separate detection and remediation scripts rather than one script that fixes everything?
quiz.answer: Detection-only runs let you measure how widespread an issue is and report on it without changing devices, and only the affected machines incur the remediation, which is safer and observable.
quiz.why: The pair model gives you a reporting/measurement phase and a controlled fix phase, so you can pilot, quantify impact, and avoid touching healthy devices.

ht2-l05-configuration-as-code.title: Configuration as code for endpoints
objectives: Explain why endpoint configuration should be declarative, versioned code
Export an existing Intune policy as JSON via Graph
Store policy definitions in Git and review changes through pull requests
Write an idempotent import that creates or updates a policy by name
Separate environment-specific values from policy templates
Understand the IntuneCM / community tooling landscape for config as code
ht2-l05-configuration-as-code.body:
## Why configuration should be code

Clicking through the Intune portal works for one device, once. It does not scale, it leaves no history, and a wrong click can hit thousands of endpoints. **Configuration as code** treats your **desired state** as declarative files — JSON policy definitions — kept in **Git** and deployed by automation. You gain a diffable **audit trail**, **peer review** through pull requests, and **rollback** to any prior commit.

The mental model: the repo is the source of truth, and Intune is just the runtime that the repo deploys to.

## Export what you already have

Start by capturing your current state. Graph exposes configuration profiles as resources you can `GET` and serialise to JSON.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All'

$policies = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/configurationPolicies' |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty value

foreach ($p in $policies) {
    $safe = $p.name -replace '[^\w\-]', '_'
    $p | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content ".\policies\$safe.json" -Encoding UTF8
}
```

Commit that `policies` folder to Git. You now have a baseline you can diff against forever.

## Idempotent import: create or update by name

The heart of config as code is an import that is **safe to re-run**. It looks the policy up by a stable key — usually `displayName` or `name` — then **updates** it if it exists and **creates** it if it does not.

```powershell
function Import-IntunePolicy {
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]
    param([Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Path)

    $def  = Get-Content $Path -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
    $base = 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/configurationPolicies'

    $existing = (Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
        -Uri "$base?`$filter=name eq '$($def.name)'").value

    if ($existing) {
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($def.name, 'Update policy')) {
            Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method PATCH `
                -Uri "$base/$($existing[0].id)" -Body ($def | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20)
        }
    }
    else {
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($def.name, 'Create policy')) {
            Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method POST `
                -Uri $base -Body ($def | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20)
        }
    }
}
```

Run it twice; the second run changes nothing. That is the property you want.

## Separate templates from environment values

Never hard-code tenant or group ids inside a policy template. Keep them in a **parameter file** per environment and inject at deploy time, so the *same* template promotes from **dev** to **prod** by swapping one file.

```powershell
$env = Get-Content '.\envs\prod.json' -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
$template = (Get-Content '.\templates\baseline.json' -Raw) `
    -replace '{{TargetGroupId}}', $env.TargetGroupId
```

## The tooling landscape

You can write your own importer, or stand on community tooling. Projects like the **IntuneCM** family and Microsoft's own samples wrap this export/import/assign loop with backup and reporting. Whatever you use, the principles are identical: declarative files, Git review, idempotent deploy.

## Your task

Build a minimal config-as-code pipeline by hand. Export at least two Intune **configurationPolicies** to JSON and commit them. Write an idempotent `Import-IntunePolicy` function (create-or-update by name, with `SupportsShouldProcess`). Move one environment-specific value — a target group id — out of the template into a per-environment JSON file and inject it at deploy time. Demonstrate a re-run that reports *no changes* the second time, and capture the `-WhatIf` output as proof of a safe dry run.

quiz.q: What is the core principle of configuration as code for endpoints?
options: Define configuration declaratively in versioned files and deploy it through automation
quiz.why: Config as code means the desired state lives in declarative, version-controlled files that are deployed by automation, giving you review, history, rollback, and repeatability.

quiz.q: Why export Intune policies to JSON and keep them in Git?
options: JSON runs faster than the portal
You get change history, peer review via pull requests, and reliable rollback
quiz.why: Versioning policy JSON in Git gives you a diffable audit trail, code review through pull requests, and the ability to roll back to a known-good state.

quiz.q: What makes an import script idempotent when applying a policy?
options: It checks whether a policy of that name exists and updates it, otherwise creates it
It always creates a new policy each run
It only runs once per tenant
quiz.why: An idempotent import is safe to re-run: it looks up the policy by a stable key (like displayName), updating if present and creating if absent, so repeated runs converge on the same state.

quiz.q: How should environment-specific values (tenant, group ids) be handled in config as code?
options: Hard-code them in each policy file
Keep them in separate parameter/variable files and inject at deploy time
Store them inside the policy displayName
quiz.why: Separating environment values from policy templates lets the same template deploy to dev and prod by swapping a parameter file, avoiding copy-paste drift.

quiz.q: Name one Graph endpoint family you would call to manage Intune device configuration profiles as code.
quiz.answer: deviceManagement/deviceConfigurations (or the settings-catalog configurationPolicies and deviceCompliancePolicies endpoints) under https://graph.microsoft.com.
quiz.why: These endpoints expose Intune configuration and compliance policies as resources you can GET to export and POST/PATCH to import, which is what config-as-code tooling drives.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why is a pull request review valuable for an Intune policy change?
quiz.answer: A reviewer can see the exact JSON diff before it reaches devices, catching mistakes like an over-broad assignment or a wrong setting before they affect the fleet.
quiz.why: Policy changes are high blast-radius; reviewing the diff in a pull request applies the same safety net to configuration that teams already apply to code.

ht2-l06-reusable-modules-error-handling.title: Building reusable automation modules with error handling
objectives: Structure a script module (.psm1) and manifest (.psd1) the right way
Control which functions are public versus internal with Export-ModuleMember
Build robust error handling with try/catch/finally and custom error records
Add structured logging and verbose output that callers can toggle
Add retry with exponential backoff as a reusable helper
Write a basic Pester test to protect a function's behaviour

quiz.q: What is the role of the module manifest (.psd1)?
options: It declares metadata, version, dependencies, and what the module exports
It is optional and ignored by PowerShell
quiz.why: The .psd1 manifest declares the module's version, author, required modules, and the functions/cmdlets it exports, while the .psm1 holds the actual code.

quiz.q: How do you keep a helper function internal to a module so callers cannot use it directly?
options: Name it with a lowercase letter
Do not list it in FunctionsToExport / Export-ModuleMember
quiz.why: Only functions you explicitly export (via Export-ModuleMember or FunctionsToExport in the manifest) are public; everything else stays private to the module scope.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of throwing a custom error record with a meaningful category and target?
options: Callers can catch specific error types and get actionable context for diagnostics
quiz.why: A well-formed ErrorRecord (message, category, target object) lets callers branch on the failure type and gives operators the context they need, rather than a generic opaque failure.

quiz.q: In a retry-with-backoff helper, why increase the wait time after each failed attempt?
options: To make the script slower on purpose
To avoid hammering a struggling or throttling service and give it time to recover
quiz.why: Exponential backoff spaces out retries so you stop pounding a service that is rate-limiting or temporarily down, which is both more polite and more likely to succeed.

quiz.q: Name the testing framework you would use to write automated tests for your PowerShell module.
quiz.answer: Pester — the de facto PowerShell testing framework, using Describe/It blocks and Should assertions to test functions and mock dependencies.
quiz.why: Pester lets you assert behaviour and mock Graph calls so you can test logic without touching a live tenant, which is essential for reliable, refactorable modules.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why prefer Write-Verbose and a logging function over Write-Host inside a module?
quiz.answer: Write-Host writes straight to the host and cannot be captured or toggled, whereas Write-Verbose and a logging function let callers control detail and redirect or persist logs.
quiz.why: Modules are consumed by other scripts and runbooks, so output must be controllable and capturable rather than hard-printed to a screen that may not exist.

ht2-l07-azure-automation-runbooks.title: Scheduled automation and runbooks with Azure Automation
objectives: Explain what Azure Automation runbooks are and when to use them over local scripts
Authenticate a runbook to Graph using a managed identity instead of stored secrets
Grant a managed identity the exact Graph application permissions it needs
Import modules into the Automation account and pin versions
Schedule a runbook and pass parameters at run time
Capture output, errors, and verbose streams in job logs for operations
ht2-l07-azure-automation-runbooks.body:
## Why run automation in the cloud

A script that only works when *you* run it on *your* laptop is not automation — it is a chore with extra steps. **Azure Automation** hosts your PowerShell as **runbooks** that run unattended on Azure compute, on a **schedule** or trigger, with no machine to leave switched on and no one to remember to click run.

Use runbooks for anything recurring at fleet scale: nightly stale-device reports, scheduled group hygiene, off-hours remediation sweeps.

## Authenticate without secrets: managed identity

The worst thing you can do is paste a credential into a script. A **managed identity** is an Azure-managed credential attached to the Automation account; Azure rotates it and you never see it. The Graph SDK connects to it with one switch.

```powershell
# Inside the runbook — no secret, no prompt
Connect-MgGraph -Identity -NoWelcome

$context = Get-MgContext
Write-Output "Connected as $($context.AppName) in tenant $($context.TenantId)"
```

Because the runbook runs **as itself** with no signed-in user, it uses **application permissions**, not delegated ones.

## Grant the identity exactly what it needs

You grant the managed identity specific **Graph application permissions** (app roles) — and only those. This is least privilege at the identity level. The grant itself can be scripted.

```powershell
# Run once by an admin to grant the runbook's identity a Graph app role
$graphSp   = Get-MgServicePrincipal -Filter "appId eq '00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000'"
$miSp      = Get-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId $managedIdentityObjectId
$appRole   = $graphSp.AppRoles | Where-Object { $_.Value -eq 'DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All' }

New-MgServicePrincipalAppRoleAssignment -ServicePrincipalId $miSp.Id `
    -PrincipalId $miSp.Id -ResourceId $graphSp.Id -AppRoleId $appRole.Id
```

## Modules and version pinning

A runbook can only use modules **imported into the Automation account**. Import the Graph sub-modules you need and **pin their versions** so a surprise update never breaks a scheduled job at 2 a.m.

```powershell
# The runbook body declares what it expects; the account provides it
#Requires -Modules @{ ModuleName='Microsoft.Graph.Authentication'; ModuleVersion='2.0.0' }
#Requires -Modules @{ ModuleName='Microsoft.Graph.DeviceManagement'; ModuleVersion='2.0.0' }
```

Import modules via the portal, or programmatically with `New-AzAutomationModule`.

## Schedule, parameterise, and log

Attach a **schedule** (daily, weekly, or a recurring interval) and pass **parameters** at run time so one runbook serves many cases. Because there is no console, design for the **job log**: every `Write-Output`, `Write-Error`, and `Write-Verbose` is captured per job.

```powershell
param(
    [int]$StaleDays = 30,
    [string]$OutputContainerUrl
)
Connect-MgGraph -Identity -NoWelcome

$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddDays(-$StaleDays)
$stale  = Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All |
    Where-Object { $_.LastSyncDateTime -lt $cutoff }

Write-Output "Found $($stale.Count) devices stale beyond $StaleDays days"
$stale | Select-Object DeviceName, LastSyncDateTime | ConvertTo-Json
```

Review the per-job streams in the Automation account's **job history** to confirm what ran and catch failures.

## Your task

Design (and where you have a sandbox, build) a runbook `Report-StaleDevices` that authenticates with `Connect-MgGraph -Identity`, accepts a `-StaleDays` parameter, lists every device stale beyond that window, and writes a JSON summary to `Write-Output`. List the **exact** Graph application permission its managed identity needs and why. Add `#Requires` lines pinning the Graph module versions, and attach a daily schedule. Describe where you would read the job log to verify the run and how you would alert on failure.

quiz.q: What is an Azure Automation runbook?
options: A local scheduled task on each device
A PowerShell (or Python) script that runs unattended in the cloud on Azure's compute
quiz.why: A runbook is a script hosted in an Azure Automation account that runs on managed cloud compute, on a schedule or trigger, with no local machine required.

quiz.q: How should a runbook authenticate to Microsoft Graph in production?
options: A system-assigned managed identity granted the needed Graph app permissions
A username and password stored in the script
A shared admin token pasted in a variable
quiz.why: A managed identity removes stored secrets entirely; Azure manages the credential, and you grant that identity the specific Graph application permissions it requires.

quiz.q: Why pin module versions in the Automation account rather than always using latest?
options: Pinning gives reproducible runs and prevents a new module version from silently breaking a runbook
quiz.why: Pinning the Microsoft.Graph module versions means a runbook behaves identically every run; an unexpected module update will not change behaviour or break a scheduled job overnight.

quiz.q: When a runbook uses a managed identity, which Connect-MgGraph parameter do you use?
quiz.why: Connect-MgGraph -Identity authenticates using the Automation account's managed identity, with no secret stored or prompt shown.

quiz.q: Name where you go to see what a runbook actually did, including errors and verbose output, after a scheduled run.
quiz.answer: The job history / job logs for that runbook in the Automation account, which capture the Output, Error, Warning, and Verbose streams for each run.
quiz.why: Unattended jobs have no console, so the per-job stream logs are your only window into success, failure, and diagnostics; design your runbook to write useful verbose/error output.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why are application permissions (not delegated) usually right for an unattended runbook?
quiz.answer: An unattended runbook has no signed-in user, so it needs application permissions granted to its identity with admin consent, scoped to only the operations it performs.
quiz.why: Delegated permissions act on behalf of a signed-in user; a scheduled runbook runs as itself, so it uses application permissions consented by an admin and kept least-privilege.

ht2-l08-lab-automate-a-tier3-workflow.title: Lab: automate a real Tier 3 workflow end to end
objectives: Decompose a real Tier 3 workflow into detect, decide, act, and report stages
Combine the module, Graph calls, remediation logic, and a runbook into one solution
Make every action safe with ShouldProcess, retry, and idempotency
Produce a machine-readable report and a human-readable summary
Authenticate the unattended path with a managed identity and least privilege
Define success criteria and a rollback plan for the automation

quiz.q: What is the right first step when automating a Tier 3 workflow end to end?
options: Decompose the workflow into clear stages: detect, decide, act, report
Write the remediation first and test in production
Grant the broadest permissions to avoid errors
Skip dry runs to save time
quiz.why: Breaking the workflow into detect, decide, act, and report stages lets you build and test each piece, add safety at the act stage, and reason about failure before touching the fleet.

quiz.q: Why run the act stage behind ShouldProcess with a pilot ring before fleet-wide rollout?
options: It removes the need for logging
A dry run and small pilot prove the logic and limit blast radius before scaling
quiz.why: Previewing with -WhatIf and piloting on a small group catches mistakes while the impact is tiny, which is essential for high blast-radius endpoint automation.

quiz.q: In the end-to-end design, what authenticates the scheduled, unattended run?
options: The Automation account's managed identity with least-privilege application permissions
quiz.why: Unattended runs use the managed identity granted only the Graph application permissions the workflow needs, removing stored secrets and limiting scope.

quiz.q: Why produce both a machine-readable report (JSON/CSV) and a human-readable summary?
options: The machine format feeds dashboards and tickets while the summary lets a human triage at a glance
Humans cannot read JSON at all
quiz.why: Structured output integrates with downstream systems, and a concise summary makes the run immediately understandable to an on-call engineer, serving two different consumers.

quiz.q: Name two safety mechanisms from this month that your end-to-end automation should include.
quiz.answer: Any two of: ShouldProcess/-WhatIf dry runs, idempotent actions, try/catch error handling, retry with exponential backoff and Retry-After handling, least-privilege scopes, and a pilot ring before fleet rollout.
quiz.why: Production endpoint automation must be previewable, idempotent, resilient to throttling/transient errors, least-privilege, and rolled out gradually — these were the recurring themes of the month.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what should your rollback plan cover for an automation that changes device or group state?
quiz.answer: It should define how to stop the schedule, reverse the change (for example remove added group members or restore the prior policy), and confirm devices returned to the known-good baseline you exported beforehand.
quiz.why: Because changes have blast radius, a tested rollback — disable schedule, reverse the action, verify against the exported baseline — turns a bad run from an incident into a non-event.

ht3-l01-zero-trust-for-endpoints.title: Zero Trust architecture for endpoints
objectives: Explain the three Zero Trust principles and why implicit trust by network location is obsolete
Map the Zero Trust pillars to endpoint controls: identity, device, app, data, network
Describe how device compliance state becomes a signal in an access decision
Differentiate authentication, authorization and continuous access evaluation at the endpoint
Design a high-level Zero Trust enforcement flow for a managed Windows device
Identify the telemetry sources that feed endpoint trust decisions
ht3-l01-zero-trust-for-endpoints.body:
## The perimeter is gone

For decades security assumed a hard shell and a soft centre: get past the firewall or onto the VPN, and you were trusted. Cloud apps, remote work and BYOD destroyed that model. **Zero Trust** replaces it with three principles: **verify explicitly**, use **least-privilege access**, and **assume breach**. Network location is no longer a trust signal. Every request — including from a device sitting in your own office — must be authenticated, authorized and validated against current signals.

For an endpoint engineer this is a mindset shift. The device stops being a passive client and becomes an active participant whose **health and compliance state** feed directly into whether access is granted.

## The pillars and how endpoints touch each

Microsoft's Zero Trust model spans **Identity, Devices, Applications, Data, Network** and Infrastructure. An endpoint sits at the intersection:

- **Identity** — the user and the device both have identities (the device identity comes from Entra join or hybrid join).
- **Devices** — compliance policy decides if the endpoint is healthy: encrypted, patched, EDR-onboarded, not jailbroken.
- **Applications** — app protection policies and managed app access.
- **Data** — encryption at rest (BitLocker) and labelling/DLP in transit.
- **Network** — segmentation so a compromised endpoint cannot roam.

## Compliance state as a signal

The heart of endpoint Zero Trust is that **device compliance becomes an input to authorization**. Intune evaluates a device against policy and stamps it compliant or non-compliant. **Conditional Access** then consumes that state. A simplified decision flow looks like this:

```text
User + device request access to resource
  -> Authenticate user (MFA / passwordless)
  -> Evaluate signals: user risk, sign-in risk, device compliance, location, app
  -> Decision: Grant / Grant with controls / Block
  -> Continuously re-evaluate (CAE) for revocation & risk change
```

Notice authorization is **not** a one-time gate. With **Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)** a disabled account, a password reset or a sudden risk spike can revoke a live session in near real time, instead of waiting for a token to expire.

## Least privilege at the endpoint

Assume breach means scoping access tightly. On the endpoint that translates to removing standing local-admin rights, using **just-in-time** elevation, and applying **just-enough-access**. You can confirm a user is not a standing admin:

```powershell
# List members of the local Administrators group
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' |
  Select-Object Name, PrincipalSource, ObjectClass
```

Every account that does not strictly need elevation is removed. A compromised standard user is far less useful to an attacker than a compromised admin.

## Telemetry feeds the decision

Zero Trust only works if the signals are trustworthy and current. Endpoint telemetry — sign-in logs, **Defender for Endpoint** alerts, Intune compliance, and device risk scores — flows into the policy engine. The richer and fresher the signal, the better the decision. This is why EDR onboarding and compliance reporting are not optional extras; they are the sensory system of your access control.

## Your task

For one managed Windows device in a test tenant, document its full Zero Trust posture: device join type, compliance policy result, BitLocker and EDR onboarding state, and the local Administrators membership. Then draw the access-decision flow for that device reaching a sensitive app, naming every signal Conditional Access would evaluate and where CAE would intervene on a revocation event.

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the core assumption of Zero Trust?
options: Devices inside the corporate network are trusted by default
Assume breach and verify every request explicitly regardless of network location
VPN-connected devices need no further checks
Trust is granted once at logon and never re-evaluated
quiz.why: Zero Trust replaces the perimeter model with explicit, per-request verification under an assume-breach posture, so network location alone never confers trust.

quiz.q: In a Zero Trust access decision for an endpoint, which is treated as a primary signal alongside user identity?
options: The device's compliance and health state
The colour of the desktop wallpaper
quiz.why: Device compliance and health (managed, encrypted, patched, not flagged by EDR) are first-class signals that Conditional Access and the access broker evaluate before granting access.

quiz.q: What does the principle of 'least privilege' add to endpoint Zero Trust?
options: It grants admin rights to all users for convenience
It limits access with just-in-time and just-enough-access and risk-based adaptive policies
It disables all auditing to reduce noise
It removes the need for MFA
quiz.why: Least privilege means scoping access tightly using JIT/JEA and adaptive, risk-based policies so a compromised endpoint or account has minimal blast radius.

quiz.q: Why is Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) important in a Zero Trust endpoint design?
options: It caches tokens forever to improve speed
It lets revocation and risk changes take effect near real time instead of waiting for token expiry
It replaces the need for device compliance
quiz.why: CAE allows critical events such as account disable, password reset or elevated risk to revoke access in near real time rather than waiting up to an hour for token lifetime to lapse.

quiz.q: Name the five core Microsoft Zero Trust pillars that an endpoint design touches.
quiz.answer: Identity, Devices (endpoints), Applications, Data, and Network (with Infrastructure often added as a sixth).
quiz.why: Microsoft's Zero Trust model spans Identity, Endpoints/Devices, Apps, Data, Network and Infrastructure; an endpoint strategy must consider how the device interacts with each.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why 'assume breach' changes how you design endpoint controls.
quiz.answer: Because you design as though an attacker is already present, you segment access, verify continuously, encrypt data and minimise privilege so a single compromised endpoint cannot move laterally or exfiltrate freely.
quiz.why: Assume breach shifts focus from keeping attackers out to limiting damage, driving micro-segmentation, least privilege, encryption and rich telemetry on every endpoint.

ht3-l02-advanced-conditional-access.title: Advanced Conditional Access and risk-based policies
objectives: Break a Conditional Access policy into its assignments and access controls and explain what each lever does
Design a layered set of policies rather than one monolithic rule, and reason about policy intersection
Distinguish sign-in risk from user risk and map each to the correct Identity Protection policy
Require phishing-resistant authentication using authentication strengths instead of the legacy MFA toggle
Apply session controls — sign-in frequency, persistent browser, app-enforced restrictions and CAE
Roll policies out safely with report-only mode and exclude break-glass emergency access accounts
ht3-l02-advanced-conditional-access.body:
## Anatomy of a Conditional Access policy

Every Conditional Access policy is an if-then statement: **if** these assignments match, **then** apply these access controls. Master the anatomy and the rest follows.

- **Assignments** define the scope. They are **users** (or workload identities), **target resources** (cloud apps, user actions like registering security info, or authentication context), and **conditions** (sign-in risk, user risk, device platform, locations, client apps, device filters).
- **Access controls** define the outcome. **Grant** controls either block or grant with requirements such as **require MFA**, **require compliant device**, **require Intune-managed or hybrid-joined device**, **require app protection policy**, or **require authentication strength**. **Session** controls shape the resulting session.

A policy with no matching assignment never fires. A policy that matches always applies its controls — and **multiple matching policies combine**: all grant requirements are ANDed together, and any single block wins.

## Design layered, not monolithic

Resist the urge to cram everything into one rule. Build small, single-purpose policies so intersection is predictable and troubleshooting is sane:

```text
CA001  Block legacy authentication            (all users)
CA002  Require phishing-resistant MFA          (admin roles)
CA003  Require compliant device                (all users, M365 apps)
CA004  Require MFA on sign-in risk = medium+   (all users)
CA005  Require password change on user risk    (all users)
CA006  Sign-in frequency 12h + no persistence  (unmanaged devices)
CA000  EXCLUDE break-glass accounts            (every policy)
```

Each policy does one thing. Together they form a defence-in-depth mesh where the grant requirements stack.

## Sign-in risk versus user risk

**Identity Protection** produces two distinct risk signals and they need different remediation.

- **Sign-in risk** is the probability that a *single authentication* is not the legitimate owner — impossible travel, anonymous IP, unfamiliar properties. Remediate in real time by **requiring MFA**.
- **User risk** is the cumulative probability that the *account itself* is compromised — leaked credentials, confirmed-compromise patterns. Remediate by **requiring a secure password change** (self-service password reset with MFA), which also dismisses the risk.

You wire these in as conditions on Conditional Access grant controls:

```json
{
  "conditions": { "signInRiskLevels": ["high", "medium"] },
  "grantControls": {
    "operator": "OR",
    "builtInControls": ["mfa"]
  }
}
```

## Strengths, session controls and locations

Drop the legacy MFA toggle for privileged access. An **authentication strength** lets you demand specific methods; the built-in **phishing-resistant** strength permits only **FIDO2**, **Windows Hello for Business** and **certificate-based** authentication.

**Session controls** govern the session after grant: **sign-in frequency** forces periodic reauthentication; **persistent browser** controls staying signed in; **app-enforced restrictions** let Office and SharePoint limit downloads on unmanaged devices; and **continuous access evaluation (CAE)** revokes sessions in near real time on critical events. **Named locations** and **device filters** sharpen conditions — for example, treating a trusted country differently or excluding a kiosk by its device attributes.

Find risky sign-ins to validate your risk policies:

```kql
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high", "medium")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName,
          RiskLevelDuringSignIn, ConditionalAccessStatus, IPAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc
```

## Roll out safely and avoid lockout

Never flip a new policy straight to On. Set it to **report-only**, let it observe real sign-ins, and read the **Conditional Access Insights** workbook and sign-in logs to see who *would* have been blocked. Surprises — service accounts, legacy clients, a forgotten region — show up here, not in a flood of help-desk tickets.

The non-negotiable safeguard: maintain two cloud-only **break-glass** accounts **excluded from every policy**, with long random passphrases, monitored sign-in alerts, and periodic testing. A policy that requires a compliant device or a downed MFA provider can otherwise lock out every admin — break-glass is your way back in.

## Your task

In a test tenant, design and document a layered set of at least five Conditional Access policies covering: block legacy auth, phishing-resistant strength for admins, compliant-device requirement, a sign-in-risk MFA policy and a user-risk password-change policy. Create each in **report-only** mode, confirm both break-glass accounts are excluded from all of them, run the Insights workbook for 48 hours, and write up the would-be impact (affected users, apps, sessions) plus any misconfiguration you caught before enabling enforcement.

quiz.q: A Conditional Access policy is structured as assignments and access controls. Which item is an ASSIGNMENT rather than an access control?
options: Require device to be marked as compliant
quiz.why: Assignments define WHO and WHAT a policy targets — users/groups, target resources, and conditions. Grant requirements like MFA, compliant device or app protection policy are access controls that fire once the assignment matches.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between sign-in risk and user risk in Microsoft Entra Identity Protection?
options: Sign-in risk is about the account being compromised over time; user risk is about a single authentication
Sign-in risk reflects the probability that a specific authentication is not the legitimate owner; user risk reflects the probability the account itself is compromised
They are identical and used interchangeably
User risk only applies to guest accounts
quiz.why: Sign-in risk is real-time and per-authentication (impossible travel, anonymous IP, unfamiliar properties), so the right remediation is MFA. User risk is a cumulative judgement that the identity is compromised (leaked credentials, confirmed-compromise patterns), so the right remediation is a secure password change.

quiz.q: You want to require phishing-resistant authentication for admins. What is the correct modern mechanism?
options: The legacy 'Require multifactor authentication' grant control
An authentication strength that allows only phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based)
Enabling the per-user MFA toggle in the legacy portal
quiz.why: Authentication strengths let you require a specific set of methods. The built-in phishing-resistant strength permits only FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business and certificate-based authentication — stronger and more precise than the generic MFA grant.

quiz.q: Which session control causes the browser session to be re-evaluated and revoked in near real time when critical events occur, rather than waiting for token expiry?
quiz.why: Continuous access evaluation lets resource providers honour near-real-time revocation events (account disable, password reset, elevated risk). Sign-in frequency forces periodic reauthentication but is not real-time; persistent browser and app-enforced restrictions serve different purposes.

quiz.q: Explain why break-glass (emergency access) accounts must be excluded from Conditional Access policies, and one safeguard you apply instead.
quiz.answer: A misconfigured or dependency-broken policy (for example one requiring a compliant device, a specific MFA provider, or a location you cannot reach) can lock every admin out of the tenant. Two cloud-only break-glass accounts excluded from all policies guarantee you can still sign in to fix it. Safeguards include long random passphrases, phishing-resistant MFA where possible, tight sign-in alerting/monitoring, and periodic credential testing.
quiz.why: Excluding break-glass accounts prevents a single bad policy or a downed MFA/identity dependency from permanently locking administrators out, while monitoring and strong credentials limit the risk those highly privileged exclusions create.

quiz.q: In one or two sentences, describe how report-only mode supports a safe Conditional Access rollout and what you inspect before enabling.
quiz.answer: Report-only mode evaluates the policy against real sign-ins and records what WOULD have happened without actually enforcing grant or block, so you can detect unintended impact. You inspect the sign-in logs and the Conditional Access Insights workbook to see which users, apps and sessions would have been affected, confirm break-glass accounts are excluded, then flip to On.
quiz.why: Report-only surfaces the real-world blast radius — including surprises like service accounts or legacy clients — before enforcement, which is the safest way to avoid mass lockouts when a new policy goes live.

ht3-l03-defender-for-endpoint-advanced-h.title: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and advanced hunting
objectives: Describe the core Defender for Endpoint capabilities: next-gen AV, EDR, ASR rules, network protection and TVM
Compare onboarding methods and explain what telemetry an onboarded device emits
Navigate the advanced hunting data model and identify the key Device* schema tables
Write KQL using where, project, summarize, parse and join across DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents and DeviceLogonEvents
Promote a validated hunting query into a custom detection rule and map findings to MITRE ATT&CK
Use the device timeline and live response for hands-on investigation and remediation
ht3-l03-defender-for-endpoint-advanced-h.body:
## What Defender for Endpoint actually is

**Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE)** is not a single antivirus product; it is a layered endpoint protection platform. The layers worth knowing: **next-generation antivirus** (cloud-backed, behaviour-based protection), **endpoint detection and response (EDR)** that records rich behavioural telemetry and raises alerts, **attack surface reduction (ASR) rules** that block risky behaviours like an Office app spawning a child process, **network protection** that blocks connections to malicious domains and IPs, and **threat & vulnerability management (TVM)** that inventories software and surfaces exploitable CVEs with remediation guidance.

The layer that makes MDE a hunting platform is EDR: every onboarded device continuously streams **behavioural telemetry** — process creations, network connections, file writes, logons, registry edits — into the cloud where you can query it.

## Onboarding and the data it produces

A device only contributes telemetry once it is **onboarded**. Common methods: **Intune** (the modern default for managed Windows), **Group Policy** or a local **onboarding script**, **Microsoft Configuration Manager**, and platform-native onboarding for macOS and Linux. Onboarding installs the sensor and connects the device to your tenant. From that moment its events flow into the **advanced hunting** schema.

## The advanced hunting data model

**Advanced hunting** is a query-based investigation tool over up to 30 days of raw event data, written in **KQL** (Kusto Query Language). The schema is organised into tables; the endpoint ones are prefixed `Device`:

- `DeviceProcessEvents` — process creations and command lines.
- `DeviceNetworkEvents` — outbound and inbound connections.
- `DeviceFileEvents` — file create, modify, rename, delete.
- `DeviceLogonEvents` — interactive, network and remote logons.
- `DeviceRegistryEvents`, `DeviceImageLoadEvents`, `DeviceEvents` — registry, DLL loads and miscellaneous sensor events.

Every row carries `DeviceId`, `Timestamp` and a set of `InitiatingProcess*` columns describing the parent process — these are the keys you join on.

## Writing KQL over the schema

KQL reads top to bottom, piping a table through operators. The core verbs are **where** (filter rows), **project** (choose columns), **summarize** (aggregate), **parse** (extract from a string) and **join** (correlate tables). Hunt for a script interpreter launched from Office:

```kql
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe", "excel.exe", "outlook.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
```

Now correlate suspicious processes with the connections they made by **joining** the process and network tables on the device and initiating process:

```kql
let suspect = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-enc", "DownloadString", "FromBase64String");
suspect
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
) on DeviceId, $left.ProcessId == $right.InitiatingProcessId
| summarize Connections = count() by DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Connections desc
```

## From query to detection and investigation

A query that reliably finds bad behaviour should not stay manual. Use **Create detection rule** to schedule the KQL, raise an alert when rows return, and optionally trigger response actions. Each alert is mapped to **MITRE ATT&CK** tactics and techniques so the behaviour gets a shared name and a place in the kill chain.

For hands-on work, the **device timeline** shows a chronological event stream, and **live response** gives you a secure remote shell:

```text
live response session (analyst):
  connect <deviceId>
  getfile "C:\Users\Public\dropper.ps1"   # collect evidence
  processes                                  # list running processes
  remediate file <SHA1>                      # quarantine
  run TriageScript.ps1                        # run a library script
```

Isolation, package collection and file quarantine can all be driven from here or automated by the detection rule.

## Your task

In a test tenant's advanced hunting, write a query that hunts for likely lateral movement: find `DeviceLogonEvents` with `LogonType == "RemoteInteractive"` (RDP) where the same `RemoteIP` produced more than five `LogonFailed` events before a `LogonSuccess` within an hour. Use `summarize` with `count()` and time bucketing, `project` only the fields an analyst needs, then join back to `DeviceProcessEvents` to show what the successful session ran. Finally, describe how you would promote it to a custom detection rule and which ATT&CK technique it maps to.

quiz.q: Which Defender for Endpoint capability proactively reduces the available attack surface by blocking risky behaviours such as Office apps spawning child processes?
quiz.why: ASR rules are configurable controls that block or audit risky behaviours (Office child processes, obfuscated scripts, credential theft from LSASS), shrinking the attack surface before an exploit can run.

quiz.q: In advanced hunting, which KQL operator is correct for selecting only the columns you want to keep in the result set?
quiz.why: project chooses and reshapes the columns returned; where filters rows. KQL has no select keyword, and parse/extract pull substrings out of a single field.

quiz.q: You want to correlate a suspicious process with the network connections it made. Which two schema tables and join key are most appropriate?
options: DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents joined on DeviceId and InitiatingProcessId
quiz.why: Process-to-network correlation joins DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents; the network table records the InitiatingProcess* fields, so you match on DeviceId plus the initiating process identity to tie a connection back to its parent process.

quiz.q: What is the effect of promoting a validated advanced hunting query into a custom detection rule?
options: It deletes the underlying telemetry to save storage
It runs the query on a schedule and generates alerts plus optional automated response actions
It exports the query to a CSV once and stops
It disables the built-in Microsoft detections
quiz.why: A custom detection rule runs your KQL on a recurring frequency, raises an alert when rows return, and can trigger response actions such as isolating the device or collecting an investigation package.

quiz.q: Name the advanced hunting schema table you would query to investigate interactive and remote sign-in activity on a device, and one field you would use to spot anomalous logons.
quiz.answer: DeviceLogonEvents. Useful fields include LogonType (for example Interactive, Network, RemoteInteractive), AccountName, RemoteIP and ActionType (LogonSuccess or LogonFailed) to spot brute force or unusual remote logons.
quiz.why: DeviceLogonEvents records authentication on the device; LogonType plus failed/success ActionType and source RemoteIP reveal lateral movement, password spraying and unexpected RemoteInteractive (RDP) sessions.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why mapping a hunting finding to MITRE ATT&CK is valuable during an investigation.
quiz.answer: Mapping to ATT&CK tactics and techniques gives the behaviour a shared, standard name so you can communicate it clearly, find related detections, anticipate the attacker's next likely step and measure your coverage gaps.
quiz.why: ATT&CK provides a common taxonomy of adversary tactics and techniques; framing findings against it turns isolated observations into an understandable kill-chain and drives consistent, comparable detection engineering.

ht3-l04-edr-and-incident-response.title: EDR and endpoint incident response
objectives: Contrast traditional signature antivirus with behaviour-based EDR and explain why telemetry and detections matter
Walk an endpoint incident through the six NIST SP 800-61 phases from preparation to lessons learned
Triage Defender for Endpoint alerts and incidents and pivot on indicators of compromise
Choose between full and selective device isolation and collect an investigation package
Use a live response session to gather artefacts and remediate while preserving evidence
Explain Automated Investigation and Response and how chain of custody is maintained
ht3-l04-edr-and-incident-response.body:
## From signatures to behaviour

Traditional **antivirus** answers one question: does this file match a known-bad signature? That works for commodity malware but fails against fileless attacks, living-off-the-land techniques and novel payloads that have no signature yet. **Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)** changes the question. An EDR agent continuously records endpoint behaviour — process creation, command lines, network connections, registry and file changes — and ships that telemetry to a cloud analytics engine. Detections fire on *behaviour*, not just file hashes, so an attacker abusing `powershell.exe` to download a payload is caught even when the file itself looks clean.

For an endpoint engineer the practical shift is this: the device is now a sensor, and your job is to triage what it reports and respond fast.

## The NIST incident response lifecycle

Discipline beats heroics. **NIST SP 800-61** defines a repeatable lifecycle that keeps responders calm and consistent:

```text
1. Preparation          build tooling, runbooks, contacts, baselines
2. Detection & Analysis confirm it is real, scope the blast radius
3. Containment          stop the spread (short-term + long-term)
4. Eradication          remove malware, accounts, persistence
5. Recovery             restore to known-good, monitor closely
6. Post-Incident        lessons learned, improve the runbook
```

NIST groups containment, eradication and recovery into one major phase, but treat them as distinct steps. The loop is iterative: lessons learned feed straight back into preparation.

## Triage and indicators of compromise

In **Defender for Endpoint**, related alerts are correlated into an **incident**. Start there, not at individual alerts. Read the attack story, identify the impacted assets, and pivot on **indicators of compromise (IOCs)** — file hashes, IP addresses, domains, registry keys. Hunt across the estate to find every device touched by the same IOC. A focused KQL query in advanced hunting confirms scope quickly:

```kql
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where SHA256 == "<suspect-hash>"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Invoke-WebRequest"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
```

Scope before you act: you cannot contain what you have not found.

## Containment: isolation and the investigation package

Defender gives you two **device isolation** modes. **Full isolation** cuts almost all connectivity, leaving only the Defender for Endpoint channel so you keep control. **Selective isolation** blocks a limited set of apps from the network while preserving more of the device — useful when you need the user partly working or want a lighter touch. Before you change anything, **collect the investigation package**: a bundle of autoruns, processes, network connections, scheduled tasks, prefetch and security event logs that preserves the device state as evidence.

## Live response and AIR

A **live response** session is a remote command shell into the isolated device for investigation and surgical remediation — all while the device stays contained.

```powershell
# Inside a live response session
getfile C:\Users\Public\suspicious.exe   # pull artefact to evidence store
processes                                # list running processes
connections                              # active network connections
remediate file C:\Users\Public\suspicious.exe
```

**Automated Investigation and Response (AIR)** can do much of this for you: when an alert fires, AIR investigates the alert tree, determines verdicts and applies approved remediation automatically, shrinking response time from hours to minutes. Always preserve **chain of custody** — record who collected each artefact, when, and where it is stored — so evidence stays trustworthy.

## Your task

In a test tenant, simulate a benign detection on one onboarded device. Walk it through the full lifecycle: triage the incident and note the IOCs, run an advanced hunting query to scope which devices share an IOC, collect the investigation package, place the device in selective isolation, open a live response session and pull one artefact to an evidence store, then write a one-page runbook entry documenting your containment decision, the chain of custody for that artefact, and the recovery and communication steps you would take.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental difference between traditional signature antivirus and EDR?
options: EDR only scans files on a fixed schedule while AV runs continuously
EDR continuously records endpoint behaviour and detects suspicious activity, not just known file signatures
EDR replaces the need for any operating system patching
AV stores full process telemetry centrally while EDR does not
quiz.why: Signature AV matches files against a database of known bad hashes; EDR continuously collects process, network and behavioural telemetry and detects anomalous activity, enabling detection of novel and fileless attacks plus investigation and response.

quiz.q: In the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, which phase directly follows Containment?
quiz.why: NIST orders the lifecycle as Preparation, Detection and Analysis, then Containment, Eradication and Recovery (often grouped), followed by Post-Incident Activity. Eradication removes the threat after the bleeding is stopped by containment.

quiz.q: When should you choose selective isolation rather than full isolation of a device in Defender for Endpoint?
options: When you want to cut all network connectivity including the Defender connection
When you need to block the device's apps from the network while keeping the Defender for Endpoint connection for investigation
When the device is already offline
When you want to permanently remove the device from the tenant
quiz.why: Selective isolation restricts a limited set of processes or apps from network access while preserving the Defender for Endpoint service connection so analysts can keep investigating and running live response; full isolation cuts almost all connectivity except the Defender channel.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of collecting an investigation package from a compromised endpoint?
options: To capture forensic artefacts such as autoruns, processes, network connections and event logs for analysis and evidence
To reinstall the operating system remotely
To deploy a new antivirus signature
quiz.why: The investigation package bundles forensic artefacts (autoruns, installed programs, network connections, prefetch, scheduled tasks, security event logs and more) so analysts can examine the device's state and preserve evidence without working live on the machine.

quiz.q: List the six phases of the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle in order.
quiz.answer: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment; Eradication; Recovery; Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned). NIST groups Containment, Eradication and Recovery into one major phase, but they are distinct steps.
quiz.why: Knowing the ordered lifecycle keeps responders disciplined: prepare first, detect and confirm, contain to stop spread, eradicate the threat, recover to normal operations, then learn so the next incident is handled faster.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why chain of custody matters when handling endpoint evidence.
quiz.answer: Chain of custody documents who collected, accessed and transferred each artefact and when, so the evidence stays trustworthy and admissible and any tampering would be detectable.
quiz.why: Without a documented, unbroken chain of custody, forensic artefacts can be challenged as altered or unreliable, undermining legal action, insurance claims and the credibility of the investigation's conclusions.

ht3-l05-hybrid-identity.title: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect and on-prem Active Directory
objectives: Explain what hybrid identity is and why organisations run on-prem AD alongside Entra ID
Describe the Entra Connect Sync architecture: connector spaces, metaverse and the sync engine
Compare Password Hash Sync, Pass-through Authentication and Federation and choose the right one
Operate the sync scheduler and trigger delta and initial sync cycles from PowerShell
Explain source anchor / immutableID, soft and hard matching, and UPN considerations
Diagnose Entra hybrid join state with dsregcmd and monitor health with Connect Health
ht3-l05-hybrid-identity.body:
## Why hybrid identity exists

Most enterprises did not start in the cloud. They have years of investment in on-premises **Active Directory** (AD) — group policy, file shares, line-of-business apps that authenticate against domain controllers. They also need Microsoft 365, Intune and Conditional Access, which live in **Microsoft Entra ID**. **Hybrid identity** bridges the two so a user has one identity, one password and one sign-on experience whether they hit an on-prem file share or a cloud app.

The bridge is **Microsoft Entra Connect** (the sync client) running **Entra Connect Sync**. It reads objects from AD, transforms them, and provisions matching objects into Entra ID, keeping them in step.

## The sync engine architecture

The engine is not a simple copy. Each connected directory has a **connector space** — a staging area holding a snapshot of that directory's objects. Inbound sync rules project objects into a central **metaverse**, the consolidated view that joins the on-prem user and the cloud user into one record. Outbound rules then export from the metaverse into the Entra ID connector space.

```text
On-prem AD ──import──> AD connector space
                              │ inbound sync rules
                              ▼
                         METAVERSE  (joined view)
                              │ outbound sync rules
                              ▼
               Entra ID connector space ──export──> Entra ID
```

Understanding this pipeline is what lets you reason about *why* an attribute did or did not flow.

## Choosing a sign-in method

Three options decide where the password is actually validated:

- **Password Hash Sync (PHS)** — a hash of the AD password hash is synced to Entra ID. Authentication happens in the cloud, survives a full on-prem outage, and is the lowest-overhead choice. Recommended default.
- **Pass-through Authentication (PTA)** — the password is validated against on-prem AD in real time by a lightweight agent. No password material in the cloud, but it depends on the agent and DCs being reachable.
- **Federation (AD FS)** — sign-in is redirected to an on-prem federation farm. Most control and most infrastructure; reserve it for specific requirements like third-party MFA or smart-card-only auth.

**Seamless single sign-on (SSO)** can sit on top of PHS or PTA to give Kerberos-style silent sign-in on domain-joined devices.

## The sync cycle and scheduler

By default the scheduler runs a **delta (incremental)** sync every 30 minutes, processing only changes. A full **initial** sync reimports everything and is triggered when you change rules. Operate it from PowerShell on the Connect server:

```powershell
# See the current schedule and whether sync is enabled
Get-ADSyncScheduler

# Force an immediate incremental (delta) run
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta

# Force a full reimport + reprocess (heavier; after rule changes)
Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial
```

## Anchors, matching and devices

Every object needs a stable **source anchor** (the **immutableID**). Modern Connect uses **ms-DS-ConsistencyGuid**, a writable attribute that makes forest migrations safe. When an on-prem object meets an existing cloud object, the engine performs a **soft match** on mail/UPN attributes; if that fails you perform a **hard match** by setting the cloud object's immutableID to the Base64 of the source anchor. Watch the **UPN**: the on-prem UPN suffix should be a verified domain in the tenant, or users end up with an `.onmicrosoft.com` UPN.

A device gets its cloud identity through **Entra hybrid join**: the domain-joined computer is registered with Entra ID (its object syncs up via Connect), so it appears as a hybrid-joined device and can satisfy Conditional Access. Verify it on the endpoint:

```text
C:\> dsregcmd /status

+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Device State                                                         |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
             AzureAdJoined : YES
          EnterpriseJoined : NO
              DomainJoined : YES
               Virtual Desktop : NOT SET
                  DeviceId : 2b8c...e91
```

Both `AzureAdJoined : YES` and `DomainJoined : YES` confirm a successful hybrid join. Use **Entra Connect Health** to monitor sync status, errors and latency, and run a **staging server** — a second Connect instance importing but not exporting — for high availability and safe upgrades.

## Your task

On a test Connect server, run `Get-ADSyncScheduler` and record the current sync interval and whether sync is enabled. Change a user's attribute (e.g. department) in on-prem AD, force a delta cycle with `Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta`, and confirm it lands in Entra ID. Then on a hybrid-joined Windows device run `dsregcmd /status`, capture the Device State and SSO State sections, and write a short note explaining which sign-in method your tenant uses and why it is the correct choice for that environment.

quiz.q: In the Entra Connect Sync engine, what is the role of the metaverse?
options: It stores the encrypted password hashes before they leave the server
It is the central aggregated view that joins objects from each connector space before export
It is the staging server's read-only replica of Entra ID
It is the cloud-side directory that Conditional Access reads from
quiz.why: The metaverse is the consolidated in-engine view. Objects flow from each connected directory into its connector space, then inbound sync rules project and join them into the metaverse, and outbound rules export the result to the target connector space.

quiz.q: An organisation needs sign-in to keep working at the cloud even if all on-prem infrastructure is offline, with the lowest operational overhead. Which sign-in method best fits?
quiz.why: Password Hash Sync synchronises a hash-of-the-hash to Entra ID, so authentication happens entirely in the cloud and survives a complete on-prem outage with minimal infrastructure. PTA and AD FS both depend on on-prem components being reachable to validate sign-ins.

quiz.q: Which attribute does Entra Connect use by default as the source anchor (immutableID) for objects synced from on-prem AD?
options: objectGUID converted, with ms-DS-ConsistencyGuid as the modern default
quiz.why: Newer Entra Connect builds use ms-DS-ConsistencyGuid as the source anchor by default (populating it from objectGUID if empty). This makes the anchor writable and portable, which is what allows safe forest migrations and rebuilds without orphaning cloud objects.

quiz.q: A user reports a change made in on-prem AD has not appeared in Entra ID after a few minutes. Which command lets you trigger an immediate incremental synchronisation?
quiz.why: Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta runs an incremental cycle that processes only changes since the last run. Initial (full) reprocesses everything and reimports rules, which is heavier and reserved for rule or configuration changes.

quiz.q: When an on-prem account is matched to an existing cloud account, explain the difference between soft match and hard match.
quiz.answer: Soft match links an on-prem object to a cloud object automatically when their primary SMTP / proxyAddresses or userPrincipalName align, with no manual action. Hard match is when you explicitly set the cloud object's immutableID to equal the Base64 of the on-prem source anchor so the next sync binds them deliberately. Soft match is convenient for clean mail attributes; hard match is the reliable fix when soft match fails or anchors must be repaired.
quiz.why: Both stop the engine creating a duplicate cloud object. Soft match relies on matching mail/UPN attributes; hard match forces the link by aligning the immutableID, and is the controlled tool when soft matching cannot find or trust the attributes.

quiz.q: On a Windows 11 device that should be Entra hybrid joined, dsregcmd /status shows AzureAdJoined : NO and DomainJoined : YES. In one or two sentences, what does this tell you and where would you look first?
quiz.answer: The device is domain-joined to on-prem AD but has not yet completed its cloud registration, so it is not hybrid joined. Check that the SCP (service connection point) points at the right tenant, that the device can reach Entra endpoints, that the computer object is syncing via Entra Connect, and review the Diagnostic Data / dsregcmd /status output and the User State section for join errors.
quiz.why: Hybrid join requires both DomainJoined : YES and AzureAdJoined : YES. AzureAdJoined : NO means the automatic device registration has not succeeded — typically an SCP, connectivity, or sync (the computer object reaching Entra) problem.

ht3-l06-certificates-and-pki.title: Certificates and PKI for endpoints
objectives: Explain asymmetric cryptography and the difference between signing and encryption
Read the key X.509 fields of a certificate and describe what each asserts
Describe a PKI hierarchy with an offline root and issuing CA, and how the chain of trust validates
Trace the certificate lifecycle: enrollment, renewal, and revocation via CRL and OCSP
Deploy device and user certificates to endpoints using AD CS auto-enrollment and Intune SCEP/PKCS profiles
Troubleshoot certificate problems on Windows endpoints using certutil and the certificate stores
ht3-l06-certificates-and-pki.body:
## Public key cryptography in two minutes

Everything in PKI rests on **asymmetric cryptography**: a mathematically linked **key pair**. The **private key** is secret and never leaves the holder; the **public key** is freely shared. The two operations matter for endpoints:

- **Signing** proves origin and integrity. You sign with your **private** key; anyone verifies with your **public** key.
- **Encryption** for confidentiality is the reverse. You encrypt to the recipient's **public** key; only their **private** key decrypts.

Getting that direction right is the single most useful thing to internalise.

## What a certificate actually is

A **digital certificate** is a public key plus identity claims, all **signed by a Certificate Authority (CA)**. The format is **X.509**. The fields you will read constantly:

- **Subject** — who the cert identifies (a user, a device, a server FQDN).
- **Issuer** — the CA that signed it.
- **Validity** — not-before and not-after dates.
- **Public key** and **signature algorithm**.
- **Subject Alternative Name (SAN)** — the real identity for TLS and 802.1X.
- **Enhanced Key Usage (EKU)** — what it is allowed to do (Client Authentication, Server Authentication, Code Signing, Secure Email).

## PKI hierarchy and the chain of trust

A production **PKI** is tiered. An **offline root CA** signs one or more **issuing (subordinate) CAs**, then is powered off to protect the ultimate trust anchor. The online **issuing CA** does the everyday signing. An endpoint trusts a leaf certificate only if it can build a chain up to a **root it already trusts** in `LocalMachine\Root`.

```text
Root CA (offline, self-signed)        <- in Trusted Root store
   |  signs
Issuing CA (online, in NTAuth/CA store)
   |  signs
Device / User leaf certificate        <- in LocalMachine\My
```

Validate a chain from a Windows endpoint:

```powershell
# Verify the full chain, revocation and trust path of a cert file
certutil -verify -urlfetch device.cer

# Inspect a CSR before submitting it to the CA
certutil -dump request.req
```

## Lifecycle: enroll, renew, revoke

Certificates are born from a **Certificate Signing Request (CSR)** — the endpoint generates a key pair, keeps the private key, and sends only the public key and subject to the CA. The CA issues against a **template**, the endpoint installs the cert, and **auto-enrollment** in AD CS renews it before expiry. When a cert must be killed early it is **revoked**; relying parties learn this from a periodically published **CRL** or a live **OCSP** lookup.

```text
Key pair generated on device
  -> CSR (public key + subject) sent to CA
  -> CA validates against template, signs, issues
  -> Cert installed in LocalMachine\My (private key stays put)
  -> Auto-enrollment renews before not-after
  -> If compromised: revoke -> appears on CRL / OCSP
```

## Getting certs onto endpoints

Domain-joined devices use **AD CS auto-enrollment** driven by certificate **templates** and Group Policy. For Intune-managed or cloud devices you choose between two profile types: a **SCEP** profile (the device generates its own key, sends a **CSR** via the NDES connector, so the private key never leaves the endpoint — ideal for device auth) or a **PKCS** profile (the key is generated centrally and imported, suited to user **S/MIME** where the same key is reused). A separate **trusted root** profile distributes the anchor. These certs then power **802.1X/Wi-Fi**, **VPN**, **TLS**, **code signing**, **S/MIME**, and **certificate-based authentication to Entra**.

## Troubleshooting with certutil

When authentication fails, certutil is your scalpel. List a store, dump a cert, check the CA-side picture:

```text
certutil -store My                 :: machine identity certs + key presence
certutil -store -user My           :: the user store instead
certutil -store -enterprise NTAuth :: CAs trusted for Entra/AD logon
certutil -dump device.cer          :: decode all X.509 fields
certutil -verify -urlfetch x.cer   :: build chain, fetch CRL/OCSP, report errors
```

The golden questions: is the private key present, does the chain reach a trusted root, has it been revoked, and is the right EKU on it.

## Your task

In a test tenant, deploy a **device certificate** to one managed Windows endpoint using an Intune **SCEP** profile (with its trusted-root and SCEP profiles), then prove it works for **certificate-based authentication**. On the endpoint, run `certutil -store My` and `certutil -verify -urlfetch` against the issued cert, and capture: the Subject, SAN, EKU, the full chain to the root, whether the private key is present, and the revocation check result. Then deliberately revoke the certificate at the CA, force a CRL/OCSP refresh, and document how the endpoint's behaviour changes and what certutil now reports.

quiz.q: A device presents a leaf certificate signed by an issuing CA, which is signed by an offline root CA. What must an endpoint validating this chain have in its trust store for validation to succeed?
options: The root CA certificate installed as a trusted root anchor
A copy of every CRL ever published
quiz.why: Chain validation walks from the leaf up to a self-signed root that must be present and trusted in the LocalMachine\Root (trusted root) store. The intermediate is usually supplied in the chain or AIA; only the root must be pre-trusted as the anchor. Private keys are never distributed for validation.

quiz.q: When a user digitally signs an email with S/MIME, which key performs the signing and which verifies it?
options: Sign with the recipient's public key; verify with the recipient's private key
Sign with the sender's private key; verify with the sender's public key
Sign with a shared symmetric key on both ends
Sign with the CA's private key; verify with the sender's private key
quiz.why: Signing proves origin and integrity, so the sender signs with their own private key and anyone verifies with the sender's public key from the certificate. Encryption is the reverse: you encrypt to the recipient's public key. Mixing these up is the classic PKI exam trap.

quiz.q: An issuing CA is compromised on a Tuesday. Which mechanism lets relying parties learn that previously valid certificates should no longer be trusted, in near real time?
quiz.why: OCSP gives a real-time per-certificate status response and is lighter than downloading a full CRL. The CRL is the periodically published revocation list; OCSP is the live lookup. Auto-enrollment, templates and key archival have nothing to do with revocation distribution.

quiz.q: You are deploying a device certificate to unmanaged-by-domain Windows endpoints via Intune so the private key never leaves the device. Which profile type is the correct choice?
options: SCEP certificate profile with an NDES connector
quiz.why: SCEP has the device generate its own key pair locally and only sends a CSR, so the private key never leaves the endpoint, which is ideal for device authentication. PKCS imported certs are generated centrally (key escrowed) and suit user S/MIME scenarios where the same key must be reused. A trusted root profile only distributes the anchor.

quiz.q: Name the certutil command that displays the certificates currently in a named Windows certificate store, and state which store holds a machine's own identity certificates.
quiz.answer: certutil -store (for example, certutil -store My for the personal/identity store, or certutil -store -enterprise NTAuth). A machine's own identity certificates live in the LocalMachine\My (Personal) store; trusted roots live in LocalMachine\Root.
quiz.why: certutil -store enumerates a store and prints each certificate's subject, serial, thumbprint and whether the private key is present. Knowing My versus Root, and machine versus user scope, is fundamental to triaging endpoint certificate issues.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why a root CA is typically kept offline while an issuing (subordinate) CA stays online.
quiz.answer: The root CA's private key is the ultimate trust anchor, so it is kept offline (powered off or air-gapped) to protect it from compromise, while the online issuing CA does the day-to-day signing and can be revoked and replaced by the root if it is ever breached.
quiz.why: If the root key is stolen the entire PKI collapses and cannot be cheaply recovered, so it signs only the issuing CA(s) and then goes offline; a compromised issuing CA, by contrast, can be revoked by the root and reissued, containing the blast radius.

ht3-l07-data-protection-bitlocker-dlp.title: Data protection: BitLocker, DLP and Purview
objectives: Describe how data must be protected at rest, in use and in transit, and which control covers each
Explain BitLocker key concepts: TPM, TPM+PIN, XTS-AES, used-space versus full encryption and recovery key escrow
Manage and audit BitLocker using manage-bde and the Get-BitLockerVolume cmdlet
Recover a BitLocker-protected drive using a recovery key escrowed to Entra ID or Active Directory
Apply Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels and classification to enforce protection that travels with the data
Design endpoint DLP policies that block or audit risky egress while balancing security against user productivity
ht3-l07-data-protection-bitlocker-dlp.body:
## Three states, three controls

Data protection is not one job; it is three. Data is vulnerable **at rest** (sitting on a disk), **in use** (open on a screen, copied to a clipboard), and **in transit** (moving over a network or onto a USB stick). A complete strategy covers all three. **BitLocker** protects data at rest by encrypting the whole volume. **Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels** protect data in use and in transit by binding classification and encryption to the file itself. **Endpoint Data Loss Prevention (DLP)** controls risky egress - copy to USB, upload to cloud, clipboard, print. No single tool is enough; you layer them.

## BitLocker: encryption at rest

**BitLocker** encrypts the entire volume with **XTS-AES** (the modern, tamper-resistant mode, default 128-bit, optionally 256-bit). The encryption key is sealed to the **Trusted Platform Module (TPM)**, a hardware chip that releases the key only if boot integrity is intact. TPM-only unlocks transparently, but adding a **PIN** (TPM+PIN) defeats pre-boot key-extraction attacks against a stolen device.

Two enrolment choices matter. **Used-space-only** encryption is fast and fine for brand-new drives; **full** encryption is mandatory for any drive that has held data, because free sectors can hold readable remnants. Critically, you must **escrow the recovery key** to Entra ID or Active Directory so a locked-out user is never stranded.

In practice you set all of this with an **Intune disk encryption policy** for fleet-wide consistency, then verify on the box:

```powershell
# Quick status and protection state
manage-bde -status C:

# List the key protectors (TPM, numerical recovery password, etc.)
manage-bde -protectors -get C:

# The PowerShell-native equivalent, richer for scripting
Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C: |
  Select-Object MountPoint, VolumeStatus, EncryptionMethod,
    ProtectionStatus, EncryptionPercentage
```

## BitLocker recovery

When the TPM measurements change - a firmware update, a BIOS change, a moved disk - BitLocker enters **recovery mode** and demands the 48-digit numerical password. Because you escrowed it, you retrieve it from Entra ID or AD and unlock:

```text
manage-bde -unlock C: -RecoveryPassword 123456-...-654321
manage-bde -protectors -disable C:   # suspend during planned firmware work
```

Suspend (not decrypt) protection before TPM-affecting maintenance so the device boots without prompting, then resume.

## Purview: classification and labels

Protection at rest is not enough once a file leaves the disk. **Microsoft Purview Information Protection** classifies content using **sensitive information types (SITs)** - pattern detectors for things like card or passport numbers - and **trainable classifiers**, machine-learning models trained on examples to spot fuzzy categories such as contracts. A **sensitivity label** (for example *Confidential*) then applies persistent encryption, rights and visual marking that **travel with the file** anywhere.

## Endpoint DLP and the productivity balance

**Endpoint DLP** enforces policy at egress points on managed devices: block or audit **copy to USB, upload to cloud, clipboard paste, and print**. Combined with labels, DLP can say "a *Confidential*-labelled file may not be written to removable media". The art is balance: blunt blocking breeds shadow IT and **insider risk**. Mature rollouts start in **audit**, scope by label and group, then enforce with a **block-with-override** that captures user justification - protecting **PII** without stopping legitimate work.

## Your task
