```yaml
    cmd: python src/split.py
    deps:
      - data/processed/features.parquet
    params:
      - split.test_size
      - split.seed
    outs:
      - data/splits/
```

Run the whole graph with `dvc repro`. DVC re-executes only stages whose dependencies or params changed—this gives caching plus reproducibility.

## Parameterizing with Configuration

Keep all tunable values in a `params.yaml` rather than hardcoding them. This makes runs explicit and diffable.

```yaml
transform:
  fillna_strategy: median
split:
  test_size: 0.2
  seed: 42
```

Changing `seed` or `test_size` produces a new, tracked pipeline run. Always set and record random seeds.

## Data Validation

Validate data before it flows downstream. Libraries like Great Expectations or Pandera define expectations:

```python
import pandera as pa
from pandera import Column, Check

schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({
    "amount": Column(float, Check.greater_than(0)),
    "customer_id": Column(int, nullable=False),
    "category": Column(str, Check.isin(["a", "b", "c"])),
})

validated = schema.validate(df)  # raises on violation
```

Fail fast: a broken schema should stop the pipeline rather than silently train on garbage.

## Connecting to Training

Training reads versioned artifacts and records which data version it used (the Git commit / DVC hash). Log this into your experiment tracker (MLflow, W&B) so every model links back to its exact dataset. This closes the loop: model → params → data → raw source.

## Best Practices

- Make every stage **deterministic and idempotent**.
- Never mutate raw data in place; treat it as immutable.
- Store config separate from code; record seeds.
- Validate early and fail loudly.
- Tie model artifacts to data + code versions for full lineage.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a pipeline stage to be idempotent?
options: It runs faster each time it executes
Running it multiple times with the same inputs yields the same output
quiz.why: Idempotency means repeated execution on identical inputs produces identical outputs, which is essential for reproducibility and safe re-runs.

quiz.q: In DVC, what is stored in Git versus remote storage?
options: Both data and code go to Git
Lightweight pointer files go to Git; actual data goes to remote storage
Data goes to Git; pointers go to remote storage
Everything is stored only in remote storage
quiz.why: DVC commits small .dvc pointer files to Git while pushing the large actual data files to remote object storage like S3 or GCS.

quiz.q: Why should random seeds be set and recorded in a data pipeline?
options: To make the pipeline run faster
To make stochastic steps like splitting reproducible
quiz.why: Recording seeds ensures stochastic operations such as train/test splits produce the same results across runs, preserving reproducibility.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of data validation before transformation/training?
options: To fail fast and catch schema or quality issues before training on bad data
quiz.why: Validation enforces expectations on schema, types, and ranges so the pipeline stops loudly instead of silently training on corrupt data.

quiz.q: Name one thing (besides code) that must be versioned to achieve full reproducibility.
quiz.answer: Data (or configuration/parameters, or the environment/dependencies)
quiz.why: Reproducibility requires versioning code, data, configuration, and environment together—any of data, config, or environment is a valid answer.

quiz.q: Why does DVC only re-run stages whose dependencies or parameters changed?
quiz.answer: It uses caching to skip unchanged stages, saving time while keeping outputs reproducible and traceable.
quiz.why: DVC tracks deps, params, and outs per stage, so it recomputes only what changed, combining efficient caching with deterministic reproducibility.

mle-m4-l02-rigorous-model-evaluation-and.title: Rigorous Model Evaluation and Validation
objectives: Diagnose overfitting and underfitting using train/validation/test gaps and learning curves
Apply appropriate validation strategies (holdout, k-fold, stratified, time-series, grouped) to different data types
Identify and prevent common sources of data leakage in feature engineering and preprocessing
Select evaluation metrics aligned with business objectives beyond accuracy
Measure and interpret fairness metrics across protected subgroups
Build a leakage-safe evaluation pipeline that generalizes to unseen data
mle-m4-l02-rigorous-model-evaluation-and.body:
## Why Rigorous Evaluation Matters

A model that scores 0.99 on your training data can fail completely in production. Rigorous evaluation is the discipline of producing **honest, generalizable estimates** of model performance before deployment. As an ML engineer, your job is not to maximize a number on a slide but to guarantee the model behaves reliably on data it has never seen.

Three silent killers undermine evaluation: **overfitting**, **data leakage**, and **bias**. This lesson gives you a practical toolkit to detect and prevent each.

## Overfitting vs. Underfitting

- **Overfitting**: the model memorizes training noise. Symptom: low training error, high validation error (a large gap).
- **Underfitting**: the model is too simple. Symptom: high error on both training and validation sets.

Use **learning curves** (error vs. training set size) and the **train-validation gap** to diagnose. Remedies for overfitting include regularization, more data, simpler models, and early stopping. Remedies for underfitting include richer features and higher-capacity models.

## Validation Strategies

The golden rule: **the test set is touched only once**, at the very end. Use a validation set (or cross-validation) for all tuning.

- **Holdout split**: simple train/validation/test. Fast but high variance on small data.
- **K-fold cross-validation**: rotate folds; average results for a robust estimate. Default for tabular data.
- **Stratified k-fold**: preserves class proportions in each fold — essential for imbalanced classification.
- **Time-series split**: never train on the future. Use expanding or rolling windows so validation always follows training chronologically.
- **Grouped k-fold**: when rows share a group (e.g., multiple records per patient), keep groups entirely on one side to avoid leakage.

## Data Leakage

Leakage is when information unavailable at prediction time sneaks into training, producing overly optimistic scores that vanish in production.

Common sources:

- **Preprocessing on full data**: fitting a scaler or imputer on the entire dataset before splitting leaks test statistics. Always fit preprocessing **inside** the training fold using a `Pipeline`.
- **Target leakage**: a feature that is a proxy for, or derived after, the target (e.g., `is_refunded` when predicting `will_churn`).
- **Temporal leakage**: using future information to predict the past.
- **Duplicate or group leakage**: near-duplicate rows split across train and test.

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

pipe = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
    ('clf', LogisticRegression())
])
# scaler is fit only on training folds -> no leakage
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5, scoring='f1')
```

## Choosing the Right Metrics

Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data. Match the metric to the cost of errors:

- **Precision / Recall / F1**: when false positives and false negatives have different costs.
- **ROC-AUC**: ranking quality across thresholds; can be optimistic on heavy imbalance.
- **PR-AUC**: better for rare positive classes.
- **Calibration** (reliability curves, Brier score): when probabilities must be trustworthy.
- **Regression**: RMSE penalizes large errors, MAE is robust, R² explains variance.

Always report a **confidence interval or fold variance**, not a single point estimate.

## Fairness-Aware Evaluation

A model can be accurate overall yet harmful to subgroups. Slice your metrics by **protected attributes** (gender, age, ethnicity, region).

Key fairness metrics:

- **Demographic parity**: positive prediction rate is similar across groups.
- **Equal opportunity**: true positive rate is similar across groups.
- **Equalized odds**: both TPR and FPR are similar across groups.

These definitions can conflict — you cannot usually satisfy all simultaneously, so choose based on context and stakeholder input. Tools like Fairlearn and Aequitas automate subgroup audits.

## A Leakage-Safe Evaluation Checklist

1. Split data **first**, before any preprocessing.
2. Wrap all preprocessing in a pipeline fit inside cross-validation.
3. Use the validation strategy that matches your data structure (time, groups, imbalance).
4. Pick metrics aligned with business cost.
5. Audit performance across subgroups.
6. Touch the test set exactly once.
7. Report variance and confidence, not just a point estimate.

quiz.q: You fit a StandardScaler on the entire dataset before splitting into train and test. What problem does this cause?
quiz.why: Fitting the scaler on all data lets test-set statistics influence training, leaking information and inflating performance. Preprocessing must be fit inside the training folds via a pipeline.

quiz.q: Which validation strategy is most appropriate for forecasting future sales from historical time-stamped data?
quiz.why: Time-series data requires that validation always follows training chronologically; random folds would train on the future and leak temporal information.

quiz.q: A model shows very low training error but high validation error. This indicates:
quiz.why: A large gap with low training error and high validation error is the classic signature of overfitting — the model memorized training noise.

quiz.q: For a highly imbalanced classification problem with rare positives, which metric gives the most honest picture?
quiz.why: PR-AUC focuses on precision and recall for the positive class, making it more informative than accuracy or even ROC-AUC when positives are rare.

quiz.q: Define 'equal opportunity' as a fairness metric in one sentence.
quiz.answer: Equal opportunity means the true positive rate is approximately equal across protected groups, so qualified individuals are correctly identified at the same rate regardless of group.
quiz.why: Equal opportunity focuses specifically on equalizing the true positive rate (recall) across subgroups, ensuring those who should receive a positive outcome do so equally.

quiz.q: Why should the test set be used only once, at the very end?
quiz.answer: Repeatedly evaluating on the test set leaks information into model and hyperparameter choices, causing the test score to overestimate true generalization performance.
quiz.why: Using the test set for tuning turns it into a de facto validation set, so its estimate of generalization becomes optimistically biased.

mle-m4-l03-deploying-models-as-apis.title: Deploying Models as APIs
objectives: Explain why models are served behind APIs and the trade-offs of online vs. batch inference
Load a serialized model and build prediction endpoints with FastAPI and Pydantic request validation
Add health checks, input/output schemas, and basic error handling to a serving API
Containerize the API with Docker, including dependency pinning and a clean entrypoint
Test the API locally and reason about scaling, latency, and monitoring concerns in production
mle-m4-l03-deploying-models-as-apis.body:
## Why Serve Models as APIs?

A trained model saved as a file (e.g., `model.pkl`) is useless to other systems until it is reachable. Wrapping it in a **REST API** lets web apps, mobile clients, and other services request predictions over HTTP without knowing anything about Python or your model internals.

**Online (real-time) inference** answers one request at a time with low latency — ideal for fraud checks or recommendations. **Batch inference** scores large datasets on a schedule and is cheaper per prediction but not interactive. This lesson focuses on online serving.

## Choosing FastAPI

FastAPI is a modern Python web framework that is fast, async-capable, and gives you:

- Automatic request validation via **Pydantic** models
- Auto-generated interactive docs at `/docs` (Swagger UI)
- Type hints that double as documentation and validation

## Anatomy of a Serving API

A minimal but solid serving service has:

1. **Model loading at startup** — load once, reuse across requests (never reload per request).
2. **A request schema** — validates incoming JSON so bad input fails fast with a clear 422 error.
3. **A prediction endpoint** — transforms input, calls `model.predict`, returns JSON.
4. **A health endpoint** — lets orchestrators (Kubernetes, load balancers) know the service is alive.

```python
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
import joblib

MODEL_VERSION = "1.0.0"


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Load the model once at startup into app.state, not at import time.
    app.state.model = joblib.load("model.joblib")
    yield


app = FastAPI(title="Iris Classifier", lifespan=lifespan)

class IrisRequest(BaseModel):
    sepal_length: float
    sepal_width: float
    petal_length: float
    petal_width: float

class IrisResponse(BaseModel):
    # Allow the model_version field (Pydantic v2 protects the "model_" prefix).
    model_config = ConfigDict(protected_namespaces=())
    prediction: int
    label: str
    model_version: str

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.post("/predict", response_model=IrisResponse)
def predict(req: IrisRequest, request: Request):
    model = request.app.state.model
    features = [[req.sepal_length, req.sepal_width,
                 req.petal_length, req.petal_width]]
    pred = int(model.predict(features)[0])
    return IrisResponse(prediction=pred, label=str(pred),
                        model_version=MODEL_VERSION)
```

Run it locally with:

```bash
uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
```

Visit `http://localhost:8000/docs` to try requests interactively.

## Error Handling and Validation

Pydantic automatically rejects malformed payloads with HTTP 422. For domain errors (e.g., model failure), raise `HTTPException`:

```python
from fastapi import HTTPException

try:
    pred = model.predict(features)
except Exception:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Inference failed")
```

Never let raw stack traces leak to clients — return clean status codes and messages.

## Containerizing with Docker

Containers package your code, dependencies, and runtime into a single portable image so it runs identically on your laptop, CI, and the cloud.

Pin dependencies in `requirements.txt`:

```
fastapi>=0.115,<0.116
uvicorn[standard]>=0.34,<0.35
gunicorn>=23.0,<24.0
scikit-learn>=1.6,<1.7
joblib>=1.4,<1.5
```

These are compatible-release ranges; regenerate and pin exact versions into a lockfile (e.g. `pip freeze > requirements.lock` or `pip-compile`) so production builds stay reproducible.

A clean `Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "app:app", "-k", "uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker", \
     "--workers", "4", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
```

Build and run:

```bash
docker build -t iris-api .
docker run -p 8000:8000 iris-api
```

**Tips:** use a `slim` base image to keep size down, copy `requirements.txt` first so dependency layers cache, and never bake secrets into the image — pass them as environment variables.

## Production Concerns

- **Concurrency:** run multiple workers to handle parallel requests — in production use Gunicorn with Uvicorn workers (e.g., `gunicorn app:app -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker --workers 4`), matching the Dockerfile `CMD`. The bare `uvicorn` command above is fine for local development. N workers each hold their own copy of the model in memory — size workers against model footprint and host RAM.
- **Latency:** keep models warm, batch where possible, and avoid heavy per-request I/O.
- **Monitoring:** log request counts, latency, and prediction distributions to detect drift.
- **Versioning:** include a model version in responses so you can trace which model produced a prediction.
- **Statelessness:** keep the API stateless so it scales horizontally behind a load balancer.

quiz.q: Why should a model be loaded once at application startup rather than inside the prediction endpoint?
options: It reduces the Docker image size
It avoids paying the load cost on every request, improving latency
It is required by Pydantic validation
It prevents the model from being versioned
quiz.why: Loading the model per request adds significant latency and wastes resources. Loading once at startup means every request reuses the in-memory model.

quiz.q: What HTTP status code does FastAPI automatically return when an incoming request fails Pydantic validation?
quiz.why: FastAPI uses 422 Unprocessable Entity for validation errors when the request body doesn't match the declared Pydantic schema.

quiz.q: In the Dockerfile, why is requirements.txt copied and installed before copying the rest of the application code?
options: To hide the source code from the image
To leverage Docker layer caching so dependencies aren't reinstalled on every code change
Because pip cannot run after COPY .
To reduce the number of API workers
quiz.why: Copying and installing requirements first lets Docker cache that layer; when only app code changes, the expensive dependency install is skipped.

quiz.q: Which characteristic should a serving API have to scale horizontally behind a load balancer?
options: It should store session state in memory
It should load the model per request
quiz.why: Stateless services can be replicated freely since any instance can handle any request, enabling horizontal scaling.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a /health endpoint in a deployed API?
quiz.answer: It lets orchestrators or load balancers check that the service is alive and ready to receive traffic.
quiz.why: Health checks allow infrastructure like Kubernetes or load balancers to detect unhealthy instances and route traffic only to healthy ones.

quiz.q: Name one production concern, other than health checks, that you should address when serving a model as an API.
quiz.answer: Monitoring latency and prediction drift (also acceptable: concurrency/multiple workers, model versioning, passing secrets via environment variables).
quiz.why: Production serving requires monitoring, scaling via workers, versioning, and secure secret handling beyond just basic functionality.

mle-m4-l04-capstone-end-to-end-ml-system.title: Capstone: End-to-End ML System
objectives: Scope a realistic ML problem and define success metrics tied to a business or user outcome
Build a reproducible pipeline from raw data through feature engineering, training, and evaluation
Deploy a trained model behind an inference API with versioning and basic monitoring
Evaluate the system rigorously, including offline metrics, error analysis, and slice-based fairness checks
Document and present the project clearly for a portfolio and technical interviews
mle-m4-l04-capstone-end-to-end-ml-system.body:
## Capstone Overview

This capstone ties together everything from the bootcamp into one shippable project. The goal is not a Kaggle-style notebook, but a **system**: data flows in, a model is trained and evaluated, and predictions are served behind an API with monitoring. Treat it as the centerpiece of your portfolio.

## 1. Scope and Problem Framing

Start by choosing a problem you can defend.

- **Define the task**: classification, regression, ranking, or forecasting.
- **Pick the metric that matters**: don't default to accuracy. Use F1, AUC, RMSE, or a business KPI (e.g., cost of false positives).
- **Set a baseline**: a trivial model (majority class, mean predictor, simple heuristic) you must beat.
- **State constraints**: latency budget, data freshness, interpretability requirements.

Write a one-page project brief before writing code.

## 2. Data Pipeline

A pipeline must be **reproducible** and **idempotent**.

- **Ingestion**: pull raw data from a source (CSV, API, database). Store an immutable raw copy.
- **Validation**: schema checks, null rates, range checks. Fail loudly on bad data.
- **Transformation**: feature engineering encapsulated in a `Pipeline`/`ColumnTransformer` so the same logic runs in training and serving.
- **Splitting**: respect time order for temporal data; avoid leakage from target-derived features.

Version both data and code (e.g., DVC + Git) so any run is repeatable.

## 3. Training and Experiment Tracking

- Use an experiment tracker (MLflow, Weights & Biases) to log params, metrics, and artifacts.
- Tune hyperparameters with cross-validation; never tune on the test set.
- Save the **fitted pipeline** (preprocessing + model) as a single artifact so serving matches training exactly.

## 4. Evaluation

Go beyond a single number.

- **Offline metrics** on a held-out test set vs. the baseline.
- **Error analysis**: inspect the worst predictions; look for patterns.
- **Slice-based evaluation**: report metrics per subgroup to catch hidden underperformance.
- **Calibration** (for classifiers) and **confidence intervals** where feasible.

## 5. Deployment

- Wrap the saved pipeline in an inference service (FastAPI) with a `/predict` endpoint.
- Validate inputs with a schema (Pydantic). Return predictions plus a model version.
- Containerize with Docker for reproducible deploys.
- Add **monitoring**: log inputs/outputs, track latency, and watch for data/prediction drift.

## 6. Documentation and Presentation

- A clear README: problem, data, approach, results, how to run.
- A model card summarizing intended use, metrics, and limitations.
- A short demo (video or live) and an architecture diagram.

The deliverable is a story: problem → data → model → results → deployment → what you'd do next.

quiz.q: Why should you save the entire fitted pipeline (preprocessing + model) rather than just the model?
options: It ensures serving applies identical transformations as training, avoiding train/serve skew
It removes the need for input validation
quiz.why: Saving preprocessing and model together guarantees the exact same feature transformations run at inference time, preventing train/serve skew.

quiz.q: Which practice best prevents data leakage in a temporal prediction problem?
options: Splitting by time so training precedes the validation/test period
quiz.why: For time-dependent data, splitting chronologically prevents the model from seeing future information during training, which would leak into evaluation.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of slice-based evaluation?
options: To detect underperformance on specific subgroups hidden by aggregate metrics
To replace the need for a test set
quiz.why: Aggregate metrics can hide poor performance on subgroups; slice-based evaluation surfaces these hidden weaknesses.

quiz.q: Why establish a trivial baseline before modeling?
options: To know the minimum performance any real model must beat
Because it is the final deliverable
quiz.why: A baseline (e.g., majority class or mean predictor) defines the floor of acceptable performance and contextualizes your model's value.

quiz.q: Name one signal you would monitor in production to know when a deployed model may need retraining.
quiz.answer: Data or prediction drift (also acceptable: rising error rate, stale input data, latency spikes)
quiz.why: Drift in incoming data or output distributions indicates the model's assumptions may no longer hold, signaling a retrain.

quiz.q: In one phrase, what should a /predict API response include besides the prediction for traceability?
quiz.answer: The model version
quiz.why: Returning the model version lets you trace which model produced a given prediction, essential for debugging and audits.

mle-m5-l01-transformers-and-the-attentio.title: Transformers and the Attention Mechanism
objectives: Explain why transformers replaced RNNs for sequence modeling
Convert text into tokens and integer IDs using subword (BPE) tokenization
Describe how embeddings and positional encoding represent tokens and order
Compute scaled dot-product self-attention from Q, K, and V matrices
Diagram multi-head attention and the encoder/decoder block at a high level
Connect the transformer architecture to how modern LLMs are pretrained and scaled
mle-m5-l01-transformers-and-the-attentio.body:
## Overview

The transformer is the architecture behind every modern large language model, from BERT to GPT to the latest 2026 frontier systems. We follow a sentence from raw text into a transformer: it is **tokenized**, turned into **embeddings**, given **positional information**, then processed by **self-attention**. This path is the single most important step toward becoming an LLM engineer.

## 1. Why Transformers Replaced RNNs

Before 2017, sequence models were dominated by recurrent neural networks (RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs). They read text one token at a time, carrying a hidden state forward. This had two weaknesses:

- **No parallelism.** Each step depends on the previous one, so you cannot use a GPU's parallelism across the sequence during training.
- **Weak long-range memory.** Information from early tokens decays as it is passed through many steps, making it hard to connect words far apart.

The transformer, introduced in *Attention Is All You Need*, throws out recurrence entirely. Every token can attend to every other token **in a single parallel step**, so long-range dependencies are just one attention hop away and training scales beautifully on modern hardware.

## 2. Tokenization: Text to IDs

A model cannot consume raw characters; it needs integers. **Tokenization** splits text into tokens and maps each to an ID in a fixed vocabulary. Modern LLMs use **subword** tokenization (e.g., Byte-Pair Encoding), representing rare words as combinations of known pieces to avoid the out-of-vocabulary problem.

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
enc = tok("Hello world")
print(enc["input_ids"])      # e.g. [101, 7592, 2088, 102]
print(tok.tokenize("tokenization"))  # ['token', '##ization']
```

Notice that 'tokenization' splits into subword pieces. The special IDs 101 and 102 are the [CLS] and [SEP] markers BERT adds automatically.

## 3. Embeddings and Positional Encoding

Each token ID indexes into an **embedding table**, producing a dense vector (say 768 numbers) that the model can learn to shape into meaning. But self-attention treats its inputs as an unordered *set* — it is **permutation-invariant**. Without extra signal, the model could not distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'.

The fix is **positional encoding**: we add a position-dependent vector to each token embedding so order is baked in. The original paper uses fixed sinusoidal functions; modern models often learn positions or use rotary embeddings (RoPE). The key idea: **token embedding + positional encoding = the input to attention.**

## 4. Self-Attention: The Core Mechanism

Self-attention lets each token gather information from all others. From every token's embedding we derive three vectors via learned linear projections:

- **Query (Q)** — what this token is looking for.
- **Key (K)** — what each token offers.
- **Value (V)** — the actual content to be passed along.

We score how well each query matches each key with a dot product, scale by `sqrt(d_k)` to keep gradients stable, apply softmax to get weights that sum to 1, and use those weights to average the values:

```text
attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
```

Here is a faithful minimal NumPy implementation:

```python
import numpy as np

def attention(Q, K, V):
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
    weights = np.exp(scores) / np.exp(scores).sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)  # softmax
    return weights @ V
```

The division by `sqrt(d_k)` matters: for large key dimensions the dot products grow large, pushing softmax into flat regions with vanishing gradients. Scaling keeps training healthy.

## 5. Multi-Head Attention and the Transformer Block

A single attention computation can only focus on one kind of relationship at a time. **Multi-head attention** runs several attention heads **in parallel**, each with its own Q/K/V projections into a smaller subspace. Their outputs are **concatenated** and linearly projected back. One head might track syntax, another coreference — the model learns a rich mix.

These heads sit inside a **transformer block**, which adds a position-wise feed-forward network plus **residual connections** and **layer normalization** to stabilize deep stacks. The original architecture pairs an **encoder** (bidirectional) with a **decoder** (masked, left-to-right). Encoder-only models like BERT excel at understanding; decoder-only models like GPT excel at generation.

## 6. From Transformers to LLMs

A large language model is, fundamentally, a transformer **scaled up**: stack dozens or hundreds of blocks, widen the layers to billions of parameters, and pretrain on enormous text corpora using a **self-supervised** objective — typically **next-token prediction** for decoder-only models or **masked language modeling** for encoder-only ones. No human labels are required; the text supervises itself.

This scaling, combined with vast data, produces the emergent capabilities we associate with modern LLMs. Once pretrained, the same model can be **fine-tuned** or **prompted** for countless downstream tasks — the foundation for the rest of this module.

## Key Takeaways

Transformers replaced RNNs by enabling parallelism and direct long-range attention. Text becomes subword tokens, then embeddings plus positional encoding, then flows through self-attention — `softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V` — generalized into multi-head attention inside stacked blocks. Scale that with self-supervised pretraining and you get a large language model.

quiz.q: What key advantage do transformers have over recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for processing sequences?
options: They require far less training data than RNNs
They are guaranteed to never overfit
They process all tokens in parallel and capture long-range dependencies directly
They eliminate the need for any matrix multiplication
quiz.why: RNNs process tokens sequentially, which is slow and tends to lose information across long distances. Transformers attend to all positions at once, enabling parallel computation and direct modeling of long-range dependencies.

quiz.q: Why is subword (BPE-style) tokenization preferred over splitting text into whole words?
options: It handles rare and unseen words by composing them from smaller known pieces
It always produces exactly one token per sentence
It removes the need for an embedding layer
It guarantees every language uses the same vocabulary size
quiz.why: Subword tokenization keeps a fixed vocabulary while representing rare or novel words as sequences of known subword units, avoiding the out-of-vocabulary problem that plagues word-level tokenizers.

quiz.q: Why must positional encoding be added to token embeddings before self-attention?
options: Because embeddings are too large to fit in memory otherwise
To convert the embeddings into integer token IDs
Because softmax requires positive inputs only
Because self-attention is permutation-invariant and has no inherent notion of token order
quiz.why: Self-attention treats its inputs as an unordered set, so without positional information the model could not tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'. Positional encoding injects order into the representations.

quiz.q: In scaled dot-product attention, attention = softmax(Q Kᵀ / sqrt(d_k)) V, what is the role of dividing by sqrt(d_k)?
options: It converts the values matrix V into probabilities
It scales the dot products so the softmax gradients stay stable for large key dimensions
It replaces the need for the value matrix V
It guarantees the attention weights sum to the key dimension
quiz.why: For large d_k the dot products Q·K grow large in magnitude, pushing softmax into regions with tiny gradients. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the scores at a reasonable scale so learning remains stable.

quiz.q: What does multi-head attention add compared to a single attention computation?
options: It removes the query and key projections entirely
It forces every head to learn identical weights
It runs several attention heads in parallel, each in its own subspace, then concatenates their outputs
It replaces attention with a recurrent loop
quiz.why: Multi-head attention projects Q, K, and V into several lower-dimensional subspaces and runs attention in each in parallel, letting different heads focus on different relationships, then concatenates and projects the results.

quiz.q: In one or two sentences, explain how a base transformer gets scaled into a modern large language model (LLM).
quiz.answer: By stacking many transformer (typically decoder) blocks with billions of parameters and pretraining on massive text corpora using a self-supervised objective such as next-token prediction.
quiz.why: LLMs are transformers scaled up in depth, width, and data: many stacked blocks are pretrained with a self-supervised objective (e.g., next-token prediction or masked language modeling) over huge corpora, after which they can be fine-tuned or prompted for downstream tasks.

mle-m5-l02-using-pretrained-models-with-.title: Using Pretrained Models with Hugging Face Transformers
objectives: Explain the pretrained-model paradigm and why transfer learning beats training from scratch
Run inference quickly for common tasks using the transformers pipeline() helper
Use AutoTokenizer and AutoModel classes for lower-level, customizable inference
Process batches of text efficiently with padding, truncation, and return_tensors
Apply device placement, torch.no_grad, batching, and quantization to run models efficiently
Choose an appropriate model by task, size, and license, and decide between hosted APIs and self-hosting
mle-m5-l02-using-pretrained-models-with-.body:
## Overview

Modern NLP rarely starts from a blank model. Instead you download a model that has already been trained on enormous text corpora and adapt it to your task. This lesson shows how to use the **Hugging Face Hub** and the **transformers** library to run pretrained models, from one-line inference to full low-level control, plus the practical tricks needed to run large models efficiently.

## 1. The Pretrained-Model Paradigm

Training a transformer from scratch costs millions of dollars and requires terabytes of text. The smarter approach is **transfer learning**: reuse a model whose weights already encode grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns, then apply it directly or fine-tune it on a small dataset.

The payoff is enormous: you get state-of-the-art results with a few lines of code, a modest GPU (or none), and little or no labeled data. The Hub hosts hundreds of thousands of these models, each identified by a name like `distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english`.

## 2. The Hub and pipeline()

The fastest way to run a model is the `pipeline()` helper. It bundles the tokenizer, model, and post-processing into a single callable.

```python
from transformers import pipeline

clf = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
print(clf("I love this course"))
# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.99}]
```

If you do not name a model, the pipeline picks a sensible default for the task. You can also request a specific one with `pipeline("summarization", model="facebook/bart-large-cnn")`. Common task strings include `sentiment-analysis`, `text-classification`, `ner`, `summarization`, `translation`, and `text-generation`.

## 3. Lower-Level Control: AutoTokenizer + AutoModel

When you need control over batching, devices, or outputs, drop down to the `Auto` classes. The tokenizer converts text to token IDs; the model maps those IDs to outputs.

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
import torch

name = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name)
```

The `AutoModelFor...` family selects the right architecture head for your task: `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`, `AutoModelForTokenClassification`, `AutoModelForCausalLM`, and `AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM` are the ones you will reach for most often.

## 4. Batch Inference Across Tasks

To classify several texts at once, tokenize them together with padding and truncation so they form a rectangular tensor, then run a forward pass.

```python
texts = ["great movie", "terrible plot"]
inputs = tok(texts, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(**inputs).logits
preds = logits.argmax(dim=-1)
labels = [model.config.id2label[i] for i in preds.tolist()]
print(labels)  # ['POSITIVE', 'NEGATIVE']
```

The same pattern adapts to other tasks: a NER pipeline tags entities per token, a summarizer returns generated text, and a classifier returns per-class scores. Batching many inputs in one call is far faster than looping one at a time.

## 5. Performance: Device, Batching, no_grad, and Quantization

Three habits make inference fast and memory-friendly:

- **Device placement.** Move the model and inputs to the GPU. For large models, let the library shard automatically with `from_pretrained(name, device_map="auto")`; otherwise call `model.to("cuda")` and `inputs.to("cuda")`.
- **Batching + no_grad.** Always wrap inference in `torch.no_grad()` so autograd does not build a graph, and group inputs into batches to maximize GPU utilization.
- **Quantization.** Billion-parameter models may not fit in GPU memory at full precision. Loading weights in 4-bit or 8-bit (via the `bitsandbytes` integration) shrinks memory use several-fold with minimal accuracy loss.

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True)
llm = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "some-7b-model", quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")
```

## 6. Choosing a Model and Hosted vs Self-Hosted

Pick a model by matching three things: the **task** (does an appropriate `AutoModelFor...` head exist?), the **size** (can it fit your latency and memory budget?), and the **license** (is commercial use permitted?). Filter the Hub by task, library, and license to narrow the field, and prefer popular, well-documented checkpoints.

Finally, decide where it runs. A **hosted inference API** removes all infrastructure work and scales on demand, ideal for prototypes and bursty traffic. **Self-hosting** gives you data privacy, predictable cost at high volume, and offline control, at the price of managing GPUs. Many teams prototype on a hosted API, then self-host once usage and requirements are clear.

## Key Takeaways

Reuse, do not rebuild: pretrained models give you strong results cheaply. Reach for `pipeline()` first, drop to `AutoTokenizer` + `AutoModelFor...` when you need control, batch your inputs under `torch.no_grad()`, and use device placement and quantization to fit large models. Choose by task, size, and license, and pick hosted versus self-hosted to match your scale and privacy needs.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using a pretrained model rather than training one from scratch?
options: It requires no data or compute under any circumstances
It always outperforms every possible custom-built model
It transfers knowledge learned on large corpora, saving data and compute
It eliminates the need for a tokenizer entirely
quiz.why: Pretrained models encode general language or vision knowledge learned on massive datasets, so reusing them via transfer learning gives strong results with far less data and compute than training from scratch.

quiz.q: Which transformers helper gives the fastest path to inference for a standard task?
quiz.why: pipeline() bundles the tokenizer, model, and post-processing into a single callable, so you can run a task like sentiment-analysis in one or two lines without manual setup.

quiz.q: When tokenizing a batch of variable-length texts, which arguments produce uniform-length PyTorch tensors ready for the model?
quiz.why: padding pads shorter sequences to a common length, truncation caps overly long ones, and return_tensors='pt' returns PyTorch tensors, giving a rectangular batch the model can consume.

quiz.q: Why should inference be wrapped in torch.no_grad()?
options: It automatically moves the model to the GPU
It disables gradient tracking, saving memory and speeding up inference
It applies softmax to the model's logits
It downloads the model weights from the Hub
quiz.why: During inference you do not need gradients; torch.no_grad() stops autograd from building the computation graph, which reduces memory usage and runs faster.

quiz.q: Which technique reduces a large model's memory footprint so it fits on a smaller GPU?
options: Quantization, such as 4-bit loading via bitsandbytes
quiz.why: Quantization stores weights at lower precision (for example 4-bit or 8-bit), dramatically cutting memory use so multi-billion-parameter models can run on consumer GPUs with minimal accuracy loss.

quiz.q: In one word, what does AutoModelForSequenceClassification output that you pass to argmax to get the predicted class?
quiz.answer: logits
quiz.why: Classification models return raw, unnormalized scores called logits; taking the argmax over the logits selects the highest-scoring class without needing an explicit softmax.

mle-m5-l03-retrieval-augmented-generatio.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Vector Databases
objectives: Explain why LLMs hallucinate and how injecting retrieved context grounds their answers
Describe how embeddings turn semantic similarity into a vector distance computation
Generate sentence embeddings locally with the sentence-transformers library
Use a vector database for approximate nearest-neighbor search and persistence instead of a brute-force scan
Assemble an end-to-end RAG pipeline: chunk, embed, store, retrieve top-k, prompt, generate
Evaluate and improve retrieval quality through chunking, top-k tuning, and re-ranking
mle-m5-l03-retrieval-augmented-generatio.body:
## Overview

Large language models are fluent but forgetful: their knowledge is frozen at training time, and they have never seen your internal wiki, your codebase, or yesterday's incident report. **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** closes this gap. Instead of fine-tuning the model, you retrieve the most relevant passages from your own data at query time and place them directly in the prompt, so the model answers from evidence rather than guessing.

## 1. The Grounding Problem

Ask a vanilla LLM a question about a private document and it will often produce a confident, plausible, and wrong answer. This is **hallucination**, and it stems from two limits: the model's knowledge is stale (bounded by its training cutoff) and incomplete (it never saw your data). RAG addresses both by injecting fresh, relevant context:

```python
prompt = f"""Answer using ONLY the context below.
If the answer is not in the context, say you don't know.

Context:
{retrieved_text}

Question: {question}"""
```

The model still does the reasoning and phrasing, but the facts come from text you retrieved and trust.

## 2. Embeddings: Meaning as Vectors

To retrieve by *meaning* rather than exact keywords, we convert text into **embeddings**: dense vectors where semantically similar texts land close together. Two paraphrases of the same idea map to nearby points even with no shared words, so retrieval becomes a nearest-neighbor search. Closeness is usually measured with **cosine similarity**:

```python
import numpy as np

def cosine(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
```

If the vectors are already unit-length (normalized), cosine similarity is just the dot product.

## 3. Building Embeddings with sentence-transformers

As an ML engineer you often want embeddings you can run and version yourself. The open-source **sentence-transformers** library does exactly this, running locally with no external API:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")  # open-source, runs locally
vecs = model.encode(
    ["How do I reset my password?", "Steps to recover account access"],
    normalize_embeddings=True,
)
print(vecs.shape)  # (2, 384)
```

The two sentences above share almost no words yet produce highly similar vectors. The pattern is provider-agnostic: managed services such as Voyage AI expose the same `encode`-then-store interface behind an API if you prefer not to self-host. Pick a model for your domain and stay consistent: queries and documents must be embedded with the *same* model.

## 4. Vector Databases: Indexing and Persistence

A brute-force cosine scan over every stored vector works for a few thousand passages but is O(N) per query and forgets everything on restart. A **vector database** adds two things: an **approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN)** index for sub-linear search as the corpus grows, and **persistence** of vectors plus metadata. Chroma gives a minimal local example:

```python
import chromadb

client = chromadb.Client()
collection = client.create_collection("docs")

collection.add(
    ids=["d1", "d2"],
    documents=["Reset your password from Settings.", "Our refund window is 30 days."],
    embeddings=model.encode(
        ["Reset your password from Settings.", "Our refund window is 30 days."],
        normalize_embeddings=True,
    ).tolist(),
)

hits = collection.query(
    query_embeddings=model.encode(["forgot my login"], normalize_embeddings=True).tolist(),
    n_results=2,
)
```

FAISS (a raw ANN index) and pgvector (vectors inside Postgres) are popular alternatives with the same shape: add vectors, query for the nearest.

## 5. The End-to-End RAG Pipeline

The full flow is six stages: **chunk** documents into passages, **embed** each chunk, **store** the vectors, **retrieve** the top-k nearest to the query, **inject** them into the prompt, and **generate**:

```python
import anthropic

hits = collection.query(
    query_embeddings=model.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True).tolist(),
    n_results=4,
)
context = "\n\n".join(hits["documents"][0])

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"}],
)
print(resp.content[0].text)
```

The generator can be any LLM: an open model served from HuggingFace, or an API. Retrieval is the part you own.

## 6. Evaluating and Improving RAG

Retrieval quality is the **ceiling** on answer quality: if the right passage never reaches the prompt, no generator can ground on it. Evaluate retrieval directly with metrics like recall@k (is the gold passage in the top-k?) before blaming the model. The main levers are **chunking** (size and overlap, so a passage holds one coherent idea), **top-k** (too low misses evidence, too high adds noise and cost), and **re-ranking** (retrieve a wide candidate set, then re-score with a stronger cross-encoder and keep the best few).

## Key Takeaways

RAG grounds an LLM in your data without retraining it. Embed with a consistent model, store in a vector database for fast persistent search, retrieve the top-k, and let the model generate from that evidence. When answers are weak, fix retrieval first.

quiz.q: Why are large language models prone to producing confident but incorrect answers about niche or recent facts?
options: They cannot process text longer than a single sentence
Their weights are updated live with every user query
They always refuse to answer factual questions
Their knowledge is frozen at training time and they have no access to your private or up-to-date data
quiz.why: An LLM only knows what was in its training data up to its cutoff. It cannot see your private documents or anything newer, so when asked outside that knowledge it may produce a fluent but fabricated answer. RAG fixes this by retrieving relevant context and placing it in the prompt.

quiz.q: What property of embedding vectors makes them useful for retrieval?
options: They compress any text into exactly eight bytes
Semantically similar texts map to nearby vectors, so similarity becomes a distance computation
They are unique cryptographic hashes of the input
They can only be compared with exact string matching
quiz.why: Embeddings place text in a high-dimensional space where meaning corresponds to geometry. Passages about the same topic land close together, so finding relevant text reduces to a nearest-neighbor (distance or cosine) search rather than keyword matching.

quiz.q: In the sentence-transformers snippet, why pass normalize_embeddings=True when encoding?
options: It translates the input text to English first
It removes stop words before encoding
It scales each vector to unit length, so cosine similarity reduces to a simple dot product
It is mandatory or the model will fail to load
quiz.why: Normalizing to unit length means the dot product of two vectors equals their cosine similarity. This makes similarity scoring cheaper and is what many vector indexes expect, so it keeps retrieval consistent and fast.

quiz.q: What does a vector database primarily add over a brute-force NumPy cosine scan?
options: Approximate nearest-neighbor indexing plus persistence, so search stays fast as the corpus grows
A guarantee that the LLM will never hallucinate
Automatic training of the embedding model for you
Removal of the need to chunk documents
quiz.why: A brute-force scan compares the query against every stored vector, which is O(N) and slow at scale. Vector databases build an approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index for sub-linear search and persist the vectors and metadata so you do not re-embed on every restart.

quiz.q: In a RAG system, why is retrieval quality often described as the ceiling on overall answer quality?
options: Because the generator ignores any retrieved context
If the correct passage is never retrieved, the generator has no grounded evidence to base its answer on
Because a larger embedding model always removes the need for retrieval
Because top-k must always be set to exactly one
quiz.why: Generation can only use what retrieval surfaces. If the relevant chunk is missing from the top-k, even the best LLM must fall back on its parametric memory and may hallucinate. Improving chunking, top-k, and re-ranking raises that ceiling.

quiz.q: In one or two words, name the first pipeline stage that splits long documents into smaller passages before they are embedded.
quiz.answer: chunking
quiz.why: Chunking breaks documents into passage-sized units so each embedding captures a focused piece of meaning and retrieved context fits within the prompt. Chunk size and overlap are key levers for retrieval quality.

mle-m5-l04-fine-tuning-with-lora-and-pef.title: Fine-Tuning with LoRA and PEFT
objectives: Decide when fine-tuning is warranted versus prompting or retrieval-augmented generation
Explain why full fine-tuning of large models is costly in memory and compute
Describe how LoRA freezes base weights and trains low-rank adapter matrices (delta-W = BA)
Implement LoRA on a Hugging Face model using LoraConfig and get_peft_model
Explain how QLoRA combines 4-bit quantization with LoRA to fit large models on one GPU
Apply a prompt-vs-RAG-vs-fine-tune decision framework and evaluate a fine-tuned model against a baseline
mle-m5-l04-fine-tuning-with-lora-and-pef.body:
## Why Fine-Tune?

A pretrained model already knows a great deal, but it may not behave exactly the way your task needs. **Fine-tuning** continues training on your own labeled data so the model internalizes a specific style, output format, or domain skill. Reach for it when you need consistent behavior that prompting cannot reliably produce, or when you want the model to learn a task (e.g. classifying support tickets) rather than just retrieve facts.

Fine-tuning is **not** always the answer. Prompting is free to iterate on, and RAG is usually better when answers depend on up-to-date or proprietary documents. Always ask whether a cheaper option is good enough first.

## Full Fine-Tuning vs PEFT

**Full fine-tuning** updates every weight in the model. For a model with billions of parameters this is brutal: you must store gradients and optimizer states for every parameter, often needing many times the model's size in GPU memory. You also end up with a full-size copy of the model for each task.

**Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)** sidesteps this by freezing the pretrained weights and training only a small number of new parameters. You get most of the quality of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory and storage cost, and a single base model can be shared across many tasks.

## LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation

LoRA is the most popular PEFT method. The insight: the *change* a task makes to a big weight matrix W can be approximated by a **low-rank** update. Instead of learning a full update matrix, LoRA learns two small matrices A and B and expresses the update as delta-W = B A. The base W stays frozen; only A and B are trained.

Because A and B are low rank (controlled by `r`), the trainable parameters are tiny, often well under 1% of the model. Only the adapters are saved, so checkpoints are megabytes, not gigabytes.

## Implementing LoRA with PEFT

The Hugging Face `peft` library wraps any `transformers` model in a few lines.

```python
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification

base = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    "distilbert-base-uncased", num_labels=2
)
config = LoraConfig(
    r=8, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_lin", "v_lin"],
)
model = get_peft_model(base, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()  # tiny % of params are trainable
```

`r` sets the adapter rank, `lora_alpha` scales the update, and `target_modules` picks which layers to adapt (here the query and value projections). You then train `model` with the normal `transformers` `Trainer`.

## QLoRA: Fitting Big Models on One GPU

LoRA shrinks the *trainable* parameters, but the frozen base still occupies memory. **QLoRA** adds 4-bit quantization of the frozen base so even a large model fits on a single GPU, while LoRA adapters train in higher precision on top.

```python
from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM
from peft import prepare_model_for_kbit_training

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True)
base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "some-base-model", quantization_config=bnb
)
base = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(base)
# then wrap with get_peft_model(base, lora_config) as before
```

`prepare_model_for_kbit_training` readies the quantized model for stable adapter training, so large-model fine-tuning can run on one consumer-class GPU.

## Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune: A Decision Framework

Pick the lightest tool that solves the problem:

- **Prompting / few-shot**: fastest to try, no training, no data pipeline. Best for general tasks and quick iteration.
- **RAG**: when answers depend on changing or proprietary facts. Keeps knowledge fresh without retraining; you update documents, not weights.
- **Fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA)**: when you need a consistent behavior, format, or specialized skill baked into the model, and you have a few hundred-plus labeled examples.

These combine: you can fine-tune for *behavior* and still use RAG for *facts*. Start cheap, measure, and only escalate when the simpler option provably underperforms.

## Mini-Project Brief

**Goal:** Fine-tune a small pretrained model on a domain text-classification dataset with LoRA, and prove it beats a no-training baseline.

**Steps:**
1. Pick a labeled text-classification dataset (e.g. a sentiment or topic dataset from the Hub).
2. Establish a **baseline**: a zero-shot or few-shot prompt with a base model, and record its accuracy/F1.
3. Wrap `distilbert-base-uncased` (or similar) with `LoraConfig` + `get_peft_model` and train with the `Trainer`.
4. Call `print_trainable_parameters()` and record the trainable-parameter count and percentage.
5. Evaluate the fine-tuned model on the held-out test set and compare to the baseline.

**Deliverables:**
- A training script/notebook that runs end to end.
- The saved LoRA adapter directory (not a full model copy).
- A short report: dataset, baseline metric, fine-tuned metric, trainable-param count and percent, and a one-paragraph reflection on whether fine-tuning was worth it versus prompting or RAG.

## Key Takeaways

Fine-tuning adapts a model's weights, but it is one option among prompting and RAG, not the default. LoRA freezes the base and trains low-rank adapters (delta-W = BA), saving only tiny adapter files. QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization to fit big models on one GPU. Choose the lightest approach that meets your quality bar, and always measure against a baseline.

quiz.q: When is fine-tuning the right tool rather than prompting or RAG?
options: Fine-tuning is always cheaper and should be the default choice
Whenever the knowledge base changes every few minutes
When you need to bake consistent task or domain-specific behavior into the model's weights and prompting or RAG fall short
Only when the pretrained model cannot perform inference at all
quiz.why: Fine-tuning updates the weights to internalize a style, format, or domain skill. It shines when prompting and RAG cannot reliably produce the desired behavior, but it is not always the cheapest option.

quiz.q: What does LoRA actually train?
options: It freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices A and B
It retrains every weight in the network at full precision
It removes layers from the model to save memory
It only fine-tunes the tokenizer vocabulary
quiz.why: LoRA keeps the large pretrained weights frozen and injects trainable low-rank matrices, so only a tiny fraction of parameters are updated and saved.

quiz.q: In LoRA, how is the update to a weight matrix expressed?
options: delta-W = W + b, a learned bias term
delta-W = B times A, the product of two low-rank matrices
quiz.why: LoRA approximates the weight update as the product of two low-rank matrices B and A, which together have far fewer parameters than the full matrix they adapt.

quiz.q: What is the key idea behind QLoRA?
options: It trains the entire model in 64-bit precision for maximum accuracy
It quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit and trains LoRA adapters on top, fitting large models on a single GPU
It eliminates the need for any GPU during training
It converts the model to ONNX before training
quiz.why: QLoRA loads the frozen base model in 4-bit precision to slash memory use, then trains small LoRA adapters in higher precision on top, enabling fine-tuning of very large models on one GPU.

quiz.q: You need the model to answer questions about a frequently changing internal knowledge base. Which approach is usually the best first choice?
options: Full fine-tuning the model every night
LoRA fine-tuning the model every hour
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the knowledge base
4-bit quantization of the base model alone
quiz.why: When information changes often and must stay current, RAG retrieves up-to-date documents at query time without retraining, making it cheaper and fresher than repeatedly fine-tuning.

quiz.q: Name one practical reason you might prefer LoRA fine-tuning over full fine-tuning.
quiz.answer: Far fewer trainable parameters, so it needs much less GPU memory and produces small adapter files (also acceptable: faster training, easy to swap adapters, base model stays shared)
quiz.why: Because LoRA freezes the base weights and trains only small low-rank adapters, it dramatically reduces memory and storage while letting you keep one shared base model and swap adapters per task.

mle-m6-l01-cloud-deployment-and-serving-.title: Cloud Deployment and Serving at Scale
objectives: Explain why a single local container cannot meet production availability, autoscaling, and rollout needs
Push a container image to a registry and deploy it to a managed ML endpoint (SageMaker, Vertex AI, or Azure ML)
Describe the core Kubernetes objects for serving: pods, Deployments, Services, and horizontal autoscaling
Compare purpose-built serving runtimes (KServe, BentoML, Ray Serve, Triton) and what they add over a hand-rolled API
Connect a model registry to deployment by pulling and serving an approved model version
Choose between a managed endpoint and self-managed Kubernetes based on cost, control, and operational burden
mle-m6-l01-cloud-deployment-and-serving-.body:
## From `docker run` on Your Laptop to the Cloud

Earlier you containerized a model. Running `docker run -p 8000:8000 my-model` proves the image works — but it is not production. A single container on one machine has three fatal gaps:

- **No high availability:** if the process crashes or the machine reboots, the service is simply down.
- **No autoscaling:** fixed capacity means spikes cause timeouts while idle periods waste money.
- **No safe rollout:** shipping a new version means stopping the old one, with no gradual rollout or rollback.

The cloud solves these by running **many replicas across many machines**, behind a load balancer, managed by a control plane that restarts failures and scales on demand.

## Step 1: Push to a Registry, Run on a Managed Service

Cloud services deploy from an **image in a container registry**, not from your local Docker daemon. The flow is: build, tag, push, then point a managed endpoint at the image.

```bash
# Tag and push to a registry (Amazon ECR shown; GCP Artifact Registry / Azure ACR are analogous)
docker build -t my-model:1.0 .
docker tag my-model:1.0 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:1.0
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:1.0
```

Managed ML endpoints then take that image and run it for you with autoscaling, health checks, and HTTPS built in. The big-three options:

- **AWS SageMaker** — real-time and serverless inference endpoints.
- **Google Cloud Vertex AI** — online prediction endpoints from a custom container.
- **Azure Machine Learning** — managed online endpoints.

They differ in API, but the mental model is identical: *registry image in, scalable HTTPS endpoint out.*

## Kubernetes Basics for ML Serving

When you need more control than a managed endpoint, **Kubernetes (K8s)** is the standard. Four objects matter for serving:

- **Pod** — the smallest unit; one or more containers sharing a network namespace.
- **Deployment** — declares *how many* identical replicas you want and keeps them running, enabling rolling updates and rollback.
- **Service** — a stable DNS name that load-balances traffic across the pods.
- **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)** — adds or removes replicas based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics.

A minimal Deployment plus Service for our model:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-model
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-model
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-model
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: server
          image: 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-model
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-model
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
```

With `replicas: 3` you immediately get redundancy and load spreading — the core reason to use K8s for multi-replica serving.

## Horizontal Autoscaling

Fixed replicas still waste money or fall over under load. An HPA scales the Deployment automatically:

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: my-model
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-model
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

Now Kubernetes keeps average CPU near 70%, scaling between 2 and 10 pods as traffic changes.

## Purpose-Built Serving Runtimes

Hand-rolling FastAPI is fine for one model, but production serving has recurring needs. **Purpose-built runtimes** provide them out of the box:

- **KServe** — Kubernetes-native model serving with autoscaling (including scale-to-zero), canary rollout, and a standard inference protocol.
- **BentoML** — focuses on packaging and serving: bundle model, code, and dependencies into a deployable artifact with adaptive batching.
- **Ray Serve** — scalable Python-first serving; compose multiple models and scale across a Ray cluster.
- **NVIDIA Triton** — high-throughput GPU inference with **dynamic batching** and concurrent models across TensorRT, PyTorch, and ONNX backends.

The common wins over a bare API are **continuous/dynamic batching** (grouping concurrent requests to use the GPU efficiently), **multi-model hosting**, and **GPU-aware autoscaling** — work you would otherwise build yourself.

## From Model Registry to Deployment

A **model registry** (MLflow Registry, SageMaker Model Registry, Vertex Model Registry) is the handoff point between training and serving. Training produces and registers versions; deployment pulls the **approved** version and serves it.

```python
import mlflow

# Pull the version currently promoted to Production, not a hardcoded path
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/fraud-detector@champion")
prediction = model.predict(features)
```

This decouples *what* is deployed from *how*: the serving config references a version alias, so promoting a new model is a registry action and the same image serves whichever version the registry points to.

## Choosing an Approach

There is no single right answer — it is a trade-off:

- **Managed endpoint (SageMaker / Vertex AI / Azure ML):** lowest operational burden; the provider handles infra, scaling, and patching. Best for small teams and fast time-to-production. Trade-offs: less control and often higher per-hour cost.
- **Self-managed Kubernetes (+ KServe/Triton):** maximum control and flexibility, portable across clouds, potentially cheaper at large scale. Trade-off: you own the platform and need real K8s expertise.

Start managed when you can; reach for Kubernetes when scale, cost, custom hardware, or portability demands it.

quiz.q: Why is running `docker run` on your laptop inadequate for a production model service?
options: Docker images are always too large to transfer over the network
Laptops are physically unable to execute Python code
A single machine offers no high availability, no autoscaling, and only manual, risky rollouts
Containers cannot expose network ports outside the host
quiz.why: One laptop is a single point of failure with fixed capacity. Production needs redundancy across machines, automatic scaling under load, and controlled rollouts — none of which a lone `docker run` provides.

quiz.q: What is typically the first step when deploying a container image to a managed cloud ML service?
options: Push the built image to a container registry the service can pull from
Email the image file to the cloud provider's support team
Rewrite the model in the provider's proprietary serving language
Delete Docker and upload the raw Python source files instead
quiz.why: Managed services deploy from an image stored in a registry such as Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, or Azure Container Registry. You push once, then point the endpoint at the image tag.

quiz.q: In Kubernetes, which object manages a desired number of identical pod replicas and recreates them if they fail?
quiz.why: A Deployment declares the desired replica count and pod template; its controller continuously reconciles reality to that desired state, replacing crashed pods and enabling rolling updates.

quiz.q: What do purpose-built serving runtimes like KServe, BentoML, Ray Serve, and Triton add over a hand-rolled FastAPI app?
options: Nothing useful; they are strictly slower than FastAPI in every case
Built-in capabilities such as autoscaling, request batching, multi-model serving, and GPU optimization
They remove the need to containerize the model at all
They only work for image-classification models and nothing else
quiz.why: These runtimes bake in concerns you would otherwise build by hand: dynamic batching, scale-to-zero/autoscaling, hosting many models per server, and efficient GPU utilization.

quiz.q: What is NVIDIA Triton Inference Server primarily optimized for?
options: Packaging Python applications into pip wheels for distribution
Provisioning and managing the underlying Kubernetes cluster nodes
High-throughput GPU inference with dynamic batching across multiple frameworks
Training large models from scratch on distributed clusters
quiz.why: Triton is an inference server focused on maximizing GPU throughput — it supports dynamic batching and concurrent model execution across backends like TensorRT, PyTorch, and ONNX. It does not train models.

quiz.q: When would you choose a fully managed endpoint (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML) over self-managing Kubernetes yourself?
quiz.answer: When you want lower operational burden — the provider handles infrastructure, scaling, patching, and uptime — and you are willing to trade some control and flexibility (and often higher per-hour cost) for speed and simplicity.
quiz.why: Managed endpoints minimize ops work and are ideal for small teams or when time-to-production matters; self-managed Kubernetes offers more control and potentially lower cost at scale but requires real platform expertise.

mle-m6-l02-testing-and-ci-cd-for-ml-syst.title: Testing and CI/CD for ML Systems
objectives: Explain why ML systems need code tests plus data tests and model tests
Write deterministic unit tests for pipeline and feature-engineering functions with pytest
Test a FastAPI prediction service using TestClient and assert status codes and response schema
Validate incoming data for ranges, nulls, and types using Great Expectations or pandera
Add a model-quality gate that fails the build when an evaluation metric drops below a threshold
Build a GitHub Actions workflow that installs dependencies, runs pytest, and deploys on merge to main
mle-m6-l02-testing-and-ci-cd-for-ml-syst.body:
## Why ML Systems Need Testing and CI/CD

Almost every machine learning engineer job description asks for "clean, versioned, tested code" and experience with **CI/CD**. The reason is simple: an ML system is software, and software that is not tested breaks in production. But ML adds two failure modes that traditional apps do not have. Your code can be correct while the **data** that flows through it is corrupt, or while the **model** has silently degraded. So an ML test suite has three layers: code tests, data tests, and model tests.

**CI/CD** stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery. CI runs your test suite automatically on every change so bugs are caught in minutes, not after release. CD automatically ships code that passes the tests. Together they turn "it worked on my laptop" into a repeatable, trustworthy pipeline.

## Unit-Testing Pipeline Functions with pytest

`pytest` is the standard Python testing framework. A test is just a function whose name starts with `test_`, containing `assert` statements. The golden rule is to make tests **deterministic**: feed a known input and assert an exact expected output.

```python
# features.py
def normalize(values):
    lo, hi = min(values), max(values)
    return [(v - lo) / (hi - lo) for v in values]

# test_features.py
from features import normalize

def test_normalize_scales_to_unit_range():
    out = normalize([0, 5, 10])
    assert out == [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]

def test_normalize_handles_negatives():
    out = normalize([-10, 0, 10])
    assert out[0] == 0.0 and out[-1] == 1.0
```

Run the whole suite with `pytest -q`. Test the deterministic transforms and feature logic that your pipeline depends on; that is where subtle bugs hide.

## Testing the Prediction API

Your serving layer is code too, so test it. FastAPI ships a `TestClient` (built on httpx) that drives your app **in-process** with no running server. You assert both the HTTP status code and the response schema.

```python
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from app import app

client = TestClient(app)

def test_predict_returns_valid_schema():
    payload = {"sepal_length": 5.1, "sepal_width": 3.5,
               "petal_length": 1.4, "petal_width": 0.2}
    resp = client.post("/predict", json=payload)
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    body = resp.json()
    assert "prediction" in body
    assert isinstance(body["prediction"], int)

def test_predict_rejects_bad_input():
    resp = client.post("/predict", json={"sepal_length": "oops"})
    assert resp.status_code == 422
```

The second test confirms that invalid input is rejected with a 422, exactly the contract Pydantic enforces.

## Data and Schema Validation Tests

Models are only as good as their inputs. A data-validation test asserts that incoming data has the right **ranges, nullability, and types** before it reaches the model. Tools like **pandera** and **Great Expectations** let you declare these expectations as a schema.

```python
import pandera as pa
from pandera import Column, Check

schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({
    "age": Column(int, Check.in_range(0, 120)),
    "income": Column(float, Check.greater_than(0), nullable=False),
    "country": Column(str, nullable=False),
})

def test_input_data_matches_schema(sample_df):
    schema.validate(sample_df)  # raises SchemaError if data is invalid
```

If a new batch contains negative ages or null incomes, validation fails fast with a clear error instead of producing garbage predictions.

## Model-Quality Gates

A model-quality gate is a test that **fails the build** when an evaluation metric drops below an agreed threshold. It protects you from merging a model that looks fine but quietly lost accuracy.

```python
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
import joblib

MIN_ACCURACY = 0.85

def test_model_meets_accuracy_threshold():
    model = joblib.load("model.pkl")
    X_test, y_test = load_holdout()
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
    assert acc >= MIN_ACCURACY, f"accuracy {acc:.3f} below {MIN_ACCURACY}"
```

Because it is an ordinary `assert`, the gate runs in the same `pytest` command as everything else, and a regression turns CI red.

## The CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions runs your tests in the cloud on every push and pull request. A workflow is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. Below, the **test** job installs dependencies and runs pytest; the **deploy** job runs only after tests pass and only on the `main` branch.

```yaml
name: ML CI/CD
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -q

  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./deploy.sh
```

The `needs: test` line makes deploy wait for green tests, and the `if` condition restricts deployment to merges into `main`. Pull requests get full test feedback but never deploy.

## Key Takeaways

Test ML systems in three layers: code, data, and model. Keep unit tests deterministic, drive your API with `TestClient`, validate data with pandera or Great Expectations, and gate merges on a model-quality assertion. Let GitHub Actions run it all and deploy only reviewed code on `main`. That is what "clean, versioned, tested code" looks like.

quiz.q: Compared with a traditional software project, what extra categories of tests does an ML system require?
options: Data tests and model tests, on top of code tests
Manual tests only, since ML cannot be automated
Just more unit tests for the same code
quiz.why: ML systems fail not only from buggy code but from bad data and degraded models, so you add data-validation tests and model-quality tests in addition to ordinary code unit tests.

quiz.q: When unit-testing a feature-engineering function with pytest, what property makes the test reliable?
options: It calls a live production database
It trains a full model first
It depends on the current system clock
It is deterministic: the same input always gives the same expected output
quiz.why: Good unit tests are deterministic. You feed a known input and assert an exact expected output, so the test passes or fails for a clear reason rather than flaking on randomness or external state.

quiz.q: How do you test a FastAPI prediction endpoint inside pytest without running a live server?
options: Wrap the app in fastapi.testclient.TestClient and call it in-process
Deploy to production and curl it
Disable validation and skip the endpoint
quiz.why: TestClient from fastapi.testclient drives the ASGI app in-process, letting you POST a request and assert on the status code and JSON body without binding a network port or starting uvicorn.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a data-validation test using a tool like Great Expectations or pandera?
options: To replace the need for unit tests
To catch bad input early by asserting ranges, nulls, and types before it reaches the model
quiz.why: Data-validation tools declare a schema or set of expectations (value ranges, non-null columns, expected dtypes) and fail loudly when data violates them, catching corruption before it silently degrades predictions.

quiz.q: In a CI pipeline, what should a model-quality gate do when the evaluation metric falls below the agreed threshold?
options: Fail the build so the regression is not merged or deployed
Silently log a warning and continue
Automatically lower the threshold to pass
Delete the test so the pipeline goes green
quiz.why: A quality gate is an assertion: if accuracy (or another metric) drops below the threshold the test fails, the CI run goes red, and the regression is blocked from merging or deploying.

quiz.q: Why is it important to gate the deploy job on the branch (for example, only run it when the ref is refs/heads/main)?
quiz.answer: So that tests run on every push and pull request for fast feedback, but deployment only happens for trusted, reviewed code merged into the main branch rather than on every feature branch or PR.
quiz.why: Running tests broadly gives early feedback on all branches, while restricting deploys to main ensures only reviewed, merged code reaches production, preventing accidental deployments from feature branches.

mle-m6-l03-monitoring-drift-and-retraini.title: Monitoring, Drift, and Retraining in Production
objectives: Explain why offline metrics are insufficient and how deployed models decay silently
Distinguish data drift from concept drift with concrete examples and the right detection strategy
Implement a runnable Evidently drift report comparing a reference window to a current window
Build a dependency-light drift check using scipy.stats.ks_2samp and reason about PSI
